Show that there exists a positive integer $M$ for which $a_{n} = a_{n+1}$ for all $n \ge M$.

negatives.text: Let $a_0$ be an arbitrary positive integer. Consider the infinite sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$, defined inductively as follows: given $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}$ define the term $a_n$ as the smallest positive integer such that $a_0 + a_1 + \dots + a_n$ is divisible by $n^2$. Prove that there exists a positive integer $M$ such that $a_{n+1} = a_n$ for all $n \ge M$.

Let $a_0$ be an arbitrary positive integer. Consider the infinite sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$, defined inductively as follows: given $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}$ define the term $a_n$ as the largest positive integer such that $a_0 + a_1 + \dots + a_n$ is divisible by $n$. Prove that there exists a positive integer $M$ such that $a_{n+1} = a_n$ for all $n \ge M$.

Let $a_0$ be an arbitrary positive integer. Consider the infinite sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$, defined inductively as follows: given $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}$ define the term $a_n$ as the smallest positive integer such that $a_0 + a_1 + \dots + a_n$ is divisible by $n!$. Prove that there exists a positive integer $M$ such that $a_{n+1} = a_n$ for all $n \ge M$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ ($BC > AC$) be an acute triangle with circumcircle $\omega$ centered at $O$. The tangent to $\omega$ at $C$ meets the line $AB$ at $D$. Let the circumcircles of triangles $BCD$, $OCD$, and $AOB$ intersect the ray $CA$ (extended beyond $A$) at points $Q$, $P$, and $K$ respectively, with $P$ between $A$ and $K$, and $K$ between $P$ and $Q$. If line $PD$ meets the circumcircle of triangle $BKQ$ again at point $T$, where $T$ and $P$ lie in opposite half-planes with respect to line $BQ$, show that $TB = TQ$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ ($BC < AC$) be an acute triangle with circumcircle $k$ centered at $O$. The tangent to $k$ at $C$ intersects the line $AB$ at the point $D$. The circumcircles of triangles $BCD$, $OCD$ and $AOB$ intersect the ray $CA$ (beyond $A$) at the points $Q$, $P$ and $K$, respectively, such that $P \in (AK)$ and $K \in (PQ)$. The line $PD$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $BKQ$ at the point $T$, so that $P$ and $T$ are in different halfplanes with respect to $BQ$. Prove that $TB = TQ$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ ($BC > AC$) be an acute triangle with circumcircle $k$ centered at $O$. The tangent to $k$ at $C$ intersects the line $AB$ at the point $D$. The circumcircles of triangles $BCD$, $OCD$ and $AOB$ intersect the ray $CA$ (beyond $A$) at the points $Q$, $P$ and $K$, respectively, such that $P \in (AK)$ and $K \in (PQ)$. The line $PD$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $BKQ$ at the point $T$, so that $P$ and $T$ are in the same halfplane with respect to $BQ$. Prove that $TB = TQ$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ ($BC > AC$) be an acute triangle with circumcircle $k$ centered at $O$. The tangent to $k$ at $C$ intersects the line $AB$ at the point $D$. The circumcircles of triangles $BCD$, $OCD$ and $AOB$ intersect the ray $CA$ (beyond $A$) at the points $Q$, $P$ and $K$, respectively, such that $P \in (AK)$ and $K \in (PQ)$. The line $PD$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $BKQ$ at the point $T$, so that $P$ and $T$ are in different halfplanes with respect to $BQ$. Prove that $TC = TQ$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, where $\angle B$ is obtuse, let $G$ and $H$ denote the centroid and orthocentre, respectively. Consider a circle $\omega$ with diameter $AG$, intersecting the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at a second point $L \neq A$. Let the tangent to $\omega$ at $L$ intersect the circumcircle again at $K \neq L$. If $AG = GH$, show that $\angle HKG = 90^\circ$.

negatives.text: Let $G$, $H$ be the centroid and orthocentre of $\triangle ABC$ which has an acute angle at $\angle B$. Let $\omega$ be the circle with diameter $AG$. $\omega$ intersects $\odot ABC$ again at $L \neq A$. The tangent to $\omega$ at $L$ intersects $\odot ABC$ at $K \neq L$. Given that $AG = GH$, prove $\angle HKG = 90^\circ$.

Let $G$, $H$ be the centroid and orthocentre of $\triangle ABC$ which has an obtuse angle at $\angle B$. Let $\omega$ be the circle with diameter $AH$. $\omega$ intersects $\odot ABC$ again at $L \neq A$. The tangent to $\omega$ at $L$ intersects $\odot ABC$ at $K \neq L$. Given that $AG = GH$, prove $\angle HKG = 90^\circ$.

Let $G$, $H$ be the centroid and orthocentre of $\triangle ABC$ which has an obtuse angle at $\angle B$. Let $\omega$ be the circle with diameter $AG$. $\omega$ intersects $\odot ABC$ again at $L \neq A$. The tangent to $\omega$ at $L$ intersects $\odot ABC$ at $K \neq L$. Given that $AG = 2GH$, prove $\angle HKG = 90^\circ$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$ and $\angle BAC = 45^\circ$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$, and $M$ the midpoint of side $BC$. Drop a perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$, meeting it at point $D$. Draw a circle centered at $C$ with radius $CD$, intersecting $AC$ at point $F$ and the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at points $Z$ and $E$, with $Z$ on arc $\widehat{BC}$ and $E$ on arc $\widehat{AC}$. Show that the lines $ZE$, $CO$, and $FM$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$ and $\angle A = 45^\circ$. Its circumcircle $(c)$ has center $O$, $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$ and $D$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$. With center $C$ and radius $CD$ we draw a circle which internally intersects $AB$ at the point $F$ and the circle $(c)$ at the points $Z$ and $E$, such that $Z$ lies on the small arc $\widehat{BC}$ and $E$ on the small arc $\widehat{AC}$. Prove that the lines $ZE$, $CO$, $FM$ are concurrent.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$ and $\angle A = 135^\circ$. Its circumcircle $(c)$ has center $O$, $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$ and $D$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$. With center $C$ and radius $CD$ we draw a circle which internally intersects $AC$ at the point $F$ and the circle $(c)$ at the points $Z$ and $E$, such that $Z$ lies on the small arc $\widehat{BC}$ and $E$ on the small arc $\widehat{AC}$. Prove that the lines $ZE$, $CO$, $FM$ are concurrent.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$ and $\angle A = 45^\circ$. Its circumcircle $(c)$ has center $O$, $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$ and $D$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$. With center $B$ and radius $CD$ we draw a circle which internally intersects $AC$ at the point $F$ and the circle $(c)$ at the points $Z$ and $E$, such that $Z$ lies on the small arc $\widehat{BC}$ and $E$ on the small arc $\widehat{AC}$. Prove that the lines $ZE$, $CO$, $FM$ are concurrent.

positive_text:
Let $f, g$ be integer-valued functions defined on the positive integers. A point moves on the integer lattice, starting at the origin $(0,0)$. At each step $n \ge 1$, the movement is of the form $(\pm f(n), \pm g(n))$ or $(\pm g(n), \pm f(n))$, with all eight combinations allowed. Does there always exist a sequence of such movements that causes the point to return to the origin $(0,0)$ infinitely often, when
(a) $f, g$ are integer-coefficient polynomials in $n$?
(b) $f, g$ are arbitrary integer-valued functions on the positive integers?

negatives.text:
Let $f, g$ be functions from the positive integers to the integers. Vlad the impala is jumping around the integer grid. His initial position is $\mathbf{x}_0 = (0,0)$, and for every $n \ge 1$, his jump is
$$
\mathbf{x}_n - \mathbf{x}_{n-1} = (f(n), g(n)) \text{ or } (g(n), f(n)),
$$
with two possibilities in total. Is it always possible that Vlad can choose his jumps to return to his initial location $(0,0)$ infinitely many times when
(a) $f, g$ are polynomials with integer coefficients?
(b) $f, g$ are any pair of functions from the positive integers to the integers?

Let $f, g$ be functions from the positive integers to the integers. Vlad the impala is jumping around the integer grid. His initial position is $\mathbf{x}_0 = (0,0)$, and for every $n \ge 1$, his jump is
$$
\mathbf{x}_n - \mathbf{x}_{n-1} = (\pm f(n), \pm g(n)) \text{ or } (\pm g(n), \pm f(n)) \text{ or } (\pm f(n), \pm f(n)),
$$
with nine possibilities in total. Is it always possible that Vlad can choose his jumps to return to his initial location $(0,0)$ infinitely many times when
(a) $f, g$ are polynomials with integer coefficients?
(b) $f, g$ are any pair of functions from the positive integers to the integers?

Let $f, g$ be functions from the positive integers to the integers. Vlad the impala is jumping around the integer grid. His initial position is $\mathbf{x}_0 = (0,0)$, and for every $n \ge 1$, his jump is
$$
\mathbf{x}_n - \mathbf{x}_{n-1} = (\pm f(n), \pm g(n)) \text{ or } (\pm g(n), \pm f(n)),
$$
with eight possibilities in total. Is it always possible that Vlad can choose his jumps to return to his initial location $(0,0)$ infinitely many times when
(a) $f, g$ are polynomials with integer coefficients and $f(n) = g(n)$ for all $n$?
(b) $f, g$ are any pair of functions from the positive integers to the integers?

positive_text:
In a peculiar nation, the Central Mint produces coins whose values lie in the interval $[0, 1]$. Determine the minimal constant $c > 0$ such that the following condition is always satisfied: 
*For any individual possessing a finite number of such coins with total value at most 1000, it is possible to partition the coins into 100 containers such that the sum of values in each container does not exceed $c$.*

negatives.text:
In an exotic country, the National Bank issues coins that can take any value in the interval $[0, 1]$. Find the smallest constant $c > 0$ such that the following holds, no matter the situation in that country: 
*Any citizen of the exotic country that has a finite number of coins, with a total value of no more than 1000, can split those coins into 100 boxes, such that the total value inside each box is at least $c$.*

In an exotic country, the National Bank issues coins that can take any value in the interval $[0, 1]$. Find the smallest constant $c > 0$ such that the following holds, no matter the situation in that country: 
*Any citizen of the exotic country that has a finite number of coins, with a total value of no more than 1000, can split those coins into 100 boxes, such that the total value inside each box is at most $c$, and each box contains at least one coin.*

In an exotic country, the National Bank issues coins that can take any value in the interval $[0, 1]$. Find the smallest constant $c > 0$ such that the following holds, no matter the situation in that country: 
*Any citizen of the exotic country that has a finite number of coins, with a total value of no more than 1000, can split those coins into 100 boxes, such that the total value inside each box is at most $c$, and the number of coins in each box is the same.*

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$ and circumcenter $O$. Let $s_a$ be the external angle bisector of $\angle A$. A line is drawn through $I$ perpendicular to $IO$, intersecting $BC$ at $P$ and $s_a$ at $Q$. Show that the segment $IQ$ is twice the length of $IP$.

negatives.text: Let $I$ and $O$ be the incenter and the circumcenter of a triangle $ABC$, respectively, and let $s_a$ be the exterior bisector of angle $\angle BAC$. The line through $I$ perpendicular to $IO$ meets the lines $BC$ and $s_a$ at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Prove that $IQ = IP$.

Let $I$ and $O$ be the incenter and the circumcenter of a triangle $ABC$, respectively, and let $s_a$ be the interior bisector of angle $\angle BAC$. The line through $I$ perpendicular to $IO$ meets the lines $BC$ and $s_a$ at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Prove that $IQ = 2IP$.

Let $I$ and $O$ be the incenter and the circumcenter of a triangle $ABC$, respectively, and let $s_a$ be the exterior bisector of angle $\angle BAC$. The line through $I$ parallel to $IO$ meets the lines $BC$ and $s_a$ at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Prove that $IQ = 2IP$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have $AB < AC$. Let $\omega$ be a circle through $B$ and $C$ such that $A$ lies inside $\omega$. Let points $X, Y$ be on $\omega$ such that $\angle BXA = \angle AYC$, with $X$ on the side of $AB$ opposite $C$ and $Y$ on the side of $AC$ opposite $B$. Prove that, as $X$ and $Y$ move along $\omega$, the line $XY$ always passes through a fixed point.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$. Let $\omega$ be a circle passing through $B, C$ and assume that $A$ is inside $\omega$. Suppose $X, Y$ lie on $\omega$ such that $\angle BXA = \angle AYC$ and $X$ lies on the same side of $AB$ as $C$ while $Y$ lies on the same side of $AC$ as $B$. Show that, as $X, Y$ vary on $\omega$, the line $XY$ passes through a fixed point.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$. Let $\omega$ be a circle passing through $B, C$ and assume that $A$ is inside $\omega$. Suppose $X, Y$ lie on $\omega$ such that $\angle BXA = \angle AYC$ and $X$ lies on the opposite side of $AB$ to $C$ while $Y$ lies on the opposite side of $AC$ to $B$. Show that, as $X, Y$ vary on $\omega$, the line $XY$ passes through a fixed circle.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$. Let $\omega$ be a circle passing through $B, C$ and assume that $A$ is inside $\omega$. Suppose $X, Y$ lie on $\omega$ such that $\angle BXA = 180^\circ - \angle AYC$ and $X$ lies on the opposite side of $AB$ to $C$ while $Y$ lies on the opposite side of $AC$ to $B$. Show that, as $X, Y$ vary on $\omega$, the line $XY$ passes through a fixed point.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with $AC > AB$ and circumcircle $\Gamma$. The tangent at $A$ to $\Gamma$ meets $BC$ at point $T$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $BC$, and let $R$ be the image of $A$ under reflection over $B$. Let $S$ be the point such that $SABT$ forms a parallelogram. Suppose $P$ lies on line $SB$ with $MP \parallel AB$, and that $P$ is also on $\Gamma$. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $STR$ is tangent to line $AC$.

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AC > AB$ and circumcircle $\Gamma$. The tangent from $A$ to $\Gamma$ intersects $BC$ at $T$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and let $R$ be the reflection of $A$ in $C$. Let $S$ be a point so that $SABT$ is a parallelogram and finally let $P$ be a point on line $SB$ such that $MP$ is parallel to $AB$.

Given that $P$ lies on $\Gamma$, prove that the circumcircle of $\triangle STR$ is tangent to line $AC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AC > AB$ and circumcircle $\Gamma$. The tangent from $A$ to $\Gamma$ intersects $BC$ at $T$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and let $R$ be the reflection of $A$ in $B$. Let $S$ be a point so that $SABT$ is a parallelogram and finally let $P$ be a point on line $SB$ such that $MP$ is parallel to $BC$.

Given that $P$ lies on $\Gamma$, prove that the circumcircle of $\triangle STR$ is tangent to line $AC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AC > AB$ and circumcircle $\Gamma$. The tangent from $A$ to $\Gamma$ intersects $BC$ at $T$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and let $R$ be the reflection of $A$ in $B$. Let $S$ be a point so that $SABT$ is a parallelogram and finally let $P$ be a point on line $SB$ such that $MP$ is parallel to $AB$.

Given that $P$ lies on the tangent from $A$ to $\Gamma$, prove that the circumcircle of $\triangle STR$ is tangent to line $AC$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$. The circumcircle of $ABC$ is denoted by $\omega$. The tangent to $\omega$ at $A$ meets $BC$ at a point $D$. Construct a circle $\Omega$ with center $D$ and radius equal to $AD$. Let $E$ be the second intersection of $\omega$ and $\Omega$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $BC$. If $BE$ intersects $\Omega$ again at $X$ and $CX$ intersects $\Omega$ at another point $Y$, prove that $A$, $Y$, and $M$ lie on a straight line.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle such that $AB < AC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$ and assume that the tangent to $\omega$ at $A$ intersects the line $BC$ at $D$. Let $\Omega$ be the circle with center $D$ and radius $DA$. Denote by $E$ the second intersection point of $\omega$ and $\Omega$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. If the line $CE$ meets $\Omega$ again at $X$, and the line $BX$ meets $\Omega$ for the second time at $Y$, show that $A, Y$ and $M$ are collinear.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle such that $AB < AC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$ and assume that the tangent to $\omega$ at $A$ intersects the line $BC$ at $D$. Let $\Omega$ be the circle with center $D$ and radius $AD$. Denote by $E$ the second intersection point of $\omega$ and $\Omega$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. If the line $BE$ meets $\Omega$ again at $X$, and the line $CE$ meets $\Omega$ for the second time at $Y$, show that $A, Y$ and $M$ are collinear.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle such that $AB < AC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$ and assume that the tangent to $\omega$ at $A$ intersects the line $BC$ at $D$. Let $\Omega$ be the circle with center $D$ and radius $AD$. Denote by $E$ the second intersection point of $\omega$ and $\Omega$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. If the line $BE$ meets $\Omega$ again at $X$, and the line $CX$ meets $\Omega$ for the second time at $Y$, show that $A, Y$ and $M$ are not collinear.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a scalene triangle with incenter $I$. Points $D$, $E$, and $F$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $I$ to $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively. Reflect $D$ over $AI$ to obtain point $K$, and define $L$ as the second intersection point of the circumcircles of $\triangle BFK$ and $\triangle CEK$. If $AC - AB = \frac{1}{3}BC$, prove that $DE = 2KL$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a scalene triangle and let $I$ be its incenter. The projections of $I$ on $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ are $D$, $E$ and $F$ respectively. Let $K$ be the reflection of $D$ over the line $AI$, and let $L$ be the second point of intersection of the circumcircles of the triangles $BFK$ and $CEK$. If $\frac{1}{3}BC = AB - AC$, prove that $DE = 2KL$.

Let $ABC$ be a scalene triangle and let $I$ be its incenter. The projections of $I$ on $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ are $D$, $E$ and $F$ respectively. Let $K$ be the reflection of $D$ over the line $AI$, and let $L$ be the second point of intersection of the circumcircles of the triangles $BFK$ and $CEK$. If $\frac{1}{3}BC = AC - AB$, prove that $DE = KL$.

Let $ABC$ be a scalene triangle and let $I$ be its incenter. The projections of $I$ on $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ are $D$, $E$ and $F$ respectively. Let $K$ be the reflection of $D$ over the line $BI$, and let $L$ be the second point of intersection of the circumcircles of the triangles $BFK$ and $CEK$. If $\frac{1}{3}BC = AC - AB$, prove that $DE = 2KL$.

positive_text:
Determine all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty)$ satisfying
$$
f(a f(b)^3 + b) = b^3 f(a) + f(b)
$$
for all $a, b > 0$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty)$ such that
$$
 f(yf(x)^3 + x) = x^3 f(y) - f(x)
$$
for all $x, y > 0$.

Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty)$ such that
$$
 f(yf(x)^3 + x) = x^3 f(y) + f(x)^2
$$
for all $x, y > 0$.

Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty)$ such that
$$
 f(yf(x)^3 + x) = x^3 f(y) + f(x)
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$.

positive_text: Let $n$ be an odd integer with $n \ge 3$, and consider an $n \times n$ board with $n^2$ squares. Each square is painted either red or blue by Dionysus. Two squares of the same colour can be connected if they share at least one vertex. Xanthias wants to place frogs on $k$ squares such that from any square, a frog can reach it through a finite number of such connections. Determine the smallest possible value of $k$ such that Xanthias can always accomplish this, regardless of Dionysus's colouring.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 3$ be an odd positive integer, and consider an $n \times n$ grid containing $n^2$ cells. Dionysus colours each cell either red or blue. A frog can hop directly between two cells if they have the same colour and share an edge. Xanthias views the colouring, and wants to place frogs on $k$ of the cells so that any cell can be reached by a frog in a finite number of hops. Find the least value of $k$ such that Xanthias can always be successful regardless of the colouring chosen by Dionysus.

Let $n \ge 3$ be an even positive integer, and consider an $n \times n$ grid containing $n^2$ cells. Dionysus colours each cell either red or blue. A frog can hop directly between two cells if they have the same colour and share at least one vertex. Xanthias views the colouring, and wants to place frogs on $k$ of the cells so that any cell can be reached by a frog in a finite number of hops. Find the least value of $k$ such that Xanthias can always be successful regardless of the colouring chosen by Dionysus.

Let $n \ge 3$ be an odd positive integer, and consider an $n \times n$ grid containing $n^2$ cells. Dionysus colours each cell either red or blue. A frog can hop directly between two cells if they have different colours and share at least one vertex. Xanthias views the colouring, and wants to place frogs on $k$ of the cells so that any cell can be reached by a frog in a finite number of hops. Find the least value of $k$ such that Xanthias can always be successful regardless of the colouring chosen by Dionysus.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have circumcircle $\omega$. Let $E$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ not containing $A$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $V$ be the second intersection of $AM$ with $\omega$, $F$ be the intersection of $AE$ with $BC$, and $X$ be the second intersection of the circumcircle of triangle $FEM$ with $\omega$. Let $X'$ be the reflection of $V$ over $M$, $A'$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$, and $S$ be the second intersection of $XA'$ with $\omega$. Let $Z \in \omega$ with $Z \neq X$ satisfy $AX = AZ$. Prove that $S$, $X'$, and $Z$ are collinear.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $\omega$ be its circumcircle. Let $E$ be the midpoint of the minor arc $BC$ of $\omega$, and $M$ the midpoint of $BC$. Let $V$ be the other point of intersection of $AM$ with $\omega$, $F$ the point of intersection of $AE$ with $BC$, $X$ the other point of intersection of the circumcircle of $FEM$ with $\omega$, $X'$ the reflection of $V$ with respect to $M$, $A'$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ and $S$ the other point of intersection of $XA'$ with $\omega$. If $Z \in \omega$ with $Z \neq X$ is such that $AX = AZ$, then prove that $S$, $X$ and $Z$ are collinear.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $\omega$ be its circumcircle. Let $E$ be the midpoint of the minor arc $BC$ of $\omega$, and $M$ the midpoint of $BC$. Let $V$ be the other point of intersection of $AM$ with $\omega$, $F$ the point of intersection of $AE$ with $BC$, $X$ the other point of intersection of the circumcircle of $FEM$ with $\omega$, $X'$ the reflection of $V$ with respect to $M$, $A'$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ and $S$ the other point of intersection of $XA'$ with $\omega$. If $Z \in \omega$ with $Z \neq X$ is such that $AX = AZ$, then prove that $S$, $X'$ and $A$ are collinear.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $\omega$ be its circumcircle. Let $E$ be the midpoint of the minor arc $BC$ of $\omega$, and $M$ the midpoint of $BC$. Let $V$ be the other point of intersection of $AM$ with $\omega$, $F$ the point of intersection of $AE$ with $BC$, $X$ the other point of intersection of the circumcircle of $FEM$ with $\omega$, $X'$ the reflection of $V$ with respect to $M$, $A'$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ and $S$ the other point of intersection of $XA'$ with $\omega$. If $Z \in \omega$ with $Z \neq X$ is such that $AX = AZ$, then prove that $S$, $X'$ and $Z$ are perpendicular.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, with $AB < AC$, let $D$ be the second point where the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersects the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$. Choose points $E$ and $F$ on segments $AB$ and $AC$ such that $AE = AF$, and let $P$ be the intersection of $AD$ with $EF$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$. Show that the line $AM$ and the circumcircles of triangles $AEF$ and $PMD$ share a common point.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$ and let $D$ be the other intersection point of the angle bisector of $A$ with the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Let $E$ and $F$ be points on the sides $AB$ and $AC$ respectively, such that $AE = AF$ and let $P$ be the point of intersection of $AD$ and $EF$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Prove that $AD$ and the circumcircles of triangles $AEF$ and $PMD$ pass through a common point.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$ and let $D$ be the other intersection point of the angle bisector of $A$ with the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Let $E$ and $F$ be points on the sides $AB$ and $AC$ respectively, such that $AE = AF$ and let $P$ be the point of intersection of $AD$ and $EF$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Prove that $AM$ and the circumcircles of triangles $AEB$ and $PMD$ pass through a common point.

positive_text: Show that there exists a constant $ c < \frac{3}{4} $ such that for any bounded sequence $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$ with $x_i \in [0, 1]$ for all $i$, there are infinitely many indices $ m > n $ for which $$ |x_m - x_n| < \frac{c}{m}. $$

negatives.text:
Prove that there exists a real number $c < \frac{3}{4}$ such that for each sequence $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$ satisfying $0 \le x_i \le 1$ for all $i$, there are infinitely many pairs $(m, n)$ with $m > n$ such that
$$
|x_m - x_n| \le \frac{c}{\sqrt{m}}.
$$

Prove that there exists a real number $c < \frac{3}{4}$ such that for each sequence $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$ satisfying $0 \le x_i \le 1$ for all $i$, there are infinitely many pairs $(m, n)$ with $m > n$ such that
$$
|x_m - x_n| \ge \frac{c}{m}.
$$

Prove that there exists a real number $c < \frac{3}{4}$ such that for each sequence $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$ satisfying $0 \le x_i \le 1$ for all $i$, there are infinitely many pairs $(m, n)$ with $m > n$ such that
$$
|x_m - x_n| \le \frac{c}{m} + \frac{1}{m^2}.
$$

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ denote the set of all positive real numbers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{R}_{>0} \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ satisfying the condition
$$
 f(x^{2023} + a(x)a(y)) = x^{2023} + y a(x)
$$
for every pair of positive real numbers $x$ and $y$, where $a(x) = f(x)$.

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ be the set of all positive real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}_{>0} \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that for all positive real numbers $x$ and $y$,
$$
f(x^{2023} - f(x)f(y)) = x^{2023} + yf(x).
$$

Let $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ be the set of all positive real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}_{>0} \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that for all positive real numbers $x$ and $y$,
$$
f(x^{2023} + f(x)f(y)) = x^{2023} - yf(x).
$$

Let $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ be the set of all positive real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}_{>0} \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that for all positive real numbers $x$ and $y$,
$$
f(x^{2023} + f(x)f(y)) = x^{2024} + yf(x).
$$

positive_text: Let $ n $ be an integer with $ n \ge 2 $. A sequence $ (1, 2, \dots, n) $ is written on a board. In one move, two numbers in the sequence whose sum is a perfect square can be exchanged. Determine all $ n $ such that any rearrangement of $ \{1, 2, \dots, n\} $ can be achieved through a series of such moves.

negatives.text: For an integer $n \ge 2$, the tuple $(1, 2, \dots, n)$ is written on a blackboard. On each turn, one can choose two numbers from the tuple such that their sum is a perfect square and swap them to obtain a new tuple. Find all integers $n \ge 2$ for which all permutations of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ cannot appear on the blackboard in this way.

For an integer $n \ge 2$, the tuple $(1, 2, \dots, n)$ is written on a blackboard. On each turn, one can choose two numbers from the tuple such that their product is a perfect square and swap them to obtain a new tuple. Find all integers $n \ge 2$ for which all permutations of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ can appear on the blackboard in this way.

For an integer $n \ge 2$, the tuple $(1, 2, \dots, n)$ is written on a blackboard. On each turn, one can choose two numbers from the tuple such that their sum is a perfect square and replace them with their average to obtain a new tuple. Find all integers $n \ge 2$ for which all permutations of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ can appear on the blackboard in this way.

positive_text: Determine the largest integer $ k $ with $ k \le 2023 $ such that, for any subset of size $ k $ chosen and marked red from $ \{1, 2, \dots, 2023\} $, there exists a subset of the remaining numbers that can be marked blue with the same total sum as the red subset.

negatives.text: Find the greatest integer $k \le 2023$ for which, regardless of how Alice colors exactly $k$ numbers among $\{1, 2, \dots, 2023\}$ in red, Bob can color some of the remaining uncolored numbers in blue, such that the sum of the red numbers is greater than the sum of the blue ones.

Find the greatest integer $k \le 2023$ for which, regardless of how Alice colors exactly $k$ numbers among $\{1^2, 2^2, \dots, 2023^2\}$ in red, Bob can color some of the remaining uncolored numbers in blue, such that the sum of the red numbers is the same as the sum of the blue ones.

Find the greatest integer $k \le 2023$ for which, regardless of how Alice colors exactly $k$ numbers among $\{1, 2, \dots, 2023\}$ in red, Bob can color some of the remaining uncolored numbers in blue, such that the product of the red numbers is the same as the product of the blue ones.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral tangent to a circle, and let $X$ be the point of intersection of its diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Denote by $I_1, I_2, I_3, I_4$ the incenters of triangles $\triangle DXC$, $\triangle BXC$, $\triangle AXB$, and $\triangle DXA$, in that order. Suppose the circumcircle of triangle $\triangle CI_1I_2$ intersects side $CB$ at $P$ and side $CD$ at $Q$, and the circumcircle of triangle $\triangle AI_3I_4$ intersects side $AB$ at $M$ and side $AD$ at $N$. Show that $$ AM + CQ = AN + CP. $$

negatives.text:
Let $ABCD$ be a circumscribed quadrilateral (i.e. convex with sides that are all tangent to a single circle) and let $X$ be the intersection point of its diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Let $I_1, I_2, I_3, I_4$ be the incenters of $\triangle DXC$, $\triangle BXC$, $\triangle AXB$, and $\triangle DXA$, respectively. The circumcircle of $\triangle CI_1I_2$ intersects the sides $CB$ and $CD$ at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The circumcircle of $\triangle AI_3I_4$ intersects the sides $AB$ and $AD$ at points $M$ and $N$, respectively.
Prove that
$$
AM - CQ = AN - CP.
$$

Let $ABCD$ be a circumscribed quadrilateral (i.e. convex with sides that are all tangent to a single circle) and let $X$ be the intersection point of its diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Let $I_1, I_2, I_3, I_4$ be the incenters of $\triangle DXC$, $\triangle BXC$, $\triangle AXB$, and $\triangle DXA$, respectively. The circumcircle of $\triangle CI_1I_2$ intersects the sides $CB$ and $CD$ at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The circumcircle of $\triangle AI_3I_4$ intersects the sides $AB$ and $AD$ at points $M$ and $N$, respectively.
Prove that
$$
AM + CQ = AN + CP + 1.
$$

Let $ABCD$ be a circumscribed quadrilateral (i.e. convex with sides that are all tangent to a single circle) and let $X$ be the intersection point of its diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Let $I_1, I_2, I_3, I_4$ be the incenters of $\triangle DXC$, $\triangle BXC$, $\triangle AXB$, and $\triangle DXA$, respectively. The circumcircle of $\triangle CI_1I_2$ intersects the sides $CB$ and $CD$ at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The circumcircle of $\triangle AI_3I_4$ intersects the sides $AB$ and $AD$ at points $M$ and $N$, respectively.
Prove that
$$
AM + CQ = AN + CP^2.
$$

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$ inside the figure. Let $E$ and $F$ be the midpoints of $BC$ and $AD$, respectively. Define a point $X$ on the side of the line $EF$ that includes $C$ such that $\triangle EXF \sim \triangle BOA$. Show that triangle $XCD$ is isosceles with $XC = XD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$ lying in the interior. Let $E$ and $F$ be the midpoints of the segments $BC$ and $AD$, respectively. Let $X$ be the point lying on the same side of the line $EF$ as the vertex $C$ such that $\triangle EXF$ and $\triangle AOB$ are similar. Prove that $XC = XD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$ lying in the interior. Let $E$ and $F$ be the midpoints of the segments $BC$ and $AD$, respectively. Let $X$ be the point lying on the same side of the line $EF$ as the vertex $C$ such that $\triangle EXF$ and $\triangle BOD$ are similar. Prove that $XC = XD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$ lying in the interior. Let $E$ and $F$ be the midpoints of the segments $BC$ and $AD$, respectively. Let $X$ be the point lying on the opposite side of the line $EF$ from the vertex $C$ such that $\triangle EXF$ and $\triangle BOA$ are similar. Prove that $XC = XD$.

positive_text: Let $n \ge 3$ be a natural number. On a regular $n$-gon, players Anna and Bob place their tokens on distinct vertices. Anna moves first, and on her $k$-th move, she shifts her token $k$ steps either clockwise or counterclockwise. On his $k$-th move, Bob shifts his token one step clockwise or counterclockwise. The game lasts for $2n$ moves, and Anna wins if at any point the tokens are on the same vertex. Otherwise, Bob wins. Determine for each $n$ who has a winning strategy.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 3$ be a natural number. Anna and Bob play the following game on the vertices of a regular $n$-gon: Anna places her token on a vertex of the $n$-gon. Afterwards Bob places his token on another vertex of the $n$-gon. Then, with Anna playing first, they move their tokens alternately as follows for $2n$ rounds: In Anna's turn on the $k$-th round, she moves her token $k$ positions clockwise or anticlockwise. In Bob's turn on the $k$-th round, he moves his token $k$ positions clockwise or anticlockwise. If at the end of any person's turn the two tokens are on the same vertex, then Anna wins the game. Otherwise Bob wins. Decide for each value of $n$ which player has a winning strategy.

Let $n \ge 3$ be a natural number. Anna and Bob play the following game on the vertices of a regular $n$-gon: Anna places her token on a vertex of the $n$-gon. Afterwards Bob places his token on another vertex of the $n$-gon. Then, with Anna playing first, they move their tokens alternately as follows for $2n$ rounds: In Anna's turn on the $k$-th round, she moves her token $k$ positions clockwise or anticlockwise. In Bob's turn on the $k$-th round, he moves his token 1 position clockwise or anticlockwise. If at the end of any person's turn the two tokens are on the same vertex or if the tokens are adjacent, then Anna wins the game. Otherwise Bob wins. Decide for each value of $n$ which player has a winning strategy.

Let $n \ge 3$ be a natural number. Anna and Bob play the following game on the vertices of a regular $n$-gon: Anna places her token on a vertex of the $n$-gon. Afterwards Bob places his token on another vertex of the $n$-gon. Then, with Anna playing first, they move their tokens alternately as follows for $n$ rounds: In Anna's turn on the $k$-th round, she moves her token $k$ positions clockwise or anticlockwise. In Bob's turn on the $k$-th round, he moves his token 1 position clockwise or anticlockwise. If at the end of any person's turn the two tokens are on the same vertex, then Anna wins the game. Otherwise Bob wins. Decide for each value of $n$ which player has a winning strategy.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$, $H$ its orthocentre, $O$ its circumcentre, and $\Gamma$ its circumcircle. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and define point $D$ such that $ADOH$ is a parallelogram. Assume there exists a point $X$ on $\Gamma$, on the side of $DH$ opposite to $A$, satisfying $\angle DXH + \angle DHA = 90^\circ$. Let $Y$ be the midpoint of $OX$. Show that if $MY = OA$, then $OA = 2OH$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, orthocentre $H$, circumcircle $\Gamma$ and circumcentre $O$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and let $D$ be a point such that $ADOH$ is a parallelogram. Suppose that there exists a point $X$ on $\Gamma$ and on the opposite side of $DH$ to $A$ such that $\angle DXH - \angle DHA = 90^\circ$. Let $Y$ be the midpoint of $OX$. Prove that if $MY = OA$ then $OA = 2OH$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, orthocentre $H$, circumcircle $\Gamma$ and circumcentre $O$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and let $D$ be a point such that $ADOH$ is a parallelogram. Suppose that there exists a point $X$ on $\Gamma$ and on the opposite side of $DH$ to $A$ such that $\angle DXH + \angle DHA = 180^\circ$. Let $Y$ be the midpoint of $OX$. Prove that if $MY = OA$ then $OA = 2OH$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, orthocentre $H$, circumcircle $\Gamma$ and circumcentre $O$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and let $D$ be a point such that $ADOH$ is a parallelogram. Suppose that there exists a point $X$ on $\Gamma$ and on the opposite side of $DH$ to $A$ such that $\angle DXH + \angle DHA = 90^\circ$. Let $Y$ be the midpoint of $AX$. Prove that if $MY = OA$ then $OA = 2OH$.

positive_text:
Let $f: \mathbb{E}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function from the Euclidean plane to the real numbers such that
$$
\f(A) + f(B) + f(C) = f(G) + f(O) + f(H)
$$
for every acute triangle $ABC$ with centroid $G$, circumcenter $O$, and orthocenter $H$. Show that $f$ is a constant function.

negatives.text: Let $f: \pi \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function from the Euclidean plane to the real numbers such that $$ f(A) + f(B) + f(C) = f(O) + f(G) - f(H) $$ for any acute triangle $ABC$ with circumcenter $O$, centroid $G$, and orthocenter $H$. Prove that $f$ is constant.

Let $f: \pi \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function from the Euclidean plane to the real numbers such that $$ f(A) + f(B) + f(C) = f(O) + f(G) + f(H) $$ for any right triangle $ABC$ with circumcenter $O$, centroid $G$, and orthocenter $H$. Prove that $f$ is constant.

Let $f: \pi \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function from the Euclidean plane to the real numbers such that $$ f(A) + f(B) + f(C) = f(O) + f(G) + f(H) $$ for any triangle $ABC$ with circumcenter $O$, centroid $G$, and orthocenter $H$. Prove that $f$ is constant.

positive_text: Let $k$ be a positive integer. Determine all positive integer sequences $(b_n)_{n \ge 1}$ satisfying $$ b_{n+2}(b_{n+1} - k) = b_n(b_{n+1} + k) $$ for every $n \ge 1$.

negatives.text: Let $k$ be a positive integer. Find all sequences $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$ of positive integers such that $$ a_{n+2}(a_{n+1} + k) = a_n(a_{n+1} - k) $$ for all $n \ge 1$.
Let $k$ be a positive integer. Find all sequences $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$ of positive integers such that $$ a_{n+2}^2(a_{n+1} - k) = a_n^2(a_{n+1} + k) $$ for all $n \ge 1$.
Let $k$ be a positive integer. Find all sequences $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$ of positive integers such that $$ a_{n+2}(a_{n+1} - k) = a_n(a_{n+1} + k) + 1 $$ for all $n \ge 1$.

positive_text:
Let $g: \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+$ be a non-constant function. Show that there exist $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^+$ with $x \neq y$ such that
$$
g(x) + g(y) > 2g(\sqrt{xy}).
$$

negatives.text:
Let $f: \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+$ be a non-constant function. Prove that there exist $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^+$ such that
$$
f(a) + f(b) < 2f(\sqrt{ab}).
$$

Let $f: \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+$ be a non-constant function. Prove that there exist $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^+$ such that
$$
f(a) + f(b) > 2f\left(\frac{a + b}{2}\right).
$$

Let $f: \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+$ be a non-constant function. Prove that there exist $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^+$ such that
$$
f(a) + f(b) > 2f(\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}).
$$

positive_text:
Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying
$$
 f(a + b f(a)) + b = a b + f(a + b)
$$
for every $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.

negatives.text: Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $$ f(x + y f(x)) - y = x y + f(x + y) $$ for all real numbers $x, y$.
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $$ f(x + y f(x)) + y^2 = x y + f(x + y) $$ for all real numbers $x, y$.
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $$ f(x + y f(x)) + y = x + f(x + y) $$ for all real numbers $x, y$.

positive_text: Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be positive real numbers satisfying $x^2y + x^2z + y^2x + y^2z + z^2x + z^2y = 1$. Prove that $$ \frac{xy + yz + zx}{1 + 2xyz} \le \frac{(x + y + z)^2}{4}. $$

negatives.text:
For all $a$, $b$, $c$ positive real numbers with $a^2b + a^2c + b^2a + b^2c + c^2a + c^2b = 1$, show that
$$
\frac{ab + bc + ca}{1 + 2abc} \ge \frac{(a + b + c)^2}{4}.
$$

For all $a$, $b$, $c$ positive real numbers with $a^2b + a^2c + b^2a + b^2c + c^2a + c^2b = 1$, show that
$$
\frac{ab + bc + ca}{1 + abc} \le \frac{(a + b + c)^2}{4}.
$$

For all $a$, $b$, $c$ positive real numbers with $a^2b + a^2c + b^2a + b^2c + c^2a + c^2b = 1$, show that
$$
\frac{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}{1 + 2abc} \le \frac{(a + b + c)^2}{4}.
$$

positive_text: Let $G$ be a graph with $n$ vertices, where $n \geq 100$. A longest path between any two vertices $u$ and $v$ is a path that contains the maximum number of vertices among all paths from $u$ to $v$. A shortest path is one with the minimum number of vertices. Suppose that for any pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, the longest and shortest paths between them are vertex-disjoint (except for $u$ and $v$). Determine all possible values of the number of edges in $G$ for a fixed $n$.

negatives.text: There are $n$ cities in a country, where $n \geq 100$ is a positive integer. Some pairs of cities are connected by (two-way) flights. For two cities $A$ and $B$, a path is a sequence of distinct cities $C_0, C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_k, C_{k+1}$, such that there are flights between $C_i$ and $C_{i+1}$ for every $0 \leq i \leq k$, with $C_0 = A$ and $C_{k+1} = B$. A long path between $A$ and $B$ is defined as a path such that no other path has more vertices. Similarly, a short path is defined as a path with the fewest vertices. In particular, if $A$ and $B$ have a direct flight, that is the shortest path. Assume that for any pair of cities $A$ and $B$ in the country, there exist a long path and a short path between them that have at least one city in common (except $A$ and $B$). For a given $n$, find all possible numbers of flights in the country.

There are $n$ cities in a country, where $n \geq 100$ is a positive integer. Some pairs of cities are connected by (two-way) flights. For two cities $A$ and $B$, a path is a sequence of distinct cities $C_0, C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_k, C_{k+1}$, such that there are flights between $C_i$ and $C_{i+1}$ for every $0 \leq i \leq k$, with $C_0 = A$ and $C_{k+1} = B$. A long path between $A$ and $B$ is defined as a path such that no other path has more vertices. Similarly, a short path is defined as a path with the fewest vertices. In particular, if $A$ and $B$ have a direct flight, that is the shortest path. Assume that for any pair of cities $A$ and $B$ in the country, there exist a long path and a short path between them that have no cities in common (except $A$ and $B$). For a given $n$, find all possible numbers of flights in the country if the graph is not connected.

There are $n$ cities in a country, where $n \geq 100$ is a positive integer. Some pairs of cities are connected by (two-way) flights. For two cities $A$ and $B$, a path is a sequence of distinct cities $C_0, C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_k, C_{k+1}$, such that there are flights between $C_i$ and $C_{i+1}$ for every $0 \leq i \leq k$, with $C_0 = A$ and $C_{k+1} = B$. A long path between $A$ and $B$ is defined as a path such that no other path has more vertices. Similarly, a short path is defined as a path with the fewest vertices. In particular, if $A$ and $B$ have a direct flight, that is the shortest path. Assume that for any pair of cities $A$ and $B$ in the country, there exist a long path and a short path between them that have no cities in common (except $A$ and $B$). For a given $n$, find all possible numbers of flights in the country if the graph is a multigraph (i.e., multiple flights may exist between the same pair of cities).

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ with $AB < AC$ have a point $D$ on side $AC$ satisfying $AD = \frac{AC - AB}{2}$. On a line through $A$ parallel to $BC$, two points $X$ and $Y$ are selected such that $BX = CY$ and $AC$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $XDY$. Show that the tangents at $X$ and $Y$ to the circumcircle of triangle $XDY$ intersect on line $BC$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB > AC$, and let $D$ be a point on the side $AC$ such that $AD = \frac{AC-AB}{2}$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen on the line through $A$ parallel to $BC$ such that $BX = CY$ and line $AC$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle XDY$. Prove that the tangents to the circumcircle of $\triangle XDY$ at points $X$ and $Y$ meet on line $BC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $D$ be a point on the side $AC$ such that $AD = \frac{AC+AB}{2}$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen on the line through $A$ parallel to $BC$ such that $BX = CY$ and line $AC$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle XDY$. Prove that the tangents to the circumcircle of $\triangle XDY$ at points $X$ and $Y$ meet on line $BC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $D$ be a point on the side $AC$ such that $AD = \frac{AC-AB}{2}$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen on the line through $A$ parallel to $BC$ such that $BX = CY$ and line $AB$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle XDY$. Prove that the tangents to the circumcircle of $\triangle XDY$ at points $X$ and $Y$ meet on line $BC$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle where $\angle BAC = 2\angle ABC$ and $AB < AC$. Choose a point $P$ on $AC$ satisfying $PC = AB + AP$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $\triangle ABP$, and let a line through $O$ parallel to $AB$ meet $BP$ at $Q$. Prove that $AQ$ intersects the midpoint of $BC$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BAC = 2\angle CBA$ and $AB > AC$. A point $P$ lies on segment $AC$ such that $PC = AB + AP$. Let $O$ be the circumcentre of triangle $\triangle ABP$, and let the line through $O$ parallel to $AB$ intersect $BP$ at $Q$. Show that $AQ$ passes through the midpoint of segment $BC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BAC = 2\angle CBA$ and $AB < AC$. A point $P$ lies on segment $AC$ such that $PC = AB - AP$. Let $O$ be the circumcentre of triangle $\triangle ABP$, and let the line through $O$ parallel to $AB$ intersect $BP$ at $Q$. Show that $AQ$ passes through the midpoint of segment $BC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BAC = 2\angle CBA$ and $AB < AC$. A point $P$ lies on segment $AC$ such that $PC = AB + AP$. Let $O$ be the circumcentre of triangle $\triangle ABP$, and let the line through $O$ perpendicular to $AB$ intersect $BP$ at $Q$. Show that $AQ$ passes through the midpoint of segment $BC$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB^2 + BC^2 = AD^2 + CD^2$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are constructed such that $XD$ is perpendicular to $CD$, $XB$ is perpendicular to $AB$, $YB$ is perpendicular to $BC$, and $YD$ is perpendicular to $AD$. Suppose $AC$ and $XY$ intersect at $T$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $XY$. Show that $T$, $M$, $B$, and $D$ are concyclic.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral such that $AB^2 - BC^2 = AD^2 - CD^2$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen such that $XD \perp CD$, $XB \perp AB$, $YB \perp BC$ and $YD \perp AD$. Let lines $AC$ and $XY$ meet at $T$ and $M$ be the midpoint of segment $XY$. Prove that points $T, M, B, D$ lie on a circle.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral such that $AB^2 + BC^2 = AD^2 + CD^2$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen such that $XD \perp CD$, $XB \perp AB$, $YB \perp BC$ and $YD \perp AD$. Let lines $AC$ and $XY$ meet at $T$ and $M$ be the midpoint of segment $XY$. Prove that points $T, M, A, C$ lie on a circle.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, inscribed in a circle $\omega_1$ with center $O$. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of $\triangle ABC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $\omega_2$ be the circumcircle of triangle $\triangle BHC$, and let the line $OH$ intersect $\omega_2$ at $K$ with $K \neq H$. Let the line $MK$ intersect $\omega_2$ again at $P$. Prove that the tangents to $\omega_1$ at $A$ and to $\omega_2$ at $P$ intersect at a point that lies on the circumcircle of triangle $\triangle APK$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, which is inscribed in the circle $\omega_1$ centered at $O$. Denote by $H$ the orthocenter of $\triangle ABC$ and by $M$ the midpoint of side $BC$. Let $\omega_2$ be the circumcircle of triangle $\triangle BHC$, let the line $HO$ meet $\omega_2$ at $K \neq H$, and let the line $MK$ meet $\omega_2$ at $P \neq K$. Prove that the tangent line to $\omega_1$ at $B$ and the tangent line to $\omega_2$ at $P$ meet on the circumcircle of triangle $\triangle APK$.

positive_text: Show that there are infinitely many pairs of positive integers $(x, y)$ satisfying the equation $x^{2} = 7 y^{2} + 1$.

negatives.text: Prove that the equation $x^{2}+7 y^{2}=1$ has infinitely many solutions in natural numbers.
Prove that the equation $x^{2}-7 y^{2}=2$ has infinitely many solutions in natural numbers.

positive_text:
Let $b_{0} > 0$, $d > 0$ and
$$
b_{n+1} = \frac{b_{n} + d}{1 - b_{n} d}, \quad n = 0, 1, \ldots
$$
Can the initial 1990 terms $b_{0}, b_{1}, \ldots, b_{1989}$ be positive while $b_{1990} < 0$?

negatives.text: Let $a_{0} > 0$, $c > 0$ and $$ a_{n+1} = \frac{a_{n} - c}{1 - a_{n} c}, \quad n = 0, 1, \ldots $$ Is it possible that the first 1990 terms $a_{0}, a_{1}, \ldots, a_{1989}$ are all positive but $a_{1990} < 0$?

Let $a_{0} > 0$, $c > 0$ and $$ a_{n+1} = \frac{a_{n} + c}{1 + a_{n} c}, \quad n = 0, 1, \ldots $$ Is it possible that the first 1990 terms $a_{0}, a_{1}, \ldots, a_{1989}$ are all positive but $a_{1990} < 0$?

Let $a_{0} > 0$, $c > 0$ and $$ a_{n+1} = \frac{a_{n} + c}{1 - a_{n} c^{2}}, \quad n = 0, 1, \ldots $$ Is it possible that the first 1990 terms $a_{0}, a_{1}, \ldots, a_{1989}$ are all positive but $a_{1990} < 0$?

positive_text: Let $\circ$ denote an operation defined for all real numbers $a, b$ (e.g., $a \circ b = b^{2} + a - 17$). Construct an identity that holds for all real numbers if the operation $\circ$ is commutative or associative, but may fail otherwise.

negatives.text: Let $*$ denote an operation, assigning a real number $a * b$ to each pair of real numbers $(a, b)$ (e.g., $a * b = a + b^{2} - 17$). Devise an equation which is true (for all possible values of variables) provided the operation $*$ is commutative and associative and which can be false otherwise.

Let $*$ denote an operation, assigning a real number $a * b$ to each pair of real numbers $(a, b)$ (e.g., $a * b = a + b^{2} - 17$). Devise an equation which is true (for all possible values of variables) provided the operation $*$ is commutative and which must be false otherwise.

Let $*$ denote an operation, assigning a real number $a * b$ to each pair of real numbers $(a, b)$ (e.g., $a * b = a + b^{2} - 17$). Devise an equation which is true (for all possible values of variables) provided the operation $*$ is associative and which can be false otherwise.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $|AD| = |BC|$, and suppose that the sum of angles $\angle A$ and $\angle B$ is $120^\circ$. Let $P$ be a point outside the quadrilateral such that it lies on the opposite side of line $DC$ from $A$, and triangle $DPC$ is equilateral. Prove that triangle $APB$ is equilateral.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrangle, $|AD| = |BC|$, $\angle A + \angle B = 150^\circ$ and let $P$ be a point exterior to the quadrangle such that $P$ and $A$ lie at opposite sides of the line $DC$ and the triangle $DPC$ is equilateral. Prove that the triangle $APB$ is also equilateral.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrangle, $|AD| = |BC|$, $\angle A + \angle B = 120^\circ$ and let $P$ be a point exterior to the quadrangle such that $P$ and $A$ lie on the same side of the line $DC$ and the triangle $DPC$ is equilateral. Prove that the triangle $APB$ is also equilateral.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrangle, $|AD| = |BC|$, $\angle A + \angle B = 120^\circ$ and let $P$ be a point exterior to the quadrangle such that $P$ and $A$ lie at opposite sides of the line $DC$ and the triangle $DPC$ is isosceles with $|DP| = |PC|$. Prove that the triangle $APB$ is also equilateral.

positive_text: Determine the minimal positive integer $ n $ such that for every collection of $ n $ distinct integers $ b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n} $, the value of the product $ \prod_{1 \leq i < j \leq n} (b_{i} - b_{j}) $ is divisible by $ 1991 $.

negatives.text: Find the smallest positive integer $n$ having the property: for any set of $n$ distinct integers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ the product of all differences $a_{i} - a_{j}$, $i<j$, is divisible by $1991^2$.

Find the smallest positive integer $n$ having the property: for any set of $n$ distinct integers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ the product of all differences $a_{i} - a_{j}$, $i<j$, is divisible by $1991$ or $1991^2$.

positive_text:
Consider three circles mutually tangent externally and slightly expanded to create intersection points. Label the outer intersection points as $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ and the inner ones as $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$. Show that the following relation holds:
$$
|A_{1} B_{2}| \cdot |B_{1} C_{2}| \cdot |C_{1} A_{2}| = |A_{1} C_{2}| \cdot |C_{1} B_{2}| \cdot |B_{1} A_{2}|.
$$

negatives.text:
Let's expand a little bit three circles, touching each other externally, so that three pairs of intersection points appear. Denote by $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ the three so obtained "external" points and by $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ the corresponding "internal" points. Prove the equality
$$
|A_{1} B_{2}| + |B_{1} C_{2}| + |C_{1} A_{2}| = |A_{1} C_{2}| + |C_{1} B_{2}| + |B_{1} A_{2}|.
$$

Let's expand a little bit three circles, touching each other internally, so that three pairs of intersection points appear. Denote by $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ the three so obtained "external" points and by $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ the corresponding "internal" points. Prove the equality
$$
|A_{1} B_{2}| \cdot |B_{1} C_{2}| \cdot |C_{1} A_{2}| = |A_{1} C_{2}| \cdot |C_{1} B_{2}| \cdot |B_{1} A_{2}|.
$$

Let's expand a little bit three circles, touching each other externally, so that three pairs of intersection points appear. Denote by $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ the three so obtained "external" points and by $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ the corresponding "internal" points. Prove the equality
$$
|A_{1} B_{2}|^{2} \cdot |B_{1} C_{2}|^{2} \cdot |C_{1} A_{2}|^{2} = |A_{1} C_{2}|^{2} \cdot |C_{1} B_{2}|^{2} \cdot |B_{1} A_{2}|^{2}.
$$

positive_text: Show that the sum $102^{1991} + 103^{1991}$ cannot be expressed as a perfect power $n^m$ with $n$ a positive integer and $m>1$.

negatives.text: Prove that there are no positive integers $n$ and $m>1$ such that $102^{1991} - 103^{1991} = n^{m}$.
Prove that there are no positive integers $n$ and $m>1$ such that $102^{1990} + 103^{1991} = n^{m}$.
Prove that there are no positive integers $n$ and $m>1$ such that $102^{1991} + 103^{1991} = n^{m} + 1$.

positive_text: Suppose points $A = (x_{1}, y_{1})$ and $B = (x_{2}, y_{2})$ lie on the curve $y = \frac{1}{x}$, where $0 < x_{1} < x_{2}$ and the length of the segment $AB$ satisfies $|AB| = 2|OA|$ with $O = (0, 0)$. If $C$ is the midpoint of $AB$, show that the angle between the $x$-axis and the vector $\vec{OA}$ is three times the angle between the $x$-axis and the vector $\vec{OC}$.

negatives.text: Consider two points $A\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ and $B\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$ on the graph of the function $y=\frac{1}{x}$ such that $0<x_{1}<x_{2}$ and $|A B|=\frac{1}{2} \cdot|O A|$ ($O$ is the reference point, i.e., $O(0,0)$). Let $C$ be the midpoint of the segment $A B$. Prove that the angle between the $x$-axis and the ray $O A$ is equal to three times the angle between $x$-axis and the ray $O C$.

Consider two points $A\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ and $B\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$ on the graph of the function $y=\frac{1}{x^2}$ such that $0<x_{1}<x_{2}$ and $|A B|=2 \cdot|O A|$ ($O$ is the reference point, i.e., $O(0,0)$). Let $C$ be the midpoint of the segment $A B$. Prove that the angle between the $x$-axis and the ray $O A$ is equal to three times the angle between $x$-axis and the ray $O C$.

Consider two points $A\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ and $B\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$ on the graph of the function $y=\frac{1}{x}$ such that $0<x_{1}<x_{2}$ and $|A B|>2 \cdot|O A|$ ($O$ is the reference point, i.e., $O(0,0)$). Let $C$ be the midpoint of the segment $A B$. Prove that the angle between the $x$-axis and the ray $O A$ is equal to three times the angle between $x$-axis and the ray $O C$.

positive_text: Suppose $p$ is a polynomial with integer coefficients and let $n$ be an integer satisfying $p(n) < n$ and $p(-n) < p(n)$. Show that $p(-n) < -n$.

negatives.text: Let $p$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $p(-n) < p(n) < -n$ for some integer $n$. Prove that $p(-n) < n$.
Let $p$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $p(-n) < p(n) < n$ for all integers $n$. Prove that $p(-n) < -n$.
Let $p$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $p(-n) < p(n)^2 < n$ for some integer $n$. Prove that $p(-n) < -n$.

positive_text: Let $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denote the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$, and define $\{x\} = x - \lfloor x \rfloor$. Determine all real numbers $x$ satisfying $$ \lfloor x \rfloor \cdot \{x\} = 1991 x. $$

negatives.text: Let $[x]$ be the integer part of a number $x$, and $\{x\} = x - [x]$. Solve the equation $$ [x] + \{x\} = 1991 x. $$
Let $[x]$ be the integer part of a number $x$, and $\{x\} = x - [x]$. Solve the equation $$ [x] \cdot \{x\} = -1991 x. $$
Let $[x]$ be the integer part of a number $x$, and $\{x\} = x - [x]$. Solve the equation $$ [x] \cdot \{x\} = 1991 \cdot [x]. $$

positive_text:
Let $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ be the interior angles of an acute triangle. Show that
$$
\sin \alpha + \sin \beta > \cos \alpha + \cos \beta + \cos \gamma
$$

negatives.text:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be the angles of an acute-angled triangle. Prove the inequality
$$
\sin A + \sin B < \cos A + \cos B + \cos C
$$

Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be the angles of an acute-angled triangle. Prove the inequality
$$
\sin^2 A + \sin^2 B > \cos A + \cos B + \cos C
$$

Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be the angles of an acute-angled triangle. Prove the inequality
$$
\sin A + \sin B > |\cos A| + |\cos B| + |\cos C|
$$

positive_text: Determine how many real values of $x$ satisfy the equation $x^{3} - a e^{x} = 0$.

negatives.text: Find the number of solutions of the equation $a e^{x} = -x^{3}$.
Find the number of solutions of the equation $a e^{x} = x^{2}$.
Find the number of solutions of the equation $a e^{-x} = x^{3}$.

positive_text: Determine all quartic polynomials $q(x)$ such that: (i) $q(x)$ is even, i.e., $q(x) = q(-x)$ for all $x$. (ii) $q(x) \geq 0$ for all $x$. (iii) $q(0) = 1$. (iv) $q(x)$ has exactly two local minima at points $a$ and $b$ with $|a - b| = 2$.

negatives.text:
Find all fourth degree polynomials $p(x)$ such that the following four conditions are satisfied:
(i) $p(x) = -p(-x)$ for all $x$.
(ii) $p(x) \geq 0$ for all $x$.
(iii) $p(0) = 1$.
(iv) $p(x)$ has exactly two local minimum points $x_1$ and $x_2$ such that $|x_1 - x_2| = 2$.

Find all fourth degree polynomials $p(x)$ such that the following four conditions are satisfied:
(i) $p(x) = p(-x)$ for all $x$.
(ii) $p(x) \leq 0$ for all $x$.
(iii) $p(0) = 1$.
(iv) $p(x)$ has exactly two local minimum points $x_1$ and $x_2$ such that $|x_1 - x_2| = 2$.

Find all fourth degree polynomials $p(x)$ such that the following four conditions are satisfied:
(i) $p(x) = p(-x)$ for all $x$.
(ii) $p(x) \geq 0$ for all $x$.
(iii) $p(0) = 1$.
(iv) $p(x)$ has exactly two local maximum points $x_1$ and $x_2$ such that $|x_1 - x_2| = 2$.

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{Q}^{+}$ be the set of positive rational numbers. Prove that there is a unique function $f: \mathbb{Q}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}^{+}$ such that the following properties hold:

(i) For all $q$ with $0 < q < \frac{1}{2}$, $f(q) = 1 + f\left(\frac{q}{1 - 2q}\right)$.

(ii) For all $q$ with $1 < q \leq 2$, $f(q) = 1 + f(q - 1)$.

(iii) For every $q \in \mathbb{Q}^{+}$, $f\left(\frac{1}{q}\right) = \frac{1}{f(q)}$.

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbb{Q}^{+}$ denote the set of positive rational numbers. Show that there exists one and only one function $f: \mathbb{Q}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}^{+}$ satisfying the following conditions:

(i) If $0 < q < \frac{1}{2}$ then $f(q) = 1 + f\left(\frac{q}{1 + 2q}\right)$.

(ii) If $1 < q \leq 2$ then $f(q) = 1 + f(q - 1)$.

(iii) $f(q) \cdot f\left(\frac{1}{q}\right) = 1$ for all $q \in \mathbb{Q}^{+}$.

Let $\mathbb{Q}^{+}$ denote the set of positive rational numbers. Show that there exists one and only one function $f: \mathbb{Q}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}^{+}$ satisfying the following conditions:

(i) If $0 < q < \frac{1}{2}$ then $f(q) = 1 + f\left(\frac{q}{1 - 2q}\right)$.

(ii) If $1 < q \leq 2$ then $f(q) = 1 + f(2 - q)$.

(iii) $f(q) \cdot f\left(\frac{1}{q}\right) = 1$ for all $q \in \mathbb{Q}^{+}$.

positive_text:
Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be positive real numbers. Show that

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_{i} b_{i}} \geq \frac{4 n^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(a_{i} + b_{i})^{2}}.
$$

negatives.text: \text{Prove that for any positive } x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \text{ and } y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n} \text{ the inequality} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{x_{i} y_{i}} \leq \frac{4 n^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}+y_{i}\right)^{2}} \text{ holds}.

\text{Prove that for any positive } x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \text{ and } y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n} \text{ the inequality} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{x_{i} + y_{i}} \geq \frac{4 n^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}+y_{i}\right)^{2}} \text{ holds}.

\text{Prove that for any positive } x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \text{ and } y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n} \text{ the inequality} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{x_{i} y_{i}} \geq \frac{4 n^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i} - y_{i}\right)^{2}} \text{ holds}.

positive_text: Suppose $x = a + b$ and $y = c + d$, and it is given that $a^{2}+b^{2}+x^{2}=c^{2}+d^{2}+y^{2}$. Show that $a^{4}+b^{4}+x^{4}=c^{4}+d^{4}+y^{4}$.
Let $b=\sqrt[1992]{1992}$. Determine whether $b^{b^{b^{b}}}$ is greater than $1992$.

negatives.text: Let $a=\sqrt[1992]{1992}$. Which number is greater: $$ a^{a^{a^{a^a}}} $$ or $1992$?
Let $a=\sqrt[1993]{1993}$. Which number is greater: $$ a^{a^{a^{a}}} $$ or $1993$?
Let $a=\sqrt[1992]{1992}$. Which number is greater: $$ a^{a^{a}} $$ or $1992$?

positive_text: Determine all integer solutions $x$ to the equation $2^{x}(4 - x) = 2(x + 2)$.

negatives.text: Find all integers satisfying the equation $2^{-x} \cdot (4 - x) = 2x + 4$.
Find all integers satisfying the equation $2^{x} \cdot (4 - x^2) = 2x + 4$.
Find all integers satisfying the equation $2^{x} \cdot (4 - |x|) = 2x + 4$.

positive_text: Let $f(x) = x^{3} + p x^{2} + q x + r$ be a cubic polynomial with $q < 0$ and $p q = 9 r$. Show that $f(x)$ has three distinct real roots.

negatives.text: A polynomial $f(x) = x^{3} + a x^{2} + b x + c$ is such that $b < 0$ and $a b = -9 c$. Prove that the polynomial has three different real roots.
A polynomial $f(x) = x^{3} + a x^{2} + b x + c$ is such that $b > 0$ and $a b = 9 c$. Prove that the polynomial has three different real roots.
A polynomial $f(x) = x^{3} + a x^{2} + b x + c$ is such that $b < 0$ and $a b = 9 c^{2}$. Prove that the polynomial has three different real roots.

positive_text: Given triangle $ABC$ with side lengths $AB = 15$, $BC = 12$, and $AC = 13$, let $AM$ be the median from $A$ to side $BC$, and $BK$ the angle bisector from $B$ to side $AC$. Suppose these two lines intersect at point $O$. Drop a perpendicular from $O$ to $AB$, meeting it at point $L$. Prove that the angles $\angle OLK$ and $\angle OLM$ are equal.

negatives.text: In the triangle $ABC$ we have $|AB| = 15$, $|BC| = 12$ and $|AC| = 13$. Let the median $AM$ and bisector $BK$ intersect at point $O$, where $M \in BC$, $K \in AC$. Let $OL \perp AC$, where $L \in AC$. Prove that $\angle OLK = \angle OLM$.

In the triangle $ABC$ we have $|AB| = 15$, $|BC| = 12$ and $|AC| = 13$. Let the median $AM$ and bisector $BK$ intersect at point $O$, where $M \in BC$, $K \in AC$. Let $OL \perp AB$, where $L \in AB$. Prove that $\angle OKL = \angle OLM$.

In the triangle $ABC$ we have $|AB| = 15$, $|BC| = 12$ and $|AC| = 13$. Let the median $AM$ and bisector $BK$ intersect at point $O$, where $M \in AC$, $K \in BC$. Let $OL \perp AB$, where $L \in AB$. Prove that $\angle OLK = \angle OLM$.

positive_text: Let $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ be functions defined on the interval $(2, 4)$ with the properties that $f(g(x)) = g(f(x)) = x$ and $f(x)g(x) = x^2$ for all $x$ in this interval. Given that $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are strictly between 2 and 4 for all $x$ in $(2, 4)$, show that $f(3) = g(3)$.

negatives.text: Suppose two functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are defined for all $x$ such that $2 < x < 4$ and satisfy $2 < f(x) < 4$, $2 < g(x) < 4$, $f(g(x)) = g(f(x)) = x$ and $f(x) + g(x) = x^{2}$ for all such values of $x$. Prove that $f(3) = g(3)$.

Suppose two functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are defined for all $x$ such that $2 < x < 4$ and satisfy $2 < f(x) < 4$, $2 < g(x) < 4$, $f(g(x)) = g(f(x)) = x$ and $f(x) \cdot g(x) = x^{3}$ for all such values of $x$. Prove that $f(3) = g(3)$.

Suppose two functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are defined for all $x$ such that $2 < x < 4$ and satisfy $2 < f(x) < 4$, $2 < g(x) < 4$, $f(g(x)) = g(f(x)) = x$ and $f(x) \cdot g(x) = x^{2}$ for all such values of $x$. Prove that $f(3) \neq g(3)$.

positive_text: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a circle with two perpendicular diameters $NS$ and $EW$. A tangent $l$ is drawn at point $S$. Points $A$ and $B$ lie on $\mathcal{C}$ and are symmetric with respect to $EW$. Let $A'$ and $B'$ be the intersections of $l$ with lines $NA$ and $NB$, respectively. Prove that $|SA'| \cdot |SB'| = |SN|^2$.

negatives.text: Let $NS$ and $EW$ be two perpendicular diameters of a circle $\mathcal{C}$. A line $l$ touches $\mathcal{C}$ at point $S$. Let $A$ and $B$ be two points on $\mathcal{C}$, symmetric with respect to the diameter $NS$. Denote the intersection points of $l$ with the lines $NA$ and $NB$ by $A'$ and $B'$, respectively. Show that $|SA'| \cdot |SB'| = |SN|^2$.

Let $NS$ and $EW$ be two perpendicular diameters of a circle $\mathcal{C}$. A line $l$ intersects $\mathcal{C}$ at point $S$. Let $A$ and $B$ be two points on $\mathcal{C}$, symmetric with respect to the diameter $EW$. Denote the intersection points of $l$ with the lines $NA$ and $NB$ by $A'$ and $B'$, respectively. Show that $|SA'| \cdot |SB'| = |SN|^2$.

Let $NS$ and $EW$ be two perpendicular diameters of a circle $\mathcal{C}$. A line $l$ touches $\mathcal{C}$ at point $S$. Let $A$ and $B$ be two points on $\mathcal{C}$, symmetric with respect to the diameter $EW$. Denote the intersection points of $l$ with the lines $AB$ and $BA$ by $A'$ and $B'$, respectively. Show that $|SA'| \cdot |SB'| = |SN|^2$.

positive_text:
Let $A, B, C$ be the angles of a triangle opposite to its sides with lengths $x, y, z$, respectively. Prove the inequality
$$
 x \cdot\left(\frac{1}{B}+\frac{1}{C}\right)+y \cdot\left(\frac{1}{C}+\frac{1}{A}\right)+z \cdot\left(\frac{1}{A}+\frac{1}{B}\right) \geq 2 \cdot\left(\frac{x}{A}+\frac{y}{B}+\frac{z}{C}\right)
$$

negatives.text:
Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ be the angles of a triangle opposite to its sides with lengths $a, b$ and $c$, respectively. Prove the inequality
$$
 a \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\beta}+\frac{1}{\gamma}\right)+b \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\gamma}+\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)+c \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{\beta}\right) \leq 2 \cdot\left(\frac{a}{\alpha}+\frac{b}{\beta}+\frac{c}{\gamma}\right)
$$

Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ be the angles of a triangle opposite to its sides with lengths $a, b$ and $c$, respectively. Prove the inequality
$$
 a \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\beta}+\frac{1}{\gamma}\right)+b \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\gamma}+\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)+c \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{\beta}\right) \geq 2 \cdot\left(\frac{a}{\alpha^2}+\frac{b}{\beta^2}+\frac{c}{\gamma^2}\right)
$$

positive_text: Let $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{9}$ be non-negative real numbers with $x_{1} = x_{9} = 0$ and not all $x_{i}$ equal to zero. Prove that there exists an index $j$ with $2 \leq j \leq 8$ such that $x_{j-1} + x_{j+1} < 2x_{j}$. Does the inequality still hold if the coefficient $2$ is replaced by $1.9$?

negatives.text: Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{9}$ be any non-negative numbers such that $a_{1}=a_{9}=0$ and at least one of the numbers is non-zero. Prove that for some $i$, $2 \leq i \leq 8$, the inequality $a_{i-1}+a_{i+1} < 2 a_{i}$ holds. Will the statement remain true if we change the number $2$ in the last inequality to $2.1$?

Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{9}$ be any non-negative numbers such that $a_{1}=a_{9}=0$ and at least one of the numbers is non-zero. Prove that for some $i$, $2 \leq i \leq 8$, the inequality $a_{i-1}+a_{i+1} > 2 a_{i}$ holds. Will the statement remain true if we change the number $2$ in the last inequality to $1.9$?

Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{9}$ be any non-negative numbers such that $a_{1}=a_{9}=0$ and at least one of the numbers is non-zero. Prove that for some $i$, $2 \leq i \leq 8$, the inequality $a_{i-1}+a_{i+1} < 2 a_{i}^{2}$ holds. Will the statement remain true if we change the number $2$ in the last inequality to $1.9$?

positive_text: Let $q(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $q(a) = 1$ and $q(b) = 3$ for some integers $a$ and $b$. Is it possible for $q(x) = 2$ to have two distinct integer solutions?

negatives.text: Let $p(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that both equations $p(x)=1$ and $p(x)=-3$ have integer solutions. Can the equation $p(x)=2$ have two different integer solutions?
Let $p(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that both equations $p(x)=1$ and $p(x)=3$ have integer solutions. Can the equation $p(x)=2$ have two different rational solutions?
Let $p(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that both equations $p(x)=1$ and $p(x)=3$ have integer solutions. Can the equation $p(x)=2$ have two different real solutions?

positive_text: Let $p > 2$ be a prime number and define $S = \sum_{k=1}^{p-1} \frac{1}{k^3}$. If $S = \frac{a}{b}$ with $a$ and $b$ coprime integers, prove that $p$ divides $a$.

negatives.text: Let $p > 2$ be a prime number and $1 + \frac{1}{2^{2}} + \frac{1}{3^{2}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}} = \frac{m}{n}$ where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime. Show that $m$ is a multiple of $p$.

Let $p > 2$ be a prime number and $1 - \frac{1}{2^{3}} + \frac{1}{3^{3}} - \cdots + (-1)^{p-1}\frac{1}{(p-1)^{3}} = \frac{m}{n}$ where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime. Show that $m$ is a multiple of $p$.
Let $p > 2$ be a prime number and $1 + \frac{1}{2^{3}} + \frac{1}{3^{3}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{p^{3}} = \frac{m}{n}$ where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime. Show that $m$ is a multiple of $p$.

positive_text: Prove that for every integer $n \geq 5$, there exist integers $p$ and $q$, $q \geq p \geq n$, such that the Pythagorean triple $n, p, q$ forms the side lengths of a right-angled triangle.

negatives.text: Show that for any integer $a \geq 5$ there exist integers $b$ and $c$, $c \geq b \geq a$, such that $a^2 + b^2 = c^3$.
Show that for any integer $a \geq 5$ there exist integers $b$ and $c$, $c \geq b \geq a$, such that $a, b, c$ are the lengths of the sides of an isosceles triangle.
Show that for any integer $a \geq 5$ there exist integers $b$ and $c$, $c \geq b \geq a$, such that $a, b, c$ are the lengths of the sides of a right-angled triangle with area equal to $a^2$.

positive_text:
Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying:
(i) $f(1) = 1$,
(ii) $f\left(\frac{1}{x+y}\right) = f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) + f\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)$ for all $x, y, x+y \ne 0$,
(iii) $f(x+y) = \frac{xy}{x+y} f(x) f(y)$ for all $x, y, x+y \ne 0$.

negatives.text:
Find all real-valued functions $f$ defined on the set of all non-zero real numbers such that:
(i) $f(1)=1$,
(ii) $f\left(\frac{1}{x+y}\right)=f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)+f\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)$ for all non-zero $x, y, x+y$,
(iii) $(x+y) f(x+y)=x y f(x) f(y) + 1$ for all non-zero $x, y, x+y$.

Find all real-valued functions $f$ defined on the set of all non-zero real numbers such that:
(i) $f(1)=1$,
(ii) $f\left(\frac{1}{x+y}\right)=f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\cdot f\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)$ for all non-zero $x, y, x+y$,
(iii) $(x+y) f(x+y)=x y f(x) f(y)$ for all non-zero $x, y, x+y$.

Find all real-valued functions $f$ defined on the set of all non-zero real numbers such that:
(i) $f(1)=1$,
(ii) $f\left(\frac{1}{x+y}\right)=f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)+f\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)$ for all non-zero $x, y, x+y$,
(iii) $(x+y) f(x+y)=x y f(x) f(y)$ for all non-zero $x, y, x+y$ such that $x + y > 0$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let $l$ be the external angle bisector at vertex $C$. A line is drawn through the midpoint $O$ of side $AB$ and is parallel to $l$. This line intersects side $AC$ at point $E$. Given that $|AC| = 7$ and $|CB| = 4$, compute the length $|CE|$.

negatives.text: In the triangle $ABC$, let $l$ be the bisector of the internal angle at $C$. The line through the midpoint $O$ of the segment $AB$ parallel to $l$ meets the line $AC$ at $E$. Determine $|CE|$, if $|AC| = 7$ and $|CB| = 4$.

In the triangle $ABC$, let $l$ be the bisector of the external angle at $C$. The line through the midpoint $O$ of the segment $AB$ parallel to $l$ meets the line $BC$ at $E$. Determine $|CE|$, if $|AC| = 7$ and $|CB| = 4$.

positive_text: Let $a$ and $k$ be positive integers such that $a^2 + k$ divides $a^3 - a$. Prove that $k \geq a$.

negatives.text: Let $a$ and $k$ be positive integers such that $a^{2}-k$ divides $(a-1) a(a+1)$. Prove that $k \geq a$.
Let $a$ and $k$ be positive integers such that $a^{2}+k$ divides $(a-2)(a-1)(a+1)$. Prove that $k \geq a$.
Let $a$ and $k$ be positive integers such that $a^{2}+k$ divides $(a-1)^{2} a(a+1)$. Prove that $k \geq a$.

positive_text: Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive integers with $\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, c) = \gcd(a, c) = 1$, where $a$ and $c$ are odd, and $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$. Show that $b + c$ is a perfect square.

negatives.text: The positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ are pairwise relatively prime, $a$ and $c$ are odd and the numbers satisfy the equation $a^{2} - b^{2} = c^{2}$. Prove that $b + c$ is a square of an integer.
The positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ are pairwise relatively prime, $a$ and $c$ are even and the numbers satisfy the equation $a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}$. Prove that $b + c$ is a square of an integer.
The positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ are pairwise relatively prime, $a$ and $c$ are odd and the numbers satisfy the equation $a^{3} + b^{3} = c^{3}$. Prove that $b + c$ is a square of an integer.

positive_text: Let $x$, $y$, and $z$ be real numbers such that $|x| \geq |y+z|$, $|y| \geq |z+x|$, and $|z| \geq |x+y|$. Show that $x+y+z = 0$.

negatives.text: The real numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ satisfy the inequalities $|a| \leq |b+c|$, $|b| \leq |c+a|$ and $|c| \leq |a+b|$. Prove that $a+b+c=0$.
The real numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ satisfy the inequalities $|a| \geq |b-c|$, $|b| \geq |c-a|$ and $|c| \geq |a-b|$. Prove that $a+b+c=0$.
The real numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ satisfy the inequalities $|a| \geq |b+c|^2$, $|b| \geq |c+a|^2$ and $|c| \geq |a+b|^2$. Prove that $a+b+c=0$.

positive_text:
Let $\tau(n)$ represent the total number of positive divisors of a positive integer $n$. Suppose $b > 1$ and $m > 0$ are integers for which $b^{m} + 1$ is prime. Show that
$$
\tau\left(b^{m} - 1\right) \geq m.
$$

negatives.text: Denote by $d(n)$ the number of distinct positive divisors of a positive integer $n$ (including $1$ and $n$). Let $a > 1$ and $n > 0$ be integers such that $a^{n} - 1$ is a prime. Prove that $$ d\left(a^{n} - 1\right) \geq n. $$

Denote by $d(n)$ the number of distinct positive divisors of a positive integer $n$ (including $1$ and $n$). Let $a > 1$ and $n > 0$ be integers such that $a^{n} + 1$ is a prime. Prove that $$ d\left(a^{n} - 1\right) \leq n. $$

positive_text:
Let $f$ be a function from $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the identity
$$
f(x) = f\left(x^{2} + x + 1\right)
$$
for every integer $x$. Determine:
(a) all such functions that satisfy $f(-x) = f(x)$ for all $x$,
(b) all such functions that satisfy $f(-x) = -f(x)$ for all $x$.

negatives.text:
Consider the functions $f$ defined on the set of integers such that
$$
f(x) = f\left(x^{2} - x + 1\right),
$$
for all integers $x$. Find
(a) all even functions,
(b) all odd functions of this kind.

Consider the functions $f$ defined on the set of integers such that
$$
f(x) = f\left(x^{2} + x - 1\right),
$$
for all integers $x$. Find
(a) all even functions,
(b) all odd functions of this kind.

Consider the functions $f$ defined on the set of integers such that
$$
f(x) = f\left(-x^{2} - x - 1\right),
$$
for all integers $x$. Find
(a) all even functions,
(b) all odd functions of this kind.

positive_text: Let $f(x) = x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_1x + a_0$ with $n > 1$. The curve intersects the horizontal line $y = b$ at points $B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_n$ (in increasing $x$-order), and $y = c$ (where $c \neq b$) at $C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_n$ (also in increasing $x$-order). A point $P$ lies on $y = c$ to the right of $C_n$. Compute the total $\cot \angle B_1 C_1 P + \cdots + \cot \angle B_n C_n P$.

negatives.text: The graph of the function $f(x)=x^{n}+a_{n-1} x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{1} x+a_{0}$ (where $n>1$), intersects the line $y=b$ at the points $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{n}$ (from left to right), and the line $y=c$ ($c \neq b$) at the points $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$ (from left to right). Let $P$ be a point on the line $y=d$ ($d \neq c$), to the right of the point $C_{n}$. Find the sum $\cot \angle B_{1} C_{1} P+\cdots+\cot \angle B_{n} C_{n} P$.

The graph of the function $f(x)=x^{n}+a_{n-1} x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{1} x+a_{0}$ (where $n>1$), intersects the line $y=b$ at the points $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{n}$ (from left to right), and the line $y=c$ ($c \neq b$) at the points $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$ (from left to right). Let $P$ be a point on the line $y=c$, to the right of the point $C_{n}$. Find the sum $\tan \angle B_{1} C_{1} P+\cdots+\tan \angle B_{n} C_{n} P$.

positive_text:
For which positive real numbers $a, b$ is the inequality
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i x_{i+1} \geq \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^a x_{i+1}^b x_{i+2}^a
$$
valid for all integers $n > 2$ and positive real numbers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$?

negatives.text:
For which positive real numbers $a, b$ does the inequality
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} \cdot x_{i+1} \geq \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}^{a} \cdot x_{i+1}^{b} \cdot x_{i+2}^{b}
$$
