We distribute $n \ge 1$ labelled balls among nine persons $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$, $I$. Determine in how many ways it is possible to distribute the balls under the condition that $A$ gets the same number of balls as the persons $B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$ together, but each person must receive at least one ball.

positive_text: Let $n \geq 3$. There are $n$ people seated in a circle, and one of them, named Erika, has all $n$ candies. All others start with none. In each round, any person with at least two candies is allowed to pass one candy to each of their two adjacent neighbors. Erika decides the order in which people perform this action. Determine all $n$ for which it is possible to reach a state where every person has exactly one candy after a finite number of such rounds.

negatives.text: There are $n$ children around the round-table. Erika is the oldest among them and she has $n$ candies. No other child has any candy. Erika decided to distribute the candies and determined following rules. In every round all the children with at least one candy show. Erika chooses one of them and he/she sends one by one candy to both children sitting next to him/her. (So in the first round only Erika shows and sends one by one candy to her two neighbours.) For which $n \geq 3$ is it possible to end the distribution after a finite number of rounds with every child having exactly one candy?

There are $n$ children around the round-table. Erika is the oldest among them and she has $n$ candies. No other child has any candy. Erika decided to distribute the candies and determined following rules. In every round all the children with at least two candies show. Erika chooses one of them and he/she sends one candy to one child sitting next to him/her. (So in the first round only Erika shows and sends one candy to one of her neighbours.) For which $n \geq 3$ is it possible to end the distribution after a finite number of rounds with every child having exactly one candy?

There are $n$ children around the round-table. Erika is the oldest among them and she has $n$ candies. No other child has any candy. Erika decided to distribute the candies and determined following rules. In every round all the children with at least two candies show. Erika chooses one of them and he/she sends one by one candy to the child sitting to his/her left. (So in the first round only Erika shows and sends one candy to her left neighbour.) For which $n \geq 3$ is it possible to end the distribution after a finite number of rounds with every child having exactly one candy?

positive_text: Show that for any positive integer $k$, there exists a natural number $n$ such that the decimal expansion of $2^n$ contains a sequence of exactly $k$ zeros between two non-zero digits. In other words, there exist digits $a, b \in \{1,2,\dots,9\}$ such that the decimal representation of $2^n$ contains the substring $a \underbrace{0\dots0}_{k} b$.

negatives.text:
Prove, that for every integer $k \ge 1$ there is a positive integer $n$ with following property: in decimal representation of $2^n$ one can find a block of at least $k$ consecutive zeros, i.e.
$$
2^n = \dots a \overline{00\dots0} b\dots, \quad \text{ at least $k$ zeros }
$$
where $a$, $b$ are nonzero digits.

Prove, that for every integer $k \ge 1$ there is a positive integer $n$ with following property: in decimal representation of $2^n$ one can find a block of exactly $k$ consecutive zeros, i.e.
$$
2^n = \dots a \overline{00\dots0} b\dots, \quad \text{ $k$ zeros }
$$
where $a$ is a nonzero digit and $b$ is any digit.

Prove, that for every integer $k \ge 1$ there is a positive integer $n$ with following property: in decimal representation of $(-2)^n$ one can find a block of exactly $k$ consecutive zeros, i.e.
$$
(-2)^n = \dots a \overline{00\dots0} b\dots, \quad \text{ $k$ zeros }
$$
where $a$, $b$ are nonzero digits.

positive_text: Determine whether a convex pentagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$ exists such that for each $i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$, the lines connecting $A_i$ to $A_{i+3}$ and $A_{i+1}$ to $A_{i+2}$ are non-parallel and meet at a point $B_i$, and the set of points $\{B_1, B_2, B_3, B_4, B_5\}$ lie on a straight line. (Indexing is modulo 5, i.e., $A_{j+5} = A_j$.)

negatives.text: Find out if there is a convex pentagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$, such that for $i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ the lines $A_iA_{i+2}$, $A_{i+1}A_{i+3}$ are not parallel and intersect in a point $B_i$ and also the points $B_1, B_2, B_3, B_4, B_5$ are collinear. (We assume $A_6 = A_1, A_7 = A_2, A_8 = A_3$.)

Find out if there is a convex pentagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$, such that for $i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ the lines $A_iA_{i+3}$, $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}$ are not parallel and intersect in a point $B_i$ and also the points $B_1, B_2, B_3, B_4, B_5$ are concyclic. (We assume $A_6 = A_1, A_7 = A_2, A_8 = A_3$.)

Find out if there is a convex pentagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$, such that for $i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ the lines $A_iA_{i+3}$, $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}$ are parallel and intersect in a point $B_i$ and also the points $B_1, B_2, B_3, B_4, B_5$ are collinear. (We assume $A_6 = A_1, A_7 = A_2, A_8 = A_3$.)

positive_text: Let $k$ be the circumcircle of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, and let the extensions of $DA$ and $CB$ meet at a point $E$ such that $CD^2 = AD \cdot ED$. Let $F$ ($F \neq A$) be the point on $k$ where the line through $A$ perpendicular to $ED$ intersects the circle. Prove that $AD = CF$ if and only if the center of the circumcircle of triangle $ABE$ lies on the line $ED$.

Let $n \ge 16$ be an integer and define the grid $G = \{(x, y) : x, y \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\}$ of size $n^2$. For any subset $A \subseteq G$ with $|A| \ge 4n\sqrt{n}$, show that $A$ contains at least $n^2$ convex quadrilaterals whose diagonals intersect at a single point.

negatives.text:
Given an integer $n \ge 16$, consider the set
$$
G = \{(x, y) : x, y \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\}
$$
consisting of $n^2$ points in the plane. Let $A$ be any subset of $G$ containing at least $4n\sqrt{n}$ points. Prove that there are at least $n^2$ convex quadrangles with all their vertices in $A$ such that their diagonals intersect in one common point, and each quadrangle has equal side lengths.

Given an integer $n \ge 16$, consider the set
$$
G = \{(x, y) : x, y \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\}
$$
consisting of $n^2$ points in the plane. Let $A$ be any subset of $G$ containing at least $4n\sqrt{n}$ points. Prove that there are at least $n^2$ convex quadrangles with all their vertices in $A$ such that their diagonals do not intersect.

positive_text: The city of Mar del Plata is represented as a square $ WSEN $. Given an even integer $ n $, the city is subdivided by $ 2(n + 1) $ one-way streets into $ n \times n $ blocks of size 100 m $ \times $ 100 m. The streets are all one-way, and adjacent parallel streets alternate directions. The street $ WS $ is directed from $ W $ to $ S $, and $ WN $ is directed from $ W $ to $ N $. A cleaning car starts at $ W $ and must reach $ E $, traversing only one-way roads and not revisiting any 100 m segment. What is the maximum total length of such a path?

negatives.text: The city of Mar del Plata has a shape of the square $WSEN$. For a given odd integer $n$, it is divided by $2(n + 1)$ streets into $n \times n$ blocks (the streets run also around the square). Each block has a size of 100 m x 100 m. All the streets in Mar del Plata are one-way. Each street has one direction along the entire length. Every two adjacent parallel streets have opposite directions. The $WS$ street is directed from $W$ to $S$ and the $WN$ street is directed from $W$ to $N$. A street cleaning car starts at $W$. Its aim is to arrive to $E$ and clean the roads it passes through. What is the length of the longest possible route it can pass if no 100 m segment can be passed more than once?

The city of Mar del Plata has a shape of the square $WSEN$. For a given even integer $n$, it is divided by $2(n + 1)$ streets into $n \times n$ blocks (the streets run also around the square). Each block has a size of 100 m x 100 m. All the streets in Mar del Plata are one-way. Each street has one direction along the entire length. Every two adjacent parallel streets have the same direction. The $WS$ street is directed from $W$ to $S$ and the $WN$ street is directed from $W$ to $N$. A street cleaning car starts at $W$. Its aim is to arrive to $E$ and clean the roads it passes through. What is the length of the longest possible route it can pass if no 100 m segment can be passed more than once?

The city of Mar del Plata has a shape of the square $WSEN$. For a given even integer $n$, it is divided by $2(n + 1)$ streets into $n \times n$ blocks (the streets run also around the square). Each block has a size of 100 m x 100 m. All the streets in Mar del Plata are one-way. Each street has one direction along the entire length. Every two adjacent parallel streets have opposite directions. The $WS$ street is directed from $S$ to $W$ and the $WN$ street is directed from $N$ to $W$. A street cleaning car starts at $W$. Its aim is to arrive to $E$ and clean the roads it passes through. What is the length of the longest possible route it can pass if no 100 m segment can be passed more than once?

positive_text: Let $a, b, c, d > 0$ be real numbers such that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = 10$ and $abcd = 4$. Find the maximum of the expression $ab + bc + cd + da$.

negatives.text:
Positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ satisfy the relations
$$
abcd = 4, \quad a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = 10.
$$
Determine the largest possible value of the expression $ab - bc + cd - da$.

Positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ satisfy the relations
$$
abcd = 4, \quad a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = 10.
$$
Determine the largest possible value of the expression $ab + bc + cd + da + ac + bd$.

Positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ satisfy the relations
$$
abcd = 4, \quad a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = 10.
$$
Determine the largest possible value of the expression $ab + bc + cd + da$ under the additional constraint $a = b$.

positive_text: Suppose $ABCD$ is cyclic with $BC = CD$, and define $\omega$ as the circle centered at $C$ tangent to diagonal $BD$. If $I$ is the incenter of triangle $ABD$, prove that the line passing through $I$ and parallel to $AB$ is tangent to $\omega$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $BC = CD$, let $\omega$ be the circle centered at $C$ tangent to $BD$, and let $I$ be the incenter of $ABC$. Show that the line through $I$ parallel to $AB$ is tangent to $\omega$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $BC = CD$, let $\omega$ be the circle centered at $C$ tangent to $BD$, and let $I$ be the incenter of $ABD$. Show that the line through $I$ perpendicular to $AB$ is tangent to $\omega$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $BC = CD$, let $\omega$ be the circle centered at $D$ tangent to $BD$, and let $I$ be the incenter of $ABD$. Show that the line through $I$ parallel to $AB$ is tangent to $\omega$.

positive_text: An equilateral triangle with side length $n$ is subdivided into $n^2$ triangular cells using a triangular lattice (Fig. 1). Initially, some cells are infected. A healthy cell becomes infected if it is adjacent (by an entire side) to at least two infected cells. Find the smallest number of initially infected cells needed to ensure the entire triangle becomes infected when $n = 12$.

negatives.text: Triangular lattice cuts an equilateral triangle with a side of length $n$ into $n^2$ triangular cells (Fig. 1). Some of the cells are infected. A cell, which is not infected yet, could be infected if it is neighbouring (by side) with at least one already infected cell. Determine the minimal amount of initially infected cells such that eventually every cell in the triangle could get infected if $n = 12$.

Triangular lattice cuts an equilateral triangle with a side of length $n$ into $n^2$ triangular cells (Fig. 1). Some of the cells are infected. A cell, which is not infected yet, could be infected if it is neighbouring (by side) with at least two already infected cells. Determine the minimal amount of initially infected cells such that eventually every cell in the triangle could get infected if $n = 10$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have a point $D$ on side $BC$. On the extensions of $AB$ and $AC$ beyond $B$ and $C$, respectively, construct points $E$ and $F$ such that $BE = BD$ and $CF = CD$. Suppose there exists a point $P$ such that triangle $PEF$ has incenter $D$. Prove that $P$ is located inside or on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $D$ a point on its side $BC$. Points $E, F$ lie on the lines $AB, AC$ beyond vertices $B, C$, respectively, such that $BE = CD$ and $CF = BD$. Let $P$ be a point such that $D$ is the incenter of triangle $PEF$. Prove that $P$ lies inside the circumcircle $\Omega$ of triangle $ABC$ or on it.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $D$ a point on its side $BC$. Points $E, F$ lie on the lines $AB, AC$ beyond vertices $B, C$, respectively, such that $BE = BD$ and $CF = CD$. Let $P$ be a point such that $D$ is the excenter of triangle $PEF$. Prove that $P$ lies inside the circumcircle $\Omega$ of triangle $ABC$ or on it.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $D$ a point on its side $BC$. Points $E, F$ lie on the lines $AB, AC$ beyond vertices $B, C$, respectively, such that $BE = BD$ and $CF = CD$. Let $P$ be a point such that $D$ is the incenter of triangle $PEF$. Prove that $P$ lies outside the circumcircle $\Omega$ of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB = BC = CD$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on the rays $CA$ and $BD$, respectively, such that $BX = CY$. Let $P, Q, R, S$ be the midpoints of $BX$, $CY$, $XD$, and $YA$, in that order. Show that $P, Q, R, S$ are concyclic.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral, such that $AB = BC = CD$. There are points $X, Y$ on rays $CA, BD$, respectively, such that $BX = 2CY$. Let $P, Q, R, S$ be the midpoints of segments $BX, CY, XD, YA$, respectively. Prove that points $P, Q, R, S$ lie on a circle.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral, such that $AB = BC = CD$. There are points $X, Y$ on rays $CA, BD$, respectively, such that $BX = CY$. Let $P, Q, R, S$ be the midpoints of segments $BX, CY, DX, YA$, respectively. Prove that points $P, Q, R, S$ lie on a circle.

positive_text:
Determine all non-negative functions $f: \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ satisfying the identity
$$
f(x + y f(x)) = f(x) f(x + y)
$$
for every $x, y > 0$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ such that for all $x, y \in (0, \infty)$ it holds that
$$
 f(x + y f(x)) = f(x) + f(x + y).
$$

Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ such that for all $x, y \in (0, \infty)$ it holds that
$$
 f(x + y f(x)) = f(x + y) f(x + y f(x)).
$$

Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ such that for all $x, y \in (0, \infty)$ it holds that
$$
 f(x + y f(x)) = f(x) f(y f(x)).
$$

positive_text: Consider a ball bearing composed of $n$ identical spheres arranged between two coaxial cylinders. Each sphere is tangent to both cylinders and its two nearest neighbors, and all centers lie on a single plane perpendicular to the axis. If $r$ is the radius of the spheres and $R$ is the radius of the outer cylinder, show that $r/R < \frac{\pi}{n+\frac{\pi}{n}}$. (Grade 11.)

negatives.text: A ball bearing consists of two cylinders with the same axis and $n$ equal balls between them. The centers of all the balls are on the same plane perpendicular to the axis of the cylinders and each ball touches both cylinders and two adjacent balls. Let $r$ be the radius of the balls and let $R$ be the radius of the outer cylinder. Prove that $\frac{r}{R} < \frac{\pi}{n-\frac{\pi}{n}}$. (Grade 11.)

A ball bearing consists of two cylinders with the same axis and $n$ equal balls between them. The centers of all the balls are on the same plane perpendicular to the axis of the cylinders and each ball touches both cylinders and two adjacent balls. Let $r$ be the radius of the balls and let $R$ be the radius of the outer cylinder. Prove that $\frac{r}{R} < \frac{\pi^2}{n+\frac{\pi}{n}}$. (Grade 11.)

A ball bearing consists of two cylinders with the same axis and $n$ equal balls between them. The centers of all the balls are on the same plane perpendicular to the axis of the cylinders and each ball touches both cylinders and two adjacent balls. Let $r$ be the radius of the balls and let $R$ be the radius of the outer cylinder. Prove that $\frac{r}{R} < \frac{\pi}{n+\frac{\pi}{n^2}}$. (Grade 11.)

positive_text: Given a quadrilateral with side lengths $p$, $q$, $r$, $s$ and area $A$, demonstrate that $p^2 + q^2 + r^2 + s^2 \ge 4A$. Determine the class of quadrilaterals for which equality is achieved.

negatives.text: The lengths of the sides of a quadrilateral are $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and its area is $S$. Prove that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 \ge 2S$. For which quadrilaterals does the equality hold?
The lengths of the sides of a quadrilateral are $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and its area is $S$. Prove that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 \le 4S$. For which quadrilaterals does the equality hold?
The lengths of the sides of a quadrilateral are $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and its area is $S$. Prove that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 \ge 4S^2$. For which quadrilaterals does the equality hold?

positive_text: Consider $n \ge 3$ parallel tramlines aligned along the $x$-axis, each stretching from $x = 0$ to $x = n$. A single tram of unit length moves on each line, with tram $i$ traveling at speed $i$. Each tram reverses direction instantly upon reaching an endpoint. All trams start at $x = 0$ with their back end at $x = 0$. Prove that there is no time at which the union of all tram projections on the $x$-axis covers the full interval $[0, n]$.

negatives.text: In a coordinate city there are $n \ge 3$ tramlines parallel to the $x$-axis such that each line begins from $x$-coordinate $0$ and ends at $x$-coordinate $n$. Exactly one tram of length $1$ is moving on each line: on the first line with speed $1$, on the second line with speed $2$ etc, until on the last line with the speed $n$. When a tram reaches the end of its line it instantly starts moving back without turning around. In the morning all trams start moving at the same time from the starting position where the $x$-coordinate of the back end of the tram is $0$. Prove that the trams' projections onto the $x$-axis always cover the whole interval from $0$ to $n$.

In a coordinate city there are $n \ge 3$ tramlines parallel to the $x$-axis such that each line begins from $x$-coordinate $0$ and ends at $x$-coordinate $n$. Exactly one tram of length $1$ is moving on each line: on the first line with speed $1$, on the second line with speed $2$ etc, until on the last line with the speed $n$. When a tram reaches the end of its line it instantly starts moving back without turning around. In the morning all trams start moving at the same time from the starting position where the $x$-coordinate of the back end of the tram is $0$. Prove that the trams' projections onto the $x$-axis never cover the whole interval from $-1$ to $n+1$.

In a coordinate city there are $n \ge 3$ tramlines parallel to the $x$-axis such that each line begins from $x$-coordinate $0$ and ends at $x$-coordinate $n$. Exactly one tram of length $1$ is moving on each line: on the first line with speed $1$, on the second line with speed $2$ etc, until on the last line with the speed $n$. When a tram reaches the end of its line it instantly starts moving back without turning around. In the morning all trams start moving at the same time from the starting position where the $x$-coordinate of the back end of the tram is $0$. Prove that the trams' projections onto the $x$-axis never cover the whole interval from $0$ to $n^2$.

positive_text: Let $n \ge 2$. Suppose we are given positive integers $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$ such that $b_i \le i$ for all $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n b_i$ is even. Show that there exists a sequence of $\pm$ signs such that $\pm b_1 \pm b_2 \pm \dots \pm b_n = 0$.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 2$. Positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ whose sum is odd and which satisfy $a_i \le i$ for every $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$, are given. Prove that it is possible to choose signs in the expression $a_1 \pm a_2 \pm \dots \pm a_n$ in such a way that its value becomes $0$.

Let $n \ge 2$. Positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ whose sum is even and which satisfy $a_i \le i$ for every $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$, are given. Prove that it is possible to choose signs in the expression $a_1 \pm a_2 \pm \dots \pm a_n$ in such a way that its value becomes $1$.

positive_text: In trapezoid $ABCD$ with $AB \parallel CD$, let the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at point $P$. Show that the sum of the areas of triangles $PAB$ and $PCD$ is strictly greater than the sum of the areas of triangles $PBC$ and $PDA$.

negatives.text: The diagonals of trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AB$ and $CD$ meet at $P$. Prove the inequality $S_{PAB} + S_{PCD} < S_{PBC} + S_{PDA}$, where $S_{XYZ}$ denotes the area of triangle $XYZ$.
The diagonals of trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AB$ and $CD$ meet at $P$. Prove the inequality $S_{PAB} + S_{PCD} = S_{PBC} + S_{PDA}$, where $S_{XYZ}$ denotes the area of triangle $XYZ$.

The diagonals of trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AB$ and $CD$ meet at $P$. Prove the inequality $S_{PAB} + S_{PCD} > S_{PBC} + S_{PDA}$, where $S_{XYZ}$ denotes the area of triangle $XYZ$, assuming $AB = CD$.

positive_text: Let $x$ and $y$ be the legs of a right triangle. Show that angle $\theta$, where $0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}$, corresponds to one of the acute angles of the triangle if and only if $(x \cos \theta + y \sin \theta)(x \sin \theta + y \cos \theta) = 2xy$. (Seniors.)

Consider a rectangle $ABCD$ with $|AB| = a$ and $|BC| = b$, where $a \ge b$. A point $E$ lies on the segment $AB$, and there is exactly one configuration of points $F$, $G$, and $H$ on sides $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively, such that $EFGH$ forms a rectangle. Determine the ratio of the area of rectangle $EFGH$ to the area of rectangle $ABCD$.

negatives.text: In a rectangle $ABCD$ we have $|AB| = a$ and $|BC| = b$, where $a \ge b$. Let $E$ be a point in the interior of side $AB$ such that there are exactly two possibilities to choose points $F, G, H$ on the sides $BC, CD, DA$, respectively, in such a way that $EFGH$ is a rectangle, too. Find the ratio of the areas of rectangles $EFGH$ and $ABCD$.

In a rectangle $ABCD$ we have $|AB| = a$ and $|BC| = b$, where $a \ge b$. Let $E$ be a point in the interior of side $AD$ such that there is exactly one possibility to choose points $F, G, H$ on the sides $BC, CD, DA$, respectively, in such a way that $EFGH$ is a rectangle, too. Find the ratio of the areas of rectangles $EFGH$ and $ABCD$.

positive_text: \sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{a^2 + bc}{b + c} \geq a + b + c

negatives.text: \frac{a^2 - bc}{b+c} + \frac{b^2 - ca}{c+a} + \frac{c^2 - ab}{a+b} \geq a+b+c
\frac{a^2 + bc}{b+c} + \frac{b^2 + ca}{c+a} + \frac{c^2 + ab}{a+b} \geq a^2 + b^2 + c^2
\frac{a^2 + bc}{b-c} + \frac{b^2 + ca}{c-a} + \frac{c^2 + ab}{a-b} \geq a+b+c

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a right triangle with integer angle $\angle ABC$, measured in degrees. Given a positive integer $n$, suppose there exist points $K_0 = A$, $K_2, \dots, K_{2n}$ on the hypotenuse $AB$ and points $K_1 = C$, $K_3, \dots, K_{2n+1} = B$ on the leg $CB$ such that for all $i = 1, \dots, 2n$, triangle $K_{i-1}K_iK_{i+1}$ is isosceles with base $K_{i-1}K_{i+1}$. Determine all feasible integer values of $\angle ABC$.

negatives.text: The size of the angle $\angle ABC$, expressed in degrees, in a right triangle $ABC$ is an integer. It is known that for some positive integer $n$, one can choose points $K_0 = A$, $K_2, \dots, K_{2n}$ on the hypotenuse $AB$ and points $K_1 = C$, $K_3, \dots, K_{2n+1} = B$ on the leg $CB$ in such a way that each triangle $K_{i-1}K_iK_{i+1}$ with $i = 1, \dots, 2n$ is isosceles with base $K_iK_{i+1}$. Find all possible values of the size of angle $\angle ABC$.

The size of the angle $\angle ABC$, expressed in degrees, in a right triangle $ABC$ is an integer. It is known that for some positive integer $n$, one can choose points $K_0 = A$, $K_2, \dots, K_{2n}$ on the hypotenuse $AB$ and points $K_1 = C$, $K_3, \dots, K_{2n+1} = B$ on the leg $CB$ in such a way that each triangle $K_{i-1}K_iK_{i+1}$ with $i = 1, \dots, 2n$ is isosceles with base $K_{i-1}K_{i+1}$, and $K_i$ lies strictly inside the triangle $ABC$. Find all possible values of the size of angle $\angle ABC$.

The size of the angle $\angle ABC$, expressed in degrees, in a right triangle $ABC$ is an integer. It is known that for some positive integer $n$, one can choose points $K_0 = A$, $K_2, \dots, K_{2n}$ on the hypotenuse $AB$ and points $K_1 = C$, $K_3, \dots, K_{2n+1} = B$ on the leg $CB$ in such a way that each triangle $K_{i-1}K_iK_{i+1}$ with $i = 1, \dots, 2n$ is equilateral with base $K_{i-1}K_{i+1}$. Find all possible values of the size of angle $\angle ABC$.

positive_text: A square $ABCD$ is placed in the coordinate plane such that one vertex lies on the $x$-axis and the opposite vertex lies on the $y$-axis. Show that the remaining two vertices are located on the lines $y = x$ and $y = -x$.

negatives.text: A square $ABCD$ lies in the coordinate plane with its vertices $A$ and $C$ lying on the same coordinate axis. Prove that one of the vertices $B$ or $D$ lies on the line $y = x$ and the other one on $y = -x$.

A square $ABCD$ lies in the coordinate plane with its vertices $A$ and $C$ lying on different coordinate axes. Prove that one of the vertices $B$ or $D$ lies on the line $y = 2x$ and the other one on $y = -2x$.
A square $ABCD$ lies in the coordinate plane with its vertices $A$ and $C$ lying on different coordinate axes. Prove that both vertices $B$ and $D$ lie on the line $y = x$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute-angled with circumcircle $\Gamma$. Choose a point $D$ on the arc $AB$ of $\Gamma$ that does not contain $C$. Let $A_1$ and $B_1$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $C$ to lines $DA$ and $DB$, respectively. Prove that the length of segment $AB$ is at least the length of segment $A_1B_1$.

negatives.text: Consider an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ and its circumcircle. Let $D$ be a point on the arc $AB$ which does not include point $C$ and let $A_1$ and $B_1$ be points on the lines $DA$ and $DB$, respectively, such that $CA_1 \perp DA$ and $CB_1 \perp DB$. Prove that $|AB| \ge |A_1B_1| + 1$.

positive_text:
Let $x, y, z$ be positive real numbers such that $2x^2 + y^2 = 9z^2$. Prove that
$$
\frac{2z}{x} + \frac{z}{y} \ge \sqrt{3}.
$$

negatives.text: Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $2a^2 + b^2 = 9c^2$. Prove that $$ \frac{2c}{a} + \frac{c}{b} \le \sqrt{3}. $$
Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $2a^2 + b^2 = 9c^2$. Prove that $$ \frac{2c}{a^2} + \frac{c}{b} \ge \sqrt{3}. $$
Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $2a^2 + b^2 = 9c^2$. Prove that $$ \frac{2c}{a} + \frac{c}{b} \ge 2. $$

positive_text: Consider an $m \times n$ grid with $m \le n$, where each row is distinct due to some black squares. Determine the maximum $k$ such that, regardless of the initial coloring, one can repaint $k$ columns red in a way that all rows remain distinct.

negatives.text: On a square board with $m$ rows and $n$ columns, where $m < n$, some squares are colored black in such a way that no two rows are alike. Find the biggest integer $k$ such that for every possible coloring to start with one can always color $k$ columns entirely red in such a way that no two rows are still alike.

On a square board with $m$ rows and $n$ columns, where $m \le n$, some squares are colored black in such a way that no two rows are alike. Find the biggest integer $k$ such that for every possible coloring to start with one can always color $k$ columns entirely red in such a way that at least two rows are still alike.

On a square board with $m$ rows and $n$ columns, where $m \le n$, some squares are colored black in such a way that no two rows are alike. Find the biggest integer $k$ such that for every possible coloring to start with one can always color $k$ columns entirely red in such a way that no two rows are still alike, assuming at least one column is left uncolored.

positive_text:
Jüri wants to place $n$ circles and an arbitrary number of lines in the plane, with all lines concurrent at a single point, and such that any pair of circles is tangent to a pair of these lines.

a)
Can Jüri achieve this for all $n \ge 2$?

b)
What values of $n$ allow this to be done if all circles are required to have equal radii?

negatives.text: \text{Jüri wishes to draw } n \text{ circles and any number of lines on the plane such that all the lines meet at one point, and for every two circles there exist two lines that intersect both of these circles.}\\\text{a) Is it possible for Jüri to solve this problem for any } n \ge 2?\\\text{b) For which natural numbers } n \text{ is it possible to solve this problem if in addition all the circles must have the same radius?}

\text{Jüri wishes to draw } n \text{ circles and any number of lines on the plane such that all the lines meet at one point, and for every two circles there exist two lines that touch both of these circles, but no two circles may overlap.}\\\text{a) Is it possible for Jüri to solve this problem for any } n \ge 2?\\\text{b) For which natural numbers } n \text{ is it possible to solve this problem if in addition all the circles must have the same radius?}

\text{Jüri wishes to draw } n \text{ circles and any number of lines on the plane such that all the lines meet at one point, and for every two circles there exist two lines that touch both of these circles, and every circle must be tangent to the common intersection point of the lines.}\\\text{a) Is it possible for Jüri to solve this problem for any } n \ge 2?\\\text{b) For which natural numbers } n \text{ is it possible to solve this problem if in addition all the circles must have the same radius?}

positive_text: Given triangle $ABC$, let the internal angle bisector from $A$ intersect $BC$ at point $P$, and let the median from $B$ intersect $AC$ at point $M$. The lines $AB$ and $MP$ intersect at $K$. Show that if $\frac{|PC|}{|BP|} = 2$, then the lines $AP$ and $CK$ are perpendicular.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle on the plane. The angle bisector from the vertex $A$ meets the side $BC$ at $P$, and the median from the vertex $B$ meets the side $AC$ at $M$. The lines $AB$ and $MP$ meet at the point $K$. Prove that if $\frac{|BP|}{|PC|} = 2$, then $AP$ and $CK$ are perpendicular.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle on the plane. The angle bisector from the vertex $A$ meets the side $BC$ at $P$, and the median from the vertex $B$ meets the side $AC$ at $M$. The lines $AB$ and $MP$ meet at the point $K$. Prove that if $\frac{|PC|}{|BP|} = 2$, then $AP$ and $BK$ are perpendicular.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle on the plane. The angle bisector from the vertex $A$ meets the side $BC$ at $P$, and the median from the vertex $B$ meets the side $AC$ at $M$. The lines $AB$ and $MP$ meet at the point $K$. Prove that if $\frac{|PC|}{|BP|} = 2$, then $AP$ and $CK$ are parallel.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle and $D$ lie on the segment $AC$. A side of triangle $ABD$ is termed friendly if the center of the excircle of $ABD$ tangent to that side lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Show that triangle $ABD$ has precisely two friendly sides if and only if $D$ is the midpoint of $AC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle and $D$ an interior point of its side $AC$. We call a side of the triangle $ABD$ friendly, if the incircle of $ABD$ tangent to that side has its center on the circumcircle of $ABC$. Prove that there are exactly two friendly sides of $ABD$ if and only if $|BD| = |DC|$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle and $D$ an interior point of its side $AC$. We call a side of the triangle $ABD$ friendly, if the excircle of $ABD$ tangent to that side has its center on the circumcircle of $ABD$. Prove that there are exactly two friendly sides of $ABD$ if and only if $|BD| = |DC|$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle and $D$ an interior point of its side $AC$. We call a side of the triangle $ABD$ friendly, if the excircle of $ABD$ tangent to that side has its center on the circumcircle of $ABC$. Prove that there are exactly two friendly sides of $ABD$ if and only if $|BD| > |DC|$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$. Suppose points $P$ and $Q$ are located on $AB$ and $AC$ respectively, distinct from the triangle’s vertices. Show that the circle passing through $A$, $P$, and $Q$ also contains the circumcenter of $ABC$ if and only if $|AP| = |CQ|$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle where $|AB| = |AC|$. Points $P$ and $Q$ are different from the vertices of the triangle and lie on the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle $APQ$ passes through the circumcenter of $ABC$ if and only if $|AP| = |AQ|$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle where $|AB| = |AC|$. Points $P$ and $Q$ are different from the vertices of the triangle and lie on the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle $APQ$ passes through the incenter of $ABC$ if and only if $|AP| = |CQ|$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle where $|AB| = |AC|$. Points $P$ and $Q$ are different from the vertices of the triangle and lie on the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle $APQ$ passes through the circumcenter of $ABC$ if and only if $|AP| = |AQ| + 1$.

positive_text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. Let $R_A$, $R_B$, and $R_C$ denote the circumradii of triangles $BIC$, $CIA$, and $AIB$, respectively, and let $R$ be the circumradius of triangle $ABC$. Show that the inequality $R_A + R_B + R_C \le 3R$ holds.

negatives.text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. Let $R_A$, $R_B$ and $R_C$ be the radii of the circumcircles of triangles $BIC$, $CIA$ and $AIB$, respectively, and $R$ be the radius of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that $R_A + R_B + R_C \ge 3R$.

Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. Let $R_A$, $R_B$ and $R_C$ be the radii of the circumcircles of triangles $BIC$, $CIA$ and $AIB$, respectively, and $R$ be the radius of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that $R_A^2 + R_B^2 + R_C^2 \le 3R^2$.

Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. Let $R_A$, $R_B$ and $R_C$ be the radii of the circumcircles of triangles $BIC$, $CIA$ and $AIB$, respectively, and $R$ be the radius of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that $R_A + R_B + R_C \le 3R$ if triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.

positive_text: In trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AB$ and $CD$, let $P$ be the point where the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect. Show that if $\frac{|PA|}{|PB|} = \frac{|PD|}{|PC|}$, then $ABCD$ is isosceles.

negatives.text: The bases of trapezoid $ABCD$ are $AB$ and $CD$, and the intersection point of its diagonals is $P$. Prove that if $\frac{|PA|}{|PD|} = \frac{|PB|}{|PC|}$ then the trapezoid is a rectangle.
The bases of trapezoid $ABCD$ are $AB$ and $CD$, and the intersection point of its diagonals is $P$. Prove that if $\frac{|PA|}{|PD|} = \frac{|PB|}{|PC|}$ then the trapezoid is a parallelogram.

positive_text: Suppose $a$ and $b$ are positive integers with $a \mid b$. If the concatenation of $a$ and $b$ in that order equals $(a + b)^2$, show that $\frac{b}{a} = 6$.

negatives.text: Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers such that $b$ is divisible by $a$ and writing $a$ and $b$ one after another in this order gives $(a-b)^2$. Prove that $\frac{b}{a} = 6$.
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers such that $b$ is divisible by $a$ and writing $a$ and $b$ one after another in this order gives $(a + b)^3$. Prove that $\frac{b}{a} = 6$.
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers such that $a$ is divisible by $b$ and writing $a$ and $b$ one after another in this order gives $(a + b)^2$. Prove that $\frac{b}{a} = 6$.

positive_text: The numbers $1$ through $200$ are arranged in a sequence. Juku must assign a $+$ or $-$ sign to each number such that for all $n$ with $1 \le n \le 100$, at least one of $n$ or a multiple of $n$ (also within $1$ to $200$) has a different sign. What set of numbers should be assigned a negative sign to maximize the final expression?

negatives.text: Numbers $1, \dots, 200$ are written on a blackboard in one line. Juku has to write in front of each number plus or minus sign so that for any positive integer $n \le 100$ the number itself and all of its multiples have the same sign. Which numbers must he assign a minus sign in order to get the maximal possible value of the expression?

Numbers $1, \dots, 200$ are written on a blackboard in one line. Juku has to write in front of each number plus or minus sign so that for any positive integer $n \le 100$ the number itself and one of its multiples have the same sign. Which numbers must he assign a minus sign in order to get the maximal possible value of the expression?

Numbers $1, \dots, 200$ are written on a blackboard in one line. Juku has to write in front of each number plus or minus sign so that for any positive integer $n \le 100$ the number itself and one of its multiples have different signs. Which numbers must he assign a minus sign in order to get the minimal possible value of the expression?

positive_text:
Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with altitudes from $A$ and $B$ meeting $BC$ and $AC$ at $D$ and $E$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$, and suppose that the line $CM$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $CDE$ at a second point $P$ and the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at a second point $Q$. Prove that
$$
MP = MQ.
$$

negatives.text: In an acute triangle the feet of altitudes drawn from vertices $A$ and $B$ are $D$ and $E$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $AB$. Line $CM$ intersects the circumcircle of $CDE$ again in point $P$ and the circumcircle of $CAB$ again in point $Q$. Prove that $$ |MP| < |MQ|. $$

positive_text: In right triangle $ABC$ with right angle at $C$, let $D$ be a point on $AB$ (distinct from $B$) such that triangle $CBD$ is isosceles with $|CB| = |CD|$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ACD$. Suppose that $OD$ intersects $CB$ at $P$ and the line through $O$ perpendicular to $AB$ intersects ray $CD$ at $Q$. If points $A$, $C$, $P$, $Q$ lie on a circle, does it follow that quadrilateral $ACPQ$ is a square?

negatives.text: Let $D$ be the point different from $B$ on the hypotenuse $AB$ of a right triangle $ABC$ such that $|CB| = |CD|$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ACD$. Rays $OD$ and $CB$ intersect at point $P$, and the line through point $O$ perpendicular to side $AC$ and ray $CD$ intersect at point $Q$. Points $A$, $C$, $P$, $Q$ are concyclic. Does this imply that $ACPQ$ is a square?

Let $D$ be the point different from $B$ on the hypotenuse $AB$ of a right triangle $ABC$ such that $|CB| = |CD|$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ACD$. Rays $OD$ and $CB$ intersect at point $P$, and the line through point $O$ perpendicular to side $AB$ and ray $CD$ intersect at point $Q$. Points $A$, $C$, $P$, $Q$ are concyclic. Does this imply that $ACPQ$ is a rectangle?

Let $D$ be the point different from $B$ on the hypotenuse $AB$ of a right triangle $ABC$ such that $|CB| = |CD|$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ACD$. Rays $OD$ and $CB$ intersect at point $P$, and the line through point $O$ perpendicular to side $AB$ and ray $CD$ intersect at point $Q$. Points $A$, $C$, $P$, $Q$ are concyclic. Does this imply that $ACPQ$ is a rhombus?

positive_text:
Define a sequence $(b_k)_{k=m}^n$ as *perfect* if:
1. There exists a base $a > 1$ such that $b_k = a^k + 1$ for all $k$ in the range $m$ to $n$;
2. Each term $b_k$ is a power of a prime number, i.e., $b_k = q^t$ for some prime $q$ and integer $t \geq 0$.
Show that for sufficiently large $n - m$, no such sequence exists, and identify all perfect sequences with the greatest number of terms.

negatives.text:
Call a tuple $(b_m, b_{m+1}, \dots, b_n)$ of integers *perfect* if both following conditions are fulfilled:
1. There exists an integer $a > 1$ such that $b_k = a^k - 1$ for all $k = m, m+1, \dots, n$;
2. For all $k = m, m+1, \dots, n$, there exists a prime number $q$ and a non-negative integer $t$ such that $b_k = q^t$.
Prove that if $n - m$ is large enough then there is no perfect tuples, and find all perfect tuples with the maximal number of components.

Call a tuple $(b_m, b_{m+1}, \dots, b_n)$ of integers *perfect* if both following conditions are fulfilled:
1. There exists an integer $a > 1$ such that $b_k = a^k + 1$ for all $k = m, m+1, \dots, n$;
2. For all $k = m, m+1, \dots, n$, there exists a prime number $q$ and a non-negative integer $t$ such that $b_k = q^t + 1$.
Prove that if $n - m$ is large enough then there is no perfect tuples, and find all perfect tuples with the maximal number of components.

Call a tuple $(b_m, b_{m+1}, \dots, b_n)$ of integers *perfect* if both following conditions are fulfilled:
1. There exists an integer $a > 1$ such that $b_k = a^k + 1$ for all $k = m, m+1, \dots, n$;
2. For all $k = m, m+1, \dots, n$, there exists a prime number $q$ and a non-negative integer $t$ such that $b_k = q^t$ and $b_k > 100$.
Prove that if $n - m$ is large enough then there is no perfect tuples, and find all perfect tuples with the maximal number of components.

positive_text: \text{Determine all positive real values of } x, y, z, w \text{ satisfying} \begin{cases} x + \frac{1}{x} = 2 + w, \\ y + \frac{1}{y} = 2 + w, \\ z + \frac{1}{z} = 2 - w, \\ y + \frac{1}{z} = 2 - w. \end{cases}

negatives.text:
Find all positive real solutions of the system of equations
$$x + \frac{1}{x} - w = 2,$$
$$y + \frac{1}{y} - w = 2,$$
$$z + \frac{1}{z} + w = 2,$$
$$y + \frac{1}{z} - w = 2.$$

Find all positive real solutions of the system of equations
$$x + \frac{1}{x} - w = 2,$$
$$y + \frac{1}{y} - w = 2,$$
$$z + \frac{1}{z^2} + w = 2,$$
$$y + \frac{1}{z} + w = 2.$$

Find all positive real solutions of the system of equations
$$x + \frac{1}{x} - w = 2,$$
$$y + \frac{1}{y} - w = 2,$$
$$z + \frac{1}{z} + w = 2,$$
$$y + \frac{1}{z} + w = 3.$$

positive_text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$ be positive integers. Define
$$ u = (a+b)(a+c)(a+d)(b+c)(b+d)(c+d) $$
and
$$ v = ab + ac + ad + bc + bd + cd. $$
Show that $3$ divides $uv$.

negatives.text:
Given positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ and
$$ (a+b)(a+c)(a+d)(b+c)(b+d)(c+d) = u, $$
$$ ab - ac + ad + bc - bd + cd = v, $$
prove that the product $uv$ is divisible by 3.

Given positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ and
$$ (a+b)(a+c)(a+d)(b+c)(b+d)(c+d) = u, $$
$$ ab + ac + ad + bc + bd + cd = v, $$
prove that the product $uv$ is divisible by 5.

Given positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ and
$$ (a+b)(a+c)(a+d)(b+c)(b+d)(c+d) = u, $$
$$ ab + ac + ad + bc + bd + cd = v, $$
prove that the product $u + v$ is divisible by 3.

positive_text: Given a unit circle, distribute $n$ points on or within it so that the smallest distance between any pair of points is maximized. Let this maximal minimal distance be $d_n$. Does the inequality $d_{n+1} < d_n$ hold for all integers $n \ge 2$?

negatives.text: Inside a square of side length $1$ (or on the boundary), one marks $n$ points in such a way that the minimal distance between two marked points is as large as possible. Let $d_n$ be this distance between the two closest points. Is it true that $d_{n+1} < d_n$ for every natural number $n \ge 2$?

Inside a circle of radius $1$ (or on the circumference), one marks $n$ points in such a way that the minimal distance between two marked points is as large as possible. Let $d_n$ be this distance between the two closest points. Is it true that $d_{n+1} > d_n$ for every natural number $n \ge 2$?

positive_text: Determine the number of integer triples $(x, y, z)$ with $0 \le x, y, z \le 36$ such that $|x - y| = |y - z|$.

negatives.text: Find the number of solutions of the equation $|a + b| = |b - c|$ in integers from $0$ to $36$.
Find the number of solutions of the equation $|a - b^2| = |b - c|$ in integers from $0$ to $36$.
Find the number of solutions of the inequality $|a - b| \geq |b - c|$ in integers from $0$ to $36$.

positive_text: Kati and Peeter play a game. Kati first writes a number $a > 2016$ on the board. Then Peeter generates new numbers by repeatedly writing $2016b + 1$, where $b$ is the largest number already on the board. Peeter wins if any of these numbers is divisible by $2017$. Kati wins otherwise. Determine if Kati can prevent Peeter from winning, and if so, find the smallest such $a$.

negatives.text: Kati and Peeter play the following game. First, Kati writes a positive integer $a > 2016$ on the blackboard. Then Peeter starts to write more numbers on the blackboard, adding at each step the number $2016b - 1$ where $b$ is the biggest number on the blackboard. Peeter wins if at some point he writes a number divisible by $2017$. Otherwise Kati wins. Can Kati win, and if yes, what is the smallest number $a$ she can write to win?

Kati and Peeter play the following game. First, Kati writes a positive integer $a > 2016$ on the blackboard. Then Peeter starts to write more numbers on the blackboard, adding at each step the number $2016b + 1$ where $b$ is the biggest number on the blackboard. Peeter wins if at some point he writes a number divisible by $2016$. Otherwise Kati wins. Can Kati win, and if yes, what is the smallest number $a$ she can write to win?

Kati and Peeter play the following game. First, Kati writes a positive integer $a > 2016$ on the blackboard. Then Peeter starts to write more numbers on the blackboard, adding at each step the number $2016b + 1$ where $b$ is the smallest number on the blackboard. Peeter wins if at some point he writes a number divisible by $2017$. Otherwise Kati wins. Can Kati win, and if yes, what is the smallest number $a$ she can write to win?

positive_text: \text{Find all real solutions to the system } x^3 + y = 4z, \ x + y^3 = z, \ xy = -1

negatives.text: Solve the system $a^3 + b = -4c$, $a + b^3 = c$, $ab = -1$
Solve the system $a^3 + b = 4c$, $a + b^3 = c$, $ab = 1$
Solve the system $a^2 + b = 4c$, $a + b^3 = c$, $ab = -1$

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, suppose $AB - BC = \frac{1}{2} AC$. Construct two semicircles with diameters $AB$ and $BC$ outside triangle $ABC$. If $X$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to the common tangent of the semicircles, determine the measure of $\angle CAX$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = \frac{AC}{2} - BC$. Consider the two semicircles outside the triangle with diameters $AB$ and $BC$. Let $X$ be the orthogonal projection of $A$ onto the common tangent line of those semicircles. Find $\angle CAX$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = \frac{AC^2}{2} + BC$. Consider the two semicircles outside the triangle with diameters $AB$ and $BC$. Let $X$ be the orthogonal projection of $A$ onto the common tangent line of those semicircles. Find $\angle CAX$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = \frac{AC}{2} + 2BC$. Consider the two semicircles outside the triangle with diameters $AB$ and $BC$. Let $X$ be the orthogonal projection of $A$ onto the common tangent line of those semicircles. Find $\angle CAX$.

positive_text: Let $A$ be the vertex of an acute angle of measure $\alpha$ in the plane. Choose points $B_0$ and $B_1$ on opposite sides of the angle so that $\angle AB_0B_1 = \beta$. For any $n \geq 2$, define $B_n$ on the side $AB_{n-2}$ such that $B_n \neq B_{n-2}$ and the length $B_{n-1}B_n$ is equal to $B_{n-2}B_{n-1}$. Show that the sequence $\{B_n\}$ must terminate after finitely many steps and find the maximal index $n$ (depending on $\alpha$ and $\beta$) for which $B_n$ is defined.

negatives.text: An acute angle with vertex $A$ and size $\alpha$ is given on a plane. Points $B_0$ and $B_1$ are chosen on different sides of the angle in such a way that $\angle AB_0B_1 = \beta$. Whenever points $B_0, B_1, \dots, B_{n-1}$ are defined, the next point $B_n$ on side $AB_{n-2}$ is allowed to be defined in such a way that $B_n \neq B_{n-2}$ and $B_{n-1}B_n = B_{n-2}B_{n-1}^2$. Prove that this process cannot last infinitely and determine the largest index $n$ (depending on $\alpha$ and $\beta$) for which $B_n$ can be defined.

An acute angle with vertex $A$ and size $\alpha$ is given on a plane. Points $B_0$ and $B_1$ are chosen on different sides of the angle in such a way that $\angle AB_0B_1 = \beta$. Whenever points $B_0, B_1, \dots, B_{n-1}$ are defined, the next point $B_n$ on side $AB_{n-2}$ is allowed to be defined in such a way that $B_n \neq B_{n-2}$ and $B_{n-1}B_n = B_{n-2}B_{n-1}$, provided $\alpha > \beta + \pi/2$. Prove that this process cannot last infinitely and determine the largest index $n$ (depending on $\alpha$ and $\beta$) for which $B_n$ can be defined.

positive_text:
Show that for all $ a > 0 $, the inequality
$$
(a+1)(a+2)(a+5) \ge 36a
$$
holds true.

negatives.text: Prove that every positive real number satisfies $$(x+1)(x+2)(x+5) \le 36x.$$
Prove that every positive real number satisfies $$(x+1)(x+2)(x+5) \ge 36x^2.$$
Prove that every positive real number satisfies $$\left(x^2+1\right)\left(x^2+2\right)\left(x^2+5\right) \ge 36x^2.$$

positive_text:
Let triangle $ABC$ be acute, and suppose that $BE$ is the altitude from $B$ to $AC$. Let $P$ lie on $AB$ such that $AP = AE$, and define $N$ such that $BCEN$ forms a parallelogram. Suppose the area of triangle $AEP$ equals the area of triangle $BNP$, and let $Q$ be the intersection of $NE$ and $AB$.

a) Prove that the line segment $PQ$ is intersected by the median from $C$ in triangle $ABC$.

b) Prove that the angle bisector of $\angle A$, the altitude from $B$, and the median from $C$ are concurrent in triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text:
Let $BE$ be an altitude of an acute triangle $ABC$ and let $P$ be the point on side $AB$ such that $AP = EB$. Let $N$ be the point for which $BCEN$ is a parallelogram. The areas of the triangles $AEP$ and $BNP$ are equal. Lines $NE$ and $AB$ intersect at $Q$.

a) Prove that the median of triangle $ABC$ drawn from the vertex $C$ intersects the line segment $PQ$.

b) Prove that in the triangle $ABC$, the bisector of the angle $A$, the altitude drawn from the vertex $B$ and the median drawn from the vertex $C$ meet in one point.

Let $BE$ be an altitude of an acute triangle $ABC$ and let $P$ be the point on side $AB$ such that $AP = AE$. Let $N$ be the point for which $BCEN$ is a parallelogram. The areas of the triangles $AEP$ and $BNP$ are not equal. Lines $NE$ and $AB$ intersect at $Q$.

a) Prove that the median of triangle $ABC$ drawn from the vertex $C$ intersects the line segment $PQ$.

b) Prove that in the triangle $ABC$, the bisector of the angle $A$, the altitude drawn from the vertex $B$ and the median drawn from the vertex $C$ meet in one point.

positive_text:
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers, $a \ge b$. A $1 \times a$ board is subdivided into $a$ unit cells, and there is an unlimited supply of $1 \times b$ stickers. A player places a sticker on the board in a move by covering $b$ adjacent cells, with at least one cell not previously covered. Players alternate, and the one who cannot play a valid move loses.

a) Prove that if $a$ and $b$ have the same parity, the first player can always win.

b) Is it necessarily the case that if $a$ and $b$ have opposite parity, the second player can always win?

negatives.text:
Let $n$ and $m$ be positive integers, $n \ge m$. There is a game board of size $1 \times n$ divided into $n$ unit squares and an unlimited supply of sticky tapes of size $1 \times m$. On each move, any player adds a tape covering $m$ consecutive unit squares on the board precisely, all of which are not yet covered by any tape. Two players move alternately and the one who can make no move loses.
a) Prove that if $n$ and $m$ are of equal parity then the first player can win regardless of how the opponent plays.
b) Is it true that, whenever $n$ and $m$ are of different parity, the second player can win regardless of how the first player plays?

Let $n$ and $m$ be positive integers, $n \ge m$. There is a game board of size $1 \times n$ divided into $n$ unit squares and an unlimited supply of sticky tapes of size $1 \times m$. On each move, any player adds a tape covering $m$ consecutive unit squares on the board precisely, at least one of which is not yet covered by any tape. Two players move alternately and the one who can make no move wins.
a) Prove that if $n$ and $m$ are of equal parity then the first player can win regardless of how the opponent plays.
b) Is it true that, whenever $n$ and $m$ are of different parity, the second player can win regardless of how the first player plays?

Let $n$ and $m$ be positive integers, $n \ge m$. There is a game board of size $1 \times n$ divided into $n$ unit squares and an unlimited supply of sticky tapes of size $1 \times m$. On each move, any player adds a tape covering $m$ consecutive unit squares on the board precisely, at least one of which is not yet covered by any tape. Two players move alternately and the one who can make no move loses.
a) Prove that if $n$ and $m$ are of equal parity then the first player can win regardless of how the opponent plays.
b) Is it true that, whenever $n$ and $m$ are of equal parity, the second player can win regardless of how the first player plays?

positive_text: Suppose $\frac{a}{b}$ and $\frac{c}{d}$ are reduced fractions of two distinct positive rational numbers $u$ and $v$, and define the mediant as $x = \frac{a + c}{b + d}$. Show that for any fixed positive rational $x$ with $x \ne u$, there are infinitely many rational numbers $v$ for which $x$ is the mediant of $u$ and $v$.

negatives.text: The mediant of two rational numbers $u$ and $v$ is $x = \frac{a + c}{b + d}$, where $\frac{a}{b}$ and $\frac{c}{d}$ are the reduced fractions of $u$ and $v$ respectively. Prove that for any two distinct positive rational numbers $u$ and $x$, there exist only finitely many positive rational numbers $v$, such that $x$ is the mediant of $u$ and $v$.

The mediant of two rational numbers $u$ and $v$ is $x = \frac{a - c}{b - d}$, where $\frac{a}{b}$ and $\frac{c}{d}$ are the reduced fractions of $u$ and $v$ respectively. Prove that for any two distinct positive rational numbers $u$ and $x$, there exist infinitely many positive rational numbers $v$, such that $x$ is the mediant of $u$ and $v$.

The mediant of two rational numbers $u$ and $v$ is $x = \frac{a + c}{b + d}$, where $\frac{a}{b}$ and $\frac{c}{d}$ are the reduced fractions of $u$ and $v$ respectively. Prove that for any two distinct positive rational numbers $u$ and $x$, there exist infinitely many positive rational numbers $v$, such that $x$ is the mediant of $u$ and $v$ and $v < u$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with midpoints $D$, $E$, and $F$ of $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively. Let $M$ be the centroid of triangle $ABC$. Reflect $M$ over $D$, $E$, and $F$ to obtain points $X$, $Y$, and $Z$, respectively. Suppose that the lines $XZ$ and $YZ$ intersect $AB$ at points $K$ and $L$. Show that the lengths $AL$ and $BK$ are equal.

negatives.text: The midpoints of the sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ of triangle $ABC$ are $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. The reflections of centroid $M$ of $ABC$ around points $D$, $E$, and $F$ are $X$, $Y$, and $Z$, respectively. Segments $XY$ and $XZ$ intersect the side $AB$ in points $K$ and $L$, respectively. Prove that $AL = BK$.

The midpoints of the sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ of triangle $ABC$ are $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. The reflections of centroid $M$ of $ABC$ around points $D$, $E$, and $F$ are $X$, $Y$, and $Z$, respectively. Segments $XZ$ and $YZ$ intersect the side $AC$ in points $K$ and $L$, respectively. Prove that $AL = BK$.

positive_text: Suppose $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral with diagonals intersecting at point $M$. Given that $AB = 2$ mm, $BC = 5$ mm, $AM = 4$ mm, and the ratio $\frac{CD}{CM} = 0.6$, determine the value of $AD$.

negatives.text: Let $M$ be the intersection of the diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$. Find the length of $AD$, if it is known that $AB = 2$ mm, $BC = 5$ mm, $AM = 4$ mm, and $\frac{CD}{CM} = -0.6$.
Let $M$ be the intersection of the diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$. Find the length of $AD$, if it is known that $AB = 2$ mm, $BC = 5$ mm, $AM = 4$ mm, and $\frac{CD^2}{CM^2} = 0.6$.

Let $M$ be the intersection of the diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$. Find the length of $AD$, if it is known that $AB = 2$ mm, $BC = 5$ mm, $AM = 4$ mm, and $\frac{CD}{CM} = 0.6$, and $ABCD$ is a rectangle.

positive_text: Suppose we have distinct points $O$, $A$, $B$, $K_1$, $\ldots$, $K_n$, $L_1$, $\ldots$, $L_n$ in the plane, with no three collinear. The open segments $K_iL_i$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$ are red, while all other points are uncoloured. A *permissible path* from $O$ to $X$ is a polygonal chain from $O$ to $X$ that avoids all red segments. For example, when $n = 1$, with $K_1 = (-1; 0)$, $L_1 = (1; 0)$, $O = (0; -1)$, and $X = (0; 1)$, $OK_1X$ and $OL_1X$ are permissible paths, and no shorter ones exist. Determine the smallest positive integer $n$ such that it is possible for the first non-$O$ vertex in any minimal permissible path from $O$ to $A$ to be closer to $B$ than to $A$, and for the first non-$O$ vertex in any minimal permissible path from $O$ to $B$ to be closer to $A$ than to $B.

negatives.text: There are distinct points $O$, $A$, $B$, $K_1$, $\ldots$, $K_n$, $L_1$, $\ldots$, $L_n$ on a plane such that no three points are collinear. The open line segments $K_1L_1$, $\ldots$, $K_nL_n$ are coloured red, other points on the plane are left uncoloured. An *allowed path* from point $O$ to point $X$ is a polygonal chain with first and last vertices at points $O$ and $X$, containing no red points. Find the least positive integer $n$ such that it is possible that the first vertex that is not $O$ on any shortest possible allowed path from $O$ to $A$ is closer to $B$ than to $A$, and the first vertex that is not $O$ on any shortest possible allowed path from $O$ to $B$ is closer to $A$ than to $B, but the condition only needs to hold for one of the two paths.

There are distinct points $O$, $A$, $B$, $K_1$, $\ldots$, $K_n$, $L_1$, $\ldots$, $L_n$ on a plane such that no three points are collinear. The open line segments $K_1L_1$, $\ldots$, $K_nL_n$ are coloured red, other points on the plane are left uncoloured. An *allowed path* from point $O$ to point $X$ is a polygonal chain with first and last vertices at points $O$ and $X$, containing no red points. Find the least positive integer $n$ such that it is possible that the first vertex that is not $O$ on any shortest possible allowed path from $O$ to $A$ is closer to $B$ than to $A$, and the first vertex that is not $O$ on any shortest possible allowed path from $O$ to $B$ is closer to $A$ than to $B, and the first vertex on any allowed path from $O$ to $A$ is distinct from the first vertex on any allowed path from $O$ to $B$.

There are distinct points $O$, $A$, $B$, $K_1$, $\ldots$, $K_n$, $L_1$, $\ldots$, $L_n$ on a plane such that no three points are collinear. The open line segments $K_1L_1$, $\ldots$, $K_nL_n$ are coloured red, other points on the plane are left uncoloured. An *allowed path* from point $O$ to point $X$ is a polygonal chain with first and last vertices at points $O$ and $X$, containing no red points. Find the least positive integer $n$ such that it is possible that the first vertex that is not $O$ on any shortest possible allowed path from $O$ to $A$ is closer to $B$ than to $A$, and the first vertex that is not $O$ on any shortest possible allowed path from $O$ to $B$ is closer to $A$ than to $B, and the paths must be of equal length.

positive_text: Consider a polynomial $P(x)$ with coefficients from the set $\{-1, 0, 1\}$. Given an integer $n > 1$, determine the minimal number of non-zero terms that $P(x)$ can have if it is of degree $n$ and satisfies $P(k) \equiv 0 \pmod{n}$ for all integers $k$.

negatives.text: Let a simple polynomial function be a polynomial function $P(x)$ whose coefficients belong to the set $\{-1, 0, 1\}$. Let $n$ be a positive integer, $n > 1$. Find the smallest possible number of non-zero coefficients in a simple polynomial function of $n$th order whose values at all integral arguments are divisible by $n^2$.

Let a simple polynomial function be a polynomial function $P(x)$ whose coefficients belong to the set $\{-1, 0, 1\}$. Let $n$ be a positive integer, $n > 1$. Find the smallest possible number of non-zero coefficients in a simple polynomial function of $n$th order whose values at all integral arguments are congruent to $1$ modulo $n$.

positive_text: Let $n$ be an integer with $n \ge 3$. Consider a regular polygon with $n$ sides. Select a maximal collection of non-intersecting diagonals such that no two diagonals cross in the polygon's interior. Assign to each diagonal a label equal to the minimal number of edges between its endpoints along the polygon's boundary. Determine the largest possible total of all such labels.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer, $n \ge 3$. In a regular $n$-gon, one draws a maximal set of diagonals, no two of which intersect in the interior of the $n$-gon. Every diagonal is labelled with the number of sides of the $n$-gon between the endpoints of the diagonal along the longest path. Find the maximum value of the sum of the labels.

Let $n$ be a positive integer, $n \ge 3$. In a regular $n$-gon, one draws a maximal set of diagonals, no two of which intersect in the interior of the $n$-gon. Every diagonal is labelled with the product of the number of sides of the $n$-gon between the endpoints of the diagonal along the shortest path. Find the maximum value of the sum of the labels.

Let $n$ be a positive integer, $n \ge 3$. In a regular $n$-gon, one draws a maximal set of diagonals, no two of which intersect on the boundary of the $n$-gon. Every diagonal is labelled with the number of sides of the $n$-gon between the endpoints of the diagonal along the shortest path. Find the maximum value of the sum of the labels.

positive_text: Is there a smallest integer $n \ge 3$ such that three distinct diagonals of a regular $n$-gon intersect at a common point that is not a vertex and not the center of the polygon?

negatives.text: Does there exist an integer $n \ge 3$ such that all 3 diagonals of a regular $n$-gon intersect at one point that is neither a vertex nor the center of the $n$-gon? If yes then find the least such $n$.
Does there exist an integer $n \ge 3$ such that some 3 diagonals of a regular $n$-gon meet in one point that is either a vertex or the center of the $n$-gon? If yes then find the least such $n$.
Does there exist an integer $n \ge 3$ such that some 2 diagonals of a regular $n$-gon meet in one point that is neither a vertex nor the center of the $n$-gon? If yes then find the least such $n$.

positive_text: \text{a. In a convex quadrilateral } ABCD, \text{ suppose } AB > AD \text{ and } CB > CD. \text{ Must } \angle ABC \text{ be greater than } \angle CDA?\\\text{b. Repeat part a for a non-convex quadrilateral.}

negatives.text: \text{a. Given a convex quadrilateral } ABCD \text{ with } AD < AB \text{ and } CD > CB, \text{ is the internal angle at } B \text{ always less than the internal angle at } D?\\\text{b. The same question for a non-convex quadrilateral.}

\text{a. Given a convex quadrilateral } ABCD \text{ with } AD < AB \text{ and } CD < CB, \text{ is the external angle at } B \text{ always less than the external angle at } D?\\\text{b. The same question for a non-convex quadrilateral.}

\text{a. Given a convex quadrilateral } ABCD \text{ with } AD < AB \text{ and } CD < CB, \text{ is the internal angle at } B \text{ always greater than the internal angle at } D?\\\text{b. The same question for a non-convex quadrilateral.}

positive_text: Let $ABCDE$ be a regular pentagon and let $A$ be the center of a circle $c$ passing through $B$ and $E$. If the line $BC$ intersects $c$ again at $F$, and a point $G$ is selected on $c$ such that $FB = FG$ and $G \neq B$, show that the lines $AB$, $EF$, and $DG$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: A circle $c$ with center $A$ passes through the vertices $B$ and $E$ of a regular pentagon $ABCDE$. The line $BC$ intersects the circle $c$ the second time at point $F$. positive_text: Suppose we have a binary sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ with values in $\{0, 1\}$. It is given that in any block of $2021$ consecutive terms, neither $0$ nor $1$ appears fewer than $1010$ times. Does it follow that the sequence eventually becomes periodic, meaning that there exist $n, p > 0$ such that $a_{n+i} = a_{n+i+p}$ for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$?

negatives.text: Every term of the sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ is either $0$ or $1$. It is known that both $0$ and $1$ occur at most $1010$ times among every $2021$ consecutive terms of the sequence. May one be sure that the sequence is periodic from some place on, i.e., there exist positive integers $n$ and $p$ such that $a_{n+i} = a_{n+i+p}$ for every natural number $i$?

Every term of the sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ is either $0$ or $1$. It is known that both $0$ and $1$ occur at least $1010$ times among every $2020$ consecutive terms of the sequence. Every term of the sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ is either $0$ or $1$. It is known that at least one of $0$ or $1$ occurs at least $1010$ times among every $2021$ consecutive terms of the sequence. May one be sure that the sequence is periodic from some place on, i.e., there exist positive integers $n$ and $p$ such that $a_{n+i} = a_{n+i+p}$ for every natural number $i$?

positive_text: In a right triangle $ABC$ with hypotenuse $AB$, let $D$ be the point on $AB$ such that $CD$ is perpendicular to $AB$. Let the inradii of triangles $ABC$, $CAD$ and $CBD$ be denoted $r$, $r_1$ and $r_2$, respectively. Show that $CD = r + r_1 + r_2$.

positive_text: There are $n$ candidate lists participating in an election. Let $h_i$ represent the total votes for the $i$th list, and let $M$ be the number of available seats. Anna's method distributes mandates by repeatedly selecting the list with the highest value of $\frac{h_i}{a_i + 1}$, where $a_i$ is the current number of seats assigned to list $i$, and incrementing $a_i$ for the chosen list. Bert's method instead calculates the number of mandates for each list as $m_i = \left\lfloor \frac{\beta h_i M}{K} \right\rfloor$, where $K = h_1 + \dots + h_n$ and $\beta$ is a scaling factor ensuring $\sum m_i = M$. Prove that if $\beta$ exists, the final seat distribution under both Anna's and Bert's methods is identical.

negatives.text:
There are $n$ lists of candidates taking part in elections. Let $h_i$ be the total number of votes given for the candidates of the $i$th list. There are $M$ seats in the representative assembly.

Anna proposes the following system for delivering mandates: For each list, one computes a reference number $v_i = \frac{h_i}{a_i + 1}$ where $a_i$ is the number of mandates already given to the $i$th list (initially $a_i = 0$, i.e., the reference number of each list equals its number of votes). On every step ($M$ times in total), one chooses the list with the greatest reference number (if several lists share the first place, one of them is chosen randomly) and adds one mandate to this list, after which the reference number of this list is recomputed.

Bert's idea for delivering mandates is to multiply the number of votes of every list by $\frac{M}{K}$ where $K = h_1 + \dots + h_n$, whereby fractional results are rounded upwards. As rounding may cause some seats to be undelivered, he proposes multiplying all numbers of votes of the lists by some suitable coefficient $\beta$, so that the number of mandates given to the $i$th list would be $m_i = \lfloor \frac{\beta h_i M}{K} \rfloor$ where $m_1 + \dots + m_n = M$.

Prove that if such coefficient $\beta$ exists then Anna's and Bert's methods lead to the same distribution of mandates.

Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer. Consider an $n \times n$ grid with three hidden adversaries located at the top-right corner and its adjacent squares. In the $2 \times 2$ region at the diagonally opposite corner of the grid, a group of frogs is placed. Multiple frogs may occupy the same square.

On the frogs' turn, each one moves as a knight in two distinct directions: two squares vertically and one square horizontally. On the adversaries' turn, they collectively make up to 3 such knight moves, but in the opposite direction: two squares down and one to the left, or one down and two to the left. Frogs move first. If any frog lands on a square occupied by an adversary, it is eliminated.

Determine the minimum number of frogs required to guarantee that at least one reaches a position from which both of its potential moves exit the grid.

negatives.text:
Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer. In an $n \times n$ grid there are three invisible monsters: one in the upper right corner square and one in each of its neighboring squares. In a $2 \times 2$ area in the opposite corner of the grid some frogs are placed. A square may contain more than one frog.

The frogs and the monsters take turns making the following moves. On the frogs' turn, each frog makes a knight move, jumping either two squares up and one to the right or one square up and two to the right. On the monsters' turn, they may make up to a total of 3 knight moves, jumping either two squares down and one to the right or one square down and two to the right. The frogs start. If a frog and a monster ever land on the same square, the monster will eat the frog.

Find the least number of frogs needed to ensure that at least one frog could make it to a spot where both possible jumps would take it off the grid.
