positive_text:
Determine all positive integer solutions $(x, y, z)$ to the equation
$$5 \cdot z! - 3 \cdot x! = 4 \cdot y!.$$

negatives.text: Find all triples $(x, y, z)$ of positive integers, such that $$3 \cdot x! - 4 \cdot y! = 5 \cdot z!.$$
Find all triples $(x, y, z)$ of positive integers, such that $$3 \cdot x! + 4 \cdot y! = 5 \cdot z^2.$$

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle and let $AD$ be the altitude from $A$ to side $BC$, with $D$ lying on $BC$. Extending $AD$ beyond $D$, it meets the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ again at point $E$. Let $F$ be the midpoint of segment $CE$. Suppose that the circumcircles of triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$ intersect again at point $G$ (distinct from $E$). If $P$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to line $FG$, prove that $DP = DA$.

negatives.text: In an acute triangle $ABC$, the extension of the altitude $AD$ over $D$ intersects the circumcircle at $E$. The midpoint of $BE$ is $F$. The circumcircles of $ABC$ and $DEF$ intersect at $G \neq E$. The foot of the altitude drawn from $A$ to $FG$ is $P$. Prove that $DA = DP$.

In an acute triangle $ABC$, the extension of the altitude $AD$ over $D$ intersects the circumcircle at $E$. The midpoint of $CE$ is $F$. The circumcircles of $ABC$ and $DGF$ intersect at $E \neq G$. The foot of the altitude drawn from $A$ to $FG$ is $P$. Prove that $DA = DP$.

In an acute triangle $ABC$, the extension of the altitude $AD$ over $D$ intersects the circumcircle at $E$. The midpoint of $CE$ is $F$. The circumcircles of $ABC$ and $DEF$ intersect at $G \neq E$. The foot of the altitude drawn from $B$ to $FG$ is $P$. Prove that $DA = DP$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$. Let the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ meet $BC$ at point $D$, and let the internal angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ meet the perpendicular bisector of segment $AD$ at point $E$. Prove that the internal angle bisector of $\angle ACB$ is perpendicular to the segment $DE$.

negatives.text: In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$, the bisector of the angle $BAC$ intersects $BC$ at $D$. The bisector of the angle $ABC$ intersects the perpendicular bisector of $AD$ at $E$. Prove that the bisector of the angle $ACB$ is parallel to $DE$.

In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$, the bisector of the angle $BAC$ intersects $BC$ at $D$. The bisector of the angle $ABC$ intersects the perpendicular bisector of $AD$ at $E$. Prove that the bisector of the angle $ABC$ is perpendicular to $DE$.

In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$, the bisector of the angle $BAC$ intersects $BC$ at $D$. The bisector of the angle $ABC$ intersects the perpendicular bisector of $AD$ at $E$. Prove that the bisector of the angle $ACB$ is perpendicular to $EC$.

positive_text: Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer. Assign real values to the vertices of a regular $n$-gon such that adjacent vertices differ by at most $1$. Determine the smallest real number $C$ for which it is guaranteed that some adjacent pair has a difference of at most $C$.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 3$ be any natural number. A real number is written into every vertex of a regular $n$-gon in such a way that numbers in any two neighbouring vertices differ by at least $1$. Find the least non-negative real number $C$ such that, regardless of the choice of the numbers in the vertices, there exist two neighbouring vertices in which numbers differ by at most $C$.

Let $n \ge 3$ be any natural number. A real number is written into every vertex of a regular $n$-gon in such a way that numbers in any two neighbouring vertices differ by at most $1$. Find the least non-negative real number $C$ such that, regardless of the choice of the numbers in the vertices, there exist two vertices (not necessarily adjacent) in which numbers differ by at most $C$.

Let $n \ge 3$ be any natural number. A real number is written into every vertex of a regular $n$-gon in such a way that numbers in any two adjacent vertices differ by at most $1$. Find the least non-negative real number $C$ such that, regardless of the choice of the numbers in the vertices, there exist two adjacent vertices in which the absolute value of the sum of their numbers is at most $C$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, where $AB < BC$ and angle $B$ is obtuse, the incircle centered at $I$ touches $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at points $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. The line $AI$ meets $BC$ at $K$. Let the ray $IB$ intersect the circumcircle of triangle $KIF$ at point $P$ ($P \neq I$), and let the ray $IC$ intersect the circumcircle of triangle $KIE$ at point $Q$ ($Q \neq I$). Prove that the segment $DK$ is bisected by the line $PQ$.

negatives.text: A triangle $ABC$ with $AB > BC$ and an obtuse angle at vertex $B$ is given. The incircle of the triangle $ABC$ with incentre $I$ touches the sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ at points $D$, $E$ and $F$, respectively. The line $AI$ intersects the side $BC$ at point $K$. The ray $IB$ intersects the circumcircle of the triangle $KIF$ at point $P$ ($P \neq I$), whereas the ray $IC$ intersects the circumcircle of the triangle $KIE$ at point $Q$ ($Q \neq I$). Prove that the line $PQ$ bisects the line segment $DK$.

A triangle $ABC$ with $AB < BC$ and an acute angle at vertex $B$ is given. The incircle of the triangle $ABC$ with incentre $I$ touches the sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ at points $D$, $E$ and $F$, respectively. The line $AI$ intersects the side $BC$ at point $K$. The ray $IB$ intersects the circumcircle of the triangle $KIF$ at point $P$ ($P \neq I$), whereas the ray $IC$ intersects the circumcircle of the triangle $KIE$ at point $Q$ ($Q \neq I$). Prove that the line $PQ$ bisects the line segment $DK$.

A triangle $ABC$ with $AB < BC$ and an obtuse angle at vertex $B$ is given. The incircle of the triangle $ABC$ with incentre $I$ touches the sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ at points $D$, $E$ and $F$, respectively. The line $AI$ intersects the side $BC$ at point $K$. The ray $IB$ intersects the circumcircle of the triangle $KIF$ at point $P$ ($P \neq I$), whereas the ray $IC$ intersects the circumcircle of the triangle $KID$ at point $Q$ ($Q \neq I$). Prove that the line $PQ$ bisects the line segment $DK$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral where $\angle DAB = \angle BCD = 90^\circ$ and $\angle ABC > \angle CDA$. Points $Q$ and $R$ lie on segments $BC$ and $CD$, respectively, and the line $QR$ meets lines $AB$ and $AD$ at points $P$ and $S$. Suppose $PQ = RS$. If $M$ is the midpoint of $BD$ and $N$ is the midpoint of $QR$, show that $M, N, A$, and $C$ are concyclic.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $\angle DAB = \angle BCD = 90^\circ$ and $\angle ABC < \angle CDA$. Let $Q$ and $R$ be points on the segments $BC$ and $CD$, respectively, such that the line $QR$ intersects lines $AB$ and $AD$ at points $P$ and $S$, respectively. It is given that $PQ = RS$. Let the midpoint of $BD$ be $M$ and the midpoint of $QR$ be $N$. Prove that $M, N, A$ and $C$ lie on a circle.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $\angle DAB = 90^\circ$ and $\angle BCD = 180^\circ$. Let $Q$ and $R$ be points on the segments $BC$ and $CD$, respectively, such that the line $QR$ intersects lines $AB$ and $AD$ at points $P$ and $S$, respectively. It is given that $PQ = RS$. Let the midpoint of $BD$ be $M$ and the midpoint of $QR$ be $N$. Prove that $M, N, A$ and $C$ lie on a circle.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $\angle DAB = 90^\circ$ and $\angle BCD = 90^\circ$. Let $Q$ and $R$ be points on the segments $BC$ and $CD$, respectively, such that the line $QR$ intersects lines $AB$ and $AD$ at points $P$ and $S$, respectively. It is given that $PQ = 2RS$. Let the midpoint of $BD$ be $M$ and the midpoint of $QR$ be $N$. Prove that $M, N, A$ and $C$ lie on a circle.

positive_text:
Determine the minimal positive integer $ k $ such that there exists a partition of $ \mathbb{Z}_{>0} $ into $ k $ subsets and a mapping $ f: \mathbb{Z}_{>0} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{>0} $ satisfying:
(i) If $ m, n $ belong to the same subset, then $ f(m+n) = f(m) + f(n) $.
(ii) There exist $ m, n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} $ such that $ f(m+n) \neq f(m) + f(n) $.

negatives.text:
Find the smallest positive integer $ k $ for which there exist a colouring of the positive integers $ \mathbb{Z}_{>0} $ with $ k $ colours and a function $ f: \mathbb{Z}_{>0} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{>0} $ with the following two properties:
(i) For all positive integers $ m, n $ of the same colour, $ f(m+n) = f(m) + f(n) $.
(ii) There are positive integers $ m, n $ such that $ f(m+n) = f(m) + f(n) $.

Find the smallest positive integer $ k $ for which there exist a colouring of the positive integers $ \mathbb{Z}_{>0} $ with $ k $ colours and a function $ f: \mathbb{Z}_{>0} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{>0} $ with the following two properties:
(i) For all positive integers $ m, n $ of the same colour, $ f(m+n) = f(m) + f(n) $.
(ii) For all positive integers $ m, n $, $ f(m+n) \neq f(m) + f(n) $.

positive_text:
Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $d_{1}<d_{2}<\ldots<d_{n}$ be positive integers. In a set of $d_{n}+1$ individuals, a collection of pairwise matches is arranged. Each pair can meet at most once. Prove that there exists a configuration of matches such that:

i) Each individual participates in a number of matches equal to one of $d_{1}, d_{2}, \ldots, d_{n}$,

ii) For all $i$ such that $1 \leq i \leq n$, there is at least one individual who participates in exactly $d_{i}$ matches.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geq 1$ be an integer and let $t_{1}<t_{2}<\ldots<t_{n}$ be positive integers. In a group of $t_{n}$ people, some games of chess are played. Two people can play each other at most once. Prove that it is possible for the following conditions to hold at the same time:

i) The number of games played by each person is one of $t_{1}, t_{2}, \ldots, t_{n}$,

ii) For every $i$ with $1 \leq i \leq n$, there is someone who has played exactly $t_{i}$ games of chess.

Let $n \geq 1$ be an integer and let $t_{1}<t_{2}<\ldots<t_{n}$ be positive integers. In a group of $t_{n}+1$ people, some games of chess are played. Two people can play each other at most once. Prove that it is possible for the following conditions to hold at the same time:

i) The number of games played by each person is one of $t_{1}^2, t_{2}^2, \ldots, t_{n}^2$,

ii) For every $i$ with $1 \leq i \leq n$, there is someone who has played exactly $t_{i}^2$ games of chess.

Let $n \geq 1$ be an integer and let $t_{1}<t_{2}<\ldots<t_{n}$ be positive integers. In a group of $t_{n}+1$ people, some games of chess are played. Two people can play each other at most once. Prove that it is possible for the following conditions to hold at the same time:

i) The number of games played by each person is strictly greater than one of $t_{1}, t_{2}, \ldots, t_{n}$,

ii) For every $i$ with $1 \leq i \leq n$, there is someone who has played strictly greater than $t_{i}$ games of chess.

positive_text:
Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer. A sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ of positive integers is termed expensive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that
$$
\prod_{i=1}^{n} (a_{i}+a_{(i \bmod n)+1}) = 2^{2k-1}.
$$
a) Determine all integers $n \geq 2$ for which such a sequence exists.
b) Show that for any given positive integer $m$, there exists an integer $n \geq 2$ for which $m$ is part of an expensive sequence.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer. An $n$-tuple $(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n})$ of positive integers is expensive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that
$$
(a_{1}+a_{2})(a_{2}+a_{3}) \cdots (a_{n-1}+a_{n})(a_{n}+a_{1})=2^{2k}.
$$
a) Find all positive integers $n \geq 2$ for which there exists an expensive $n$-tuple.
b) Prove that for every positive integer $m$ there exists an integer $n \geq 2$ such that $m$ belongs to an expensive $n$-tuple.
There are exactly $n$ factors in the product on the left hand side.

Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer. An $n$-tuple $(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n})$ of positive integers is expensive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that
$$
(a_{1}-a_{2})(a_{2}-a_{3}) \cdots (a_{n-1}-a_{n})(a_{n}-a_{1})=2^{2k-1}.
$$
a) Find all positive integers $n \geq 2$ for which there exists an expensive $n$-tuple.
b) Prove that for every positive integer $m$ there exists an integer $n \geq 2$ such that $m$ belongs to an expensive $n$-tuple.
There are exactly $n$ factors in the product on the left hand side.

Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer. An $n$-tuple $(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n})$ of positive integers is expensive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that
$$
(a_{1}+a_{2})(a_{2}+a_{3}) \cdots (a_{n-1}+a_{n})(a_{n}+a_{1})=2^{2k-1} + 1.
$$
a) Find all positive integers $n \geq 2$ for which there exists an expensive $n$-tuple.
b) Prove that for every positive integer $m$ there exists an integer $n \geq 2$ such that $m$ belongs to an expensive $n$-tuple.
There are exactly $n$ factors in the product on the left hand side.

positive_text:
Consider an infinite set $V$ of nodes representing users on Mugbook, with a finite number of edges connecting each node to others (each node has finitely many neighbors), and every node has at least one neighbor. Edges are undirected.

Each node selects one of its neighbors as a 'primary link.' A node is a 1-primary link if it is selected by someone else. For $n > 1$, a node is an $n$-primary link if it is selected by a node that is an $(n-1)$-primary link. A node is considered influential if it is an $n$-primary link for all positive integers $n$.

a. Prove that every influential node is the primary link of an influential node.

b. Show that if the degree of each node is unbounded, it is possible for an influential node to not be the primary link of an influential node.

negatives.text:
There are infinitely many people registered on the social network Mugbook. Some pairs of (different) users are registered as friends, but each person has only finitely many friends. Every user has at least one friend. (Friendship is symmetric; that is, if $A$ is a friend of $B$, then $B$ is a friend of $A$.)

Each person is required to designate one of their friends as their best friend. If $A$ designates $B$ as her best friend, then (unfortunately) it does not follow that $B$ necessarily designates $A$ as her best friend. Someone designated as a best friend is called a 1-best friend. More generally, if $n>1$ is a positive integer, then a user is an $n$-best friend provided that they have been designated the best friend of someone who is an $(n-1)$-best friend. Someone who is a $k$-best friend for every positive integer $k$ is called popular.

a. Prove that every popular person is the best friend of a non-popular person.

b. Show that if people can have infinitely many friends, then it is possible that a popular person is not the best friend of a popular person.

Every user has at least one friend. (Friendship is symmetric; that is, if $A$ is a friend of $B$, then $B$ is a friend of $A$.)

Someone who is a $k$-best friend for every positive integer $k$ is called popular.

a. Prove that every popular person is the best friend of a person who is not a 2-best friend.

b. Show that if people can have infinitely many friends, then it is possible that a popular person is not the best friend of a popular person.
