Let $AP$ meet $BC$ at $D$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Also, let $E$ be the point such that $AE \perp AB$ and $BE \perp MP$. Prove that $AE = DE$.

positive_text: Let $n$ be an even integer greater than or equal to 4, and consider an $n \times n$ board with alternating black and white cells. Suppose $A$ and $B$ are non-border cells with opposite colours. Show that there exists a Hamiltonian path starting at $A$ and ending at $B$, traversing each cell exactly once.

negatives.text: There is an $n \times n$ chessboard where $n \ge 4$ is a positive even number. The cells of the chessboard are coloured black and white such that adjacent cells sharing a common side have different colours. Let $A$ and $B$ be two interior cells of the same colour. Prove that a chess piece can move from $A$ to $B$ by moving across adjacent cells such that every cell of the chessboard is passed through exactly once.

There is an $n \times n$ chessboard where $n \ge 4$ is a positive even number. The cells of the chessboard are coloured black and white such that adjacent cells sharing a common side have different colours. Let $A$ and $B$ be two interior cells of distinct colours. Prove that a chess piece can move from $A$ to $B$ by moving across adjacent cells such that every cell of the chessboard is passed through at most twice.

There is an $n \times n$ chessboard where $n \ge 4$ is a positive odd number. The cells of the chessboard are coloured black and white such that adjacent cells sharing a common side have different colours. Let $A$ and $B$ be two interior cells of distinct colours. Prove that a chess piece can move from $A$ to $B$ by moving across adjacent cells such that every cell of the chessboard is passed through exactly once.

positive_text:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with centroid $G$ and midpoint $M$ of $BC$. Choose a point $D$ on $GM$, and let a line through $D$ intersect $AB$ at $E$ and $AC$ at $F$ (with $E, F \ne A$). Prove that
$$
[BEGF] + [CFGE] \ge \frac{4}{9}[ABC].
$$
Determine the condition for equality.

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and let $G$ be the centroid of $\triangle ABC$. Let $D$ be a point on the segment $GM$. A straight line passing through $D$ meets the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$ respectively (with $E, F \ne A$). Show that
$$
[BEGF] + [CFGE] \ge \frac{2}{3}[ABC].
$$
When does the equality hold? (Here $[WXYZ]$ is the area of the polygon $WXYZ$, etc.)

Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and let $G$ be the centroid of $\triangle ABC$. Let $D$ be a point on the segment $GM$. A straight line passing through $D$ meets the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$ respectively (with $E, F \ne A$). Show that
$$
[BEGF] + [CFGE] \le \frac{4}{9}[ABC].
$$
When does the equality hold? (Here $[WXYZ]$ is the area of the polygon $WXYZ$, etc.)

Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and let $G$ be the centroid of $\triangle ABC$. Let $D$ be a point on the segment $GM$. A straight line passing through $D$ meets the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$ respectively (with $E, F \ne A$). Show that
$$
[BEGF] + [CFGE] \ge \frac{4}{9}[ABC] + 1.
$$
When does the equality hold? (Here $[WXYZ]$ is the area of the polygon $WXYZ$, etc.)

positive_text: Let $n$ be an integer and let $A$ be a set of $4n+2$ integers from $\{0, 1, 2, \dots, 5^n\}$. Show that there are three distinct elements $a, b, c$ in $A$ with $a < b < c$ satisfying $c - 3b + 2a > 0$.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be an integer, and let $A$ be a subset of $\{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots, 5^n\}$ consisting of $4n+2$ numbers. Prove that there exist $a, b, c \in A$ such that $a < b < c$ and $c + 2a < 3b$.
Let $n$ be an integer, and let $A$ be a subset of $\{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots, 5^n\}$ consisting of $4n+2$ numbers. Prove that there exist $a, b, c \in A$ such that $a < b < c$ and $c + 2a = 3b$.
Let $n$ be an integer, and let $A$ be a subset of $\{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots, 5^n\}$ consisting of $4n+2$ numbers. Prove that there exist $a, b, c \in A$ such that $a < b < c$ and $c + a > 3b$.

positive_text: \text{\textit{ABCD}} is a parallelogram with \angle B acute. A circle is tangent to sides \textit{CD}, \textit{DA}, and \textit{BC}. It intersects diagonal \textit{AC} at two points \textit{M} and \textit{N}, with \textit{M} closer to vertex \textit{A}. Given that \textit{AM} = 9, \textit{MN} = 16, and \textit{NC} = 2, compute the area of quadrilateral \textit{ABCD}.

negatives.text: \text{\textit{ABCD}} is a parallelogram with \angle B acute. A circle is tangent to \textit{BC}, \textit{CD} and \textit{DA}. The circle intersects \textit{AC} at \textit{M} and \textit{N}, where \textit{M} is closer to \textit{A} than \textit{N}. If \textit{AM} = 9, \textit{MN} = 16 and \textit{NC} = -2, find the area of \textit{ABCD}.

\text{\textit{ABCD}} is a parallelogram with \angle B acute. A circle is tangent to \textit{BC}, \textit{CD} and \textit{DA}. The circle intersects \textit{AC} at \textit{M} and \textit{N}, where \textit{M} is closer to \textit{A} than \textit{N}. If \textit{AM} = 9, \textit{MN} = 16 and \textit{NC} = 2, find the perimeter of \textit{ABCD}.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be such that $AB < AC$. The internal angle bisector of $\angle A$ intersects $BC$ at point $D$, and the external angle bisector of $\angle A$ intersects the extension of $BC$ beyond $B$ at point $E$. Given $EB = 2022$ and that $BD$ and $DC$ are positive integers, determine how many distinct values $BD$ can take.

negatives.text: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB < AC$. The internal bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $BC$ at $D$, while the external bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $BC$ produced at $E$. If $EC = 2022$ and the lengths of $BD$ and $DC$ are integers, how many possible lengths of $BD$ are there?

In $\triangle ABC$, $AB < AC$. The internal bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $BC$ at $D$, while the external bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $CB$ produced at $E$. If $EB = 2022$ and the lengths of $BD$ and $DC$ are integers, how many possible lengths of $BD$ are there such that $BD > DC$?

positive_text: Let $x^4 - 2022x^2 + 2023 = 0$ be an equation with roots $a^3$ and $b^3$. If $p = a^3 + 3a b^2$ and $q = b^3 + 3a^2 b$, find the value of $(p+q)^{\frac{1}{3}} + (p-q)^{\frac{1}{3}}$.

negatives.text: Let $a$ and $b$ be the two roots of the equation $x^{\frac{4}{3}} + 2022x^{\frac{2}{3}} + 2023 = 0$. If $p = a + 3a^{\frac{1}{3}}b^{\frac{2}{3}}$ and $q = b + 3a^{\frac{2}{3}}b^{\frac{1}{3}}$, find the value of $(p+q)^{\frac{1}{3}} + (p-q)^{\frac{1}{3}}$.

Let $a$ and $b$ be the two roots of the equation $x^{\frac{4}{3}} - 2022x^{\frac{2}{3}} + 2023 = 0$. If $p = a + 3a^{\frac{1}{3}}b^{\frac{2}{3}}$ and $q = b + 3a^{\frac{2}{3}}b^{\frac{1}{3}}$, find the value of $(p+q)^{\frac{1}{3}} - (p-q)^{\frac{1}{3}}$.

Let $a$ and $b$ be the two roots of the equation $x^{\frac{4}{3}} - 2022x^{\frac{2}{3}} + 2023 = 0$. If $p = a + 3a^{\frac{1}{3}}b^{\frac{2}{3}}$ and $q = b + 3a^{\frac{2}{3}}b^{\frac{1}{3}}$, find the value of $(p+q)^{\frac{1}{2}} + (p-q)^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

positive_text: Let $Q(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Define a sequence $\{b_n\}$ recursively by $b_0 = 0$ and $b_n = Q(b_{n-1})$ for all $n \ge 1$. Prove that if $b_m = 0$ for some positive integer $m$, then either $b_1 = 0$ or $b_2 = 0$.

negatives.text: Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Define a sequence $\{a_n\}$ by $a_0 = 0$ and $a_n = P(a_{n-1})$ for all $n \ge 1$. Prove that if there exists a positive integer $m$ for which $a_m = 0$, then $a_1 = 0$ and $a_2 = 0$.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Define a sequence $\{a_n\}$ by $a_0 = 0$ and $a_n = P(a_{n-1})$ for all $n \ge 1$. Prove that if there exists a positive integer $m$ for which $a_m = 0$, then $a_1 = 0$ or $a_3 = 0$.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Define a sequence $\{a_n\}$ by $a_0 = 0$ and $a_n = P(a_{n-1})$ for all $n \ge 1$. Prove that if there exists a positive integer $m$ for which $a_m = 0$, then $a_1 = 0$ or $a_2 = 1$.

positive_text: Given a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ with diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersecting at point $E$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on segment $AC$ in the order $A$, $E$, $Q$, $P$, $C$, with $BP$ bisecting $\angle ABC$ and $DQ$ bisecting $\angle ADC$. If $AE = 4$, $EQ = 2$ and $QP = 3$, compute the value of $PC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral and $E$ be the intersection of $AC$ and $BD$. $P$ and $Q$ are two points on $AC$ such that the points $A$, $E$, $Q$, $P$, $C$ lie on the same straight line in this order, and that $BP$ bisects $\angle ABC$ whereas $DQ$ bisects $\angle ADC$. If $AE = 4$, $EQ = -2$ and $QP = 3$, find the length of $PC$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral and $E$ be the intersection of $AC$ and $BD$. $P$ and $Q$ are two points on $AC$ such that the points $A$, $E$, $Q$, $P$, $C$ lie on the same straight line in this order, and that $BP$ bisects $\angle ABC$ whereas $DQ$ bisects $\angle ADC$. If $AE = 4$, $EQ = 2$ and $QP^2 = 3$, find the length of $PC$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral and $E$ be the intersection of $AC$ and $BD$. $P$ and $Q$ are two points on $AC$ such that the points $A$, $E$, $Q$, $P$, $C$ lie on the same straight line in this order, and that $BP$ bisects $\angle ABC$ whereas $DQ$ bisects $\angle ADC$. If $AE = 4$, $EQ = 2$ and $QP = 3$, find the length of $PC$ given that $PC < 1$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$. Let $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $E$. Points $F$ and $G$ lie on $AB$ and $CD$ respectively with $AF = 15$, $FB = 13$, $BE = 30$, $ED = 13$, $DG = 7.5$, and $GC = 6.5$. Suppose $P$ is a point such that $PF \perp AB$ and $PG \perp CD$. Determine the value of $\frac{PE}{PO}$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcentre $O$. Diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $E$. $F$ and $G$ are points on segments $AB$ and $CD$ respectively. Suppose $AF = 15$, $FB = 13$, $BE = 30$, $ED = 13$, $DG = 6.5$ and $GC = 7.5$. Let $P$ be a point such that $PF \perp AB$ and $PG \perp CD$. Find $\frac{PE}{PO}$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcentre $O$. Diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $E$. $F$ and $G$ are points on segments $AB$ and $CD$ respectively. Suppose $AF = 15$, $FB = 13$, $BE = 30$, $ED = 13$, $DG = 7.5$ and $GC = 6.5$. Let $P$ be a point such that $PF \perp AB$ and $PG \perp CD$. Find $\frac{PO}{PE}$.

positive_text: Suppose we have $n$ binary sequences of length 200 such that any two sequences have Hamming distance at least 101. Is it possible for $n$ to be at least 101?

negatives.text: There is a set of $n$ 01-sequences of length 200. Every pair of 01-sequences differ at most at 101 positions. (For example, the two 01-sequences of length 6, 111100 and 010001 differ at four positions, 1st, 3rd, 4th and 6th positions, counting from the left.) Is it possible that $n \ge 101$?

There is a set of $n$ 01-sequences of length 200. Every pair of 01-sequences differ at least at 100 positions. (For example, the two 01-sequences of length 6, 111100 and 010001 differ at four positions, 1st, 3rd, 4th and 6th positions, counting from the left.) Is it possible that $n \ge 101$?

positive_text: Given a convex polygon $P = V_1V_2\dots V_n$ with $n \ge 4$, define $g(k)$ as the largest angle $\angle V_kV_jV_{k+1}$, where $V_j$ is any vertex distinct from $V_k$ and $V_{k+1}$ (with $V_{n+1} = V_1$). Determine the minimum possible value of $g(1) + g(2) + \dots + g(n)$ over all such polygons for a fixed $n$.

negatives.text: Let $A_1A_2\dots A_n$ be a convex polygon where $n \ge 4$. For each $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$, let $f(i)$ be the minimum of the angles $\angle A_iA_jA_{i+1}$ where $A_j$ can be any vertex different from $A_i$ and $A_{i+1}$ (with $A_{n+1} = A_1$). For each $n$, find the smallest possible value of $f(1) + f(2) + \dots + f(n)$.

Let $A_1A_2\dots A_n$ be a convex polygon where $n \ge 4$. For each $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$, let $f(i)$ be the maximum of the angles $\angle A_iA_jA_{i+1}$ where $A_j$ can be any vertex different from $A_i$ and $A_{i+1}$ (with $A_{n+1} = A_1$). For each $n$, find the largest possible value of $f(1) + f(2) + \dots + f(n)$.

positive_text: In an acute triangle $ABC$, let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AM$. Let the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ meet $BC$ again at a point $E$ distinct from $B$. If a point $F$ lies on segment $AE$ such that $FB = FC$, show that $F$ is the midpoint of $AE$.

negatives.text: Let $M$ be the midpoint of the side $BC$ of an acute $\triangle ABC$, and let $D$ be the foot of perpendicular from $C$ to $AM$. The circumcircle of $\triangle ABD$ intersects the side $BC$ again at $E \neq B$. Suppose $F$ is a point on the segment $AE$ such that $FB = FD$. Prove that $F$ is the midpoint of $AE$.

Let $M$ be the midpoint of the side $BC$ of an acute $\triangle ABC$, and let $D$ be the foot of perpendicular from $C$ to $AM$. The circumcircle of $\triangle ABD$ intersects the side $BC$ again at $E \neq B$. Suppose $F$ is a point on the segment $AE$ such that $FB = FC$ and $\angle FBC = \angle FCB$. Prove that $F$ is the midpoint of $AE$.

Let $M$ be the midpoint of the side $BC$ of an acute $\triangle ABC$, and let $D$ be the foot of perpendicular from $C$ to $AM$. The circumcircle of $\triangle ABD$ intersects the side $BC$ again at $E \neq B$. Suppose $F$ is a point on the segment $AE$ such that $FB = FC$. Prove that $F$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$.

positive_text: \text{\textit{ABCD}} is an isosceles trapezium with \text{\textit{AD}} \parallel \text{\textit{BC}}, \text{\textit{AD}} > \text{\textit{BC}}, and non-parallel sides equal. A point \text{\textit{P}} satisfies \text{\textit{PA}} = 1, \text{\textit{PB}} = 2, \text{\textit{PC}} = 3, \text{\textit{PD}} = 4. Determine the ratio \text{\textit{AD}} : \text{\textit{BC}}.

negatives.text: \text{\textit{ABCD}} \text{ is a trapezium with } AD \parallel BC, AD < BC \text{ and } AB = CD. P \text{ is a point on the plane whose distance from } A, B, C, D \text{ are } 1, 2, 3, 4 \text{ respectively. Find } AD : BC.

\text{\textit{ABCD}} \text{ is a trapezium with } AD \parallel BC, AD > BC \text{ and } AB \ne CD. P \text{ is a point on the plane whose distance from } A, B, C, D \text{ are } 1, 2, 3, 4 \text{ respectively. Find } AD : BC.

\text{\textit{ABCD}} \text{ is a trapezium with } AD \parallel BC, AD > BC \text{ and } AB = CD. P \text{ is a point on the plane whose distance from } A, B, C, D \text{ are } 1, 2, 3, 3 \text{ respectively. Find } AD : BC.

positive_text: \text{Let } ABCD \text{ be a square and } P \text{ a point inside it. Given that } \angle APD + \angle BPC = 180^\circ \text{ and } \angle BPC < 90^\circ, \text{ with } PB = 3 \text{ and } PC = 4, \text{ determine the length of } BC.

negatives.text: \text{\$ABCD\$ is a square. \$P\$ is a point inside \$ABCD\$ such that \$\angle APD + \angle BPC = 180^\circ\$ and \$\angle BPC\$ is acute. If \$PB = 3\$ and \$PC = 4\$, find \$AC\$.}

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, $\angle BAC = 75^\circ$ and $\angle C = 45^\circ$. If point $T$ lies on the extension of $BC$ such that $CT = BC$, and $M$ is the midpoint of $AT$, determine the measure of $\angle BMC$.

negatives.text: Given $\triangle ABC$, $\angle CAB = 75^\circ$ and $\angle ACB = 45^\circ$. $BC$ is extended to $T$ so that $BC = CT$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the segment $BT$. Find $\angle BMC$.
Given $\triangle ABC$, $\angle CAB = 75^\circ$ and $\angle ACB = 45^\circ$. $BC$ is extended to $T$ so that $BC = CT$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the segment $AT$. Find $\angle MCT$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, $I$ the incenter of $\triangle ABC$, and $D$ the projection of $I$ onto $BC$. Let $E$ be the second intersection of the line through $A$ perpendicular to $BC$ with the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$. If $\angle MID = \angle ACB - \angle ABC$, show that $\triangle DEI$ is isosceles with $DE = DI$.

negatives.text: Given an acute $\triangle ABC$ with $AB > AC$, let $M$ be the midpoint of the side $BC$. Let $I$ be the incentre of $\triangle ABC$, and let $D$ be the foot of perpendicular from $I$ to $BC$. The line passing through $A$ and perpendicular to $BC$ meets the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ again at $E \neq A$. Suppose $\angle MID = \angle ABC - \angle ACB$. Prove that $DE = DI$.

Given an acute $\triangle ABC$ with $AB > AC$, let $M$ be the midpoint of the side $BC$. Let $I$ be the incentre of $\triangle ABC$, and let $D$ be the foot of perpendicular from $I$ to $BC$. The line passing through $A$ and perpendicular to $BC$ meets the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ again at $E \neq A$. Suppose $\angle MID = \angle ACB + \angle ABC$. Prove that $DE = DI$.

Given an acute $\triangle ABC$ with $AB > AC$, let $M$ be the midpoint of the side $BC$. Let $I$ be the incentre of $\triangle ABC$, and let $D$ be the foot of perpendicular from $I$ to $BC$. The line passing through $A$ and perpendicular to $BC$ meets the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ again at $E \neq A$. Suppose $\angle MID = 2(\angle ACB - \angle ABC)$. Prove that $DE = DI$.

positive_text: Let $a, b, c$ be positive integers, with $b$ and $c$ not exceeding $2023$, such that $a - b = 2c$ and $(a^2 + c^2)(b^2 + c^2)$ is divisible by $17^2$. How many ordered triples $(a, b, c)$ satisfy these conditions?

In triangle $ABC$, with $AB < AC$, let $AD$ be the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$, where $D$ lies on $BC$. Let $\Gamma$ be a circle through $A$ and $D$ that is tangent to $BC$ at $D$. This circle intersects $AB$ again at $E$ (other than $A$). Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of $\triangle BDE$, and let the tangent to $\omega$ at $D$ intersect $\Gamma$ again at $F$. Let $P$ be the intersection of $EF$ and $AC$. Show that $PD$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

negatives.text: Given $\triangle ABC$ with $AB < AC$, let $AD$ be the bisector of $\angle BAC$ with $D$ on the side $BC$. Let $\Gamma$ be a circle passing through $A$ and $D$ which is tangent to $BC$ at $D$. Suppose $\Gamma$ cuts the side $AB$ again at $E \neq A$. The tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle CDE$ at $D$ intersects $\Gamma$ again at $F \neq D$. Let $P$ be the intersection point of the segments $EF$ and $AC$. Prove that $PD$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

Given $\triangle ABC$ with $AB < AC$, let $AD$ be the bisector of $\angle BAC$ with $D$ on the side $BC$. Let $\Gamma$ be a circle passing through $A$ and $D$ which is tangent to $BC$ at $D$. Suppose $\Gamma$ cuts the side $AB$ again at $E \neq A$. The tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle BDE$ at $E$ intersects $\Gamma$ again at $F \neq D$. Let $P$ be the intersection point of the segments $EF$ and $AC$. Prove that $PD$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

Given $\triangle ABC$ with $AB < AC$, let $AD$ be the bisector of $\angle BAC$ with $D$ on the side $BC$. Let $\Gamma$ be a circle passing through $A$ and $D$ which is tangent to $BC$ at $D$. Suppose $\Gamma$ cuts the side $AB$ again at $E \neq A$. The tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle BDE$ at $D$ intersects $\Gamma$ again at $F \neq D$. Let $P$ be the intersection point of the segments $EF$ and $AB$. Prove that $PD$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle, and let a point $P$ lie within it satisfying $AP = 15$ and $BP = 8$. Determine the maximum total area of triangles $ABP$ and $BCP$.

negatives.text: A point $P$ lies inside an equilateral triangle $ABC$ such that $AP = 15$ and $BP = 8$. Find the minimum possible value of the sum of areas of triangles $ABP$ and $BCP$.
A point $P$ lies inside an equilateral triangle $ABC$ such that $AP^2 = 15$ and $BP^2 = 8$. Find the maximum possible value of the sum of areas of triangles $ABP$ and $BCP$.
A point $P$ lies inside an equilateral triangle $ABC$ such that $AP = 15$ and $BP = 8$. Find the maximum possible value of the product of areas of triangles $ABP$ and $BCP$.

positive_text: In convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, suppose $AB = 5$, $AD = 17$, and $CD = 6$. If the internal angle bisectors of $\angle DAB$ and $\angle CDA$ intersect at the center of segment $BC$, determine the area of quadrilateral $ABCD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = 5$, $AD = 17$, and $CD = 6$. If the angle bisectors of $\angle BAD$ and $\angle ADC$ intersect at the midpoint of $AC$, find the area of $ABCD$.
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = 5$, $AD = 17$, and $CD = 6$. If the angle bisectors of $\angle BCD$ and $\angle ADC$ intersect at the midpoint of $BC$, find the area of $ABCD$.
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = 5$, $AD = 17$, and $CD = 6$. If the angle bisectors of $\angle BAD$ and $\angle ADC$ intersect at the midpoint of $BC$, find the perimeter of $ABCD$.

positive_text: Determine the number of real values of $x$ that satisfy the equation $\frac{\ln x}{\ln 3} = 3 \sin(3\pi x)$.

negatives.text: How many solutions are there to the equation $\log_3 x = -3 \sin(3\pi x)$?
How many solutions are there to the equation $\log_3 x = 3 \sin(\pi x)$?
How many solutions are there to the equation $\log_3 x = 3 |\sin(3\pi x)|$?

positive_text:
Let $\{x_n\}$ be a sequence of real numbers with initial value $x_0$ and recurrence relation
$$
x_{n+1} = \lfloor x_n \rfloor \cdot (x_n - \lfloor x_n \rfloor) \quad \text{for all } n \geq 0.
$$
Show that $x_n = x_{n+2}$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

negatives.text:
A sequence of real numbers $a_{0}, a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ is defined by the formula
$$
a_{i+1}=\left\lfloor a_{i}\right\rfloor +\left\langle a_{i}\right\rangle \quad \text{ for } \quad i \geq 0
$$
here $a_{0}$ is an arbitrary real number, $\left\lfloor a_{i}\right\rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer not exceeding $a_{i}$, and $\left\langle a_{i}\right\rangle=a_{i}-\left\lfloor a_{i}\right\rfloor$. Prove that $a_{i}=a_{i+2}$ for $i$ sufficiently large.

A sequence of real numbers $a_{0}, a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ is defined by the formula
$$
a_{i+1}=\left\lceil a_{i}\right\rceil \cdot\left\langle a_{i}\right\rangle \quad \text{ for } \quad i \geq 0
$$
here $a_{0}$ is an arbitrary real number, $\left\lceil a_{i}\right\rceil$ denotes the least integer greater than or equal to $a_{i}$, and $\left\langle a_{i}\right\rangle=a_{i}-\left\lfloor a_{i}\right\rfloor$. Prove that $a_{i}=a_{i+2}$ for $i$ sufficiently large.

A sequence of real numbers $a_{0}, a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ is defined by the formula
$$
a_{i+1}=\left\lfloor a_{i}\right\rfloor \cdot\left\langle a_{i}\right\rangle^{2} \quad \text{ for } \quad i \geq 0
$$
here $a_{0}$ is an arbitrary real number, $\left\lfloor a_{i}\right\rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer not exceeding $a_{i}$, and $\left\langle a_{i}\right\rangle=a_{i}-\left\lfloor a_{i}\right\rfloor$. Prove that $a_{i}=a_{i+2}$ for $i$ sufficiently large.

positive_text:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$. Suppose a point $P$ lies inside triangle $ABC$ and satisfies
$$
\angle ABP + \angle ACP = \angle CBP + \angle BCP.
$$
Prove that $AP \geq AI$ and that equality occurs precisely when $P = I$.

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incentre $I$. A point $P$ in the interior of the triangle satisfies
$$
\angle PBA + \angle PCA = 2(\angle PBC + \angle PCB).
$$
Show that $AP \geq AI$ and that equality holds if and only if $P$ coincides with $I$.

positive_text:
Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with $AB \parallel CD$ and $AB > CD$. Let points $K$ and $L$ be on segments $AB$ and $CD$, respectively, such that $\frac{AK}{KB} = \frac{DL}{LC}$. Suppose there exist points $P$ and $Q$ on segment $KL$ with
$$
\angle APB = \angle BCD \quad \text{and} \quad \angle CQD = \angle ABC.
$$
Show that the four points $P$, $Q$, $B$, and $C$ lie on a circle.

negatives.text:
Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with parallel sides $AB > CD$. Points $K$ and $L$ lie on the line segments $AB$ and $CD$, respectively, so that $AK / KB = DL / LC$. Suppose that there are points $P$ and $Q$ on the line segment $KL$ satisfying
$$
\angle APB = \angle CDB \quad \text{and} \quad \angle CQD = \angle ABC.
$$
Prove that the points $P$, $Q$, $B$ and $C$ are concyclic.

Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with parallel sides $AB > CD$. Points $K$ and $L$ lie on the line segments $AB$ and $CD$, respectively, so that $AK / KB = DL / LC$. Suppose that there are points $P$ and $Q$ on the line segment $KL$ satisfying
$$
\angle APB = \angle BCD \quad \text{and} \quad \angle CQD = \angle BAC.
$$
Prove that the points $P$, $Q$, $B$ and $C$ are concyclic.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have $\angle C < \angle A < 90^\circ$, and let point $D$ lie on side $AC$ such that $BD = BA$. Suppose the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches $AB$ and $AC$ at points $K$ and $L$, respectively. Let $J$ be the incentre of triangle $BCD$. Prove that the line $KL$ cuts $AJ$ at its midpoint.

negatives.text: A point $D$ is chosen on the side $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$ with $\angle C < \angle A < 90^\circ$ in such a way that $BD = BC$. The incircle of $ABC$ is tangent to $AB$ and $AC$ at points $K$ and $L$, respectively. Let $J$ be the incentre of triangle $BCD$. Prove that the line $KL$ intersects the line segment $AJ$ at its midpoint.

A point $D$ is chosen on the side $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$ with $\angle C < \angle A < 90^\circ$ in such a way that $BD = BA$. The incircle of $ABC$ is tangent to $AB$ and $AC$ at points $K$ and $L$, respectively. Let $J$ be the circumcenter of triangle $BCD$. Prove that the line $KL$ intersects the line segment $AJ$ at its midpoint.

A point $D$ is chosen on the side $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$ with $\angle C < \angle A < 90^\circ$ in such a way that $BD = BA$. The incircle of $ABC$ is tangent to $AB$ and $BC$ at points $K$ and $L$, respectively. Let $J$ be the incentre of triangle $BCD$. Prove that the line $KL$ intersects the line segment $AJ$ at its midpoint.

positive_text:
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. Suppose there exists a point $P$ inside the quadrilateral such that $P$ lies on two circles: one through $A$ and $D$, and another through $B$ and $C$, and these circles are externally tangent at $P$. Given that
$$
\angle PAB + \angle PDC \leq \frac{\pi}{2} \quad \text{ and } \quad \angle PBA + \angle PCD \leq \frac{\pi}{2},
$$
prove that $AB + CD \geq BC + AD$.

negatives.text:
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. A circle passing through the points $A$ and $D$ and a circle passing through the points $B$ and $C$ are internally tangent at a point $P$ inside the quadrilateral. Suppose that
$$
\angle PAB + \angle PDC \leq 90^\circ \quad \text{ and } \quad \angle PBA + \angle PCD \leq 90^\circ.
$$
Prove that $AB + CD \geq BC + AD$.

positive_text: Let $m > n > 1$ be coprime positive integers. For each integer $d$, define $W(d)$ to be the smallest value of $|p| + |q|$ such that $m p + n q = d$ for integers $p$ and $q$. A number $d$ is called a local champion if $W(d) \geq W(d + m)$, $W(d) \geq W(d - m)$, $W(d) \geq W(d + n)$, and $W(d) \geq W(d - n)$. Determine all such local champions and their count.

negatives.text: Let $a > b > 1$ be relatively prime positive integers. Define the weight of an integer $c$, denoted by $w(c)$, to be the minimal possible value of $|x| + |y|$ taken over all pairs of integers $x$ and $y$ such that $$ a x - b y = c. $$ An integer $c$ is called a local champion if $w(c) \geq w(c \pm a)$ and $w(c) \geq w(c \pm b)$. Find all local champions and determine their number.

Let $a > b > 1$ be relatively prime positive integers. Define the weight of an integer $c$, denoted by $w(c)$, to be the minimal possible value of $|x|^2 + |y|^2$ taken over all pairs of integers $x$ and $y$ such that $$ a x + b y = c. $$ An integer $c$ is called a local champion if $w(c) \geq w(c \pm a)$ and $w(c) \geq w(c \pm b)$. Find all local champions and determine their number.

positive_text:
Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be a sequence of real numbers. For each $i$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$), define
$$
\quad d_{i} = \text{maximum of } \{a_j \mid 1 \leq j \leq i\} - \text{minimum of } \{a_j \mid i \leq j \leq n\}
$$
and let $d$ be the maximum of all $d_i$.

a. Prove that for any non-decreasing sequence $x_1 \leq x_2 \leq \ldots \leq x_n$ of real numbers,
$$
\begin{equation*}
\max_{1 \leq i \leq n} |x_i - a_i| \geq \frac{d}{2}.
\end{equation*}
$$

b. Demonstrate the existence of such a sequence $x_1 \leq x_2 \leq \ldots \leq x_n$ for which equality is achieved.

negatives.text:
Given a sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ of real numbers. For each $i$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$) define
$$
\text{d}_{i}=\min \{a_{j}: 1 \leq j \leq i\}-\max \{a_{j}: i \leq j \leq n\}
$$
and let
$$
\text{d}=\max \{\text{d}_{i}: 1 \leq i \leq n\} .
$$

a. Prove that for arbitrary real numbers $x_{1} \leq x_{2} \leq \ldots \leq x_{n}$,
$$
\begin{equation*}
\max \{\left|x_{i}-a_{i}\right|: 1 \leq i \leq n\} \geq \frac{\text{d}}{2} .
\end{equation*}
$$

b. Show that there exists a sequence $x_{1} \leq x_{2} \leq \ldots \leq x_{n}$ of real numbers such that we have equality in (1).

Given a sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ of real numbers. For each $i$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$) define
$$
\text{d}_{i}=\max \{a_{j}: 1 \leq j \leq i\}-\min \{a_{j}: i \leq j \leq n\}
$$
and let
$$
\text{d}=\min \{\text{d}_{i}: 1 \leq i \leq n\} .
$$

a. Prove that for arbitrary real numbers $x_{1} \leq x_{2} \leq \ldots \leq x_{n}$,
$$
\begin{equation*}
\max \{\left|x_{i}-a_{i}\right|: 1 \leq i \leq n\} \geq \frac{\text{d}}{2} .
\end{equation*}
$$

b. Show that there exists a sequence $x_{1} \leq x_{2} \leq \ldots \leq x_{n}$ of real numbers such that we have equality in (1).

Given a sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ of real numbers. For each $i$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$) define
$$
\text{d}_{i}=\max \{a_{j}: 1 \leq j \leq i\}-\min \{a_{j}: i \leq j \leq n\}
$$
and let
$$
\text{d}=\max \{\text{d}_{i}: 1 \leq i \leq n\} .
$$

a. Prove that for arbitrary real numbers $x_{1} \leq x_{2} \leq \ldots \leq x_{n}$,
$$
\begin{equation*}
\min \{\left|x_{i}-a_{i}\right|: 1 \leq i \leq n\} \geq \frac{\text{d}}{2} .
\end{equation*}
$$

b. Show that there exists a sequence $x_{1} \leq x_{2} \leq \ldots \leq x_{n}$ of real numbers such that we have equality in (1).

positive_text:
Let $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ be a function such that
$$
 f(a+b) \geq f(a)+f(f(b))-1
$$
for all $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$. Determine all possible values of $f(2007)$.

negatives.text:
Consider those functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ which satisfy the condition
$$
 f(m+n) \leq f(m)+f(f(n))-1
$$
for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Find all possible values of $f(2007)$.

($\mathbb{N}$ denotes the set of all positive integers.)

Consider those functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ which satisfy the condition
$$
 f(m+n) = f(m)+f(f(n))-1
$$
for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Find all possible values of $f(2007)$.

($\mathbb{N}$ denotes the set of all positive integers.)

Consider those functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ which satisfy the condition
$$
 f(m+n) \geq f(m)+f(n)-1
$$
for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Find all possible values of $f(2007)$.

($\mathbb{N}$ denotes the set of all positive integers.)

Let $n > 1$ be an integer. Find all sequences $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n^{2}+n}$ satisfying the following conditions: (a) $a_{i} \in \{0,1\}$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n^{2}+n$; (b) $a_{i+1}+a_{i+2}+\ldots+a_{i+n} > a_{i+n+1}+a_{i+n+2}+\ldots+a_{i+2n}$ for all $0 \leq i \leq n^{2}-n$.

Let $n > 1$ be an integer. Find all sequences $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n^{2}+n}$ satisfying the following conditions: (a) $a_{i} \in \{0,1\}$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n^{2}+n$; (b) $a_{i+1}^{2}+a_{i+2}^{2}+\ldots+a_{i+n}^{2} < a_{i+n+1}^{2}+a_{i+n+2}^{2}+\ldots+a_{i+2n}^{2}$ for all $0 \leq i \leq n^{2}-n$.

positive_text: Let $R$ be a unit square partitioned into $n > 1$ rectangles with sides parallel to the sides of $R$. Suppose every line parallel to an edge of $R$ that intersects the interior of $R$ also intersects the interior of at least one rectangle in the partition. Prove that there is at least one rectangle in the partition that does not share any edge with the boundary of $R$.

negatives.text: A unit square is dissected into $n>1$ rectangles such that their sides are parallel to the sides of the square. Any line, parallel to a side of the square and intersecting its interior, also intersects the interior of some rectangle. Prove that in this dissection, there exists a rectangle having all points on the boundary of the square.

A unit square is dissected into $n>1$ rectangles such that their sides are parallel to the sides of the square. Any line, parallel to a side of the square and intersecting its interior, also intersects the interior of some rectangle. Prove that in this dissection, all rectangles have at least one point on the boundary of the square.

A unit square is dissected into $n>1$ rectangles such that their sides are parallel to the sides of the square. Any line, parallel to a side of the square and intersecting its interior, also intersects the interior of some rectangle. Prove that in this dissection, there exists a rectangle having no point on the boundary of the square, if $n$ is odd.

positive_text:
Let $S_{0} = (s_{1}, \ldots, s_{n})$ be a finite sequence of real numbers. For each $m \geq 0$, from the sequence $S_{m} = (x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n})$ we construct a new sequence $S_{m+1}$ as follows.
1. Choose a partition $\{1, \ldots, n\} = P \cup Q$, with $P$ and $Q$ disjoint, such that the value
$$
\left|\sum_{p \in P} x_{p} - \sum_{q \in Q} x_{q}\right|
$$
is minimized. (Empty subsets are allowed and contribute $0$ to the sum.) In case of multiple partitions, choose arbitrarily.
2. Define $S_{m+1} = (y_{1}, \ldots, y_{n})$, where $y_{i} = x_{i} + 1$ if $i \in P$, and $y_{i} = x_{i} - 1$ if $i \in Q$.
Prove that there exists an $m$ such that some element $x$ of $S_{m}$ satisfies $|x| \geq n / 2$.

negatives.text:
Let $A_{0} = (a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n})$ be a finite sequence of real numbers. For each $k \geq 0$, from the sequence $A_{k} = (x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n})$ we construct a new sequence $A_{k+1}$ in the following way.
1. We choose a partition $\{1, \ldots, n\} = I \cup J$, where $I$ and $J$ are two disjoint sets, such that the expression
$$
\left|\sum_{i \in I} x_{i} + \sum_{j \in J} x_{j}\right|
$$
attains the smallest possible value. (We allow the sets $I$ or $J$ to be empty; in this case the corresponding sum is $0$.) If there are several such partitions, one is chosen arbitrarily.
2. We set $A_{k+1} = (y_{1}, \ldots, y_{n})$, where $y_{i} = x_{i} + 1$ if $i \in I$, and $y_{i} = x_{i} - 1$ if $i \in J$.
Prove that for some $k$, the sequence $A_{k}$ contains an element $x$ such that $|x| \geq n / 2$.

Let $A_{0} = (a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n})$ be a finite sequence of real numbers. For each $k \geq 0$, from the sequence $A_{k} = (x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n})$ we construct a new sequence $A_{k+1}$ in the following way.
1. We choose a partition $\{1, \ldots, n\} = I \cup J$, where $I$ and $J$ are two disjoint sets, such that the expression
$$
\left|\sum_{i \in I} x_{i} - \sum_{j \in J} x_{j}\right|
$$
attains the largest possible value. (We allow the sets $I$ or $J$ to be empty; in this case the corresponding sum is $0$.) If there are several such partitions, one is chosen arbitrarily.
2. We set $A_{k+1} = (y_{1}, \ldots, y_{n})$, where $y_{i} = x_{i} + 1$ if $i \in I$, and $y_{i} = x_{i} - 1$ if $i \in J$.
Prove that for some $k$, the sequence $A_{k}$ contains an element $x$ such that $|x| \geq n / 2$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $X$ be a variable point on the arc $MA$ (not containing $B$) of the circumcircle of triangle $ABM$. Let $T$ lie in the interior of angle $BMA$ such that $\angle TMX = 90^\circ$ and $TX = BX$. Prove that the value of $\angle MTB - \angle CTM$ is constant, regardless of the position of $X$.

negatives.text: Given an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$. The midpoint of side $BC$ is denoted by $M$. Let $X$ be a variable point on the shorter arc $MA$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABM$. Let $T$ be the point in the angle domain $BMA$, for which $\angle TMX = 90^\circ$ and $TX = AX$. Prove that $\angle MTB - \angle CTM$ does not depend on $X$.

Given an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$. The midpoint of side $BC$ is denoted by $M$. Let $X$ be a variable point on the shorter arc $MA$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABM$. Let $T$ be the point in the angle domain $BMA$, for which $\angle TMX = 180^\circ$ and $TX = BX$. Prove that $\angle MTB - \angle CTM$ does not depend on $X$.

positive_text: Find the minimal positive real number $ k $ such that the inequality $ k S_{1} \geq S $ holds for all convex quadrilaterals $ ABCD $, with points $ A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}, D_{1} $ on sides $ AB, BC, CD, DA $ respectively. Let $ S $ be the sum of the two smallest areas among triangles $ AA_{1}D_{1}, BB_{1}A_{1}, CC_{1}B_{1}, DD_{1}C_{1} $, and let $ S_{1} $ be the area of $ A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}D_{1} $.

negatives.text: Determine the smallest positive real number $ k $ with the following property. Let $ ABCD $ be a convex quadrilateral, and let points $ A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1} $ and $ D_{1} $ lie on sides $ AB, BC $, $ CD $ and $ DA $, respectively. Consider the areas of triangles $ AA_{1}D_{1}, BB_{1}A_{1}, CC_{1}B_{1} $, and $ DD_{1}C_{1} $; let $ S $ be the sum of the two largest ones, and let $ S_{1} $ be the area of quadrilateral $ A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}D_{1} $. Then we always have $ k S_{1} \geq S $.

Determine the smallest positive real number $ k $ with the following property. Let $ ABCD $ be a convex quadrilateral, and let points $ A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1} $ and $ D_{1} $ lie on sides $ AB, BC $, $ CD $ and $ DA $, respectively. Consider the areas of triangles $ AA_{1}D_{1}, BB_{1}A_{1}, CC_{1}B_{1} $, and $ DD_{1}C_{1} $; let $ S $ be the sum of the two smallest ones, and let $ S_{1} $ be the area of triangle $ A_{1}B_{1}C_{1} $. Then we always have $ k S_{1} \geq S $.

positive_text:
Let $x$, $y$, $z$, $w$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
xyzw = 1 \quad \text{ and } \quad x + y + z + w > \frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{z} + \frac{z}{w} + \frac{w}{x}
$$
Prove that
$$
x + y + z + w < \frac{y}{x} + \frac{z}{y} + \frac{w}{z} + \frac{x}{w}
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
ab cd = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad a + b + c + d > \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{d} + \frac{d}{a}
$$
Prove that
$$
a + b + c + d < \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{d} + \frac{d}{a}
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
ab cd = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad a + b + c + d > \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{d} + \frac{d}{a}
$$
Prove that
$$
a + b + c + d < \frac{b}{a} + \frac{c}{b} + \frac{d}{a} + \frac{a}{d}
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
ab cd = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad a + b + c + d < \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{d} + \frac{d}{a}
$$
Prove that
$$
a + b + c + d < \frac{b}{a} + \frac{c}{b} + \frac{d}{c} + \frac{a}{d}
$$

positive_text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be positive real numbers. Show that the following inequality is always satisfied:
$$
\sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{(a-b)(a-c)}{a+b+c} \geq 0
$$
and characterize when equality occurs.

negatives.text: \text{Prove that for any four positive real numbers } a, b, c, d \text{ the inequality} \quad \frac{(a+b)(a-c)}{a+b+c}+\frac{(b-c)(b+d)}{b+c+d}+\frac{(c-d)(c-a)}{c+d+a}+\frac{(d-a)(d-b)}{d+a+b} \geq 0 \text{ holds. Determine all cases of equality.}

\text{Prove that for any four positive real numbers } a, b, c, d \text{ the inequality} \quad \frac{(a-b)(a-c)}{a+b+c}+\frac{(b-c)(b-d)}{b+c+d}+\frac{(c-d)(c-a)}{c+d+a}+\frac{(d-a)(d-b)}{d+a+b} \leq 0 \text{ holds. Determine all cases of equality.}

\text{Prove that for any four positive real numbers } a, b, c, d \text{ the inequality} \quad \frac{(a-b)^2(a-c)}{a+b+c}+\frac{(b-c)^2(b-d)}{b+c+d}+\frac{(c-d)^2(c-a)}{c+d+a}+\frac{(d-a)^2(d-b)}{d+a+b} \geq 0 \text{ holds. Determine all cases of equality.}

positive_text: Let $\tau(n)$ denote the number of positive divisors of $n$. Determine all functions $g: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ satisfying the conditions: (a) $\tau(g(k)) = k$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$; (b) $g(k m)$ divides $(k - 1) m^{k m - 1} g(k)$ for all $k, m \in \mathbb{N}$.

Determine all real-valued functions $f$ defined on $\mathbb{R}$ such that for all real numbers $a$ and $b$, the following identity holds:
$$
 f(a f(a + b)) = f(b f(a)) + a^2.
$$

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f$ from the set of real numbers into the set of real numbers which satisfy for all real $x, y$ the identity
$$
 f(x f(x+y))=f(y f(x))-x^{2} .
$$

Find all functions $f$ from the set of real numbers into the set of real numbers which satisfy for all real $x, y$ the identity
$$
 f(x f(x+y))=f(y f(x))+|x|^{2} .
$$

Find all functions $f$ from the set of real numbers into the set of real numbers which satisfy for all real $x, y$ the identity
$$
 f(x f(x+y))=f(y f(x))+x^{3} .
$$

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let the incircle touch $AB$ and $AC$ at $Z$ and $Y$, respectively. Suppose $BY$ and $CZ$ intersect at point $G$. Define $R$ and $S$ such that $BCYR$ and $BCSZ$ are parallelograms. Show that the distances from $G$ to $R$ and $S$ are equal.

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle. The incircle of $ABC$ touches the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at the points $Z$ and $Y$, respectively. Let $G$ be the point where the lines $BY$ and $CZ$ meet, and let $R$ and $S$ be points such that the two quadrilaterals $BCYR$ and $BCSZ$ are rectangles.
Prove that $GR = GS$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle. The incircle of $ABC$ touches the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at the points $Z$ and $Y$, respectively. Let $G$ be the point where the lines $BY$ and $CZ$ meet, and let $R$ and $S$ be points such that the two quadrilaterals $BCYR$ and $BCSZ$ are parallelograms.
Prove that $GR > GS$.

positive_text:
Let $P$ be a convex polygon invariant under a 180-degree rotation about a point $O$. Show there exists a parallelogram $R$ containing $P$ such that
$$
\frac{\text{Area}(R)}{\text{Area}(P)} \leq \sqrt{2}.
$$

negatives.text: Let $P$ be a polygon that is convex and symmetric to some point $O$. Prove that for some parallelogram $R$ satisfying $P \subset R$ we have $$ \frac{|R|}{|P|} \leq 2 $$ where $|R|$ and $|P|$ denote the area of the sets $R$ and $P$, respectively.

Let $P$ be a polygon that is convex and symmetric to some line $L$. Prove that for some parallelogram $R$ satisfying $P \subset R$ we have $$ \frac{|R|}{|P|} \leq \sqrt{2} $$ where $|R|$ and $|P|$ denote the area of the sets $R$ and $P$, respectively.

Let $P$ be a polygon that is convex and symmetric to some point $O$. Prove that for some rectangle $R$ satisfying $P \subset R$ we have $$ \frac{|R|}{|P|} \leq \sqrt{2} $$ where $|R|$ and $|P|$ denote the area of the sets $R$ and $P$, respectively.

positive_text: \text{Suppose } n \geq 4 \text{ players compete in a round-robin tennis tournament with no draws. A group of four players is termed bad if one is defeated by the other three, and each of these three has one win and one loss among themselves. If the tournament has no bad groups, and } w_i \text{ and } \ell_i \text{ denote the number of wins and losses for the } i\text{th player, show that} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n}(w_i - \ell_i)^3 \geq 0

negatives.text:
Let $ n \geq 4 $ players participated in a tennis tournament. Any two Players have played exactly one game, and there was no tie game. We call a company of four players bad if one player was defeated by the other three players, and each of these three players won a game and lost another game among themselves. Suppose that there is at least one bad company in this tournament. Let $ w_{i} $ and $ \ell_{i} $ be respectively the number of wins and losses of the $ i $th player. Prove that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(w_{i}-\ell_{i}\right)^{3} \geq 0
$$

positive_text: Suppose $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{s}$ are integer arithmetic progressions such that: (i) every integer is covered by at least one $P_i$; (ii) for each $P_i$, there exists an integer in $P_i$ that is not in any other $P_j$. Let $n$ be the least common multiple of the differences of these progressions, with prime factorization $n = p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}$. Show that $$ s \geq 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_{i}(p_{i} - 1). $$

negatives.text:
Let $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{s}$ be arithmetic progressions of integers, the following conditions being satisfied:
(i) each integer belongs to at least one of them;
(ii) each progression contains a number which does not belong to other progressions.
Denote by $n$ the greatest common divisor of steps of these progressions; let $n=p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}$ be its prime factorization. Prove that
$$
 s \geq 1+\sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_{i}\left(p_{i}-1\right)
$$

Let $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{s}$ be arithmetic progressions of integers, the following conditions being satisfied:
(i) each integer belongs to at least one of them;
(ii) each progression contains a number which does not belong to other progressions.
Denote by $n$ the least common multiple of steps of these progressions; let $n=p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}$ be its prime factorization. Prove that
$$
 s \geq 1+\sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_{i}\left(p_{i}+1\right)
$$

Let $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{s}$ be arithmetic progressions of integers, the following conditions being satisfied:
(i) each integer belongs to at least one of them;
(ii) each progression contains a number which does not belong to other progressions.
Denote by $n$ the least common multiple of steps of these progressions; let $n=p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}$ be its prime factorization. Prove that
$$
 s \geq 1+\sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_{i}\left(p_{i}-1\right)^2
$$

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$, and let $D$ be the midpoint of segment $AC$. The internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets the circumcircle of triangle $BDC$ at a point $E$ inside $\triangle ABC$. If the line $BD$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $AEB$ at points $B$ and $F$, and if lines $AF$ and $BE$ intersect at $I$, and lines $CI$ and $BD$ intersect at $K$, prove that $I$ is the incenter of triangle $KAB$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $D$ be the midpoint of $AC$. The angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersects the circle through $D$, $B$, and $C$ in a point $E$ outside the triangle $ABC$. The line $BD$ intersects the circle through $A$, $E$, and $B$ in two points $B$ and $F$. The lines $AF$ and $BE$ meet at a point $I$, and the lines $CI$ and $BD$ meet at a point $K$. Show that $I$ is the incenter of triangle $KAB$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $D$ be the midpoint of $BC$. The angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersects the circle through $D$, $B$, and $C$ in a point $E$ inside the triangle $ABC$. The line $BD$ intersects the circle through $A$, $E$, and $B$ in two points $B$ and $F$. The lines $AF$ and $BE$ meet at a point $I$, and the lines $CI$ and $BD$ meet at a point $K$. Show that $I$ is the incenter of triangle $KAB$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $D$ be the midpoint of $AC$. The angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersects the circle through $D$, $B$, and $C$ in a point $E$ inside the triangle $ABC$. The line $CD$ intersects the circle through $A$, $E$, and $B$ in two points $B$ and $F$. The lines $AF$ and $BE$ meet at a point $I$, and the lines $CI$ and $BD$ meet at a point $K$. Show that $I$ is the incenter of triangle $KAB$.

positive_text: Let $P Q R S T U$ be a convex hexagon such that each side is tangent to a circle $\omega$ centered at $O$. Assume that the circumcircle of triangle $P R T$ coincides in center with $\omega$. Let $M$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $Q$ to $R S$. Suppose the perpendicular from $Q$ to $S U$ intersects the line $T O$ at point $N$. Let $N$ be used to drop a perpendicular to $S T$, landing at point $M'$. Prove that $S M = S M'$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon all of whose sides are tangent to a circle $\omega$ with center $O$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $ACE$ is concentric with $\omega$. Let $J$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to $CD$. Suppose that the perpendicular from $B$ to $DF$ intersects the line $EO$ at a point $K$. Let $L$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $K$ to $DE$. Prove that $DJ = DF$.

Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon all of whose sides are tangent to a circle $\omega$ with center $O$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $ACE$ is concentric with $\omega$. Let $J$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to $CD$. Suppose that the perpendicular from $B$ to $DF$ intersects the line $EO$ at a point $K$. Let $L$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $K$ to $DE$. Prove that $DJ = DE$.

Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon all of whose sides are tangent to a circle $\omega$ with center $O$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $ACE$ is concentric with $\omega$. Let $J$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to $CD$. Suppose that the perpendicular from $B$ to $DF$ intersects the line $EO$ at a point $K$. Let $L$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $K$ to $DE$. Prove that $DJ = DK$.

positive_text: Let $k$ be a positive integer and define $p = 2^k + 1$. Prove that $p$ is prime if and only if there exists a rearrangement $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{p-1}$ of the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, p-1\}$ and a sequence of integers $h_1, h_2, \ldots, h_{p-1}$ such that $p$ divides $h_i^{b_i} - b_{i+1}$ for all $i = 1, 2, \ldots, p-1$, where $b_p = b_1$.

negatives.text: Let $k$ be a positive integer and set $n=2^{k}+1$. Prove that $n$ is a prime number if and only if the following holds: there is a permutation $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n-1}$ of the numbers $1,2, \ldots, n-1$ and a sequence of integers $g_{1}, g_{2}, \ldots, g_{n-1}$ such that $n$ divides $g_{i}^{a_{i}}+a_{i+1}$ for every $i \in\{1,2, \ldots, n-1\}$, where we set $a_{n}=a_{1}$.

Let $k$ be a positive integer and set $n=2^{k}+1$. Prove that $n$ is a prime number if and only if the following holds: there is a permutation $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n-1}$ of the numbers $1,2, \ldots, n-1$ and a sequence of integers $g_{1}, g_{2}, \ldots, g_{n-1}$ such that $n$ divides $g_{i}^{a_{i}}-a_{i}$ for every $i \in\{1,2, \ldots, n-1\}$, where we set $a_{n}=a_{1}$.

Let $k$ be a positive integer and set $n=2^{k}+1$. Prove that $n$ is a prime number if and only if the following holds: there is a permutation $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n-1}$ of the numbers $1,2, \ldots, n-1$ and a sequence of integers $g_{1}, g_{2}, \ldots, g_{n-1}$ such that $n$ divides $g_{i}^{a_{i}}-a_{i+1}$ for every $i \in\{1,2, \ldots, n\}$, where we set $a_{n+1}=a_{1}$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a right triangle at $C$, and let $C_0$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$. Let $X$ be a point inside the segment $CC_0$. On $AX$ and $BX$, mark points $K$ and $L$ such that $BK = BC$ and $AL = AC$. Let $M$ be the point where $AL$ and $BK$ intersect. Prove that $MK = ML$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BCA = 90^\circ$, and let $C_0$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$. Choose a point $X$ in the interior of the segment $CC_0$, and let $K, L$ be the points on the segments $AX, BX$ for which $BK = BC$ and $AL = AC$ respectively. Denote by $M$ the intersection of $AL$ and $BK$. Show that $MK = ML^2$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BCA = 90^\circ$, and let $C_0$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$. Choose a point $X$ in the interior of the segment $CC_0$, and let $K, L$ be the points on the segments $AX, BX$ for which $BK = BC$ and $AL = AC$ respectively. Denote by $M$ the intersection of $AL$ and $BK$. Show that $MK = MC$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BCA = 90^\circ$, and let $C_0$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$. Choose a point $X$ in the interior of the segment $CC_0$, and let $K, L$ be the points on the segments $AX, BX$ for which $BK = AC$ and $AL = BC$ respectively. Denote by $M$ the intersection of $AL$ and $BK$. Show that $MK = ML$.

positive_text:
Given any set of $2000$ distinct real numbers, show that there exist two distinct ordered pairs $(x, y)$ and $(u, v)$ with $x > y$ and $u > v$, such that
$$
\left|\frac{x - y}{u - v} - 1\right| < \frac{1}{100000}
$$

negatives.text:
Prove that in any set of $2000$ distinct real numbers there exist two pairs $a > b$ and $c > d$ with $a \neq c$ or $b \neq d$, such that
$$
\left|\frac{a-b}{c-d}+1\right|<\frac{1}{100000}
$$

Prove that in any set of $2000$ distinct real numbers there exist two pairs $a > b$ and $c > d$ with $a \neq c$ or $b \neq d$, such that
$$
\left|\left(\frac{a-b}{c-d}\right)^2-1\right|<\frac{1}{100000}
$$

Prove that in any set of $2000$ distinct real numbers there exist two pairs $a > b$ and $c > d$ with $a \neq c$ or $b \neq d$, such that
$$
\left|\frac{a-b}{c-d}-1\right|<\frac{1}{1000000}
$$

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer, and define a non-decreasing sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ of positive integers such that $a_{n} \leqslant a_{1} + n$. Extend this sequence periodically to infinity by setting $a_{n+i} = a_{i}$ for all $i \geq 1$. If for all $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$, it holds that $a_{a_{i}} \leq n + i - 1$, show that the total sum of the sequence satisfies $a_{1} + a_{2} + \cdots + a_{n} \leq n^2$.

Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer. Define a circular arrangement as a cyclic permutation of the numbers $0, 1, \ldots, n$, where rotations are considered identical. An arrangement is beautiful if, for all distinct $0 \leq a, b, c, d \leq n$ satisfying $a + c = b + d$, the chords connecting $a$ to $c$ and $b$ to $d$ do not cross. Let $M$ denote the number of such beautiful arrangements. Let $N$ be the count of positive integer pairs $(x, y)$ with $x + y \leq n$ and $\gcd(x, y) = 1$. Prove that $$M = N + 1.$$

negatives.text: Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Consider all circular arrangements of the numbers $0,1, \ldots, n$; the $n+1$ rotations of an arrangement are considered to be equal. A circular arrangement is called beautiful if, for any four distinct numbers $0 \leqslant a, b, c, d \leqslant n$ with $a+c = b+d$, the chord joining numbers $a$ and $c$ does intersect the chord joining numbers $b$ and $d$. Let $M$ be the number of beautiful arrangements of $0,1, \ldots, n$. Let $N$ be the number of pairs $(x, y)$ of positive integers such that $x+y \leqslant n$ and $\operatorname{gcd}(x, y) = 1$. Prove that $$M = N + 1.$$

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Consider all circular arrangements of the numbers $0,1, \ldots, n$; the $n+1$ rotations of an arrangement are considered to be equal. A circular arrangement is called beautiful if, for any four distinct numbers $0 \leqslant a, b, c, d \leqslant n$ with $a^2 + c^2 = b^2 + d^2$, the chord joining numbers $a$ and $c$ does not intersect the chord joining numbers $b$ and $d$. Let $M$ be the number of beautiful arrangements of $0,1, \ldots, n$. Let $N$ be the number of pairs $(x, y)$ of positive integers such that $x+y \leqslant n$ and $\operatorname{gcd}(x, y) = 1$. Prove that $$M = N + 1.$$

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Consider all circular arrangements of the numbers $0,1, \ldots, n$; the $n+1$ rotations of an arrangement are considered to be equal. A circular arrangement is called beautiful if, for any four distinct numbers $0 \leqslant a, b, c, d \leqslant n$ with $a+c = b+d$, the chord joining numbers $a$ and $c$ does not intersect the chord joining numbers $b$ and $d$. Let $M$ be the number of beautiful arrangements of $0,1, \ldots, n$. Let $N$ be the number of pairs $(x, y)$ of positive integers such that $x+y < n$ and $\operatorname{gcd}(x, y) = 1$. Prove that $$M = N + 1.$$

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $\angle B > \angle C$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on line $AC$ such that $\angle PBA = \angle QBA = \angle C$. Assume $A$ lies between $P$ and $C$. If a point $D$ on segment $BQ$ satisfies $PD = PB$, and the ray $AD$ meets the circumcircle of $ABC$ again at $R$, show that $QR = QB$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle B > \angle C$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be two different points on line $AC$ such that $\angle PBA = \angle QBA = \angle CAB$ and $A$ is located between $P$ and $C$. Suppose that there exists an interior point $D$ of segment $BQ$ for which $PD = PB$. Let the ray $AD$ intersect the circle $ABC$ at $R \neq A$. Prove that $QB = QR$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle B > \angle C$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be two different points on line $AC$ such that $\angle PBA = \angle QBA = \angle ACB$ and $C$ is located between $P$ and $A$. Suppose that there exists an interior point $D$ of segment $BQ$ for which $PD = PB$. Let the ray $AD$ intersect the circle $ABC$ at $R \neq A$. Prove that $QB = QR$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle B > \angle C$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be two different points on line $AC$ such that $\angle PBA = \angle QBA = \angle ACB$ and $A$ is located between $P$ and $C$. Suppose that there exists an interior point $D$ of segment $BQ$ for which $PD = PC$. Let the ray $AD$ intersect the circle $ABC$ at $R \neq A$. Prove that $QB = QR$.

positive_text: Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon such that $AB = DE$, $BC = EF$, $CD = FA$, and $\angle A - \angle D = \angle C - \angle F = \angle E - \angle B$. Show that the lines $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ meet at a common point.

negatives.text: Let $AB C D E F$ be a convex hexagon with $AB = DE$, $BC = EF$, $CD = FA$, and $\angle A + \angle D = \angle C + \angle F = \angle E + \angle B$. Prove that the diagonals $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ are concurrent.

Let $AB C D E F$ be a convex hexagon with $AB = DE$, $BC = EF$, $CD = FA$, and $\angle A - \angle D = \angle C - \angle F = \angle B - \angle E$. Prove that the diagonals $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ are concurrent.

Let $AB C D E F$ be a convex hexagon with $AB = DE$, $BC = EF$, $CD = FA$, and $\angle A - \angle D = \angle C - \angle F = \angle E - \angle B + 180^\circ$. Prove that the diagonals $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ are concurrent.

positive_text: Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer. Suppose an $n \times n$ grid is given, and a set of $n$ rooks is placed such that each row and each column contains precisely one rook. Determine the largest integer $k$ with the property that in any such placement, there exists a $k \times k$ subgrid that contains no rooks at all.

negatives.text: Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Consider an $n \times n$ chessboard divided into $n^{2}$ unit squares. We call a configuration of $n$ rooks on this board happy if every row and every column contains exactly one rook. Find the greatest positive integer $k$ such that for every happy configuration of rooks, we can find a $k \times k$ square with at least one rook on at least one of its $k^{2}$ unit squares.

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Consider an $n \times n$ chessboard divided into $n^{2}$ unit squares. We call a configuration of $n$ rooks on this board happy if every row and every column contains exactly one rook. Find the greatest positive integer $k$ such that for every happy configuration of rooks, we can find a $k \times k$ square with exactly one rook on its $k^{2}$ unit squares.

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Consider an $n \times n$ chessboard divided into $n^{2}$ unit squares. We call a configuration of $n$ rooks on this board happy if every row and every column contains exactly one rook. Find the greatest positive integer $k$ such that for every happy configuration of rooks, we can find a $k \times k$ square without a rook on at least one of its $k^{2}$ unit squares.

positive_text: Let $n \geq 3$ distinct lines be given in the plane, with the condition that no two are parallel and no three intersect at a common point. Let $\mathcal{F}$ denote the collection of bounded regions formed by these lines. Show that there exists a subset of $\lceil\sqrt{n / 2}\rceil$ lines that can be marked blue such that no region in $\mathcal{F}$ is surrounded entirely by blue lines.

negatives.text: Consider $n \geqslant 3$ lines in the plane such that no two lines are parallel and no three have a common point. These lines divide the plane into polygonal regions; let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of regions having finite area. Prove that it is possible to colour $\lfloor\sqrt{n / 2}\rfloor$ of the lines blue in such a way that no region in $\mathcal{F}$ has a completely blue boundary. (For a real number $x,\lfloor x\rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer which is not larger than $x$.)

Consider $n \geqslant 3$ lines in the plane such that no two lines are parallel and no three have a common point. These lines divide the plane into polygonal regions; let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of regions having finite area. Prove that it is possible to colour $\lceil\sqrt{n / 3}\rceil$ of the lines blue in such a way that no region in $\mathcal{F}$ has a completely blue boundary. (For a real number $x,\lceil x\rceil$ denotes the least integer which is not smaller than $x$.)

Consider $n \geqslant 3$ lines in the plane such that no two lines are parallel and no three have a common point. These lines divide the plane into polygonal regions; let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of regions having finite area. Prove that it is possible to colour $\lceil\sqrt{n / 2}\rceil$ of the lines blue in such a way that all regions in $\mathcal{F}$ have a completely blue boundary.

positive_text: Let $P$ be a set of $n \geqslant 4$ non-collinear points in the plane. They are initially connected with $n$ line segments such that each point is an endpoint of exactly two segments. At each move, two intersecting segments $AB$ and $CD$ are replaced with $AC$ and $BD$, provided both new segments do not already exist. Show that the number of such moves cannot exceed $\frac{n^{3}}{4}$.

negatives.text: Let $M$ be a set of $n \geqslant 4$ points in the plane, no three of which are collinear. Initially these points are connected with $n$ segments so that each point in $M$ is the endpoint of exactly two segments. Then, at each step, one may choose two segments $AB$ and $CD$ sharing a common interior point and replace them by the segments $AC$ and $BD$ if none of them is present at this moment. Prove that it is impossible to perform $n^{3} / 2$ or more such moves.

positive_text: In an acute triangle $ABC$, let $P$ and $Q$ lie on side $BC$ such that $\angle PAB = \angle ACB$ and $\angle QAC = \angle CBA$. Define $M$ and $N$ as the points on the extensions of $AP$ and $AQ$, respectively, with $PM = AP$ and $QN = AQ$. Prove that the lines $BM$ and $CN$ meet at a point lying on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: The points $P$ and $Q$ are chosen on the side $BC$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ so that $\angle PAB = \angle ACB$ and $\angle QAC = \angle CBA$. The points $M$ and $N$ are taken on the rays $AP$ and $AQ$, respectively, so that $AP = 2PM$ and $AQ = 2QN$. Prove that the lines $BM$ and $CN$ intersect on the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$.

The points $P$ and $Q$ are chosen on the side $BC$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ so that $\angle PAB = \angle ACB$ and $\angle QAC = \angle CBA$. The points $M$ and $N$ are taken on the rays $AP$ and $AQ$, respectively, so that $AP = PM$ and $AQ = QN$. Prove that the lines $CM$ and $BN$ intersect on the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle and $O$ the circumcentre of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, where $AB > BC$. The angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ meets $\Omega$ again at $M$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with diameter $BM$. The angle bisectors of $\angle AOB$ and $\angle BOC$ intersect $\Gamma$ again at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Choose a point $R$ on line $PQ$ such that $BR = MR$. Prove that $BR$ is parallel to $AC$.

negatives.text: Let $\Omega$ and $O$ be the circumcircle and the circumcentre of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ with $AB > BC$. The angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects $\Omega$ at $M \neq B$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with diameter $BM$. The angle bisectors of $\angle AOB$ and $\angle BOC$ intersect $\Gamma$ at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The point $R$ is chosen on the line $PQ$ so that $BR = BR$. Prove that $BR \parallel AC$.

positive_text: Consider $n \geqslant 1$ cities placed in a straight line from left to right. Each city is equipped with a leftward-facing bulldozer to its left and a rightward-facing bulldozer to its right. All $2n$ bulldozers are of distinct sizes. When a right-facing and a left-facing bulldozer meet, the one with the larger size pushes the smaller one off the road. However, if one bulldozer reaches the back of another, it pushes the other off regardless of size. For two cities $A$ and $B$, with $A$ to the left of $B$, city $A$ is said to be able to clear city $B$ if its right bulldozer can move to $B$ and eliminate all intervening bulldozers. Likewise, $B$ can clear $A$ if its left bulldozer can move left and eliminate all bulldozers in its path. Show that there is precisely one city that cannot be cleared by any other city.

negatives.text: In Lineland there are $n \geqslant 1$ towns, arranged along a road running from left to right. Each town has a left bulldozer (put to the left of the town and facing left) and a right bulldozer (put to the right of the town and facing right). The sizes of the $2n$ bulldozers are distinct. Every time when a right and a left bulldozer confront each other, the smaller bulldozer pushes the larger one off the road. On the other hand, the bulldozers are quite unprotected at their rears; so, if a bulldozer reaches the rear-end of another one, the first one pushes the second one off the road, regardless of their sizes. Let $A$ and $B$ be two towns, with $B$ being to the right of $A$. We say that town $A$ can sweep town $B$ away if the right bulldozer of $A$ can move over to $B$ pushing off all bulldozers it meets. Similarly, $B$ can sweep $A$ away if the left bulldozer of $B$ can move to $A$ pushing off all bulldozers of all towns on its way. Prove that there is exactly one town which cannot be swept away by any other one.

In Lineland there are $n \geqslant 1$ towns, arranged along a road running from left to right. Each town has a left bulldozer (put to the left of the town and facing left) and a right bulldozer (put to the right of the town and facing right). The sizes of the $2n$ bulldozers are not necessarily distinct. Every time when a right and a left bulldozer confront each other, the larger bulldozer pushes the smaller one off the road. On the other hand, the bulldozers are quite unprotected at their rears; so, if a bulldozer reaches the rear-end of another one, the first one pushes the second one off the road, regardless of their sizes. Let $A$ and $B$ be two towns, with $B$ being to the right of $A$. We say that town $A$ can sweep town $B$ away if the right bulldozer of $A$ can move over to $B$ pushing off all bulldozers it meets. Similarly, $B$ can sweep $A$ away if the left bulldozer of $B$ can move to $A$ pushing off all bulldozers of all towns on its way. Prove that there is exactly one town which cannot be swept away by any other one.

positive_text:
Let $S$ be a finite set of points in the plane. Define $S$ to be symmetric if for any two distinct points $X, Y \in S$, there exists a point $Z \in S$ such that the distances $XZ$ and $YZ$ are equal. Define $S$ to be non-concentric if there is no point $Q \in S$ such that $QX = QY = QZ$ for any three distinct points $X, Y, Z \in S$.

a. Prove that for each integer $n \geq 3$, a symmetric set of size $n$ exists.

b. Determine all integers $n \geq 3$ for which a symmetric, non-concentric set of size $n$ exists.

negatives.text:
Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is balanced if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{V}$, there exists a point $C \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $AC < BC$. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is center-free if for any distinct points $A, B, C \in \mathcal{V}$, there does not exist a point $P \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $PA = PB = PC$.

a. Show that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a balanced set consisting of $n$ points.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ does there exist a balanced, center-free set consisting of $n$ points?

Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is balanced if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{V}$, there exists a point $C \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $AC = BC$ or $AC = 2BC$. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is center-free if for any distinct points $A, B, C \in \mathcal{V}$, there does not exist a point $P \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $PA = PB = PC$.

a. Show that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a balanced set consisting of $n$ points.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ does there exist a balanced, center-free set consisting of $n$ points?

positive_text:
Determine all integers $n \geqslant 3$ such that for any real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ with $\left|a_{k}\right| + \left|b_{k}\right| = 1$ for all $1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$, there exists a choice of signs $\varepsilon_{1}, \varepsilon_{2}, \ldots, \varepsilon_{n} \in \{-1, 1\}$ satisfying
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} \varepsilon_{k} a_{k}\right| + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} \varepsilon_{k} b_{k}\right| \leqslant 1
$$

negatives.text:
Find all integers $n \geqslant 3$ with the following property: for all real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ satisfying $\left|a_{k}\right|+\left|b_{k}\right|=1$ for $1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$, there exist $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$, each of which is either $-1$ or $1$, such that
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} a_{k}\right|^{2}+\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} b_{k}\right|^{2} \leqslant 1
$$

Find all integers $n \geqslant 3$ with the following property: for all real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ satisfying $\left|a_{k}\right|+\left|b_{k}\right|=1$ for $1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$, there exist $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$, each of which is either $-1$ or $1$, such that
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} a_{k}\right|+\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} b_{k}\right| \geqslant 1
$$

positive_text:
Given $n \geqslant 2$ segments in the plane such that every pair intersects in the interior and no three meet at one point, let $n-1$ be the number of claps Jeff makes. At each clap, snails placed at the endpoints move to the next intersection point along their segments. After $n-1$ claps, snails reach the furthest intersection from their start.

a) Show that for odd $n$, Jeff can always choose the initial positions of the snails so that no collision occurs at any intersection point.

b) Demonstrate that for even $n$, regardless of how Jeff initializes the snails, a collision is unavoidable at some point in time.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. In the plane, there are $n$ segments given in such a way that any two segments have an intersection point in the interior, and no three segments intersect at a single point. Jeff places a snail at one of the endpoints of each of the segments and claps his hands $n-1$ times. Each time when he claps his hands, all the snails move along their own segments and stay at the next intersection points until the next clap. Since there are $n-1$ intersection points on each segment, all snails will reach the furthest intersection points from their starting points after $n-1$ claps.

a) Prove that if $n$ is odd then Jeff can always place the snails so that no two of them ever occupy the same endpoint.

b) Prove that if $n$ is even then there must be a moment when some two snails occupy the same endpoint no matter how Jeff places the snails.

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. In the plane, there are $n$ segments given in such a way that any two segments have an intersection point in the interior, and no three segments intersect at a single point. Jeff places a snail at one of the endpoints of each of the segments and claps his hands $n$ times. Each time when he claps his hands, all the snails move along their own segments and stay at the next intersection points until the next clap. Since there are $n$ intersection points on each segment, all snails will reach the furthest intersection points from their starting points after $n$ claps.

a) Prove that if $n$ is odd then Jeff can always place the snails so that no two of them ever occupy the same intersection point.

b) Prove that if $n$ is even then there must be a moment when some two snails occupy the same intersection point no matter how Jeff places the snails.

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. In the plane, there are $n$ segments given in such a way that any two segments have an intersection point in the interior, and no three segments intersect at a single point. Jeff places a snail at one of the endpoints of each of the segments and claps his hands $n-1$ times.
