b) Prove that if $n$ is odd then there must be a moment when some two snails occupy the same intersection point no matter how Jeff places the snails.

positive_text: Determine all integer-coefficient polynomials $P(x)$ of odd degree $d$ such that for any positive integer $n$, there exist $n$ positive integers $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ where $\frac{P(x_i)}{P(x_j)}$ lies in $\left(\frac{1}{2}, 2\right)$ and is a $d$-th power of a rational number for all $1 \leq i, j \leq n$.

Let $ f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ be a function such that $ f(x)+y = f(y)+x $ holds for all $ x, y \in \mathbb{R} $ with $ (f(x)+y)(f(y)+x) > 0 $. Show that $ f(x)+y \leqslant f(y)+x $ for all real numbers $ x $ and $ y $ satisfying $ x > y $.

negatives.text: Assume that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies the following condition: For every $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $(f(x)+y)(f(y)+x) < 0$, we have $f(x)+y=f(y)+x$. Prove that $f(x)+y \leqslant f(y)+x$ whenever $x>y$.

Assume that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies the following condition: For every $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $(f(x)+y)(f(y)+x) > 0$, we have $f(x)+y=f(y)+x$. Prove that $f(x)+y \geqslant f(y)+x$ whenever $x>y$.

Assume that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies the following condition: For every $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $(f(x)+x)(f(y)+y) > 0$, we have $f(x)+y=f(y)+x$. Prove that $f(x)+y \leqslant f(y)+x$ whenever $x>y$.

positive_text: Let $n$ be an integer with $n \geq 3$. Suppose $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ are two regular $n$-gons in the plane. Show that the set of vertices of $\mathcal{A}$ contained in the closure of $\mathcal{B}$ forms a contiguous arc of the cyclic sequence of vertices of $\mathcal{A}$. (In other words, there exists a straight line that separates the vertices of $\mathcal{A}$ inside or on $\mathcal{B}$ from the remaining vertices of $\mathcal{A}$.)

negatives.text: Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. Two regular $n$-gons $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ are given in the plane. Prove that the vertices of $\mathcal{A}$ that lie inside $\mathcal{B}$ or on its boundary are at most two disjoint intervals.

Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. Two regular $n$-gons $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ are given in the plane. Prove that the vertices of $\mathcal{A}$ that lie inside $\mathcal{B}$ or on its boundary are symmetric with respect to the center of $\mathcal{A}$.

positive_text:
Let $n \geq 2018$ be an integer, and suppose that $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ are distinct positive integers with each $a_i, b_i \leq 5n$. If the sequence of ratios
$$
\frac{a_{i}}{b_{i}}
$$
for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$ forms an arithmetic progression, prove that all the ratios are equal.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2018$ be an integer, and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be pairwise distinct positive integers not exceeding $5n$. Suppose that the sequence
$$
\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}, \frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}
$$
forms a geometric progression. Prove that the terms of the sequence are equal.

Let $n \geqslant 2018$ be an integer, and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be pairwise distinct positive integers not exceeding $5n$. Suppose that the sequence
$$
\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}, \frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}
$$
forms an arithmetic progression. Prove that the common difference is strictly positive.

Let $n \geqslant 2018$ be an integer, and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be pairwise distinct positive integers not exceeding $2n$. Suppose that the sequence
$$
\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}, \frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}
$$
forms an arithmetic progression. Prove that the terms of the sequence are equal.

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $x$ and $y$,
$$
f(2x) + 2f(y) = f(f(x+y)).
$$

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
 f(2a) - 2f(b) = f(f(a+b)).
$$

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
 f(2a) + 2f(b) = f(f(a-b)).
$$

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
 f(2a) + 2f(b) = f(f(a^2 + b)).
$$

positive_text:
Let $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{2019}$ be real numbers such that
$$
x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{2019}=0 \quad \text{and} \quad x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+\cdots+x_{2019}^{2}=1 .$$
Let $m=\min \left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{2019}\right)$ and $M=\max \left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{2019}\right)$. Prove that
$$
mM \leqslant-\frac{1}{2019}$$

negatives.text:
Let $u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}$ be real numbers satisfying
$$
u_{1}+u_{2}+\cdots+u_{2019}=0 \quad \text{and} \quad u_{1}^{3}+u_{2}^{3}+\cdots+u_{2019}^{3}=1 .$$
Let $a=\min \left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}\right)$ and $b=\max \left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}\right)$. Prove that
$$
a b \leqslant-\frac{1}{2019}$$

Let $u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}$ be real numbers satisfying
$$
u_{1}+u_{2}+\cdots+u_{2019}=1 \quad \text{and} \quad u_{1}^{2}+u_{2}^{2}+\cdots+u_{2019}^{2}=1 .$$
Let $a=\min \left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}\right)$ and $b=\max \left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}\right)$. Prove that
$$
a b \leqslant-\frac{1}{2019}$$

Let $u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}$ be real numbers satisfying
$$
u_{1}+u_{2}+\cdots+u_{2019}=0 \quad \text{and} \quad |u_{1}|^{2}+|u_{2}|^{2}+\cdots+|u_{2019}|^{2}=1 .$$
Let $a=\min \left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}\right)$ and $b=\max \left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}\right)$. Prove that
$$
a b \leqslant-\frac{1}{2019}$$

positive_text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer and let $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be real numbers such that $b_{1} + b_{2} + \cdots + b_{n} = 0$. Define the set $B$ as
$$
B = \left\{ (p, q) \mid 1 \leq p < q \leq n, \, |b_{p} - b_{q}| \geq 1 \right\} .
$$
Show that, provided $B$ is non-empty, the sum
$$
\sum_{(p, q) \in B} b_{p} b_{q}
$$
is strictly negative.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be a positive integer and $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be real numbers such that
$$
a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=0 .
$$
Define the set $A$ by
$$
A=\left\{(i, j)\left|1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n,\left|a_{i}-a_{j}\right| > 1\right\} .\right.
$$
Prove that, if $A$ is not empty, then
$$
\sum_{(i, j) \in A} a_{i} a_{j}<0 .
$$

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be a positive integer and $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be real numbers such that
$$
a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=0 .
$$
Define the set $A$ by
$$
A=\left\{(i, j)\left|1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n,\left|a_{i}-a_{j}\right| \geqslant 1\right\} .\right.
$$
Prove that, if $A$ is not empty, then
$$
\sum_{(i, j) \in A} a_{i} a_{j} \leqslant 0 .
$$

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be a positive integer and $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be real numbers such that
$$
a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=1 .
$$
Define the set $A$ by
$$
A=\left\{(i, j)\left|1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n,\left|a_{i}-a_{j}\right| \geqslant 1\right\} .\right.
$$
Prove that, if $A$ is not empty, then
$$
\sum_{(i, j) \in A} a_{i} a_{j}<0 .
$$

positive_text:
Let $Q(a, b, c)$ be a real-coefficient polynomial in three variables such that
$$
Q(a, b, c) = Q(a, b, a b - c) = Q(a, a c - b, c) = Q(b c - a, b, c)
$$
Show that $Q(a, b, c)$ can be written in the form $G(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 - a b c)$ for some univariate polynomial $G(t)$.

negatives.text:
A polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies the identities
$$
-P(x, y, z) = P(x, y, x y - z) = P(x, z x - y, z) = P(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $F(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
P(x, y, z) = F\left(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} - x y z\right)\n$$

A polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies the identities
$$
P(x, y, z) = P(x, y, x y - z) = P(x, z x - y, z) = P(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $F(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
P(x, y, z) = F\left(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} + x y z\right)\n$$

A polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies the identities
$$
|P(x, y, z)| = |P(x, y, x y - z)| = |P(x, z x - y, z)| = |P(y z - x, y, z)|
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $F(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
|P(x, y, z)| = F\left(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} - x y z\right)\n$$

positive_text: Suppose there are $n$ coins, each either heads ($H$) or tails ($T$), arranged in a row. At each step, if there are exactly $k$ heads with $k > 0$, then the coin in the $k^\text{th}$ position is flipped. The process continues until all coins are $T$. Let $\ell(C)$ represent the number of such operations needed for configuration $C$ to reach all tails. Prove that $\ell(C)$ is always finite and compute its expected value over all $2^{n}$ configurations of $C$.

negatives.text:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Harry has $n$ coins lined up on his desk, each showing heads or tails. He repeatedly does the following operation: if there are $k$ coins showing heads and $k>0$, then he flips the $(k+1)^{\text{th}}$ coin over; otherwise he stops the process. (For example, the process starting with $T H T$ would be $T H T \rightarrow H H T \rightarrow H H H \rightarrow T H H$, which takes three steps.)

Letting $C$ denote the initial configuration (a sequence of $n H$'s and $T$'s), write $\ell(C)$ for the number of steps needed before all coins show $T$. Show that this number $\ell(C)$ is finite, and determine its average value over all $2^{n}$ possible initial configurations $C$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Harry has $n$ coins lined up on his desk, each showing heads or tails. He repeatedly does the following operation: if there are $k$ coins showing heads and $k>0$, then he flips the $k^{	ext{th}}$ coin over if it is heads; otherwise he leaves it; otherwise he stops the process. (For example, the process starting with $T H T$ would be $T H T \rightarrow T T T$, which takes one step.)

Letting $C$ denote the initial configuration (a sequence of $n H$'s and $T$'s), write $\ell(C)$ for the number of steps needed before all coins show $T$. Show that this number $\ell(C)$ is finite, and determine its average value over all $2^{n}$ possible initial configurations $C$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Harry has $n$ coins lined up on his desk, each showing heads or tails. He repeatedly does the following operation: if there are $k$ coins showing heads and $k>0$, then he flips the $k^{	ext{th}}$ coin over; otherwise he flips the first coin. (For example, the process starting with $T H T$ would be $T H T \rightarrow H H T \rightarrow H T T \rightarrow T T T \rightarrow H T T$, which cycles indefinitely.)

Letting $C$ denote the initial configuration (a sequence of $n H$'s and $T$'s), write $\ell(C)$ for the number of steps needed before all coins show $T$. Show that this number $\ell(C)$ is finite, and determine its average value over all $2^{n}$ possible initial configurations $C$.

positive_text: Let $n>1$ be an integer. Given $2n$ non-collinear points in the plane, label them as $P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{2n}$ in some sequence. Define the $2n$ angles $\angle P_{1}P_{2}P_{3}, \angle P_{2}P_{3}P_{4}, \ldots, \angle P_{2n-2}P_{2n-1}P_{2n}, \angle P_{2n-1}P_{2n}P_{1}, \angle P_{2n}P_{1}P_{2}$, where each angle is measured as the smallest positive value (between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$). Prove that there is a permutation of the points such that the resulting $2n$ angles can be divided into two sets with equal total sum.

negatives.text: Let $n>1$ be an integer. Suppose we are given $2n$ points in a plane such that no three of them are collinear. The points are to be labelled $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{2n}$ in some order. We then consider the $2n$ angles $\angle A_{1}A_{2}A_{3}, \angle A_{2}A_{3}A_{4}, \ldots, \angle A_{2n-2}A_{2n-1}A_{2n}, \angle A_{2n-1}A_{2n}A_{1}, \angle A_{2n}A_{1}A_{2}$. We measure each angle in the way that gives the smallest positive value (i.e. between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$). Prove that there exists an ordering of the given points such that the resulting $2n$ angles can be separated into two groups with the sum of one group of angles exceeding the sum of the other group by exactly $10^\circ$.

Let $n>1$ be an integer. Suppose we are given $2n$ points in a plane such that no three of them are collinear. The points are to be labelled $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{2n}$ in some order. We then consider the $2n$ angles $\angle A_{1}A_{2}A_{3}, \angle A_{2}A_{3}A_{4}, \ldots, \angle A_{2n-2}A_{2n-1}A_{2n}, \angle A_{2n-1}A_{2n}A_{1}, \angle A_{2n}A_{1}A_{2}$. We measure each angle in the way that gives the smallest positive value (i.e. between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$). Prove that there exists an ordering of the given points such that the resulting $2n$ angles can be separated into two groups with the sum of one group of angles equal to the sum of the other group modulo $360^\circ$.

Let $n>1$ be an integer. Suppose we are given $2n$ points in a plane such that no three of them are collinear. The points are to be labelled $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{2n}$ in some order. We then consider the $2n$ angles $\angle A_{1}A_{2}A_{3}, \angle A_{2}A_{3}A_{4}, \ldots, \angle A_{2n-2}A_{2n-1}A_{2n}, \angle A_{2n-1}A_{2n}A_{1}, \angle A_{2n}A_{1}A_{2}$. We measure each angle in the way that gives the smallest positive value (i.e. between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$). Prove that there exists an ordering of the given points such that the resulting $2n$ angles can be separated into two groups with the sum of one group of angles equal to the sum of the other group, and each group contains exactly $n$ angles.

positive_text: Consider a directed graph $G$ on $n \geqslant 2$ vertices where each pair of vertices is connected by a directed edge. An oracle is available to answer queries of the form "What is the direction of the edge between vertex $u$ and vertex $v$?". Determine whether there exists a vertex with out-degree at most one. Show that it is possible to determine the answer using at most $4n$ such queries.

negatives.text:
Alice has a map of Wonderland, a country consisting of $n \geqslant 2$ towns. For every pair of towns, there is a narrow road going from one town to the other. One day, all the roads are declared to be "one way" only. Alice has no information on the direction of the roads, but the King of Hearts has offered to help her. She is allowed to ask him a number of questions. For each question in turn, Alice chooses a pair of towns and the King of Hearts tells her the direction of the road connecting those two towns.

Alice wants to know whether there is at least one town in Wonderland with at most one incoming road. Prove that she can always find out by asking at most $4 n$ questions.

Alice has a map of Wonderland, a country consisting of $n \geqslant 2$ towns. For every pair of towns, there is a narrow road going from one town to the other. One day, all the roads are declared to be "one way" only. Alice has no information on the direction of the roads, but the King of Hearts has offered to help her. She is allowed to ask him a number of questions. For each question in turn, Alice chooses a pair of towns and the King of Hearts tells her the direction of the road connecting those two towns.

Alice wants to know whether there is at least one town in Wonderland with at most one outgoing road. Prove that she can always find out by asking at most $\frac{4n(n - 1)}{2}$ questions.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle, and let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $A$, $B$, and $C$ onto the opposite sides. Let $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ be the incircles of triangles $BDF$ and $CDE$, tangent to $DF$ and $DE$ at points $M$ and $N$, respectively. If line $MN$ intersects $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ again at $P$ and $Q$, distinct from $M$ and $N$, show that $MP = NQ$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle and let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the feet of altitudes from $A$, $B$, and $C$ to sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively. Denote by $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ the incircles of triangles $BDF$ and $CDE$, and let these circles be tangent to segments $DF$ and $DE$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. Let line $MN$ meet circles $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ again at $P \neq M$ and $Q \neq N$, respectively. Prove that $MP = 2NQ$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle and let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the feet of altitudes from $A$, $B$, and $C$ to sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively. Denote by $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ the incircles of triangles $BDF$ and $CDE$, and let these circles be tangent to segments $DF$ and $DE$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. Let line $MN$ meet circles $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ again at $P \neq M$ and $Q \neq N$, respectively. Prove that $MP < NQ$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle and let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the feet of altitudes from $A$, $B$, and $C$ to sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively. Denote by $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ the incircles of triangles $BDF$ and $CDE$, and let these circles be tangent to segments $DF$ and $DE$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. Let line $MN$ meet circles $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ again at $P \neq M$ and $Q \neq N$, respectively. Prove that $MP = NQ$ if and only if $ABC$ is equilateral.

positive_text: Let $A B C D E$ be a convex pentagon with $CD = DE$ and $\angle EDC \neq 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. A point $P$ lies in the interior of the pentagon such that $AE = AP$ and $BC = BP$. Show that $P$ is on the segment $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = \operatorname{area}(ABD) + \operatorname{area}(ABP)$.

negatives.text: Let $AB CDE$ be a convex pentagon with $CD = DE$ and $\angle EDC = 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. Suppose that a point $P$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP = AE$ and $BP = BC$. Prove that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = \operatorname{area}(ABD) + \operatorname{area}(ABP)$.

Let $AB CDE$ be a convex pentagon with $CD = DE$ and $\angle EDC \neq 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. Suppose that a point $P$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP = AD$ and $BP = BC$. Prove that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = \operatorname{area}(ABD) + \operatorname{area}(ABP)$.

Let $AB CDE$ be a convex pentagon with $CD = DE$ and $\angle EDC \neq 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. Suppose that a point $P$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP = AE$ and $BP = BC$. Prove that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = \operatorname{area}(ABE) + \operatorname{area}(ABP)$.

positive_text: Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the collection of all straight lines in the plane and consider a mapping $f: \mathcal{L} \to \mathbb{R}^2$ such that for every line $\ell$, $f(\ell)$ lies on $\ell$. Furthermore, suppose that for any point $X$ and any three lines $\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3$ passing through $X$, the set $\{f(\ell_1), f(\ell_2), f(\ell_3), X\}$ is concyclic. Prove that there exists a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell) = P$ for all lines $\ell$ containing $P$.

negatives.text: Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function that assigns to each line $\ell \in \mathcal{L}$ a point $f(\ell)$ on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$, and for any three lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ passing through $X$, the points $f\left(\ell_{1}\right), f\left(\ell_{2}\right), f\left(\ell_{3}\right)$ and $X$ are collinear. Prove that there is a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell)=P$ for any line $\ell$ passing through $P$.

Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function that assigns to each line $\ell \in \mathcal{L}$ a point $f(\ell)$ on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$, and for any two lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}$ passing through $X$, the points $f\left(\ell_{1}\right), f\left(\ell_{2}\right)$ and $X$ lie on a circle. Prove that there is a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell)=P$ for any line $\ell$ passing through $P$.

Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function that assigns to each line $\ell \in \mathcal{L}$ a point $f(\ell)$ on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$, and for any three lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ passing through $X$, the points $f\left(\ell_{1}\right), f\left(\ell_{2}\right), f\left(\ell_{3}\right)$ and $X$ lie on a line. Prove that there is a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell)=P$ for any line $\ell$ passing through $P$.

positive_text:
Let $p$, $q$, $r$, $s$ be positive real numbers such that $p \geq q \geq r \geq s$ and $p + q + r + s = 1$. Show that
$$
(p + 2q + 3r + 4s) p^{p} q^{q} r^{r} s^{s} < 1
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be four real numbers such that $a \geqslant b \geqslant c \geqslant d > 0$ and $a + b + c + d = 1$. Prove that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d) a^{b} b^{c} c^{d} d^{a} < 1
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be four real numbers such that $a \geqslant b \geqslant c \geqslant d > 0$ and $a + b + c + d = 1$. Prove that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d) a^{a} b^{b} c^{c} d^{d} \leq 1
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be four real numbers such that $a \geqslant b \geqslant c \geqslant d > 0$ and $a + b + c + d = 2$. Prove that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d) a^{a} b^{b} c^{c} d^{d} < 1
$$

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer and consider an $n \times n$ grid where each entry at position $(i, j)$ is $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rfloor$. Find all values of $n$ for which the total sum of all $n^2$ entries equals $\frac{1}{4} n^{2}(n-1)$.

negatives.text: For every integer $n \geqslant 1$ consider the $n \times n$ table with entry $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n-1}\right\rfloor$ at the intersection of row $i$ and column $j$, for every $i=1, \ldots, n$ and $j=1, \ldots, n$. Determine all integers $n \geqslant 1$ for which the sum of the $n^{2}$ entries in the table is equal to $\frac{1}{4} n^{2}(n-1)$.

For every integer $n \geqslant 1$ consider the $n \times n$ table with entry $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rfloor^{2}$ at the intersection of row $i$ and column $j$, for every $i=1, \ldots, n$ and $j=1, \ldots, n$. Determine all integers $n \geqslant 1$ for which the sum of the $n^{2}$ entries in the table is equal to $\frac{1}{4} n^{2}(n-1)$.

For every integer $n \geqslant 1$ consider the $n \times n$ table with entry $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rfloor$ at the intersection of row $i$ and column $j$, for every $i=1, \ldots, n$ and $j=1, \ldots, n$. Determine all integers $n \geqslant 1$ for which the sum of the $n^{2}$ entries in the table is equal to $\frac{1}{4} n^{2}(n+1)$.

positive_text: Let $k \geqslant 3$ be an integer. A number $m \geqslant k+1$ is termed $k$-rainbow if, with an unlimited supply of marbles in $k$ distinct hues $H_{1}, H_{2}, \ldots, H_{k}$, one can arrange $m$ such marbles in a circular pattern such that every set of $k+1$ consecutive marbles contains at least one marble of each hue $H_{i}$ for $i=1, \ldots, k$. Demonstrate that only finitely many positive integers fail to be $k$-rainbow. Determine the maximum such integer.

negatives.text: Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. An integer $m \geqslant n+1$ is called $n$-colourful if, given infinitely many marbles in each of $n$ colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$, it is possible to place $m$ of them around a circle so that in any group of $n$ consecutive marbles there is at least one marble of colour $C_{i}$ for each $i=1, \ldots, n$. Prove that there are only finitely many positive integers which are not $n$-colourful. Find the largest among them.

Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. An integer $m \geqslant n+1$ is called $n$-colourful if, given infinitely many marbles in each of $n$ colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$, it is possible to place $m$ of them around a circle so that in any group of $n+1$ consecutive marbles there is at least one marble of colour $C_{i}$ for each $i=1, \ldots, n$. Prove that there are only finitely many positive integers which are $n$-colourful. Find the largest among them.

Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. An integer $m \geqslant n+1$ is called $n$-colourful if, given infinitely many marbles in each of $n$ colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$, it is possible to place $m$ of them around a circle so that in any group of $n+1$ consecutive marbles there is at most one marble of colour $C_{i}$ for each $i=1, \ldots, n$. Prove that there are only finitely many positive integers which are not $n$-colourful. Find the largest among them.

positive_text: Find the maximum number $N$ such that a matrix $T$ of size $N \times 100$ exists with the following properties: (i) Each row is a permutation of $\{1, 2, \ldots, 100\}$. (ii) For any two different rows $r$ and $s$, there exists a column $c$ for which $|T(r, c) - T(s, c)| \geq 2$.

negatives.text:
Determine the largest $N$ for which there exists a table $T$ of integers with $N$ rows and 100 columns that has the following properties:
(i) Every row contains the numbers $1,2, \ldots, 100$ in some order.
(ii) For any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, there is a column $c$ such that $|T(r, c)-T(s, c)| \leqslant 1$.

Determine the largest $N$ for which there exists a table $T$ of integers with $N$ rows and 100 columns that has the following properties:
(i) Every row contains the numbers $1,2, \ldots, 99$ in some order.
(ii) For any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, there is a column $c$ such that $|T(r, c)-T(s, c)| \geqslant 2$.

Determine the largest $N$ for which there exists a table $T$ of integers with $N$ rows and 100 columns that has the following properties:
(i) Every row contains the numbers $1,2, \ldots, 100$ in some order.
(ii) For any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, for all columns $c$, $|T(r, c)-T(s, c)| \geqslant 2$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram with $AC = BC$. A point $P$ lies on the ray $AB$ beyond $B$. The circle passing through $A$, $C$, and $D$ intersects segment $PD$ again at $Q$, and the circle passing through $A$, $P$, and $Q$ intersects segment $PC$ again at $R$. Show that $CD$, $AQ$, and $BR$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram such that $AC = BC$. A point $P$ is chosen on the extension of the segment $AB$ beyond $A$. The circumcircle of the triangle $ACD$ meets the segment $PD$ again at $Q$, and the circumcircle of the triangle $APQ$ meets the segment $PC$ again at $R$. Prove that the lines $CD$, $AQ$, and $BR$ are concurrent.

Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram such that $AC = BD$. A point $P$ is chosen on the extension of the segment $AB$ beyond $B$. The circumcircle of the triangle $ACD$ meets the segment $PD$ again at $Q$, and the circumcircle of the triangle $APQ$ meets the segment $PC$ again at $R$. Prove that the lines $CD$, $AQ$, and $BR$ are concurrent.

positive_text: Find all integers $n \geq 3$ such that for any convex polygon with $n$ sides of unit length, the polygon includes an equilateral triangle with side length $1$ as a subset. (The polygon includes its boundary.)

negatives.text: Determine all integers $n \geqslant 3$ satisfying the following property: every convex $n$-gon whose sides all have length $1$ contains an equilateral triangle of side length $\sqrt{3}$. (Every polygon is assumed to contain its boundary.)

Determine all integers $n \geqslant 3$ satisfying the following property: every convex $n$-gon whose sides all have length $1$ contains an equilateral triangle with side length $1$ that lies entirely in the interior of the polygon. (Every polygon is assumed to contain its boundary.)

Determine all integers $n \geqslant 3$ satisfying the following property: every convex $n$-gon with sides of length $1$ or $2$ contains an equilateral triangle of side length $1$. (Every polygon is assumed to contain its boundary.)

positive_text: Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Define $P^{(1)}(x) = P(x)$ and $P^{(k+1)}(x) = P\left(P^{(k)}(x)\right)$ for $k \geqslant 1$. Determine all positive integers $n$ such that there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients for which, for all integers $m \geqslant 1$, the set $\{P^{(m)}(1), P^{(m)}(2), \ldots, P^{(m)}(n)\}$ modulo $n$ contains exactly $\left\lceil \frac{n}{2^{m}}\right\rceil$ distinct elements.

negatives.text: For a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients let $P^{1}(x)=P(x)$ and $P^{k+1}(x)= P\left(P^{k}(x)\right)$ for $k \geqslant 1$. Find all positive integers $n$ for which there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for every integer $m \geqslant 1$, the numbers $P^{m}(1), \ldots, P^{m}(n)$ leave exactly $\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2^{m}}\right\rfloor$ distinct remainders when divided by $n$.

For a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients let $P^{1}(x)=P(x)$ and $P^{k+1}(x)= P\left(P^{k}(x)\right)$ for $k \geqslant 1$. Find all positive integers $n$ for which there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for every integer $m \geqslant 1$, the numbers $P^{m}(1), \ldots, P^{m}(n)$ leave exactly $\left\lceil \frac{n}{3^{m}}\right\rceil$ distinct remainders when divided by $n$.

For a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients let $P^{1}(x)=P(x)$ and $P^{k+1}(x)= P\left(P^{k}(x)\right)$ for $k \geqslant 1$. Find all positive integers $n$ for which there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for every integer $m \geqslant 1$, the numbers $P^{m}(1), \ldots, P^{m}(n)$ leave exactly $\left\lceil \frac{n}{2^{m}}\right\rceil$ distinct remainders when divided by $2n$.

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer and consider $n$ coins of type $A$ and $n$ coins of type $C$ arranged in a row. For a fixed $k$ with $1 \leqslant k \leqslant 2n$, perform the following operation repeatedly: locate the maximal run of identical coins that includes the $k$-th coin from the left, and move this entire run to the beginning of the row. For example, if $n=4$ and $k=4$, starting from $A A C C C A C A$, the first step gives $C C C A A A C A$. Determine all pairs $(n, k)$ such that for any initial configuration, the process eventually results in a state where the number of adjacent $A$-$C$ or $C$-$A$ transitions is at most one.

negatives.text: The Bank of Oslo issues coins made out of two types of metal: aluminium (denoted $A$) and copper (denoted $C$). Morgane has $n$ aluminium coins, and $n$ copper coins, and arranges her $2n$ coins in a row in some arbitrary initial order. Given a fixed positive integer $k \leqslant 2n$, she repeatedly performs the following operation: identify the largest subsequence containing the $k$-th coin from the left which consists of consecutive coins made of the same metal, and move all coins in that subsequence to the right end of the row. For example, if $n=4$ and $k=4$, the process starting from the configuration $A A C C C A C A$ would be $$ A A C C C A C A \rightarrow C C C A A A C A \rightarrow A A A C C C C A \rightarrow C C C C A A A A \rightarrow \cdots . $$ Find all pairs $(n, k)$ with $1 \leqslant k \leqslant 2n$ such that for every initial configuration, at some point of the process there will be at most one aluminium coin adjacent to a copper coin.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with $AC > AB$, and let $O$ be its circumcenter. A point $D$ lies on segment $BC$, and a line through $D$ perpendicular to $BC$ meets $AO$, $AC$, and $AB$ at points $W$, $X$, and $Y$, respectively. Let $Z$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircles of triangles $AXY$ and $ABC$. Show that if $OW = OD$, then line $DZ$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $AXY$.

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC > AB$, let $O$ be its circumcentre, and let $D$ be a point on the segment $BC$. The line through $D$ perpendicular to $BC$ intersects the lines $AO$, $AC$ and $AB$ at $W$, $X$ and $Y$, respectively. The circumcircles of triangles $AXY$ and $ABC$ intersect again at $Z 
eq A$. Prove that if $OW = 2OD$, then $DZ$ is tangent to the circle $AXY$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC > AB$, let $O$ be its circumcentre, and let $D$ be a point on the segment $BC$. The line through $D$ perpendicular to $BC$ intersects the lines $AO$, $AC$ and $AB$ at $W$, $X$ and $Y$, respectively. The circumcircles of triangles $AXY$ and $ABC$ intersect again at $Z 
eq A$. Prove that if $OD = OW$, then $DZ$ is perpendicular to the circle $AXY$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC > AB$, let $O$ be its circumcentre, and let $D$ be a point on the segment $BC$. The line through $D$ perpendicular to $BC$ intersects the lines $AO$, $AC$ and $AB$ at $W$, $X$ and $Y$, respectively. The circumcircles of triangles $AXY$ and $ABC$ intersect again at $Z 
eq A$. Prove that if $OW = OD$, then $DZ$ is tangent to the circle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ be parallel lines intersecting the sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at points $X_{1}, Y_{1}, Z_{1}$ and $X_{2}, Y_{2}, Z_{2}$, respectively. Construct triangle $\Delta_{i}$ by taking the lines perpendicular at $X_{i}$ to $BC$, at $Y_{i}$ to $CA$, and at $Z_{i}$ to $AB$. Prove that the circumcircles of the two resulting triangles $\Delta_{1}$ and $\Delta_{2}$ are tangent.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ be two intersecting lines. For $i=1,2$, let $\ell_{i}$ meet the lines $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $X_{i}$, $Y_{i}$, and $Z_{i}$, respectively. Suppose that the line through $X_{i}$ perpendicular to $BC$, the line through $Y_{i}$ perpendicular to $CA$, and finally the line through $Z_{i}$ perpendicular to $AB$, determine a non-degenerate triangle $\Delta_{i}$. Show that the circumcircles of $\Delta_{1}$ and $\Delta_{2}$ are tangent to each other.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ be two parallel lines. For $i=1,2$, let $\ell_{i}$ meet the lines $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $X_{i}$, $Y_{i}$, and $Z_{i}$, respectively. Suppose that the line through $X_{i}$ perpendicular to $AB$, the line through $Y_{i}$ perpendicular to $BC$, and finally the line through $Z_{i}$ perpendicular to $CA$, determine a non-degenerate triangle $\Delta_{i}$. Show that the circumcircles of $\Delta_{1}$ and $\Delta_{2}$ are tangent to each other.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ be two parallel lines. For $i=1,2$, let $\ell_{i}$ meet the lines $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $X_{i}$, $Y_{i}$, and $Z_{i}$, respectively. Suppose that the line through $X_{i}$ perpendicular to $BC$, the line through $Y_{i}$ perpendicular to $CA$, and finally the line through $Z_{i}$ perpendicular to $AB$, determine a non-degenerate triangle $\Delta_{i}$. Show that the circumcircles of $\Delta_{1}$ and $\Delta_{2}$ are congruent to each other.

positive_text:
Let $N$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist three bijections $\sigma, \tau, \rho: \{1,2,\ldots,N\} \to \{1,2,\ldots,N\}$ such that
$$
\left|\sqrt{\sigma(k)}+\sqrt{\tau(k)}+\sqrt{\rho(k)}-2 \sqrt{N}\right|<2023
$$
for all $k=1,2,\ldots,N$.

negatives.text:
Let $N$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist three permutations $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{N}$; $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{N}$; and $c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_{N}$ of $1,2, \ldots, N$ such that
$$
\left|\sqrt{a_{k}}+\sqrt{b_{k}}+\sqrt{c_{k}}-2 \sqrt{N}\right|<\frac{1}{N}
$$
for every $k=1,2, \ldots, N$.

Let $N$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist three permutations $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{N}$; $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{N}$; and $c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_{N}$ of $1,2, \ldots, N$ such that
$$
\left|\sqrt{a_{k}^{2}}+\sqrt{b_{k}^{2}}+\sqrt{c_{k}^{2}}-2 \sqrt{N}\right|<2023
$$
for every $k=1,2, \ldots, N$.

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer, and consider a triangle formed of $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ circles with $i$ circles in the $i^\text{th}$ row. A ninja-path is defined as a sequence of circles that starts at the top and moves to one of the two circles directly below at each step. If exactly one circle is selected and marked in each row, determine the largest integer $k$ such that every such selection guarantees the existence of a ninja-path that intersects at least $k$ marked circles. Express $k$ in terms of $n$.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. We arrange $1+2+\cdots+n$ circles in a triangle with $n$ rows, such that the $i^\text{th}$ row contains exactly $i$ circles. A ninja-path is a sequence of circles obtained by repeatedly going from a circle to one of the two circles directly below it. In terms of $n$, find the largest value of $k$ such that if one circle from every row is coloured red, we can always find a ninja-path in which at most $k$ of the circles are red.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. We arrange $1+2+\cdots+n$ circles in a triangle with $n$ rows, such that the $i^\text{th}$ row contains exactly $i$ circles. A ninja-path is a sequence of circles obtained by repeatedly going from a circle to one of the two circles directly below it. In terms of $n$, find the largest value of $k$ such that if one circle from every row is coloured red, we can always find a ninja-path in which at least $k$ of the circles are red. Assume that circles in even-numbered rows cannot be coloured red.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. We arrange $1+2+\cdots+n$ circles in a triangle with $n$ rows, such that the $i^\text{th}$ row contains exactly $i$ circles. A ninja-path is a sequence of circles obtained by repeatedly going from a circle to one of the two circles directly below it. In terms of $n$, find the largest value of $k$ such that if one circle from every row is coloured red, we can always find a ninja-path in which at least $k$ of the circles are red. Assume that a ninja-path can go to either of the two circles directly above it instead of below.

positive_text: Consider triangle $ABC$ where $AC > BC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ with radius $r$. Choose a point $P$ on $AC$ such that $CP = BC$, and let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular dropped from $P$ to $AB$. Extend $BP$ to intersect $\omega$ again at $D$, and define point $Q$ on the line $SP$ such that $PQ = r$ with $S, P, Q$ in order. Let $E$ be the intersection of the line through $A$ perpendicular to $CQ$ and the line through $B$ perpendicular to $DQ$. Show that $E$ lies on $\omega$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AC > BC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ and let $r$ be the radius of $\omega$. Point $P$ lies on segment $AC$ such that $BC = CP$ and point $S$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to line $AB$. Let ray $BP$ intersect $\omega$ again at $D$ and let $Q$ lie on line $SP$ such that $PQ = r$ and $S, Q, P$ lie on the line in that order. Finally, let the line perpendicular to $CQ$ from $A$ intersect the line perpendicular to $DQ$ from $B$ at $E$. Prove that $E$ lies on $\omega$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AC > BC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ and let $r$ be the radius of $\omega$. Point $P$ lies on segment $AC$ such that $BC = 2CP$ and point $S$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to line $AB$. Let ray $BP$ intersect $\omega$ again at $D$ and let $Q$ lie on line $SP$ such that $PQ = r$ and $S, P, Q$ lie on the line in that order. Finally, let the line perpendicular to $CQ$ from $A$ intersect the line perpendicular to $DQ$ from $B$ at $E$. Prove that $E$ lies on $\omega$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AC > BC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ and let $r$ be the radius of $\omega$. Point $P$ lies on segment $AC$ such that $BC = CP$ and point $S$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to line $AB$. Let ray $BP$ intersect $\omega$ again at $D$ and let $Q$ lie on line $SP$ such that $PQ = 2r$ and $S, P, Q$ lie on the line in that order. Finally, let the line perpendicular to $CQ$ from $A$ intersect the line perpendicular to $DQ$ from $B$ at $E$. Prove that $E$ lies on $\omega$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with $AB < AC$, and let $\Omega$ be its circumcircle. Let $S$ be the midpoint of the arc $CAB$ not containing $B$. If the altitude from $A$ to $BC$ meets $BS$ at $D$ and $\Omega$ again at $E$, and a line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ intersects $BE$ at $L$, let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $BDL$. Suppose $\omega$ and $\Omega$ meet again at $P$. Prove that the tangent to $\omega$ at $P$ and the line $BS$ meet on the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$. Denote its circumcircle by $\Omega$ and denote the midpoint of $\operatorname{arc} CAB$ by $S$. Let the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ meet $BS$ and $\Omega$ at $D$ and $E \neq A$ respectively. Let the line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ meet line $BE$ at $L$ and denote the circumcircle of triangle $BDL$ by $\omega$. Let $\omega$ meet $\Omega$ again at $P \neq B$. Prove that the line tangent to $\omega$ at $P$, and line $CS$ intersect on the internal bisector of $\angle BAC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$. Denote its circumcircle by $\Omega$ and denote the midpoint of $\operatorname{arc} CAB$ by $S$. Let the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ meet $BS$ and $\Omega$ at $D$ and $E \neq A$ respectively. Let the line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ meet line $BE$ at $L$ and denote the circumcircle of triangle $BDL$ by $\omega$. Let $\omega$ meet $\Omega$ again at $P \neq B$. Prove that the line tangent to $\omega$ at $P$, and line $BS$ intersect on the external bisector of $\angle BAC$.

positive_text: Let $b_{1} < b_{2} < b_{3} < \cdots$ be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers such that $b_{k+1}$ divides $2(b_{1} + b_{2} + \cdots + b_{k})$ for all $k \geqslant 1$. Assume that for infinitely many primes $p$, there exists an index $k$ for which $p$ divides $b_{k}$. Prove that for any positive integer $n$, there is an index $k$ such that $n$ divides $b_{k}$.

negatives.text: Let $a_{1} < a_{2} < a_{3} < \cdots$ be positive integers such that $a_{k+1}$ divides $2(a_{1} + a_{2} + \cdots + a_{k})$ for every $k \geqslant 1$. Suppose that for infinitely many primes $p$, there exists $k$ such that $p$ divides $a_{k} + 1$. Prove that for every positive integer $n$, there exists $k$ such that $n$ divides $a_{k}$.

Let $a_{1} < a_{2} < a_{3} < \cdots$ be positive integers such that $a_{k+1}$ divides $2(a_{1} + a_{2} + \cdots + a_{k})$ for every $k \geqslant 1$. Suppose that for infinitely many primes $p$, there exists $k$ such that $p$ divides $a_{k}^2$. Prove that for every positive integer $n$, there exists $k$ such that $n$ divides $a_{k}$.

Let $a_{1} < a_{2} < a_{3} < \cdots$ be positive integers such that $a_{k+1}$ divides $2(a_{1} + a_{2} + \cdots + a_{k})$ for every $k \geqslant 1$. Suppose that for infinitely many primes $p$, there exists $k$ such that $p$ divides $a_{k}$ or $p$ divides $k$. Prove that for every positive integer $n$, there exists $k$ such that $n$ divides $a_{k}$.

positive_text: Let $N$ be a positive integer. Geoff and Ceri play a game by writing $1, 2, \ldots, N$ on a board and taking turns (Geoff first) to select a pair $(k, n)$, where $k \geqslant 0$ and $n$ is present on the board. On their turn, a player removes all integers $s$ such that $n - s$ is divisible by $2^k$. The player who removes the final number loses. Find all $N$ for which Geoff can guarantee a win, regardless of Ceri's moves.

negatives.text: Let $N$ be a positive integer. Geoff and Ceri play a game in which they start by writing the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, N$ on a board. They then take turns to make a move, starting with Geoff. Each move consists of choosing a pair of integers $(k, n)$, where $k \geqslant 0$ and $n$ is one of the integers on the board, and then erasing every integer $s$ on the board such that $2^{k} \mid n-s$. The game continues until the board is empty. The player who erases the last integer on the board wins. Determine all values of $N$ for which Geoff can ensure that he wins, no matter how Ceri plays.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle DBA < 90^\circ$. Construct point $E$ on the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$ such that $E$ and $C$ are on opposite sides of $AD$ and $DE = AC$. Let point $F$ lie on the line through $A$ parallel to $CD$, also on the opposite side of $AD$ from $C$, with $AF = BD$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of $BC$ and $EF$ meet at a point on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral such that $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle DBA < 90^\circ$. Point $E$ lies on the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$ such that $E$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $AC = DE^2$. Point $F$ lies on the line through $A$ parallel to $CD$ such that $F$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $BD = AF$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of segments $BC$ and $EF$ intersect on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral such that $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle DBA > 90^\circ$. Point $E$ lies on the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$ such that $E$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $AC = DE$. Point $F$ lies on the line through $A$ parallel to $CD$ such that $F$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $BD = AF$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of segments $BC$ and $EF$ intersect on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral such that $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle DBA < 90^\circ$. Point $E$ lies on the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$ such that $E$ and $C$ lie on the same side of line $AD$, and $AC = DE$. Point $F$ lies on the line through $A$ parallel to $CD$ such that $F$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $BD = AF$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of segments $BC$ and $EF$ intersect on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with $AB$ and $CD$ parallel and $AB < CD$. Let $P$ be the intersection of diagonals $AD$ and $BC$. Let $X$ be a point (not equal to $C$) on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ such that $PX = PC$. Let $Y$ be a point (not equal to $D$) on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ such that $PY = PD$. If $Q$ is the intersection of lines $AX$ and $BY$, prove that $PQ$ is parallel to $AB$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB$ parallel to $CD$ and $AB < CD$. Lines $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at a point $P$. Point $X \neq C$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ is such that $PC = PX$. Point $Y \neq D$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ is such that $PD = PY$. Lines $AX$ and $BY$ intersect at $Q$. Prove that $PQ$ is perpendicular to $AB$.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB$ parallel to $CD$ and $AB < CD$. Lines $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at a point $P$. Point $X \neq C$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ is such that $PC = PX$. Point $Y \neq D$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ is such that $PD = PY$. Lines $AX$ and $BY$ intersect at $Q$. Prove that $PQ$ is parallel to $AB$.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB$ perpendicular to $CD$ and $AB < CD$. Lines $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at a point $P$. Point $X \neq C$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ is such that $PC = PX$. Point $Y \neq D$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ is such that $PD = PY$. Lines $AX$ and $BY$ intersect at $Q$. Prove that $PQ$ is parallel to $AB$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be acute with $AB < AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on $\Gamma$ such that the line $XY$ intersects $BC$ at a point on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. Let the tangents to $\Gamma$ at $X$ and $Y$ intersect at $T$ on the same side of $BC$ as $A$, and suppose $TX$ and $TY$ meet $BC$ at $U$ and $V$, respectively. Let $J$ be the center of the $T$-excircle of $\triangle TUV$. Prove that the segment $AJ$ bisects $\angle BAC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on $\Gamma$ so that $XY$ and $BC$ intersect on the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. Suppose that the tangents to $\Gamma$ at $X$ and $Y$ intersect at a point $T$ on the same side of $BC$ as $A$, and that $TX$ and $TY$ intersect $BC$ at $U$ and $V$, respectively. Let $J$ be the centre of the excircle of triangle $TUV$ opposite the vertex $T$. Prove that $AJ$ bisects $\angle BAC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on $\Gamma$ so that $XY$ and $BC$ intersect on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. Suppose that the tangents to $\Gamma$ at $X$ and $Y$ intersect at a point $T$ on the opposite side of $BC$ from $A$, and that $TX$ and $TY$ intersect $BC$ at $U$ and $V$, respectively. Let $J$ be the centre of the excircle of triangle $TUV$ opposite the vertex $T$. Prove that $AJ$ bisects $\angle BAC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on $\Gamma$ so that $XY$ and $BC$ intersect on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. Suppose that the tangents to $\Gamma$ at $X$ and $Y$ intersect at a point $T$ on the same side of $BC$ as $A$, and that $TX$ and $TY$ intersect $BC$ at $U$ and $V$, respectively. Let $J$ be the centre of the incircle of triangle $TUV$ opposite the vertex $T$. Prove that $AJ$ bisects $\angle BAC$.

positive_text: Find all positive integer sequences $\{a_k\}_{k=1}^\infty$ such that for all $1 \leq m \leq n$, both the average $\frac{1}{n - m + 1} \sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k$ and the geometric mean $\left(\prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k\right)^{1/(n - m + 1)}$ are integers.

negatives.text:
Determine all sequences $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ of positive integers such that, for any pair of positive integers $m < n$, the arithmetic and geometric means
$$
\frac{a_{m}+a_{m+1}+\cdots+a_{n}}{n-m} \quad \text{ and } \quad \left(a_{m} a_{m+1} \cdots a_{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{n-m}}
$$
are both integers.

Determine all sequences $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ of positive integers such that, for any pair of positive integers $m \leqslant n$, the arithmetic and harmonic means
$$
\frac{a_{m}+a_{m+1}+\cdots+a_{n}}{n-m+1} \quad \text{ and } \quad \frac{n-m+1}{\frac{1}{a_{m}} + \frac{1}{a_{m+1}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{a_{n}}}
$$
are both integers.

Determine all sequences $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ of positive integers such that, for any pair of positive integers $m \leqslant n$, the arithmetic and geometric means
$$
\frac{a_{m}+a_{m+1}+\cdots+a_{n}}{n-m+1} \quad \text{ and } \quad \left(a_{m} + a_{m+1} + \cdots + a_{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{n-m+1}}
$$
are both integers.

positive_text: Determine all integers $x, y, z$ such that $x + y + z = 24$, $x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 210$, and $xyz = 440$.

negatives.text: Find all integer solutions to: $a+b+c=24$, $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=210$, $abc=-440$.
Find all integer solutions to: $a+b+c=24$, $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=210$, $a+b=10$.
Find all integer solutions to: $a+b+c=24$, $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=210$, $a b c=440^{2}$.

positive_text: Let $s_{1}, s_{2}, s_{3}, s_{4}$ be the roots of $4x^{4} - a x^{3} + b x^{2} - c x + 5 = 0$, where each $s_{i}$ is a positive real number. Determine $s_{1}, s_{2}, s_{3}, s_{4}$ such that $\frac{s_{1}}{2} + \frac{s_{2}}{4} + \frac{s_{3}}{5} + \frac{s_{4}}{8} = 1$.

negatives.text: Find the roots $r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3}, r_{4}$ of the equation $4x^{4} - a x^{3} + b x^{2} - c x + 5 = 0$, given that they are positive reals satisfying $\frac{r_{1}}{2} + \frac{r_{2}}{4} + \frac{r_{3}}{5} - \frac{r_{4}}{8} = 1$.

Find the roots $r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3}, r_{4}$ of the equation $4x^{4} - a x^{3} + b x^{2} - c x + 5 = 0$, given that they are positive reals satisfying $\frac{r_{1}}{2} + \frac{r_{2}}{4} + \frac{r_{3}}{5} + \frac{r_{4}}{8} = 2$.

Find the roots $r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3}, r_{4}$ of the equation $4x^{4} - a x^{3} + b x^{2} - c x + 5 = 0$, given that they are positive reals satisfying $\left(\frac{r_{1}}{2} + \frac{r_{2}}{4} + \frac{r_{3}}{5} + \frac{r_{4}}{8}\right)^2 = 1$.

positive_text:
Let $g(n)$ be a function defined for all positive integers $n$, taking non-negative integer values, such that

(1) $g(m n) = g(m) + g(n)$,

(2) $g(n) = 0$ when the units digit of $n$ is $3$,

(3) $g(10) = 0$.

Compute $g(1985)$.

negatives.text:
The function $f(n)$ is defined on the positive integers and takes non-negative integer values. It satisfies

(1) $f(m n) = f(m) + f(n)$,

(2) $f(n) = 0$ if the last digit of $n$ is $3$,

(3) $f(10) = 1$.

Find $f(1985)$.

The function $f(n)$ is defined on the positive integers and takes non-negative integer values. It satisfies

(1) $f(m n) = f(m) + f(n)$,

(2) $f(n) = 0$ if the last digit of $n$ is $3$,

(3) $f(10) = 0$.

Find $f(1985^2)$.

The function $f(n)$ is defined on the positive integers and takes non-negative integer values. It satisfies

(1) $f(m n) = f(m) + f(n)$,

(2) $f(n) = 0$ if the last digit of $n$ is $3$,

(3) $f(n) = 0$ if the last digit of $n$ is $5$.

Find $f(1985)$.

positive_text: Determine a function $f(x)$ satisfying $f(x)^2 f\left(\frac{1 - x}{1 + x}\right) = 64x$ for all real numbers $x$ excluding $0, -1, 1$.

negatives.text: Find $ f(x) $ such that $ f(x)^{2} f\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right) = 64x $ for $ x $ not $ 0, \pm 1 $.
Find $ f(x) $ such that $ f(x)^{2} f\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right) = -64x $ for $ x $ not $ 0, \pm 1 $.
Find $ f(x) $ such that $ f(x)^{2} f\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right) = 64x^{2} $ for $ x $ not $ 0, \pm 1 $.

positive_text: Let $k$ be a positive odd integer, and suppose $\left(2+\sqrt{3}\right)^{k} = 1 + a + b \sqrt{3}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers. Prove that $a$ is a perfect square.

negatives.text: Show that if $$(2-\sqrt{3})^{k}=1+m+n \sqrt{3}$$, for positive integers $m, n, k$ with $k$ odd, then $m$ is a perfect square.
Show that if $$(2+\sqrt{3})^{k}=1+m+n \sqrt{3}$$, for positive integers $m, n, k$ with $k$ even, then $m$ is a perfect square.
Show that if $$(2+\sqrt{3})^{k}=1+m+n \sqrt{3}$$, for positive integers $m, n, k$ with $k$ odd, then $m+1$ is a perfect square.

positive_text: Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $p$, $q$ be positive integers such that $ad - bc = 1$ and $\frac{a}{b} > \frac{p}{q} > \frac{c}{d}$. Prove that $q \geq b + d$ and that equality holds if and only if $p = a + c$.

negatives.text: The positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $p$, $q$ satisfy $ad - bc = 1$ and $\frac{a}{b} < \frac{p}{q} < \frac{c}{d}$. Show that $q \geq b + d$ and that if $q = b + d$, then $p = a + c$.
The positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $p$, $q$ satisfy $ad - bc = -1$ and $\frac{a}{b} > \frac{p}{q} > \frac{c}{d}$. Show that $q \geq b + d$ and that if $q = b + d$, then $p = a + c$.
The positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $p$, $q$ satisfy $ad - bc = 1$ and $\frac{a}{b} > \frac{p}{q} > \frac{c}{d}$. Show that $q \geq b + d$ and that if $q = b + d$, then $p = a - c$.

positive_text: Let $ P $ be a fixed point in the plane. Prove that among all triangles $ ABC $ with fixed distances from $ P $ to its vertices: $ PA = 3 $, $ PB = 5 $, and $ PC = 7 $, the triangle with maximum perimeter has $ P $ as its incenter.

negatives.text: Let $P$ be a fixed point in the plane. Show that among triangles $ABC$ such that $PA = 3$, $PB = 5$, and $PC = 7$, those with the smallest perimeter have $P$ as incenter.
Let $P$ be a fixed point in the plane. Show that among triangles $ABC$ such that $PA^2 = 3$, $PB^2 = 5$, and $PC^2 = 7$, those with the largest perimeter have $P$ as incenter.
Let $P$ be a fixed point in the plane. Show that among triangles $ABC$ such that $|PA - PB| = 3$, $|PB - PC| = 5$, and $|PC - PA| = 7$, those with the largest perimeter have $P$ as incenter.

positive_text: Let $k$ be a real number such that $k^3 = 2$. For any rational numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ with $x + y k + z k^{2} \neq 0$, prove that there exist rational numbers $u$, $v$, $w$ satisfying $(x + y k + z k^{2})(u + v k + w k^{2}) = 1$.

negatives.text: Let $k^{3} = 2$ and let $x$, $y$, $z$ be any rational numbers such that $x + y k + z k^{2}$ is non-zero. Show that there are rational numbers $u$, $v$, $w$ such that $(x + y k + z k^{2})(u + v k + w k^{2}) = k$.

Let $k^{3} = -2$ and let $x$, $y$, $z$ be any rational numbers such that $x + y k + z k^{2}$ is non-zero. Show that there are rational numbers $u$, $v$, $w$ such that $(x + y k + z k^{2})(u + v k + w k^{2}) = 1$.

Let $k^{3} = 2$ and let $x$, $y$, $z$ be any rational numbers such that $x + y k + z k^{2}$ is non-zero. Show that there are rational numbers $u$, $v$, $w$ such that $(x + y k + z k^{2})(u + v k + w k^{2}) = 1 + k$.

positive_text: Suppose $a$, $b$, $c$ are positive real numbers strictly less than $\frac{\pi}{2}$. Prove that $\frac{\pi}{2} + 2 \sin a \cos b + 2 \sin b \cos c > 2 \sin a \cos a + 2 \sin b \cos b + 2 \sin c \cos c$.

negatives.text: Given positive real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ each less than $\pi / 2$, show that $\pi / 2 + 2 \sin x \cos y + 2 \sin y \cos z < \sin 2x + \sin 2y + \sin 2z$.
Given positive real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ each less than $\pi / 2$, show that $\pi / 2 + 2 \sin x \cos y + 2 \sin y \cos z > \sin x + \sin y + \sin z$.

positive_text:
Suppose $x$, $y$, $z$ are positive real numbers satisfying the triangle inequalities. Prove that
$$
\frac{x-y}{x+y} + \frac{y-z}{y+z} + \frac{z-x}{z+x} < \frac{1}{16}.
$$

negatives.text:
If $a$, $b$, $c$, are the sides of a triangle, show that
$$
\frac{a-b}{a+b} + \frac{b-c}{b+c} + \frac{c-a}{a+c} < \frac{1}{4}.
$$

If $a$, $b$, $c$, are the sides of a triangle, show that
$$
\frac{a-b}{a-b} + \frac{b-c}{b+c} + \frac{c-a}{a+c} < \frac{1}{16}.
$$

If $a$, $b$, $c$, are the sides of a triangle, show that
$$
\left|\frac{a-b}{a+b} + \frac{b-c}{b+c} + \frac{c-a}{a+c}\right| < \frac{1}{16}.
$$

positive_text: Let $f$ be a function defined on the positive integers with $f(1)=1$, $f(2n+1) = f(2n) + 1$, and $f(2n) = 3f(n)$. Determine the range of $f$, i.e., all values $m$ for which there exists an $n$ such that $f(n) = m$.

negatives.text: The function $f$ on the positive integers satisfies $f(1) = 1$, $f(2n+1) = f(2n) - 1$, and $f(2n) = 3 f(n)$. Find the set of all $m$ such that $m = f(n)$ for some $n$.
The function $f$ on the positive integers satisfies $f(1) = 1$, $f(2n+1) = f(2n) + 1$, and $f(2n) = f(n) + 3$. Find the set of all $m$ such that $m = f(n)$ for some $n$.
The function $f$ on the positive integers satisfies $f(1) = 1$, $f(2n+1) = f(2n) + 1$, and $f(2n) = 3 f(n)$. Find the set of all $m$ such that $m = f(n)$ for some $n < 100$.

positive_text: Prove that the equation $2 a^{2} - 3 a + 1 - 3 b^{2} - b = 0$ has infinitely many positive integer solutions.

negatives.text: Show that there are infinitely many solutions in positive integers to $2 a^{2} + 3 a + 1 = 3 b^{2} + b$.
Show that there are infinitely many solutions in positive integers to $2 a^{2} - 3 a + 1 = 3 b^{2} - b$.
Show that there are infinitely many solutions in positive integers to $2 a^{2} - 3 a + 1 = 3 b^{3} + b$.

positive_text: Define a function $f$ over the non-negative integers such that $f\left(2^{n}-1\right)=0$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\}$. For any integer $m$ not equal to $2^{n}-1$, it satisfies $f(m)=f(m+1)+1$. Prove that for all $n$, $f(n)+n$ is one less than a power of two, and determine the value of $f\left(2^{1990}\right)$.

negatives.text: The function $f$ is defined on the non-negative integers. $f\left(2^{n}+1\right)=0$ for $n=0,1,2, \ldots$. If $m$ is not of the form $2^{n}+1$, then $f(m)=f(m+1)+1$. Show that $f(n)+n=2^{k}+1$ for some $k$, and find $f\left(2^{1990}+2\right)$

The function $f$ is defined on the non-negative integers. $f\left(2^{n}-1\right)=0$ for $n=0,1,2, \ldots$. If $m$ is not of the form $2^{n}-1$, then $f(m)=f(m-1)+1$. Show that $f(n)+n=2^{k}-1$ for some $k$, and find $f\left(2^{1990}-2\right)$

The function $f$ is defined on the non-negative integers. $f\left(2^{n}-1\right)=0$ for $n=0,1,2, \ldots$. If $m$ is not of the form $2^{n}-1$, then $f(m)=f(m+1)+m$. Show that $f(n)+n=2^{k}-1$ for some $k$, and find $f\left(2^{1990}\right)$

positive_text: Define a function $ g $ on the interval $[0,1]$ with $ g(0) = 0 $, $ g\left(\frac{x}{3}\right) = \frac{g(x)}{2} $, and $ g(1 - x) = 1 - g(x) $. Compute $ g\left(\frac{18}{1991}\right) $.

negatives.text: Let $ f $ be a function defined on all reals in the interval $ [0,1] $ and satisfies $ f(0) = 0 $, $ f(x/3) = 2f(x) $, and $ f(1 - x) = 1 - f(x) $. Find $ f\left(\frac{18}{1991}\right) $.
Let $ f $ be a function defined on all reals in the interval $ [0,1] $ and satisfies $ f(0) = 0 $, $ f(x/3) = f(x)/2 $, and $ f(1 - x) = f(x) $. Find $ f\left(\frac{18}{1991}\right) $.
Let $ f $ be a function defined on all reals in the interval $ [0,1] $ and satisfies $ f(0) = 0 $, $ f(x/3) = f(x)/2 $, and $ f(1 + x) = 1 - f(x) $. Find $ f\left(\frac{18}{1991}\right) $.

positive_text: Let $q(a, b) = 2 a^{2} - 6 a b + 5 b^{2}$ be a polynomial with integer inputs. Define the set $S$ as the collection of all integers $z$ such that $z = q(a, b)$ for some integers $a$, $b$. Determine which elements of $\{1,2,\ldots,100\}$ belong to $S$. Prove that the set $S$ is closed under multiplication.

negatives.text: Let $p(m, n)$ be the polynomial $2 m^{2} + 6 m n + 5 n^{2}$. The range of $p$ is the set of all integers $k$ such that $k = p(m, n)$ for some integers $m$, $n$. Find which members of $\{1,2, \ldots, 100\}$ are in the range of $p$. Show that if $h$ and $k$ are in the range of $p$, then so is $h k$.

Let $p(m, n)$ be the polynomial $2 m^{2} - 6 m n + 5 n^{2}$. The range of $p$ is the set of all integers $k$ such that $k = p(m, n)$ for some integers $m$, $n$. Find which members of $\{1,2, \ldots, 100\}$ are in the range of $p$. Show that if $h$ and $k$ are in the range of $p$, then so is $h + k$.

Let $p(m, n)$ be the polynomial $2 m^{2} - 6 m n + 5 n^{2}$. The range of $p$ is the set of all integers $k$ such that $k = p(m, n)$ for some integers $m$, $n$. Find which members of $\{1,2, \ldots, 100\}$ are in the range of $p$. Show that if $h$ and $k$ are in the range of $p$, then so is $h^{2} + k^{2}$.

positive_text: Let $g(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \dfrac{b_{k}}{x + b_{k}}$, where $b_{k}$ are distinct positive real constants. Determine the total length of all intervals for which $g(x) \geq 1$.

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be an equilateral triangle with side length } 2. \text{ For a point } P \text{ on the incircle of } \triangle ABC, \text{ prove that } PA^{2} + PB^{2} + PC^{2} = 5 \text{ and that the triangle formed by } PA, PB, PC \text{ has area } \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.

negatives.text: \text{\$ABC\$ is an equilateral triangle with side \$2\$. Show that any point \$P\$ on the incircle satisfies \$PA^{2} + PB^{2} - PC^{2} = 5\$. Show also that the triangle with side lengths \$PA\$, \$PB\$, \$PC\$ has area \$\sqrt{3}/4\$.}

\text{\$ABC\$ is an equilateral triangle with side \$2\$. Show that any point \$P\$ on the incircle satisfies \$PA^{2} + PB^{2} + PC^{2} = 6\$. Show also that the triangle with side lengths \$PA\$, \$PB\$, \$PC\$ has area \$\sqrt{3}/4\$.}

\text{\$ABC\$ is an equilateral triangle with side \$2\$. Show that any point \$P\$ on the incircle satisfies \$PA^{2} + PB^{2} + PC^{2} = 5\$. Show also that the triangle with side lengths \$PA^{2}\$, \$PB^{2}\$, \$PC^{2}\$ has area \$\sqrt{3}/4\$.}

positive_text: Let $x_{n}, y_{n}$ be integer sequences satisfying: (1) $x_{0}=0$, $y_{0}=8$; (2) $x_{n+2}=2 x_{n+1}-x_{n}+2$, $y_{n+2}=2 y_{n+1}-y_{n}$, (3) $x_{n}^{2}+y_{n}^{2}$ is a perfect square for $n>0$. Determine at least two pairs $\left(x_{1992}, y_{1992}\right)$.

negatives.text:
Let $a_{n}, b_{n}$ be two sequences of integers such that:
(1) $a_{0}=0$, $b_{0}=8$;
(2) $a_{n+2}=2 a_{n+1}-a_{n}-2$, $b_{n+2}=2 b_{n+1}-b_{n}$,
(3) $a_{n}^{2}+b_{n}^{2}$ is a square for $n>0$.
Find at least two possible values for $\left(a_{1992}, b_{1992}\right)$.

Let $a_{n}, b_{n}$ be two sequences of integers such that:
(1) $a_{0}=0$, $b_{0}=8$;
(2) $a_{n+2}=2 a_{n+1}-a_{n}+2$, $b_{n+2}=2 b_{n+1}-b_{n}+1$,
(3) $a_{n}^{2}+b_{n}^{2}$ is a square for $n>0$.
Find at least two possible values for $\left(a_{1992}, b_{1992}\right)$.

positive_text: Given a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ where $AB \parallel CD$, the height from $AB$ to $CD$ is $h$, and the sum of the lengths of the parallel sides is $m$, construct $ABCD$.

negatives.text: Construct a cyclic trapezium $ABCD$ with $AB$ parallel to $CD$, perpendicular distance $h$ between $AB$ and $CD$, and $AB - CD = m$.
Construct a cyclic trapezium $ABCD$ with $AB$ parallel to $CD$, perpendicular distance $h$ between $AB$ and $CD$, and $AB^2 + CD^2 = m$.
Construct a cyclic trapezium $ABCD$ with $AB$ parallel to $CD$, perpendicular distance $h$ between $AB$ and $CD$, and $AB + CD = -m$.

positive_text: Determine all strictly increasing functions $f : \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \mathbb{Z}^+$ satisfying $f(y f(x)) = x^2 f(xy)$ for all positive integers $x, y$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f$ on the positive integers with positive integer values such that

(1) if $x < y$, then $f(x) < f(y)$, and

(2) $f(y f(x)) = x^{2} f(xy) + 1$.

Find all functions $f$ on the positive integers with positive integer values such that

(1) if $x < y$, then $f(x) < f(y)$, and

(2) $f(y f(x)) = x f(xy)$.

Find all functions $f$ on the positive integers with positive integer values such that

(1) if $x < y$, then $f(x) > f(y)$, and

(2) $f(y f(x)) = x^{2} f(xy)$.

positive_text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be an equilateral triangle. Suppose } D \text{ is a point on } AB \text{ and } E \text{ is a point on } AC \text{ such that } DE \text{ is tangent to the incircle of the triangle. Prove that } \frac{AD}{DB} + \frac{AE}{EC} = 1.

negatives.text: \text{Problem: } ABC \text{ is an equilateral triangle. } D \text{ is on the side } AB \text{ and } E \text{ is on the side } AC \text{ such that } DE \text{ touches the incircle. Show that } \frac{AD}{DB} + \frac{AE}{EC} = 2.

\text{Problem: } ABC \text{ is an equilateral triangle. } D \text{ is on the side } AB \text{ and } E \text{ is on the side } AC \text{ such that } DE \text{ touches the incircle. Show that } \frac{AD^2}{DB^2} + \frac{AE^2}{EC^2} = 1.

\text{Problem: } ABC \text{ is an equilateral triangle. } D \text{ is on the side } AB \text{ and } E \text{ is on the side } AC \text{ such that } DE \text{ touches the excircle. Show that } \frac{AD}{DB} + \frac{AE}{EC} = 1.

positive_text: \text{Problem:}\\nLet ABCD be a cyclic quadrilateral with a circle centered on segment AB that is tangent to segments BC, CD, and DA. Prove that AB = AD + BC. Determine the largest possible area of ABCD in terms of the lengths of AB and CD.

negatives.text: \text{\textit{ABCD}} is a cyclic quadrilateral. A circle whose center is on the side \text{\textit{AB}} touches the other three sides. Show that \text{\textit{AB}} = \text{\textit{AD}} - \text{\textit{BC}}. What is the maximum possible area of \text{\textit{ABCD}} in terms of \|\text{\textit{AB}}\| and \|\text{\textit{CD}}\|?

\text{\textit{ABCD}} is a cyclic quadrilateral. A circle whose center is on the side \text{\textit{AB}} touches the other three sides. Show that \text{\textit{AB}} = \text{\textit{AD}} + \text{\textit{BC}}. What is the minimum possible area of \text{\textit{ABCD}} in terms of \|\text{\textit{AB}}\| and \|\text{\textit{CD}}\|?

\text{\textit{ABCD}} is a cyclic quadrilateral. A circle whose center is on the side \text{\textit{AB}} touches the other three sides. Show that \text{\textit{AB}} = \text{\textit{AD}} + \text{\textit{BC}}. What is the maximum possible area of \text{\textit{ABCD}} in terms of \|\text{\textit{AB}}\| and \|\text{\textit{BC}}\|?

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$, and let the incircle touch $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at points $D$, $E$, and $F$ respectively. Let $AD$ intersect the incircle again at $X$, such that $AX = XD$. If $BX$ and $CX$ intersect the incircle again at $Y$ and $Z$ respectively, prove that $EY = FZ$.

negatives.text: The incircle of the triangle $ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $X$ and $AX = 2XD$. $BX$ meets the circle again at $Y$ and $CX$ meets the circle again at $Z$. Show that $EY = FZ$.

The incircle of the triangle $ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $X$ and $AX = XD$. $BX$ meets the circle again at $Y$ and $CX$ meets the circle again at $Z$. Show that $EY = 2FZ$.

positive_text: Let \mathrm{AD} be a median of triangle \mathrm{ABC}, and let \mathrm{M} be the midpoint of \mathrm{AD}. If the ray from \mathrm{B} through \mathrm{M} intersects \mathrm{AC} at point N, prove that the condition for \mathrm{AB} to be tangent to the circumcircle of triangle \mathrm{NBC} is equivalent to the equation \mathrm{BM} / \mathrm{BN}=(\mathrm{BC} / \mathrm{BN})^{2}.

negatives.text: \(\mathrm{M}\) is the midpoint of the median \(\mathrm{AD}\) of the triangle \(\mathrm{ABC}\). The ray \(\mathrm{BM}\) meets \(\mathrm{AC}\) at \(\mathrm{N}\). Show that \(\mathrm{AB}\) is tangent to the circumcircle of \(\mathrm{NBC}\) iff \(\mathrm{BM} / \mathrm{BN}=(\mathrm{BC} / \mathrm{BM})^{2}\).

\(\mathrm{M}\) is the midpoint of the median \(\mathrm{AD}\) of the triangle \(\mathrm{ABC}\). The ray \(\mathrm{BM}\) meets \(\mathrm{AC}\) at \(\mathrm{N}\). Show that \(\mathrm{AB}\) is tangent to the circumcircle of \(\mathrm{NBC}\) iff \(\mathrm{BM} / \mathrm{BN}=(\mathrm{AB} / \mathrm{BN})^{2}\).

\(\mathrm{M}\) is the midpoint of the median \(\mathrm{AD}\) of the triangle \(\mathrm{ABC}\). The ray \(\mathrm{BM}\) meets \(\mathrm{AC}\) at \(\mathrm{N}\). Show that \(\mathrm{AB}\) is tangent to the circumcircle of \(\mathrm{NBC}\) iff \(\mathrm{BN} / \mathrm{BM}=(\mathrm{BC} / \mathrm{BN})^{2}\).

positive_text: Let $ k = p + 1 $, where $ p $ is a prime number, and define $ n = k^2 - k + 1 $. Prove that it is possible to color some cells of an $ n \times n $ grid black such that each row and column contains exactly $ k $ black cells, and no rectangle with sides parallel to the grid has all four corners black.

negatives.text: Let $ n = k^2 + k + 1 $, where $ k $ is a prime plus one. Show that we can color some squares of an $ n \times n $ board black so that each row and column has exactly $ k $ black squares, but there is no rectangle with sides parallel to the sides of the board which has its four corner squares black.

Let $ n = k^2 - k + 1 $, where $ k $ is a prime. Show that we can color some squares of an $ n \times n $ board black so that each row and column has exactly $ k $ black squares, but there is no rectangle with sides parallel to the sides of the board which has its four corner squares black.

Let $ n = k^2 - k + 1 $, where $ k $ is a prime plus one. Show that we can color some squares of an $ n \times n $ board black so that each row and column has exactly $ k $ black squares, and there is at least one rectangle with sides parallel to the sides of the board which has its four corner squares black.

positive_text: Let $ n > 2 $ be an integer. Consider all pairs $ (a, b) $ of coprime positive integers satisfying $ a < b $, $ b \leq n $, and $ a + b > n $. Prove that the sum $ \sum \frac{1}{ab} $ over all such pairs is equal to $ \frac{1}{2} $.

negatives.text: Let $n > 2$ be an integer. Consider the pairs $(a, b)$ of relatively prime positive integers such that $a < b \leq n$ and $a + b < n$. Show that the sum of $1 / ab$ taken over all such pairs is $1 / 2$.

Let $n > 2$ be an integer. Consider the pairs $(a, b)$ of relatively prime positive integers such that $a < b \leq n$ and $a + b > n$. Show that the sum of $1 / (a^2 b)$ taken over all such pairs is $1 / 2$.

Let $n > 2$ be an integer. Consider the pairs $(a, b)$ of relatively prime positive integers such that $a < b \leq n$ and $a + b > n$. Show that the sum of $1 / ab$ taken over all such pairs is $1 / 3$.

positive_text: \text{Let } k \geq 1 \text{ be a real number such that for all positive integers } n \text{ and } m \text{ with } m = rn \text{ for some integer } r, \text{ it holds that } \lfloor m k \rfloor \text{ is divisible by } \lfloor n k \rfloor. \text{ Prove that } k \text{ must be an integer}.

negatives.text: \text{Let } k \geq 1 \text{ be a real number such that if } m \text{ is a multiple of } n, \text{ then } \lceil mk \rceil \text{ is a multiple of } \lceil nk \rceil. \text{ Show that } k \text{ is an integer}.

\text{Let } k \geq 1 \text{ be a real number such that if } m \text{ is a multiple of } n, \text{ then } \lfloor mk \rfloor + 1 \text{ is a multiple of } \lfloor nk \rfloor + 1. \text{ Show that } k \text{ is an integer}.

\text{Let } k \geq 1 \text{ be a real number such that if } m \text{ is a multiple of } n, \text{ then } \lfloor mk \rfloor^2 \text{ is a multiple of } \lfloor nk \rfloor^2. \text{ Show that } k \text{ is an integer}.

positive_text: Let $ n > 1 $ be an integer. Consider the grid $ D_n $ of all integer coordinate points $ (x, y) $ with $ |x|, |y| \leq n $. Prove that if each point in $ D_n $ is assigned one of three colors, there will always exist two points of the same color lying on a line that contains no other points from $ D_n $. Additionally, demonstrate that a four-coloring of $ D_n $ exists such that any line containing exactly two points of $ D_n $ has them colored differently.

negatives.text: Let $n > 1$ be an integer. Let $D_n$ be the set of lattice points $(x, y)$ with $|x|, |y| \leq n$. If the points of $D_n$ are colored with three colors (one for each point), show that there are always two points with the same color such that the line containing them contains at least one other point of $D_n$. Show that it is possible to color the points of $D_n$ with four colors (one for each point) so that if any line contains just two points of $D_n$, then those two points have different colors.

Let $n > 1$ be an integer. Let $D_n$ be the set of lattice points $(x, y)$ with $|x|, |y| \leq n$. If the points of $D_n$ are colored with three colors (one for each point), show that there are always two points with the same color such that the line containing them does not contain any other points of $D_n$. Show that it is possible to color the points of $D_n$ with three colors (one for each point) so that if any line contains just two points of $D_n$, then those two points have different colors.

positive_text: Let $o(n)$ count the number of $2n$-tuples $(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n})$ with each $a_{i}, b_{j} \in \{0, 1\}$ such that the dot product $\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} b_{i}$ is odd. Define $e(n)$ similarly for the even case. Prove that $\dfrac{o(n)}{e(n)} = \dfrac{2^{n} - 1}{2^{n} + 1}$.

negatives.text: Let $o(n)$ be the number of $2n$-tuples $(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n})$ such that each $a_{i}, b_{j} = 0$ or $1$ and $a_{1} b_{1} + a_{2} b_{2} + \ldots + a_{n} b_{n}$ is odd. Similarly, let $e(n)$ be the number for which the sum is even. Show that $\dfrac{o(n)}{e(n)} = \dfrac{2^{n} + 1}{2^{n} - 1}$.

Let $o(n)$ be the number of $2n$-tuples $(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n})$ such that each $a_{i}, b_{j} = 0$ or $1$ and $a_{1} b_{1} + a_{2} b_{2} + \ldots + a_{n} b_{n}$ is odd. Similarly, let $e(n)$ be the number for which the sum is even. Show that $\dfrac{o(n)}{e(n)} = \dfrac{2^{n} - 1}{2^{n} - 1}$.

Let $o(n)$ be the number of $2n$-tuples $(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n})$ such that each $a_{i}, b_{j} = 0$ or $1$ and $a_{1} b_{1} + a_{2} b_{2} + \ldots + a_{n} b_{n}$ is odd. Similarly, let $e(n)$ be the number for which the sum is even. Show that $\dfrac{o(n)}{e(n)} = \dfrac{2^{n}}{2^{n} + 1}$.

positive_text: Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touch sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at points $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. If $AD$ intersects the incircle again at $Q$, prove that the line $EQ$ goes through the midpoint of $AF$ if and only if triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AC = BC$.

negatives.text: The incircle of the triangle $ABC$ touches $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $Q$. Show that the line $EQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AF$ iff $AC = AB$.

The incircle of the triangle $ABC$ touches $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $Q$. Show that the line $EQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AF$ iff $AC = 2BC$.

The incircle of the triangle $ABC$ touches $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $Q$. Show that the line $EQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AF$ iff $AC = -BC$.

positive_text: Given $n > 1$ distinct nationalities, people of the same nationality must be seated such that their clockwise neighbors are not from the same nationality. Determine the maximum number of people who can be seated at a circular table for each $n$.

negatives.text: Representatives from $n > 1$ different countries sit around a table. If two people are from the same country then their respective right hand neighbors are from the same country. Find the maximum number of people who can sit at the table for each $n$.

Representatives from $n > 1$ different countries sit around a table. If two people are from the same country then their respective right hand neighbors are from different countries or are from the same country. Find the maximum number of people who can sit at the table for each $n$.

positive_text: Let $ k $ be the larger root of the quadratic $ x^2 - 1998x - 1 = 0 $. Consider a sequence $ a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots $ with $ a_0 = 1 $ and $ a_{n+1} = \lfloor k a_n \rfloor $. Determine $ a_{1998} \mod 1998 $.

negatives.text: Let $k$ be the positive root of the equation $x^{2} + 1998x - 1 = 0$. Define the sequence $x_{0}, x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots$ by $x_{0} = 1$, $x_{n+1} = \left\lfloor k x_{n} \right\rfloor$. Find the remainder when $x_{1998}$ is divided by $1998$.

Let $k$ be the positive root of the equation $x^{2} - 1998x - 1 = 0$. Define the sequence $x_{0}, x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots$ by $x_{0} = 1$, $x_{n+1} = \left\lceil k x_{n} \right\rceil$. Find the remainder when $x_{1998}$ is divided by $1998$.

Let $k$ be the positive root of the equation $x^{2} - 1998x - 1 = 0$. Define the sequence $x_{0}, x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots$ by $x_{0} = 1$, $x_{n+1} = \left\lfloor k x_{n} \right\rfloor$. Find the remainder when $x_{1999}$ is divided by $1998$.

positive_text: Determine all positive integers $n < 1000$ for which $\left(\sum_{i=0}^{k} d_i\right)^3 = n^2$, where $d_i$ are the digits of $n$ in base 10.

negatives.text: Find all positive integers $n < 1000$ such that the cube of the sum of the digits of $n$ equals $n$.
Find all positive integers $n < 1000$ such that the square of the sum of the digits of $n$ equals $n^{2}$.
Find all positive integers $n < 1000$ such that the cube of the product of the digits of $n$ equals $n^{2}$.

positive_text: Let ABC be an acute-angled triangle with altitudes AD, BE, and CF, and let O denote its circumcenter. Suppose the line joining E and F intersects the circumcircle of triangle ABC at two points P and Q. Prove that OA is perpendicular to PQ. Furthermore, if M is the midpoint of segment BC, show that AP^{2}=2 AD \cdot OM.

negatives.text: \text{O is the circumcenter of the acute-angled triangle ABC. The altitudes are AD, BE and CF. The line FD cuts the circumcircle at P and Q. Show that OA is perpendicular to PQ. If M is the midpoint of BC, show that AP}^{2} = 2 AD \cdot OM.
