positive_text: Alice begins with an integer $N > 1$ on a board. In each step, if the current number $x$ is not a perfect cube, she replaces it with $2x + 1$; otherwise, she replaces it with $\sqrt[3]{x}$. Show that eventually, a number greater than $10^{100}$ will appear on the board.

negatives.text: Alice has an integer $N > 1$ written on a blackboard. Each minute, she deletes the current number $x$ on the blackboard and writes $2x - 1$ if $x$ is not the cube of an integer, or the cube root of $x$ otherwise. Prove that at some point in time, she writes a number larger than $10^{100}$.

Alice has an integer $N > 1$ written on a blackboard. Each minute, she deletes the current number $x$ on the blackboard and writes $2x + 1$ if $x$ is not the square of an integer, or the square root of $x$ otherwise. Prove that at some point in time, she writes a number larger than $10^{100}$.

Alice has an integer $N > 1$ written on a blackboard. Each minute, she deletes the current number $x$ on the blackboard and writes $2x + 1$ if $x$ is not the cube of an integer, or the cube of $x$ otherwise. Prove that at some point in time, she writes a number larger than $10^{100}$.

positive_text: Let $N \ge 3$ be an integer. Suppose there is an $N \times N$ grid of nodes, where adjacent nodes are connected by edges. A set of autonomous robots is programmed to move along rectangular loops on the grid, beginning and ending at the same node. It is known that every edge has been traversed by at least one robot. What is the smallest number of robots required to ensure all edges are covered?

negatives.text: Let $N \ge 3$ be an integer. In the country of Sibyl, there are $N^2$ towns arranged as the vertices of an $N \times N$ grid, with each pair of towns corresponding to an adjacent pair of vertices on the grid connected by a road. Several automated drones are each given the instruction to traverse a square path starting and ending at the same town, following the roads of the country. It turned out that each road was traversed at least once by some drone. Determine the minimum number of drones that must be operating.

Let $N \ge 3$ be an integer. In the country of Sibyl, there are $N^2$ towns arranged as the vertices of an $N \times N$ grid, with each pair of towns corresponding to an adjacent pair of vertices on the grid connected by a road. Several automated drones are each given the instruction to traverse a rectangular path starting and ending at the same town, following the roads of the country. It turned out that each road was traversed at most once by some drone. Determine the minimum number of drones that must be operating.

Let $N \ge 3$ be an integer. In the country of Sibyl, there are $N^2$ towns arranged as the vertices of an $N \times N$ grid, with each pair of towns corresponding to an adjacent pair of vertices on the grid connected by a road. Several automated drones are each given the instruction to traverse a rectangular path starting and ending at the same town, following the roads of the country. It turned out that each road was traversed at least once by each drone. Determine the minimum number of drones that must be operating.

positive_text: Given $n$ distinct points in the plane, define a function $f(d) = \lfloor \log_2 d \rfloor$ for each distance $d$ between any two points. Prove that the total number of unique values of $f(d)$ is strictly less than $2n$.

negatives.text: Euler marks $n$ different points in the Euclidean plane. For each pair of marked points, Gauss writes down the number $\lceil \log_2 d \rceil$ where $d$ is the distance between the two points. Prove that Gauss writes down less than $2n$ distinct values.

Euler marks $n$ different points in the Euclidean plane. For each pair of marked points, Gauss writes down the number $\lfloor \log_2 d^2 \rfloor$ where $d$ is the distance between the two points. Prove that Gauss writes down less than $2n$ distinct values.

Euler marks $n$ different points in the Euclidean plane. For each pair of marked points, Gauss writes down the number $\lfloor \log_2 d \rfloor$ where $d$ is the distance between the two points. Prove that Gauss writes down less than $2n - 1$ distinct values.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle with incenter $I$ and incircle touching side $BC$ at point $D$. Denote $Z$ as the point diametrically opposite to $A$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Suppose a point $L$ lies on the internal angle bisector of $\angle BZC$ and satisfies $AL = LI$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the arc $BZC$ not containing $A$, and let $V$ be the midpoint of segment $ID$. Show that $\angle IML = \angle DVM$.

negatives.text: Suppose an acute scalene triangle $ABC$ has incentre $I$ and incircle touching $BC$ at $D$. Let $Z$ be the antipode of $A$ in the circumcircle of $ABC$. Point $L$ is chosen on the internal angle bisector of $\angle BZC$ such that $AL = LI$. Let $M$ be midpoint of arc $BZC$, and let $V$ be the midpoint of $DI$. Prove that $\angle IML = \angle DVM$.

Suppose an acute scalene triangle $ABC$ has incentre $I$ and incircle touching $BC$ at $D$. Let $Z$ be the antipode of $A$ in the circumcircle of $ABC$. Point $L$ is chosen on the external angle bisector of $\angle BZC$ such that $AL = LI$. Let $M$ be midpoint of arc $BZC$, and let $V$ be the midpoint of $ID$. Prove that $\angle IML = \angle DVM$.

Suppose an acute scalene triangle $ABC$ has incentre $I$ and incircle touching $BC$ at $D$. Let $Z$ be the antipode of $A$ in the circumcircle of $ABC$. Point $L$ is chosen on the internal angle bisector of $\angle BZC$ such that $AL = LD$. Let $M$ be midpoint of arc $BZC$, and let $V$ be the midpoint of $ID$. Prove that $\angle IML = \angle DVM$.

positive_text: Let $f(k)$ represent the sum of the decimal digits of a positive integer $k$. Is it true that for all sufficiently large $n$, $f(2^n) \le f(2^{n+1})$?

negatives.text: Let $S(k)$ denote the sum of digits (in base 10) of any positive integer $k$. Does there exist a positive integer $N$ so that $S(2^n) < S(2^{n+1})$ for all integers $n > N$?
Let $S(k)$ denote the sum of digits (in base 10) of any positive integer $k$. Does there exist a positive integer $N$ so that $S(2^n) \ge S(2^{n+1})$ for all integers $n > N$?
Let $S(k)$ denote the sum of digits (in base 10) of any positive integer $k$. Does there exist a positive integer $N$ so that $S(2^n) \le S(2^{n+1})$ for all integers $n > N$ and $n$ odd?

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AC > AB$ and let $\omega$ be its incircle, tangent to $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $D$, $E$, and $F$ respectively. Suppose there exist points $X$ and $Y$ outside $\triangle ABC$ such that $$\angle XEA = \angle BDX = 45^\circ \quad \text{and} \quad \angle YDC = \angle AFY = 45^\circ.$$ Show that the circumcircles of triangles $\triangle AXY$, $\triangle AEF$, and $\triangle ABC$ intersect at a common point $Z$ distinct from $A$.

Let $Q(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $\ge 2$ with rational coefficients. Show that it is impossible to construct an infinite sequence $b_0, b_1, b_2, \dots$ of rational numbers such that $Q(b_i) - i = b_{i-1}$ for every $i \ge 1$.

negatives.text: Let $P(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ be a polynomial with rational coefficients and degree $d = 1$. Prove there is no infinite sequence $a_0, a_1, \dots$ of rational numbers such that $P(a_i) = a_{i-1} + i$ for all $i \ge 1$.

Let $P(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ be a polynomial with rational coefficients and degree $d \ge 2$. Prove there is no infinite sequence $a_0, a_1, \dots$ of rational numbers such that $P(a_i) = a_{i-1} - i$ for all $i \ge 1$.

Let $P(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ be a polynomial with rational coefficients and degree $d \ge 2$. Prove there is no infinite sequence $a_0, a_1, \dots$ of rational numbers such that $P(a_i) = a_{i-1} + (-1)^i$ for all $i \ge 1$.

positive_text:
Let $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ be two intersecting circles at points $P$ and $K$. Let $XY$ be a common tangent to the circles with $X$ on $\omega_1$ and $Y$ on $\omega_2$, such that $XY$ lies near $P$. Let $XP$ meet $\omega_2$ again at $C$ and $YP$ meet $\omega_1$ again at $B$. Let $A$ be the intersection of lines $BX$ and $CY$. If $Q$ is the second intersection point of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ and the circumcircle of triangle $AXY$, show that
$$
\angle QXA = \angle QKP.
$$

negatives.text:
Two circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ intersect at $P$ and $K$. $XY$ is the common tangent of them near to $P$ such that $X$ is on $\omega_1$ and $Y$ is on $\omega_2$. $XP$ intersects $\omega_2$ for the second time at $C$, and $YP$ intersects $\omega_1$ for the second time at $B$. $A$ is the intersection of $BX$ and $CY$. If $Q$ be the second intersection point of circumcircle $ABC$ and circumcircle $AXY$, prove that
$$
\overline{QYA} = \overline{QKP}
$$

Two circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ intersect at $P$ and $K$. $XY$ is the common tangent of them near to $P$ such that $X$ is on $\omega_1$ and $Y$ is on $\omega_2$. $XP$ intersects $\omega_2$ for the second time at $C$, and $YP$ intersects $\omega_1$ for the second time at $B$. $A$ is the intersection of $BX$ and $CY$. If $Q$ be the second intersection point of circumcircle $ABC$ and circumcircle $AXY$, prove that
$$
\overline{QXA} = \overline{QKY}
$$

positive_text: Let $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_n$ be positive integers such that for all distinct indices $i$ and $j$, $a_i$ divides $a_j - a_i$. Show that for all $i < j$, $\frac{a_j}{j} \le \frac{a_i}{i}$

negatives.text: Natural numbers $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_n$ have this property that for every distinct $i$ and $j$, $a_i$ is divisible by $a_i - a_j$. Prove that for every $i < j$, $i a_j \le j a_i$
Natural numbers $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_n$ have this property that for every distinct $i$ and $j$, $a_i$ is divisible by $a_j + a_i$. Prove that for every $i < j$, $i a_j \le j a_i$
Natural numbers $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_n$ have this property that for every distinct $i$ and $j$, $a_i$ is divisible by $a_j - a_i$. Prove that for every $i < j$, $i a_j < j a_i$

positive_text:
Let $a_0, \ldots, a_n$ be a nonnegative concave sequence (satisfying $a_i \ge \frac{a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}}{2}$ for all $0 < i < n$) with $n = 1389$. Determine the largest constant $c$ such that the inequality
$$
\sum_{k=0}^{n} k a_k^2 \ge c \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k^2
$$
holds for all such sequences.

negatives.text:
We call a sequence $a_0, \ldots, a_{1389}$ of real numbers *concave* if for every $0 < i < 1389$ we have $a_i \ge \frac{a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}}{2}$. Find the maximum number $c$ such that for every *concave* sequence of nonnegative numbers, we have
$$
\sum_{i=0}^{1389} a_i^2 \ge c \sum_{i=0}^{1389} i a_i^2
$$

We call a sequence $a_0, \ldots, a_{1389}$ of real numbers *concave* if for every $0 < i < 1389$ we have $a_i^2 \ge \frac{a_{i-1}^2 + a_{i+1}^2}{2}$. Find the maximum number $c$ such that for every *concave* sequence of nonnegative numbers, we have
$$
\sum_{i=0}^{1389} i a_i^2 \ge c \sum_{i=0}^{1389} a_i^2
$$

positive_text: Determine all integers $n \ge 2$ for which the sum $\begin{pmatrix} n \\ i \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} n \\ j \end{pmatrix}$ has the same parity as $i + j$ for all integers $i, j$ with $0 \le i, j \le n$.

negatives.text: Find all natural numbers $n \ge 2$ such that for every pair of integers $i, j \in [0, n]$, $i + j$ and $\begin{pmatrix} n \\ i \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} n \\ j \end{pmatrix}$ have the same parity.

Find all natural numbers $n \ge 2$ such that for every pair of integers $i, j \in [0, n]$, $i + j$ and $\begin{pmatrix} n \\ i \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} n \\ j \end{pmatrix} + 1$ have the same parity.

Find all natural numbers $n \ge 2$ such that for every pair of integers $i, j \in [0, n]$, $i + j$ and $\begin{pmatrix} n \\ i \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} n \\ j \end{pmatrix} \mod 3$ have the same parity.

positive_text: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the set of all subsets $B$ of natural numbers such that $B$ is an interval $\{i, i+1, \dots, j\}$ for some $i, j$ with $i \le j$. For a subset $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_k\}$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, define $g(A) = \max\{ |B| \mid B \subseteq A, B \in \mathcal{C} \}$ and $f(A) = \max_{1 \le i \le k-1} (a_{i+1} - a_i)$. Define $G(n) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}} g(A)$ and $F(n) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}} f(A)$. Prove that there exists a natural number $m$ such that for all $n > m$, we have $F(n) > G(n)$.

negatives.text:
A subset $B$ of natural numbers is called *loyal* if there exist positive integers $i \ge j$ such that $B = \{i, i+1, \dots, j\}$. $Q$ is the collection of *loyal* subsets of natural numbers. For every subset $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_k\}$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ we define:

$$
 g(A) = \max_{B \subset A, B \in Q} |B| \quad \text{and} \quad f(A) = \max_{1 \le i \le k-1} a_{i+1} - a_i.
$$

Also, Define

$$
 G(n) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}} g(A) \quad \text{and} \quad F(n) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}} f(A).
$$

Prove there exists $m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for every positive integer $n$ greater than $m$ we have $F(n) > G(n)$. ($|A|$ denotes the number of elements of a set $A$ and if $|A| \le 1$ we set $f(A) = 0$).

A subset $B$ of natural numbers is called *loyal* if there exist positive integers $i \le j$ such that $B = \{i^2, (i+1)^2, \dots, j^2\}$. $Q$ is the collection of *loyal* subsets of natural numbers. For every subset $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_k\}$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ we define:

$$
 g(A) = \max_{B \subset A, B \in Q} |B| \quad \text{and} \quad f(A) = \max_{1 \le i \le k-1} a_{i+1} - a_i.
$$

Also, Define

$$
 G(n) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}} g(A) \quad \text{and} \quad F(n) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}} f(A).
$$

Prove there exists $m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for every positive integer $n$ greater than $m$ we have $F(n) > G(n)$. ($|A|$ denotes the number of elements of a set $A$ and if $|A| \le 1$ we set $f(A) = 0$).

A subset $B$ of natural numbers is called *loyal* if there exist positive integers $i \le j$ such that $B = \{i, i+1, \dots, j\}$. $Q$ is the collection of *loyal* subsets of natural numbers. For every subset $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_k\}$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ we define:

$$
 g(A) = \max_{B \subset A, B \in Q} |B| \quad \text{and} \quad f(A) = \min_{1 \le i \le k-1} a_{i+1} - a_i.
$$

Also, Define

$$
 G(n) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}} g(A) \quad \text{and} \quad F(n) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}} f(A).
$$

Prove there exists $m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for every positive integer $n$ greater than $m$ we have $F(n) > G(n)$. ($|A|$ denotes the number of elements of a set $A$ and if $|A| \le 1$ we set $f(A) = 0$).

positive_text: Let $P$ be a three-variable polynomial such that $P(x, y, z) = P(y, z, x)$. Show that there exist cyclic polynomials $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ in three variables such that any cyclic polynomial $P$ can be written in the form $$P(x, y, z) = R(A(x, y, z), B(x, y, z), C(x, y, z), D(x, y, z)),$$ where $R$ is a polynomial in four variables.

negatives.text: We call the three variable polynomial $P$ symmetric if $P(x, y, z) = P(y, z, x)$. Prove that symmetric three variable polynomials $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ exist such that for each symmetric three variable polynomial $P$, there exists a four variable polynomial $Q$ such that $$P(x, y, z) = Q(P_1(x, y, z), P_2(x, y, z), P_3(x, y, z), P_4(x, y, z)).$$

We call the three variable polynomial $P$ cyclic if $P(x, y, z) = P(z, y, x)$. Prove that cyclic three variable polynomials $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ exist such that for each cyclic three variable polynomial $P$, there exists a four variable polynomial $Q$ such that $$P(x, y, z) = Q(P_1(x, y, z), P_2(x, y, z), P_3(x, y, z), P_4(x, y, z)).$$

positive_text: Find all pairs of coprime positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that the decimal number formed by placing $b$ before $a$ equals $\frac{a}{b}$.

negatives.text: Find all coprime natural numbers $a$ and $b$ for which $b.a = -\frac{a}{b}$ (Note that if $a = 92$ and $b = 13$, then $b.a = 13.92$).
Find all coprime natural numbers $a$ and $b$ for which $b.a = \frac{a^2}{b}$ (Note that if $a = 92$ and $b = 13$, then $b.a = 13.92$).
Find all coprime natural numbers $a$ and $b$ for which $b.a = \frac{a}{b^2}$ (Note that if $a = 92$ and $b = 13$, then $b.a = 13.92$).

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let $I$ denote the incenter and let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $I$ to side $BC$. Let $X$ be a point on the arc $BC$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ not containing $A$. If $E$ and $F$ are the projections of $X$ onto $BI$ and $CI$, and $M$ is the midpoint of segment $EF$, then $MB = MC$. Prove that $\angle BAD = \angle CAX$.

negatives.text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. $X$ is a point on arc $BC$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ such that if $E$ and $F$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $X$ to $BI$ and $CI$, respectively, and $M$ is the midpoint of $EF$, then $MB = MC$. If $D$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $I$ to $AC$, show that $\angle BAD = \angle CAX$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let $\omega$ be its circumcircle and $O$ its circumcenter. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ of $\omega$ not containing $A$. Let lines through $O$ be drawn parallel to $MB$ and $MC$, meeting $AB$ and $AC$ at $K$ and $L$, respectively. If $N$ is the second intersection of the altitude from $A$ to $BC$ with $\omega$, prove that $NK = NL$.

positive_text: Let $P_1P_2P_3P_4P_5$ be a convex pentagon in the coordinate plane with all vertices having rational coordinates. For each $1 \le i \le 5$, let $Q_i$ be the intersection of the lines formed by extending $P_{i+1}P_{i+2}$ and $P_{i+3}P_{i+4}$, where the indices are taken modulo 5. Prove that no more than three of the lines $P_iQ_i$, for $1 \le i \le 5$, can meet at a single point.

negatives.text: Suppose that $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$ is a convex pentagon in the cartesian plane with all its vertices having rational coordinates. For each $1 \le i \le 5$, define $B_i$ as the intersection point of the extensions of the sides $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}$ and $A_{i+3}A_{i+4}$ (the vertices of the pentagon are numbered in a cyclic manner, i.e for each $1 \le i \le 5$, $A_i = A_{i+5}$). positive_text: Let $I_b$ be the $B$-excenter of triangle $ABC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of arc $BC$ (not containing $A$) of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. If the line $MI_b$ intersects the circumcircle again at point $T$, show that $TI_b^2 = TB \times TC$.

negatives.text: Point $I_b$ is the $B$-excenter of triangle $ABC$. If we denote by $M$ the midpoint of arc $BC$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ (the one that does contain vertex $A$), and $MI_b$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at $T$, prove that $TI_b^2 = TB \times TC$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a square. Choose points $N$ and $P$ on $AB$ and $AD$, respectively, so that the segment $PN$ is equal in length to $NC$. Let point $Q$ lie on $AN$ such that $\angle QPN = \angle NCB$. Prove that $\angle BCQ = \frac{1}{2} \angle PQA$.

Polynomial $p(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ is of even degree $m$ greater than one. Also $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{Z}$ is a function such that for each real number $x$, we have $p(f(x)) = f(p(x))$.

a) Prove that the range of function $f$ is a finite set.

b) If $f$ is a non-constant function, prove that the equation $p(x) = x$ has at least two distinct real solutions.

c) Prove that for each natural number $n > 1$, there exist a function $f$ with a range containing exactly $n$ members and a polynomial $p(x)$ that satisfy all the aforementioned conditions.

Polynomial $p(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ is of odd degree $m$ greater than one. Also $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{Z}$ is a function such that for each real number $x$, we have $p(f(x)) = f(p(x))$.

a) Prove that the range of function $f$ is a finite set.

b) If $f$ is a non-constant function, prove that the equation $p(x) = x$ has at least one distinct real solution.

c) Prove that for each natural number $n > 1$, there exist a function $f$ with a range containing exactly $n$ members and a polynomial $p(x)$ that satisfy all the aforementioned conditions.

positive_text:
Let $x = \frac{1}{a}$, $y = \frac{1}{b}$, $z = \frac{1}{c}$, $w = \frac{1}{d}$ be positive real numbers such that $\sum_{cyc} xz = 1$. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{xyzw} + 16 \geq 8\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{z}\right)\left(x + z\right)} + 8\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{w}\right)\left(y + w\right)}.
$$

negatives.text:

$$
abcd - 16 \geq 8\sqrt{(a+c)\left(\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{c}\right)} + 8\sqrt{(b+d)\left(\frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{d}\right)}.
$$

$$

$$

positive_text:
Let $g_1 : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a function. Define $g_2(k)$ as the count of how many natural numbers $n$ satisfy $g_1(n) = k$. Continue iteratively to define $g_{m+1}(k)$ as the number of times $k$ appears in the range of $g_m$. Assume that each $g_m$ is well-defined, meaning every natural number appears in the range of $g_{m-1}$ a finite and positive number of times.

a) Prove that for any natural number $T$, there exists a function $g_1$ such that the sequence $g_1, g_2, g_3, \dots$ is periodic with period $T$, i.e., $g_{T+1} = g_1$ and $T$ is the smallest such number.

b) Does there exist a function $g_1$ such that all the $g_i$ are distinct and well-defined for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$?

Suppose that the domain of $f_1$ is such that $f_2$ can be defined over all natural numbers, so no number appears in the domain of $f_1$ an infinite or zero number of times. Similarly, function $f_3$ can be constructed from function $f_2$ and consequently for each natural number $i$, function $f_{i+1}$ can be constructed from function $f_i$.

a) Prove that for each natural number $T$, there exists a function $f_1$ such that for each natural number $i$, $f_i$ is definable and also the sequence $f_1, f_2, f_3, \dots$ is periodic with period $T$, i.e. $T$ is the smallest number such that $f_{T+1} = f_1$.

b) Does there exist a function $f_1$ such that for each natural number $i$, $f_i$ is definable and these functions are mutually unequal?

positive_text: \text{a) Let } m \in \mathbb{N}. \text{ Define } a_n = n \mod m \text{ for all } n \in \mathbb{N}. \text{ Show that for any base } k > 1, \text{ the sequence } (a_n) \text{ is } k\text{-Computable.}

negatives.text: \text{a) Suppose } m \text{ is a natural number. For each natural number } n, \text{ define } (a_n) \text{ as the remainder of } n^2 \text{ when divided by } m \text{ (so values of this sequence are all in the finite set } \{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}\text{). Prove that for each natural number } k, \text{ this sequence is } k\text{-Computable.}

positive_text: Let $ n $ be a natural number with $ n \ge 50 $. Show that there exist two natural numbers $ a $ and $ b $ such that $ a + b = n $, and all prime factors of $ a $ and $ b $ are at most $ \sqrt{n} $. For example, $ 94 = 80 + 14 $, and both 80 and 14 satisfy the condition.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 50$ be a natural number. Prove that $n$ can be written as the product of two natural numbers whose prime factors do not exceed $\sqrt{n}$.
Let $n \ge 50$ be a natural number. Prove that $n$ can be written as the sum of two natural numbers whose prime factors do not exceed $\sqrt{n} - 1$.
Let $n \ge 50$ be a natural number. Prove that $n$ can be written as the sum of two natural numbers whose prime factors do not exceed $\sqrt{n}$, where both numbers must be distinct.

positive_text:
\text{Let } P = (p_1, p_2) \text{ and } Q = (q_1, q_2) \text{ be two arbitrary points in } \mathbb{R}^2. \text{ Define the distance between them as} $$ d(P, Q) = |p_1 - q_1| + |p_2 - q_2|. $$ a) Describe the set of all points equidistant from $P$ and $Q$ under this metric.
 b) Given a constant $k > 0$, $k \ne 1$, define the set of all points $X$ such that $$ \frac{d(X, P)}{d(X, Q)} = k. $$ Determine its structure.
 c) The distance from a point $X$ to a line $m$ is defined as the minimum of $d(X, Y)$ over all $Y$ on $m$. A parabola is the set of points $X$ for which $d(X, F) = d(X, m)$, where $F$ is a fixed point and $m$ is a fixed line. Describe the shape of such a parabola under the given distance metric.
 d) Let triangle $PQR$ be given, and let $R_a$ be a point on side $QR$ such that $$ d(P, Q) + d(Q, R_a) = d(P, R) + d(R, R_a). $$ Define $R_b$ and $R_c$ similarly. Are the lines $PR_a$, $QR_b$, and $RR_c$ concurrent?
 e) Can there exist infinitely many points in the plane such that all pairwise distances are perfect squares?

negatives.text:
For two points $A = (x_1, y_1)$ and $B = (x_2, y_2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, their distance can be defined as,
$$
d(A, B) = |x_1 - x_2| - |y_1 - y_2|.
$$

For two points $A = (x_1, y_1)$ and $B = (x_2, y_2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, their distance can be defined as,
$$
d(A, B) = \sqrt{|x_1 - x_2|^2 + |y_1 - y_2|^2}.
$$

For two points $A = (x_1, y_1)$ and $B = (x_2, y_2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, their distance can be defined as,
$$
d(A, B) = \max\{|x_1 - x_2|, |y_1 - y_2|\}.
$$

Suppose the perpendicular bisectors of segments $DQ$ and $DP$ meet $AB$ and $AC$ at $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Show that the midpoint of side $BC$ lies on the line $XY$.

Assuming that the perpendicular bisector of $DQ$ intersects $AB$ at $X$ and the perpendicular bisector of $DP$ intersects $BC$ at $Y$, prove that the midpoint of $BC$ lies on line $XY$.

Assuming that the perpendicular bisector of $DQ$ intersects $AB$ at $X$ and the perpendicular bisector of $DP$ intersects $AC$ at $Y$, prove that the midpoint of $AB$ lies on line $XY$.

Assuming that the perpendicular bisector of $DQ$ intersects $AB$ at $X$ and the perpendicular bisector of $DP$ intersects $AC$ at $Y$, prove that the midpoint of $XY$ lies on line $BC$.

positive_text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$ be positive real numbers such that $a + b + c + d = 2$. Show that
$$
\frac{(a+c)^2}{ad+bc} + \frac{(b+d)^2}{ac+bd} + 4 \ge 4 \left( \frac{a+b+1}{c+d+1} + \frac{c+d+1}{a+b+1} \right).
$$

negatives.text: Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ be positive real numbers with $a + b + c + d = 2$. Prove that $$\frac{(a+c)^2}{ad+bc} + \frac{(b+d)^2}{ac+bd} + 4 \le 4 \left( \frac{a+b+1}{c+d+1} + \frac{c+d+1}{a+b+1} \right).$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ be positive real numbers with $a + b + c + d = 2$. Prove that $$\frac{(a+c)^2}{ad+bc} + \frac{(b+d)^2}{ac+bd} + 4 \ge 4 \left( \frac{a+b+2}{c+d+2} + \frac{c+d+2}{a+b+2} \right).$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ be positive real numbers with $a + b + c + d = 2$. Prove that $$\frac{(a+c)^2}{ad+bc} + \frac{(b+d)^2}{ac+bd} + 4 \ge 4 \left( \frac{a+b+1}{c+d+1} + \frac{a+b+1}{c+d+1} \right).$$

positive_text:
Let $\mathcal{H} = (h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ be an $(n + 1)$-tuple of $n$-variable polynomials with real coefficients. We call $\mathcal{H}$ **effective** if the following condition is satisfied: For any $n$ functions $g_1, g_2, \dots, g_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, if for all $1 \le i \le n + 1$, $Q_i(x) = h_i(g_1(x), g_2(x), \dots, g_n(x))$ is a polynomial in $x$, then each $g_j(x)$ is a polynomial.

a) Show that for all positive integers $n$, there exists an **effective** $(n+1)$-tuple $\mathcal{H}$ where each $h_i$ has degree strictly greater than one.

b) Demonstrate that for all integers $n > 1$, there is no **effective** $(n+1)$-tuple $\mathcal{H}$ consisting entirely of symmetric polynomials.

negatives.text:
A $(n + 1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ where for every $1 \le i \le n + 1$, $h_i(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n)$ is an $n$-variable polynomial with real coefficients is called **good** if the following condition holds. For any $n$ functions $f_1, f_2, \dots, f_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, if for all $1 \le i \le n + 1$, $P_i(x) = h_i(f_1(x), f_2(x), \dots, f_n(x))$ is a rational function in variable $x$, then $f_1(x), f_2(x), \dots, f_n(x)$ are polynomials.

a) Prove that for all positive integers $n$, there exists a **good** $(n+1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ such that the degree of each $h_i$ is more than one.

b) Prove that there does not exist any integer $n > 1$ for which there is a **good** $(n+1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ such that all $h_i$ are symmetric polynomials.

A $(n + 1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ where for every $1 \le i \le n + 1$, $h_i(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n)$ is an $n$-variable polynomial with real coefficients is called **good** if the following condition holds. For any $n$ functions $f_1, f_2, \dots, f_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, if for all $1 \le i \le n + 1$, $P_i(x) = h_i(f_1(x), f_2(x), \dots, f_n(x))$ is a polynomial in variable $x$ of degree at most $2$, then $f_1(x), f_2(x), \dots, f_n(x)$ are polynomials.

a) Prove that for all positive integers $n$, there exists a **good** $(n+1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ such that the degree of each $h_i$ is more than one.

b) Prove that there does not exist any integer $n > 1$ for which there is a **good** $(n+1)$-tuple $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ such that all $h_i$ are symmetric polynomials.

positive_text: \text{In triangle } ABC, \text{ let } \omega_1 \text{ be its circumcircle and } \angle C = 2\angle B. \text{ A line tangent to } \omega_1 \text{ at } A \text{ meets } BC \text{ at } E. \text{ A circle } \omega_2 \text{ passes through } B \text{ and is tangent to } AC \text{ at } C, intersecting } AB \text{ again at } F. \text{ A tangent from } E \text{ to } \omega_2 \text{ touches it at } K (\text{with } BC \text{ between } A \text{ and } K). \text{ Let } M \text{ be the midpoint of arc } BC \text{ on } \omega_1 \text{ not containing } A. \text{ Prove that } M, F, A, K \text{ lie on a circle.}

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with circumcircle } \omega_1 \text{ and } \angle C = -2\angle B. \text{ A tangent line to } \omega_1 \text{ at } A \text{ intersects } BC \text{ at } E. \text{ Let } \omega_2 \text{ be a circle passing through } B \text{ and tangent to } AC \text{ at } C. \text{ This circle intersects } AB \text{ for the second time at } F. \text{ A line through } E \text{ is tangent to } \omega_2 \text{ at } K \text{ (where } BC \text{ lies between } A \text{ and } K). \text{ Let } M \text{ be the midpoint of arc } BC \text{ of } \omega_1 \text{ (not containing } A). \text{ Prove that } MFAK \text{ is a cyclic quadrilateral.}

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with circumcircle } \omega_1 \text{ and } \angle C = 2\angle B. \text{ A tangent line to } \omega_1 \text{ at } A \text{ intersects } BC \text{ at } E. \text{ Let } \omega_2 \text{ be a circle passing through } B \text{ and tangent to } AC^2 \text{ at } C. \text{ This circle intersects } AB \text{ for the second time at } F. \text{ A line through } E \text{ is tangent to } \omega_2 \text{ at } K \text{ (where } BC \text{ lies between } A \text{ and } K). \text{ Let } M \text{ be the midpoint of arc } BC \text{ of } \omega_1 \text{ (not containing } A). \text{ Prove that } MFAK \text{ is a cyclic quadrilateral.}

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with circumcircle } \omega_1 \text{ and } \angle C = 2\angle B. \text{ A tangent line to } \omega_1 \text{ at } A \text{ intersects } BC \text{ at } E. \text{ Let } \omega_2 \text{ be a circle passing through } B \text{ and tangent to } AC \text{ at } A. \text{ This circle intersects } AB \text{ for the second time at } F. \text{ A line through } E \text{ is tangent to } \omega_2 \text{ at } K \text{ (where } BC \text{ lies between } A \text{ and } K). \text{ Let } M \text{ be the midpoint of arc } BC \text{ of } \omega_1 \text{ (not containing } A). \text{ Prove that } MFAK \text{ is a cyclic quadrilateral.}

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with points $P$ and $Q$ on side $BC$ such that $BP = CQ$ and $P$ lies between $B$ and $Q$. Let the circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ intersect $AB$ and $AC$ at points $E$ and $F$, respectively. Let $T$ be the intersection of $EP$ and $FQ$. If $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$, and two lines through $M$ are drawn parallel to $AB$ and $AC$, intersecting $EP$ and $FQ$ at $X$ and $Y$, respectively, prove that the circumcircles of triangles $TXY$ and $APQ$ are tangent.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, arbitrary points $P, Q$ lie on side $BC$ such that $BP = CQ$ and $P$ lies between $B, Q$. The circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ intersects sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. The point $T$ is the intersection point of $EP$ and $FQ$. Two lines passing through the midpoint of $BC$ and parallel to $AB$ and $AC$, intersect $AB$ and $AC$ at points $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $TXY$ and $APQ$ are tangent to each other.

In triangle $ABC$, arbitrary points $P, Q$ lie on side $BC$ such that $BP = 2CQ$ and $P$ lies between $B, Q$. The circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ intersects sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. The point $T$ is the intersection point of $EP$ and $FQ$. Two lines passing through the midpoint of $BC$ and parallel to $AB$ and $AC$, intersect $EP$ and $FQ$ at points $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $TXY$ and $APQ$ are tangent to each other.

In triangle $ABC$, arbitrary points $P, Q$ lie on side $BC$ such that $BP = CQ$ and $Q$ lies between $B, P$. The circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ intersects sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. The point $T$ is the intersection point of $EP$ and $FQ$. Two lines passing through the midpoint of $BC$ and parallel to $AB$ and $AC$, intersect $EP$ and $FQ$ at points $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $TXY$ and $APQ$ are tangent to each other.

positive_text:
Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that:
* $f(x) + f(y) \equiv 0 \pmod{x + y}$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}^+$,
* and $2f(x) \le x^3$ for all integers $x \ge 1395$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{Z}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^+$ satisfying the following conditions:
* For all $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}^+$, $f(x) + f(y)$ is divisible by $x + y$.
* For any integer $x \ge 1395$, the inequality $2f(x) \ge x^3$ holds.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{Z}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^+$ satisfying the following conditions:
* For all $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}^+$, $f(x) - f(y)$ is divisible by $x + y$.
* For any integer $x \ge 1395$, the inequality $2f(x) \le x^3$ holds.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{Z}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^+$ satisfying the following conditions:
* For all $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}^+$, $f(x) + f(y)$ is divisible by $x - y$.
* For any integer $x \ge 1395$, the inequality $2f(x) \le x^3$ holds.

positive_text: Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$. Choose a point $Q$ on segment $BC$ and a point $P$ on $\omega$ such that $AQ = AP$. Suppose the line $AP$ intersects $BC$ at $R$. Show that the tangents from $B$ and $C$ to the incircle of triangle $AQR$, distinct from $BC$, meet at a point on $\omega$.

negatives.text: Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of isosceles triangle $ABC$ where $AB = AC$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $\omega$ and $BC$ respectively such that $AP = AQ$. Lines $AP$ and $BC$ intersect at $R$. Prove that the tangents from $B$ and $C$ to the excircle of triangle $AQR$ (different from $BC$) are concurrent on $\omega$.

Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of isosceles triangle $ABC$ where $AB = AC$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $\omega$ and $BC$ respectively such that $AP = AQ$. Lines $AP$ and $BC$ intersect at $R$. Prove that the tangents from $B$ and $C$ to the incircle of triangle $AQR$ (different from $BC$) are concurrent on the circumcircle of triangle $ABQ$.

Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of isosceles triangle $ABC$ where $AB = AC$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $\omega$ and $BC$ respectively such that $AP = AQ$. Lines $BP$ and $BC$ intersect at $R$. Prove that the tangents from $B$ and $C$ to the incircle of triangle $AQR$ (different from $BC$) are concurrent on $\omega$.

positive_text: Let $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ be two intersecting circles at $A$ and $B$, with $O$ as the center of $\omega_1$ and also lying on $\omega_2$. If $S$ is the projection of $O$ onto $AB$, and $OS$ meets $\omega_2$ again at $P$, let the angle bisector of $\angle ASP$ intersect $\omega_1$ at $L$ (with $L$ and $A$ on the same side of $OP$). If $K$ is on $\omega_2$ such that $PK = PS$ (with $K$ and $A$ on the same side of $OP$), prove that $SL = KL$.

negatives.text: Two circles $\omega_1(O)$ and $\omega_2$ intersect each other at $A, B$. And $O$ lies on $\omega_2$. Let $S$ be the foot of perpendicular line to $AB$ from $O$. Line $OS$ intersects $\omega_2$ for the second time at $P$. The bisector of $\angle ASP$ intersects $\omega_1$ at $L$ ($A$ and $L$ are on the same side of the line $OP$). Let $K$ be a point on $\omega_2$ such that $PS = -PK$ ($A$ and $K$ are on the same side of the line $OP$). Prove that $SL = KL$.

Two circles $\omega_1(O)$ and $\omega_2$ intersect each other at $A, B$. And $O$ lies on $\omega_2$. Let $S$ be the foot of perpendicular line to $AB$ from $O$. Line $OS$ intersects $\omega_2$ for the second time at $P$. The bisector of $\angle ASP$ intersects $\omega_1$ at $L$ ($A$ and $L$ are on the same side of the line $OP$). Let $K$ be a point on $\omega_2$ such that $PS = PK^2$ ($A$ and $K$ are on the same side of the line $OP$). Prove that $SL = KL$.

Two circles $\omega_1(O)$ and $\omega_2$ intersect each other at $A, B$. And $O$ lies on $\omega_2$. Let $S$ be the foot of perpendicular line to $AB$ from $O$. Line $OS$ intersects $\omega_2$ for the second time at $P$. The bisector of $\angle ASP$ intersects $\omega_1$ at $L$ ($A$ and $L$ are on the same side of the line $OP$). Let $K$ be a point on $\omega_2$ such that $PS = PK$ ($A$ and $K$ are on the opposite side of the line $OP$). Prove that $SL = KL$.

positive_text: Determine all positive real-valued functions $ f $ defined on $ \mathbb{R}^+ $ satisfying $$ \frac{x + f(y)}{x f(y)} = f\left(f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) + \frac{1}{y} \right) $$ for all $ x, y \in \mathbb{R}^+ $.

negatives.text: Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$ such that for all positive real numbers $x$, $y$ $$ \frac{x - f(y)}{x f(y)} = f\left(\frac{1}{y} + f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\right) $$
Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$ such that for all positive real numbers $x$, $y$ $$ \frac{x + f(y)}{x f(y)} = f\left(\frac{1}{y} + f\left(x\right)\right) $$
Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$ such that for all positive real numbers $x$, $y$ $$ \frac{x + f(y)}{x f(y)} = f\left(\frac{1}{y} + f\left(\frac{1}{x^2}\right)\right) $$

positive_text: Let $ P $ be a point inside the isosceles trapezoid $ ABCD $, with $ AB \parallel CD $, such that $ \angle APB $ is greater than $ \angle ADC $ and $ \angle DPC $ is greater than $ \angle ABC $. Show that the sum of the bases $ AB + CD $ exceeds the sum of the legs $ AD + BC $.

negatives.text: The point $P$ is chosen in the interior of the isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$, where $AB \parallel CD$, such that $\angle APB < \angle ADC$ and $\angle DPC < \angle ABC$. Prove that $AB + CD > AD + BC$.
The point $P$ is chosen in the interior of the isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$, where $AB \parallel CD$, such that $\angle APB > \angle ADC$ and $\angle DPC > \angle ABC$. Prove that $AB + CD < AD + BC$.
The point $P$ is chosen in the interior of the isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$, where $AB \parallel CD$, such that $\angle APB > \angle ADC$ and $\angle DPC > \angle ABC$. Prove that $AB + CD = AD + BC$.

positive_text: Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$ in triangle $ABC$. Let $\omega$ be a circle tangent to sides $AB$ and $AC$ at points $E$ and $F$, respectively. From point $M$, draw two tangents to $\omega$ that touch the circle at points $P$ and $Q$, such that $P$ lies on the same side of line $AM$ as $B$. Define $X$ as the intersection of lines $PM$ and $BF$, and $Y$ as the intersection of lines $QM$ and $CE$. If $BC = 2PM$, show that segment $XY$ is tangent to circle $\omega$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$ let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $\omega$ be a circle inside of $ABC$ and tangent to $AB, AC$ at $E, F$, respectively. The tangents from $M$ to $\omega$ meet this circle at $P, Q$ such that $P$ and $B$ lie on the same side of $AM$. Lines $PM, CE$ cut each other at $X$, and $Y$ is the intersection of $QM, BF$. If $2PM = BC$, prove that $XY$ is tangent to $\omega$.

In triangle $ABC$ let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $\omega$ be a circle inside of $ABC$ and tangent to $AB, AC$ at $E, F$, respectively. The tangents from $M$ to $\omega$ meet this circle at $P, Q$ such that $P$ and $B$ lie on the same side of $AM$. Lines $PM, BF$ cut each other at $X$, and $Y$ is the intersection of $QM, CE$. If $PM = BC$, prove that $XY$ is tangent to $\omega$.

In triangle $ABC$ let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $\omega$ be a circle inside of $ABC$ and tangent to $AB, AC$ at $E, F$, respectively. The tangents from $M$ to $\omega$ meet this circle at $P, Q$ such that $P$ and $B$ lie on the same side of $AM$. Lines $PM, BF$ cut each other at $X$, and $Y$ is the intersection of $QM, CE$. If $2PM = AB$, prove that $XY$ is tangent to $\omega$.

positive_text:
Suppose $a$ and $b$ are distinct real numbers with $a^4 - b^4 = a - b$. Show that
$$
\frac{a - b}{a^6 - b^6} \le \frac{4}{3}(a + b)
$$

negatives.text: Let $x$, $y$ be distinct real numbers such that $x^4 - y^4 = x - y$. Prove that $$\frac{x - y}{x^6 - y^6} \ge \frac{4}{3}(x + y)$$
Let $x$, $y$ be distinct real numbers such that $x^4 - y^4 = x - y$. Prove that $$\frac{x + y}{x^6 - y^6} \le \frac{4}{3}(x + y)$$
Let $x$, $y$ be distinct real numbers such that $x^4 - y^4 = x + y$. Prove that $$\frac{x - y}{x^6 - y^6} \le \frac{4}{3}(x + y)$$

positive_text:
Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that:
(a) $f(y + f(x)) - f(x + f(y)) = y - x$, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$
(b) The set $J = \left\{\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b} \mid a, b \in \mathbb{R}, a \neq b\right\}$ is an interval. (i.e., $J$ contains all values between any two of its elements)

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that satisfy the following conditions:
(a) $x + f(y + f(x)) = y - f(x + f(y))$, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$
(b) The set $I = \left\{\frac{f(x)-f(y)}{x-y} \mid x, y \in \mathbb{R}, x \neq y\right\}$ is an interval.

Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that satisfy the following conditions:
(a) $x + f(y + f(x)) = y + f(x + f(y))$, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$
(b) The set $I = \left\{\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{x-y} \mid x, y \in \mathbb{R}, x \neq y\right\}$ is an interval.

Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that satisfy the following conditions:
(a) $x + f(y + f(x)) = y + f(x + f(y))$, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$
(b) The set $I = \left\{\frac{f(x)-f(y)}{x-y} \mid x, y \in \mathbb{R}, x \neq y\right\}$ is a finite interval.

positive_text: In isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$ with $AD = BC$ and $AB \parallel CD$, let diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at point $P$. Suppose the circumcircle of triangle $APB$ intersects line $BC$ again at point $X$. Let $Y$ lie on segment $AX$ such that $DY \parallel BC$, with $Y$ and $C$ on opposite sides of $AD$. Prove that $\angle YDA = 2 \times \angle YCA$.

negatives.text: In isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$ where $BC = AD$ and $AB \parallel CD$, point $P$ is the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Let $X$ be the second intersection point of $AD$ and circumcircle of triangle $APB$ and let $Y$ be a point on $AX$ such that $DY \parallel BC$ ($C$ and $Y$ are on different sides of line $AD$). Prove that $\angle YDA = 2 \times \angle YCA$.

In isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$ where $BC = AD$ and $AB \parallel CD$, point $P$ is the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Let $X$ be the second intersection point of $BC$ and circumcircle of triangle $APB$ and let $Y$ be a point on $AX$ such that $DY \parallel BC$ ($C$ and $Y$ are on the same side of line $AD$). Prove that $\angle YDA = 2 \times \angle YCA$.

positive_text: Let $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ be intersecting circles. Points $A, C$ are on $\omega_1$, and $B, D$ are on $\omega_2$, such that $AB$ and $CD$ are common external tangents of the two circles. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Let $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ be the tangents from $M$ to $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ (distinct from $AB$) meeting $CD$ at $Y$ and $X$, respectively. If $I$ is the incenter of triangle $MXY$, show that $IC = ID$.

negatives.text: Given two intersecting circles $\omega_1, \omega_2$. Points $A, C$ lie on $\omega_1$ and points $B, D$ lie on $\omega_2$ so that $AB, CD$ are common tangents of $\omega_1, \omega_2$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Tangent lines through $M$ to $\omega_1, \omega_2$ (other than $AB$) intersect $CD$ at $Y, X$. If $I$ be the incenter of triangle $MXY$, prove that $IC = IB$.

Given two intersecting circles $\omega_1, \omega_2$. Points $A, C$ lie on $\omega_1$ and points $B, D$ lie on $\omega_2$ so that $AB, CD$ are common tangents of $\omega_1, \omega_2$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Tangent lines through $M$ to $\omega_1, \omega_2$ (other than $AB$) intersect $CD$ at $Y, X$. If $I$ be the incenter of triangle $MXY$, prove that $IC = ID$ and $\angle CID = 90^\circ$.

Given two intersecting circles $\omega_1, \omega_2$. Points $A, C$ lie on $\omega_1$ and points $B, D$ lie on $\omega_2$ so that $AB, CD$ are common tangents of $\omega_1, \omega_2$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Tangent lines through $M$ to $\omega_1, \omega_2$ (other than $AB$) intersect $CD$ at $Y, X$. If $I$ be the incenter of triangle $MXY$, prove that $IC = ID$ assuming $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ are externally tangent.

positive_text:
Let $P(x)$ be a non-constant polynomial with real coefficients such that $P(0) = 0$. For any positive real number $M$, show there exists a positive integer $d$ such that for any monic polynomial $Q(x)$ with degree $\deg Q(x) \geq d$, the number of integer values $k$ for which
$$
|P(Q(k))| \leq M
$$
is less than or equal to $\deg Q(x)$.

negatives.text:
Let $P(x)$ be a non-constant polynomial with real coefficients such that $P(0) = 0$. For all positive real numbers $M$, prove that there is a positive integer $d$ such that for any monic polynomial $Q(x)$ of degree greater than or equal to $d$, total number of integers $k$ where
$$
|P(Q(k))| \geq M,
$$
is at most $\deg Q(x)$.

positive_text: Given an acute triangle $ABC$ with orthocenter $H$ and circumcenter $O$, let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the feet of the altitudes from $B$ and $C$, respectively. Choose a point $P$ on segment $EF$ such that $HP$ is perpendicular to $HO$. Let $Q$ lie on segment $HA$ so that $PQ$ is perpendicular to $HM$. Show that $QA = 3QH$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle. The altitudes $BE$, $CF$ meet at $H$. $O$ is the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$. $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$. $P$ is the point on $EF$ such that $HP \perp HO$. $Q$ is the point on $HA$ such that $PQ \perp HM$. Prove that $QA = 2QH$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle. The altitudes $BE$, $CF$ meet at $H$. $O$ is the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$. $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$. $P$ is the point on $EF$ such that $HP \perp HO$. $Q$ is the point on $HB$ such that $PQ \perp HM$. Prove that $QA = 3QH$.

positive_text: In an isosceles triangle $\triangle ABC$ with $AB = AC$, let $I$ be the incenter. Suppose a circle $\omega$ goes through $C$ and $I$ and is tangent to the angle bisector $AI$. This circle intersects side $AC$ and the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at points $Q$ and $D$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$, and $N$ the midpoint of $CQ$. Show that the lines $AD$, $MN$, and $BC$ meet at a single point.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle ($AB = AC$) with incenter $I$. Circle $\omega$ passes through $C$ and $I$ and is tangent to $BI$. The circle $\omega$ intersects $AC$ and circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at $Q$ and $D$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $N$ be the midpoint of $CQ$. Prove that $AD$, $MN$ and $BC$ are concurrent.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle ($AB = AC$) with incenter $I$. Circle $\omega$ passes through $C$ and $I$ and is tangent to $AI$. The circle $\omega$ intersects $AB$ and circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at $Q$ and $D$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $N$ be the midpoint of $CQ$. Prove that $AD$, $MN$ and $BC$ are concurrent.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle ($AB = AC$) with incenter $I$. Circle $\omega$ passes through $C$ and $I$ and is tangent to $AI$. The circle $\omega$ intersects $AC$ and circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at $Q$ and $D$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and $N$ be the midpoint of $CQ$. Prove that $AD$, $MN$ and $BC$ are concurrent.

positive_text: Given any integer $k$ with $2 \leq k < 1398$, show there exists a real number $x$ such that for all $1 < n < 1398$: $$ \{x^{n-1}\} > \{x^n\} \iff n \equiv 0 \pmod{k}. $$

negatives.text:
For every positive integer $k > 1$ prove that there exists a real number $x$ such that for every positive integer $n < 1398$:
$$
\{x^n\} > \{x^{n-1}\} \iff k \mid n.
$$

For every positive integer $k > 1$ prove that there exists a real number $x$ such that for every positive integer $n < 1398$:
$$
\{x^n\} < \{x^{n+1}\} \iff k \mid n.
$$

For every positive integer $k > 1$ prove that there exists a real number $x$ such that for every positive integer $n < 1398$:
$$
\{x^{n^2}\} < \{x^{(n-1)^2}\} \iff k \mid n.
$$

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$ and $\angle A > 60^\circ$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$. Suppose $P$ is a point on the circumcircle of triangle $BOC$ such that $BP$ is parallel to $AC$, and let $K$ be a point on $AP$ with $BK = BC$. Show that the line $CK$ passes through the midpoint of the arc $\widearc{BC}$ of the circumcircle of $\triangle BOC$.

negatives.text: Consider an acute-angled triangle $\triangle ABC$ with $AB = AC$ and $\angle A > 60^\circ$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$. Point $P$ lies on the circumcircle of $\triangle BOC$ such that $BP \parallel AC$, and point $K$ lies on segment $AP$ such that $BK = AB$. Prove that line $CK$ bisects the arc $\widearc{BC}$ of circumcircle of $\triangle BOC$.

Consider an acute-angled triangle $\triangle ABC$ with $AB = AC$ and $\angle A > 60^\circ$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$. Point $P$ lies on the circumcircle of $\triangle BOC$ such that $BP \parallel AC$, and point $K$ lies on segment $AP$ such that $BK = BC$. Prove that line $CK$ bisects the arc $\widearc{AB}$ of circumcircle of $\triangle BOC$.

positive_text: Let $n > 2$ be a natural number. Show that the equation $\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^3$ has no solutions where each $x_i$ is a positive integer greater than 1.

negatives.text: Let $n > 2$ be a natural number. Prove that the following equation has no solution $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ in positive integers numbers greater than 1: $$ (x_1x_2\dots x_n)^2 = x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \dots + x_n^2 $$

Let $n > 2$ be a natural number. Prove that the following equation has no solution $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ in positive integers numbers greater than 1: $$ (x_1x_2\dots x_n)^2 = -x_1^3 - x_2^3 - \dots - x_n^3 $$

positive_text:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. We say $n$ is interesting if for every permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, there exist polynomials $Q_1, Q_2, \dots, Q_n$ and a real number $\epsilon > 0$ such that:
$$
\text{i)}\ Q_1(0) = Q_2(0) = \dots = Q_n(0),
$$
$$
\text{ii)}\ Q_1(x) > Q_2(x) > \dots > Q_n(x) \text{ for } x \in (-\epsilon, 0),
$$
$$
\text{iii)}\ Q_{\sigma(1)}(x) > Q_{\sigma(2)}(x) > \dots > Q_{\sigma(n)}(x) \text{ for } x \in (0, \epsilon).
$$
Determine all such interesting numbers.

negatives.text:
We call an integer number $n > 0$ interesting if for each permutation $\sigma$ of $1, 2, \dots, n$ there exist polynomials $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ and $\epsilon > 0$ such that:
$$
\text{i)}\ P_1(0) = P_2(0) = \dots = P_n(0).
$$
$$
\text{ii)}\ P_1(x) < P_2(x) < \dots < P_n(x) \text{ for } -\epsilon < x < 0.
$$
$$
\text{iii)}\ P_{\sigma(1)}(x) > P_{\sigma(2)}(x) > \dots > P_{\sigma(n)}(x) \text{ for } 0 < x < \epsilon.
$$
Find all interesting numbers.

We call an integer number $n > 0$ interesting if for each permutation $\sigma$ of $1, 2, \dots, n$ there exist polynomials $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ and $\epsilon > 0$ such that:
$$
\text{i)}\ P_1(0) = P_2(0) = \dots = P_n(0).
$$
$$
\text{ii)}\ P_1(x) > P_2(x) > \dots > P_n(x) \text{ for } -\epsilon < x < 0.
$$
$$
\text{iii)}\ P_{\sigma(1)}(x) < P_{\sigma(2)}(x) < \dots < P_{\sigma(n)}(x) \text{ for } 0 < x < \epsilon.
$$
Find all interesting numbers.

positive_text: Let $f : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function with the property that for any division of $[0, 1]$ into non-empty disjoint sets $P$ and $Q$, either there exists $x \in P$ with $f(x) \in Q$ or $x \in Q$ with $f(x) \in P$. Additionally, $f(x) > x$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$. Prove that $f(x) = 1$ for infinitely many $x$ in $[0, 1]$.

negatives.text: Given a function $g : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for every non-empty partition of the interval $[0, 1]$ into subsets $A, B$ either $\exists x \in A : g(x) \in B$ or $\exists x \in B : g(x) \in A$. Furthermore, $g(x) < x$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$. Prove that $g(x) = 1$, for infinitely many $x$ in its domain.

Given a function $g : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for every non-empty partition of the interval $[0, 1]$ into subsets $A, B$ either $\exists x \in A : g(x) \in A$ or $\exists x \in B : g(x) \in B$. Furthermore, $g(x) > x$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$. Prove that $g(x) = 1$, for infinitely many $x$ in its domain.

positive_text: An infinite subset $ S $ of the positive integers is termed *good* if for any three distinct elements $ a $, $ b $, and $ c $ in $ S $, every positive divisor of $ \frac{a^c - b^c}{a - b} $ also belongs to $ S $. Prove that for each integer $ n > 1 $, there exists a good set $ S $ that does not contain $ n $.

negatives.text: We call an infinite set $ S \subseteq \mathbb{N} $ *good* if for all pairwise distinct integers $ a $, $ b $, $ c \in S $, all positive divisors of $ \frac{a^c + b^c}{a - b} $ are in $ S $. For all positive integers $ n > 1 $, prove that there exists a good set $ S $ such that $ n \notin S $.

We call an infinite set $ S \subseteq \mathbb{N} $ *good* if for all pairwise distinct integers $ a $, $ b $, $ c \in S $, all positive divisors of $ \frac{a^c - b^c}{a + b} $ are in $ S $. For all positive integers $ n > 1 $, prove that there exists a good set $ S $ such that $ n \notin S $.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$, and let $P$ be the intersection point of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of segments $AD$ and $BC$, respectively. Let $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$, and $\omega_3$ denote the circumcircles of triangles $ADP$, $BCP$, and $OMN$, respectively. Define $E$ as the intersection point of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_3$ not lying on the arc $APD$ of $\omega_1$, and $F$ as the intersection point of $\omega_2$ and $\omega_3$ not on the arc $BPC$ of $\omega_2$. Show that $OE = OF$.

negatives.text: Cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ with circumcenter $O$ is given. Point $P$ is the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Let $M$ and $N$ be midpoints of the sides $AD$ and $BC$, respectively. Suppose that $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$ and $\omega_3$ are circumcircles of triangles $ABP$, $CDP$ and $OMN$, respectively. Let $E$ and $F$ be intersection points of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_3$, which is not on the arc $APB$ of $\omega_1$, and the intersection point of $\omega_2$ and $\omega_3$, which is not on the arc $CPD$ of $\omega_2$, respectively. Prove that $OE = OF$.

positive_text: Let $P = \{p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n\}$ be a set of $n \ge 6$ points in general position in the plane (i.e., no three collinear). A "connection system" is a connected graph on $P$ with straight-line edges and no intersecting edges. Show that it is possible to construct three such connection systems $C_1, C_2, C_3$ where no pair $C_i, C_j$ share an edge.

negatives.text: Consider $n \ge 6$ points $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ on the plane such that no three of them are colinear. We call a graph with vertices $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ a "road network" if it is connected, each of its edges is a line segment, and no two edges intersect at a point other than its vertices. Prove that there are three road networks $G_1, G_2, G_3$ such that $G_i$ and $G_j$ share at least one edge for $1 \le i, j \le 3$.

Consider $n \ge 6$ points $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ on the plane such that no three of them are colinear. We call a graph with vertices $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ a "road network" if it is connected, each of its edges is a line segment, and no two edges intersect at a point other than its vertices. Prove that there are three road networks $G_1, G_2, G_3$ such that $G_i$ and $G_j$ don't have a common edge for $1 \le i < j \le 4$.

Consider $n \ge 6$ points $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ on the plane such that no three of them are colinear. We call a graph with vertices $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ a "road network" if it is connected, each of its edges is a line segment, and no two edges intersect at a point other than its vertices. Prove that there are three road networks $G_1, G_2, G_3$ such that $G_i$ and $G_j$ don't have a common edge for $1 \le i, j \le 3$, and each network has at most $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ edges.

positive_text: Let $n$ be a natural number with $n \ge 3$. Determine the largest natural number $k$ for which there exist $n$ real numbers $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$ in the interval $[0, 1)$ such that for each $j$ with $1 \le j \le k$, there is a subset of the $b_i$'s whose sum equals $j$.

negatives.text: Suppose that $3 \le n$ is a natural number. Find the maximum value of the natural number $k$, for which, there are real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n \in [0, 1]$ (not necessarily distinct) such that for every natural number $j$ satisfying $j \le k$, there exists a sum of a certain number of $a_i$'s equal to $j$.

Suppose that $3 \le n$ is a natural number. Find the maximum value of the natural number $k$, for which, there are real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n \in [0, 1)$ (not necessarily distinct) such that for every natural number $j$ satisfying $j \le k$, there exists a sum of a certain number of $a_i$'s less than or equal to $j$.

Suppose that $3 \le n$ is a natural number. Find the maximum value of the natural number $k$, for which, there are real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n \in [0, 1)$ (not necessarily distinct) such that for every natural number $j$ satisfying $j \le k$, there exists a sum of a certain number of $a_i$'s equal to $\frac{1}{j}$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be isosceles with $BA = BC$, and let $P$ be an arbitrary point on the altitude from $B$. The circumcircle of triangle $\triangle BAP$ intersects $AC$ again at point $M$. If $N$ is the reflection of $M$ over the midpoint of $AC$, then the line $NP$ intersects the circumcircle of $\triangle BAP$ again at $X$ ($X \neq P$). The line $AB$ intersects the circumcircle of $\triangle NAP$ again at $Y$ ($Y \neq A$). The tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle NAP$ at $A$ meets $BP$ at $Z$. Prove that $CZ$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $\triangle XYP$.

negatives.text: In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ ($BC = BA$), point $P$ is arbitrarily chosen on the altitude from vertex $B$. Suppose that the circumcircle of $BAP$ intersects $AC$ for the second time at point $M$. Let $N$ be the reflection of $M$ with respect to the midpoint of $AC$. $NP$ intersects the circumcircle of $BAP$ at $X$ ($X \neq P$), and $AB$ intersects the circumcircle of $NAP$ at $Y$ ($Y \neq A$). The tangent to the circumcircle of $NAP$ at $A$ intersects $BP$ at $Z$. Prove that $BZ$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $XYP$.

In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ ($BC = BA$), point $P$ is arbitrarily chosen on the altitude from vertex $B$. Suppose that the circumcircle of $BAP$ intersects $AC$ for the second time at point $M$. Let $N$ be the reflection of $M$ with respect to the midpoint of $AC$. $NP$ intersects the circumcircle of $BAP$ at $X$ ($X \neq P$), and $AB$ intersects the circumcircle of $NAP$ at $Y$ ($Y \neq A$). The tangent to the circumcircle of $NAP$ at $P$ intersects $BP$ at $Z$. Prove that $CZ$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $XYP$.

In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ ($BC = BA$), point $P$ is arbitrarily chosen on the altitude from vertex $B$. Suppose that the circumcircle of $BAP$ intersects $AC$ for the second time at point $M$. Let $N$ be the reflection of $M$ with respect to the midpoint of $AC$. $NP$ intersects the circumcircle of $BAP$ at $X$ ($X \neq P$), and $AB$ intersects the circumcircle of $NAP$ at $Y$ ($Y \neq A$). The tangent to the circumcircle of $NAP$ at $A$ intersects $BP$ at $Z$. Prove that $CZ$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $XYM$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have incenter $I$ and circumcircle $\Gamma$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ of $\Gamma$ not containing $A$. A point $X$ lies on the external bisector of $\angle BAC$. The line $BX$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $BIC$ again at $T$. Define $Y$ as a point on $\Gamma$ such that $MY = MA$. Show that $TC$ is parallel to $AY$.

negatives.text: In the triangle $ABC$, $I$ is the incenter and $M$ is the midpoint of the part of arc $BC$ on the circumcircle of $ABC$ that doesn't contain $A$. $X$ is a point on the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. The line $BX$ meets the circumcircle of $BIC$ at $T$, for the second time. The point $Y$ is on the circumcircle of $ABC$ such that $MA = MY$. Prove that $TC \parallel AY$.

In the triangle $ABC$, $I$ is the incenter and $M$ is the midpoint of the part of arc $BC$ on the circumcircle of $ABC$ that doesn't contain $A$. $X$ is a point on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. The line $CX$ meets the circumcircle of $BIC$ at $T$, for the second time. The point $Y$ is on the circumcircle of $ABC$ such that $MA = MY$. Prove that $TC \parallel AY$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have midpoints $M$ and $N$ of $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Let $BN$ and $CM$ meet the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ again at $N'$ and $M'$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on the line through $BC$ with $X$ on the extension beyond $B$ and $Y$ beyond $C$. Suppose $$\angle BXM' = \angle ACM, \quad \angle CYN' = \angle ABN.$$ Show that $AX = AY$.

negatives.text:
In triangle $ABC$ the points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. The lines $BN$ and $CM$ intersect the circumcircle of $ABC$, for the second time, at $N'$ and $M'$, respectively. Points $X$ and $Y$ are on the extension of $BC$ such that, point $B$ is between $X$ and $C$ and point $C$ is between $B$ and $Y$.

$$
\angle BXM' = \angle ABM, \angle CYN' = \angle ACN
$$

Prove that $AY = AX$.

In triangle $ABC$ the points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. The lines $BN$ and $CM$ intersect the circumcircle of $ABC$, for the second time, at $N'$ and $M'$, respectively. Points $X$ and $Y$ are on the extension of $BC$ such that, point $B$ is between $X$ and $C$ and point $C$ is between $B$ and $Y$.

$$
\angle BXM' = \angle ACM, \angle CYN' = -\angle ABN
$$

Prove that $AY = AX$.

In triangle $ABC$ the points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. The lines $BN$ and $CM$ intersect the circumcircle of $ABC$, for the second time, at $N'$ and $M'$, respectively. Points $X$ and $Y$ are on the extension of $BC$ such that, point $B$ is between $X$ and $C$ and point $C$ is between $B$ and $Y$.

$$
\angle BXM' = \angle ACM, \angle CYN' = \angle ABN^2
$$

Prove that $AY = AX$.

positive_text:
Suppose $x, y, z$ are positive integers with $y > x > 1$ and $\gcd(z, xy) = 1$. Show that there is some $k \in \mathbb{N}$ for which
$$
z \mid \binom{y^k}{x^k}
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a, b, c$ be natural numbers such that $b > a > 1$ and $\gcd(c, ab) = 1$. Prove that there exists a natural number $n$ such that
$$
c \mid \binom{b^n + a^n}{a^n}
$$

Let $a, b, c$ be natural numbers such that $b > a > 1$ and $\gcd(c, ab) = 1$. Prove that there exists a natural number $n$ such that
$$
c \mid \binom{a^n}{b^n}
$$

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer such that $n \ge 4$. Consider all permutations $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n)$ of the numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$. For each permutation, compute $$ a_1 + 2a_2 + 3a_3 + \dots + na_n $$ and record the result. How many unique results will appear on the board in total?

negatives.text:
Let $n$ be a positive integer such that $n \ge 4$. For every permutation $(s_1, s_2, \dots, s_n)$ of the numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$, we calculate the following expression and write the result on the board:
$$
1s_1 + 2s_2 + 3s_3 + \dots + ns_n
$$
However, if the permutation is decreasing, we do not write its value. In the end, how many distinct values will be written on the board?

Let $n$ be a positive integer such that $n \ge 4$. For every permutation $(s_1, s_2, \dots, s_n)$ of the numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$, we calculate the following expression and write the result on the board:
$$
1s_1 - 2s_2 + 3s_3 - \dots + (-1)^{n+1} ns_n
$$
In the end, how many distinct values will be written on the board?

Let $n$ be a positive integer such that $n \ge 4$. For every permutation $(s_1, s_2, \dots, s_n)$ of the numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$, we calculate the following expression and write the result on the board:
$$
1s_1 + 2s_2^2 + 3s_3^2 + \dots + ns_n^2
$$
In the end, how many distinct values will be written on the board?

positive_text:
Determine all sequences $(b_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of positive integers such that for all $n \ge 3$,
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n-2} \frac{1}{b_k b_{k+2}} = 1 - \frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n-1} b_j^2}.
$$

negatives.text:
Find all sequences $(a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of positive integers such that for every $n \ge 3$ we have:
$$
\frac{1}{a_1 a_3} + \frac{1}{a_2 a_4} + \frac{1}{a_3 a_5} + \dots + \frac{1}{a_{n-2} a_n} = 1 + \frac{1}{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + \dots + a_{n-1}^2}
$$

Find all sequences $(a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of positive integers such that for every $n \ge 3$ we have:
$$
\frac{1}{a_1 a_3} + \frac{1}{a_2 a_4} + \frac{1}{a_3 a_5} + \dots + \frac{1}{a_{n-2} a_n} = 1 - \frac{1}{(a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_{n-1})^2}
$$

Find all sequences $(a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of positive integers such that for every $n \ge 3$ we have:
$$
\frac{1}{a_1 a_3} + \frac{1}{a_2 a_4} + \frac{1}{a_3 a_5} + \dots + \frac{1}{a_{n-2} a_n} = 1 - \frac{1}{a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_{n-1}}
$$

positive_text: Let $ n > 10 $ be a positive integer. A set of $ n $ lines is drawn in the plane such that no two are parallel and no three meet at a single point. Suppose that among the bounded regions formed, at least $ \frac{n^2}{8} + 1 $ are colored black. A triangle formed by three of these lines is said to be *good* if it contains exactly one black region. Prove that the number of good triangles is at least $ \frac{n}{2} $.

negatives.text: Let $n > 10$ be a positive integer. $n$ lines are drawn on the plane such that no three are concurrent and no two are parallel. Among the finite regions formed by these lines, at least $\frac{n^2}{8} - 1$ of them were blacked. We call a triangle formed by three lines *good* if there is only one black region inside of it. Prove that we at least have $\frac{n}{2}$ good triangles.

Let $n > 10$ be a positive integer. $n$ lines are drawn on the plane such that no three are concurrent and no two are parallel. Among the finite regions formed by these lines, at least $\frac{n^2}{8} + 1$ of them were blacked. We call a triangle formed by three lines *good* if there are only two black regions inside of it. Prove that we at least have $\frac{n}{2}$ good triangles.

Let $n > 10$ be a positive integer. $n$ lines are drawn on the plane such that no three are concurrent and no two are parallel. Among the finite regions formed by these lines, at least $\frac{n^2}{8} + 1$ of them were blacked. We call a triangle formed by three lines *good* if there is only one black region inside of it. Prove that we at least have $\frac{n}{3}$ good triangles.

positive_text:
Let $\triangle ABC$ have side lengths $BC = a$, $CA = b$, $AB = c$, and let the internal angle bisectors of $\angle A, \angle B, \angle C$ intersect the opposite sides at points $D, E, F$, respectively. Let $d, e, f$ denote the lengths of the segments $AD, BE, CF$, respectively. Show that
$$
def = \frac{4abc(a+b+c)K}{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)},
$$
where $K$ is the area of $\triangle ABC$.

negatives.text:
Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle the lengths of whose sides $BC, CA, AB$, respectively, are denoted by $a, b, c$, respectively. Let the internal bisectors of the angles $\angle BAC, \angle ABC, \angle BCA$, respectively, meet the sides $BC, CA, AB$, respectively, at $D, E, F$, respectively. Denote the lengths of the line segments $AD, BE, CF$, respectively, by $d, e, f$, respectively. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{def} = \frac{4abc(a+b+c)\Delta}{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)},
$$
where $\Delta$ stands for the area of the triangle $ABC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle the lengths of whose sides $BC, CA, AB$, respectively, are denoted by $a, b, c$, respectively. Let the internal bisectors of the angles $\angle BAC, \angle ABC, \angle BCA$, respectively, meet the sides $BC, CA, AB$, respectively, at $D, E, F$, respectively. Denote the lengths of the line segments $AD, BE, CF$, respectively, by $d, e, f$, respectively. Prove that
$$
def = \frac{4abc(a+b+c)\Delta^2}{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)},
$$
where $\Delta$ stands for the area of the triangle $ABC$.

positive_text:
Let $r$ and $n$ be nonnegative integers with $r \le n$.

a. Show that the expression
$$
\binom{n}{r} \cdot \frac{n+1-2r}{n+1-r}
$$
results in an integer.

b. Demonstrate that the inequality
$$
\sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} \binom{n}{r} \cdot \frac{n+1-2r}{n+1-r} < 2^{n-2}
$$
holds for all $n \ge 9$.

negatives.text:
\text{Let } r \text{ and } n \text{ be nonnegative integers such that } r \le n.
\begin{itemize}
\item[a.] Prove that
$$
\frac{n-1-2r}{n+1-r} \binom{n}{r}
$$
is an integer.
\item[b.] Prove that
$$
\sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} \frac{n-1-2r}{n+1-r} \binom{n}{r} < 2^{n-2}
$$
for all } n \ge 9.

\text{Let } r \text{ and } n \text{ be nonnegative integers such that } r \le n.
\begin{itemize}
\item[a.] Prove that
$$
\frac{n+1-2r}{n+1-r} \binom{n}{r}
$$
is an integer.
\item[b.] Prove that
$$
\sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} \frac{n+1-2r}{n+1-r} \binom{n}{r} > 2^{n-2}
$$
for all } n \ge 9.

\text{Let } r \text{ and } n \text{ be nonnegative integers such that } r \le n.
\begin{itemize}
\item[a.] Prove that
$$
\frac{n+1-2r}{n+1-r} \binom{n}{r}
$$
is an integer.
\item[b.] Prove that
$$
\sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} \frac{n+1-2r}{n+1-r} \binom{n}{r} < 2^{n-2}
$$
for all } n \ge 2.

positive_text:
Given $k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ and a positive integer $n$, let $f_k(n)$ be the number of sequences $x_1, \dots, x_n$, where $x_i \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$, such that the sum $S = x_1 + \cdots + x_n$ satisfies $S \equiv k \mod 4$.

a. Prove that $f_1(n) = f_3(n)$ for all positive integers $n$.

b. Prove that
$$
 f_0(n) = \frac{3^n + 2 + (-1)^n}{4}
$$
for all positive integers $n$.

negatives.text:
Given $k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ and a positive integer $n$, let $f_k(n)$ be the number of sequences $x_1, \dots, x_n$, where $x_i \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$, and
$$
x_1 + \cdots + x_n \equiv k \mod 3.
$$

a. Prove that $f_1(n) = f_2(n)$ for all positive integers $n$.

b. Prove that
$$
f_0(n) = \frac{3^n + 2 + (-1)^n}{4}
$$
for all positive integers $n$.

Given $k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ and a positive integer $n$, let $f_k(n)$ be the number of sequences $x_1, \dots, x_n$, where $x_i \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$, and
$$
x_1 + \cdots + x_n \equiv k \mod 4.
$$

a. Prove that $f_1(n) = f_2(n)$ for all positive integers $n$.

b. Prove that
$$
f_0(n) = \frac{3^n + 2 + (-1)^n}{4}
$$
for all positive integers $n$.

Given $k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ and a positive integer $n$, let $f_k(n)$ be the number of sequences $x_1, \dots, x_n$, where $x_i \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$, and
$$
x_1 + \cdots + x_n \equiv k \mod 4.
$$

a. Prove that $f_1(n) = f_3(n)$ for all positive integers $n$.

b. Prove that
$$
f_0(n) = \frac{3^n + 2 - (-1)^n}{4}
$$
for all positive integers $n$.

positive_text:
Let $p(x)$ be a polynomial with rational coefficients. Show that there exists a positive integer $n$ for which the polynomial $q(x)$, defined as
$$
q(x) = p(x + n) - p(x),
$$
has all integer coefficients.

negatives.text: Let $p(x)$ be a polynomial with rational coefficients. Prove that there exists a positive integer $n$ such that the polynomial $q(x)$ defined by $$ q(x) = p(x + n) + p(x) $$ has integer coefficients.

Let $p(x)$ be a polynomial with rational coefficients. Prove that there exists a positive integer $n$ such that the polynomial $q(x)$ defined by $$ q(x) = p(x + n) - p(x - n) $$ has integer coefficients.

Let $p(x)$ be a polynomial with rational coefficients. Prove that there exists a positive integer $n$ such that the polynomial $q(x)$ defined by $$ q(x) = p(x + n)^2 - p(x)^2 $$ has integer coefficients.

positive_text: Suppose $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles with $|AB| = |AC|$. Let $D$ lie on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ such that $D$ and $A$ are on the same side of $BC$. Prove that $$ |DB| + |DC| \le 2|AB| $$ with equality precisely when $D = A$. Use this to show that among all triangles inscribed in a fixed circle, the equilateral triangle has the maximum perimeter.

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $|AB| = |AC|$. If $D$ is a point on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ on the same side of $BC$ as $A$, prove
$$
|AB| + |AC| \le |DB| + |DC|
$$
with equality if and only if $D = A$. Hence prove, of all triangles described in a circle, the equilateral triangle has the greatest perimeter.

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $|AB| = |AC|$. If $D$ is a point on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ on the same side of $BC$ as $A$, prove
$$
|AB| + |AC| \ge |DB| + |DC| + 1
$$
with equality if and only if $D = A$. Hence prove, of all triangles described in a circle, the equilateral triangle has the greatest perimeter.

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $|AB| = |AC|$. If $D$ is a point on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ on the opposite side of $BC$ from $A$, prove
$$
|AB| + |AC| \ge |DB| + |DC|
$$
with equality if and only if $D = A$. Hence prove, of all triangles described in a circle, the equilateral triangle has the greatest perimeter.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a square with a point $P$ inside such that $PA = 3$, $PB = 7$, and $PD = 5$. Determine the area of square $ABCD$.

negatives.text:
A square $ABCD$ contains a point $P$ such that
$$
|PA| = 3, \quad |PB| = 7 \quad \text{and} \quad |PC| = 5.
$$
Find the area of the square.

A square $ABCD$ contains a point $P$ such that
$$
|PA| = 3, \quad |PB| = 7 \quad \text{and} \quad |PD| = -5.
$$
Find the area of the square.

A square $ABCD$ contains a point $P$ such that
$$
|PA| = 3^2, \quad |PB| = 7^2 \quad \text{and} \quad |PD| = 5^2.
$$
Find the area of the square.

positive_text:
Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle, and suppose a line passes through vertex $A$ and intersects side $BC$ at point $D$, and the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at point $P$ (distinct from $A$). Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{|PD|} = \frac{1}{|PB|} + \frac{1}{|PC|}
$$

negatives.text:
A line drawn from the vertex $A$ of an equilateral triangle $ABC$ meets the side $BC$ at $D$ and the circumcircle at $P$. Show that
$$
\frac{1}{|PD|} = \frac{1}{|PB|} - \frac{1}{|PC|}
$$

A line drawn from the vertex $A$ of an equilateral triangle $ABC$ meets the side $BC$ at $D$ and the circumcircle at $P$. Show that
$$
\frac{1}{|PD|^2} = \frac{1}{|PB|} + \frac{1}{|PC|}
$$

A line drawn from the vertex $A$ of an equilateral triangle $ABC$ meets the side $BC$ at $D$ and the circumcircle at $P$. Show that
$$
\frac{1}{|PD|} = \frac{1}{|PB|} + \frac{1}{|PC|} + \frac{1}{|AB|}
$$

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a square. A point $H$ lies on $AB$ such that $|AH|^2 = |AB| \cdot |BH|$. If $E$ is the midpoint of $AD$ and $X$ is the midpoint of $AH$, and $Y$ is a point on $EB$ with $XY$ perpendicular to $BE$, prove that $|XY| = |XH|$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a square. The line segment $AB$ is divided internally at $H$ so that $|AB| \cdot |AH| = |BH|^2$. Let $E$ be the midpoint of $AD$ and $X$ be the midpoint of $AH$. Let $Y$ be the point on $EB$ such that $XY$ is perpendicular to $BE$. Prove that $|XY| = |XH|$.

Let $ABCD$ be a square. The line segment $AB$ is divided internally at $H$ so that $|AB| \cdot |BH| = |AH|^2$. Let $E$ be the midpoint of $AD$ and $X$ be the midpoint of $AH$. Let $Y$ be the point on $EB$ such that $XY$ is parallel to $BE$. Prove that $|XY| = |XH|$.

positive_text: In Harpland, coins are categorized as green, white, or orange. Each coin has a positive integer value in shillings, though same-colored coins may differ in value. These coins are arranged in an equilateral triangle with side length $n$, such that no two adjacent coins share the same color and the total value of coins along any row parallel to a triangle side is divisible by three. Show that the sum of shilling values of all green coins is divisible by three.

negatives.text: The country of Harpland has three types of coin: green, white and orange. The unit of currency in Harpland is the shilling. Any coin is worth a positive integer number of shillings, but coins of the same colour may be worth different amounts. A set of coins is stacked in the form of an equilateral triangle of side $n$ coins, as shown below for the case of $n = 6$. The stacking has the following properties: 1. no coin touches another coin of the same colour; 2. the total worth, in shillings, of the coins lying on any line parallel to one of the sides of the triangle is divisible by three. Prove that the total worth in shillings of the *green* coins in the triangle is divisible by two.

The country of Harpland has three types of coin: green, white and orange. The unit of currency in Harpland is the shilling. Any coin is worth a positive integer number of shillings, but coins of the same colour may be worth different amounts. A set of coins is stacked in the form of an equilateral triangle of side $n$ coins, as shown below for the case of $n = 6$. The stacking has the following properties: 1. no coin touches another coin of the same colour; 2. the total worth, in shillings, of the coins lying on any line parallel to one of the sides of the triangle is divisible by three. Prove that the total worth in shillings of the *green* coins in the triangle is divisible by three if all coins are worth the same number of shillings.

The country of Harpland has three types of coin: green, white and orange. The unit of currency in Harpland is the shilling. Any coin is worth a positive integer number of shillings, but coins of the same colour may be worth different amounts. A set of coins is stacked in the form of an equilateral triangle of side $n$ coins, as shown below for the case of $n = 6$. The stacking has the following properties: 1. no coin touches another coin of the same colour; 2. the total worth, in shillings, of the coins lying on any line parallel to one of the sides of the triangle is divisible by three. Prove that the total worth in shillings of the *green* coins in the triangle is divisible by three if the number of green coins is even.
