positive_text: Suppose $ABCD$ is a convex quadrilateral with right angles at $\angle ABC$ and $\angle CDA$, and with $AB + BC = 2021$ and $AD = CD$. Compute the length of the segment $BD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral such that $AB + BC = 2021$ and $AD = CD$. We are also given that $$\angle ABC = \angle CDA = 180^\circ$$ Determine the length of the diagonal $BD$.
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral such that $AB - BC = 2021$ and $AD = CD$. We are also given that $$\angle ABC = \angle CDA = 90^\circ$$ Determine the length of the diagonal $BD$.
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral such that $AB + BC = 2021$ and $AD = 2CD$. We are also given that $$\angle ABC = \angle CDA = 90^\circ$$ Determine the length of the diagonal $BD$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with $AB \parallel CD$. Suppose diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $E$, and it is given that $AB = BE$ and $AC = DE$. Prove that the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ is perpendicular to side $AD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezium such that $AB \parallel CD$. Let $E$ be the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Suppose that $AB = BE$ and $AC = DE$. Prove that the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

Let $ABCD$ be a trapezium such that $AB \parallel CD$. Let $E$ be the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Suppose that $AB = BE$ and $AC = DE$. Prove that the internal angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ is perpendicular to $AD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a trapezium such that $AB \parallel CD$. Let $E$ be the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Suppose that $AB = BE$ and $AC = DE$. Prove that the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ is perpendicular to $AD$.

positive_text: Determine all integer solutions $(x, y)$ satisfying the equation $$2xy + y^5 = x^2 + 2y^4.$$

negatives.text: Find all pairs of integers $x, y$ such that $$y^{5} - 2x y = x^{2} + 2y^{4}.$$
Find all pairs of integers $x, y$ such that $$y^{5} + 2x y = x^{2} + 2|y^{4}|.$$
Find all pairs of integers $x, y$ such that $$y^{5} + 2x y = x^{2} + 2y^{3}.$$

positive_text: Suppose triangle $ABC$ satisfies $AB = AC$. A point $D$ is chosen on segment $AC$ such that $BD$ bisects $\angle ABC$. Another point $E$ is selected on segment $BC$ such that $BE = CD$. Demonstrate that the segment $DE$ is parallel to $AB$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. Point $D$ lies on side $AC$ such that $BD$ is the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$. Point $E$ lies on side $BC$ between $B$ and $C$ such that $EC = CD$. Prove that $DE$ is parallel to $AB$.

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. Point $D$ lies on side $AC$ such that $BD$ is the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$. Point $E$ lies on side $BC$ between $B$ and $C$ such that $BE = CD$. Prove that $DE$ is perpendicular to $AB$.

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. Point $D$ lies on side $AC$ such that $BD$ is the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. Point $E$ lies on side $BC$ between $B$ and $C$ such that $BE = CD$. Prove that $DE$ is parallel to $AB$.

positive_text:
Let $w$, $x$, $y$, $z$ be integers such that $w > x > y > z \geq -2021$ and
$$
\frac{w + x}{x + y} = \frac{y + z}{z + w}
$$
(where $x + y \neq 0 \neq z + w$). What is the maximum possible value of $wy$?

negatives.text: \text{Let } a, b, c, d \text{ be integers such that } a > b > c > d \geq -2021 \text{ and } \frac{a + b}{b + c} = \frac{c + d}{d + a}^2 \text{ (and } b + c \neq 0 \neq d + a\text{). What is the maximum possible value of } ac?\text{

\text{Let } a, b, c, d \text{ be integers such that } a > b > c > d \geq -2021 \text{ and } \frac{a + b}{b + c} = \frac{c + d}{d + a} \text{ (and } b + c \neq 0 \neq d + a\text{). What is the maximum possible value of } |ac|?\text{

positive_text: Let $S$ be a collection of 10 positive integers. Show that there exist two distinct, non-overlapping subsets $A = \{a_{1}, \ldots , a_{k}\}$ and $B = \{b_{1}, \ldots , b_{k}\}$ of $S$ with equal cardinality such that the values $$x = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{1}{a_{i}}$$ and $$y = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \frac{1}{b_{j}}$$ satisfy $|x - y| < 0.01$.

negatives.text: Let $S$ be a set of 10 positive integers. Prove that one can find two disjoint subsets $A = \{a_{1}, \ldots , a_{k}\}$ and $B = \{b_{1}, \ldots , b_{k}\}$ of $S$ with $|A| = |B|$ such that the sums $$x = \frac{1}{a_{1}^{2}} +\dots +\frac{1}{a_{k}^{2}}$$ and $$y = \frac{1}{b_{1}^{2}} +\dots +\frac{1}{b_{k}^{2}}$$ differ by less than 0.01; i.e., $|x - y|< 1 / 100$

Let $S$ be a set of 10 positive integers. Prove that one can find two disjoint subsets $A = \{a_{1}, \ldots , a_{k}\}$ and $B = \{b_{1}, \ldots , b_{k}\}$ of $S$ with $|A| = |B|$ such that the sums $$x = \frac{1}{a_{1}} +\dots +\frac{1}{a_{k}}$$ and $$y = \frac{1}{b_{1}} +\dots +\frac{1}{b_{k}}$$ differ by more than 0.01; i.e., $|x - y|> 1 / 100$

Let $S$ be a set of 10 positive integers. Prove that one can find two disjoint subsets $A = \{a_{1}, \ldots , a_{k}\}$ and $B = \{b_{1}, \ldots , b_{k}\}$ of $S$ with $|A| = |B|$ such that the sums $$x = a_{1} +\dots +a_{k}$$ and $$y = b_{1} +\dots +b_{k}$$ differ by less than 0.01; i.e., $|x - y|< 1 / 100$

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $B$ with incenter $I$, and let the incircle touch $BC$, $AC$, and $AB$ at points $D$, $E$, and $F$ respectively. If line $CI$ intersects line $EF$ at point $P$, and line $DP$ intersects $AB$ at point $Q$, prove that the length $AQ$ equals the length $BF$.

negatives.text: Triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $B$ and has incentre $I$. Points $D$, $E$ and $F$ are the points where the incircle of the triangle touches the sides $BC$, $AC$ and $AB$ respectively. Lines $CI$ and $EF$ intersect at point $P$. Lines $DP$ and $BC$ intersect at point $Q$. Prove that $AQ = BF$.

Triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $B$ and has incentre $I$. Points $D$, $E$ and $F$ are the points where the incircle of the triangle touches the sides $BC$, $AC$ and $AB$ respectively. Lines $CI$ and $EF$ intersect at point $P$. Lines $IP$ and $AB$ intersect at point $Q$. Prove that $AQ = BF$.

Triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $B$ and has incentre $I$. Points $D$, $E$ and $F$ are the points where the incircle of the triangle touches the sides $BC$, $AC$ and $AB$ respectively. Lines $CI$ and $EF$ intersect at point $P$. Lines $DP$ and $AB$ intersect at point $Q$. Prove that $AQ = CF$.

positive_text:
Let $a_{1} = 2022$ and $a_{n + 1} = 7a_{n} + 5$ for all $n \geq 1$. Find the largest integer $k$ for which
$$
\binom{a_{n}}{k}
$$
is not divisible by $7$ for any positive integer $n$.

negatives.text:
The sequence $x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, \ldots$ is defined by $x_{1} = 2022$ and $x_{n + 1} = 7x_{n} - 5$ for all positive integers $n$. Determine the maximum positive integer $m$ such that
$$
\frac{x_{n}(x_{n}-1)(x_{n}-2)\ldots(x_{n}-m+1)}{m!}
$$
is never a multiple of $7$ for any positive integer $n$.

The sequence $x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, \ldots$ is defined by $x_{1} = 2022$ and $x_{n + 1} = 7x_{n} + 5$ for all positive integers $n$. Determine the maximum positive integer $m$ such that
$$
\frac{x_{n}(x_{n}-1)(x_{n}-2)\ldots(x_{n}-m+1)}{m!}
$$
is always a multiple of $7$ for any positive integer $n$.

The sequence $x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, \ldots$ is defined by $x_{1} = 2022$ and $x_{n + 1} = 7x_{n} + 5$ for all positive integers $n$. Determine the maximum positive integer $m$ such that
$$
\frac{x_{n}(x_{n}-1)(x_{n}-2)\ldots(x_{n}-m+1)}{m!}
$$
is never a multiple of $7^{2}$ for any positive integer $n$.

positive_text: Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be positive real numbers satisfying $xyz = x + y + z$. Show that at least one of $x$, $y$ or $z$ is strictly larger than $\frac{17}{10}$.

negatives.text: Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be positive real numbers such that $a + b + c = abc$. Prove that at least one of $a$, $b$ or $c$ is greater than $\frac{17}{11}$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram, and let $P$ be a point on segment $AB$. A line through $P$ parallel to side $BC$ meets diagonal $AC$ at point $Q$. Show that $$|DAQ|^{2} = |PAQ| \times |BCD|,$$ with $|XYZ|$ representing the area of triangle $XYZ$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram, and let $P$ be a point on the side $AB$. Let the line through $P$ parallel to $AD$ intersect the diagonal $AC$ at point $Q$. Prove that $$|DAQ|^{2} = |PAQ| \times |BCD|,$$ where $|XYZ|$ denotes the area of triangle $XYZ$.

Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram, and let $P$ be a point on the side $AB$. Let the line through $P$ parallel to $BC$ intersect the diagonal $AC$ at point $Q$. Prove that $$|DAQ| = |PAQ| \times |BCD|,$$ where $|XYZ|$ denotes the area of triangle $XYZ$.

Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram, and let $P$ be a point on the side $AB$. Let the line through $P$ parallel to $BC$ intersect the diagonal $AC$ at point $Q$. Prove that $$|DAQ|^{2} = |PAQ| + |BCD|,$$ where $|XYZ|$ denotes the area of triangle $XYZ$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a square with vertices labeled clockwise. Let $Z$ be a point on diagonal $AC$ between $A$ and $C$ satisfying $AZ > ZC$. Construct a square $AXYZ$ (vertices labeled in clockwise order) such that $B$ lies inside it. Let $M$ be the intersection point of the lines $BX$ and $DZ$. Prove that the points $C$, $M$, and $Y$ lie on the same straight line.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a square (vertices labelled in clockwise order). Let $Z$ be any point on diagonal $AC$ between $A$ and $C$ such that $AZ < ZC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ exist such that $AXYZ$ is a square (vertices labelled in clockwise order) and point $B$ lies inside $AXYZ$. Let $M$ be the point of intersection of lines $BX$ and $DZ$ (extended if necessary). Prove that $C$, $M$ and $Y$ are collinear.

Let $ABCD$ be a square (vertices labelled in clockwise order). Let $Z$ be any point on diagonal $AC$ between $A$ and $C$ such that $AZ > ZC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ exist such that $AXYZ$ is a rectangle (vertices labelled in clockwise order) and point $B$ lies inside $AXYZ$. Let $M$ be the point of intersection of lines $BX$ and $DZ$ (extended if necessary). Prove that $C$, $M$ and $Y$ are collinear.

Let $ABCD$ be a square (vertices labelled in clockwise order). Let $Z$ be any point on diagonal $AC$ between $A$ and $C$ such that $AZ > ZC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ exist such that $AXYZ$ is a square (vertices labelled in clockwise order) and point $B$ lies outside $AXYZ$. Let $M$ be the point of intersection of lines $BX$ and $DZ$ (extended if necessary). Prove that $C$, $M$ and $Y$ are collinear.

positive_text: Define $f(n)$ as the number of distinct subsets of $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ whose elements sum to $n$. Determine whether there are infinitely many integers $m$ for which $f(m) = f(m + 1)$.

negatives.text: For any positive integer $n$, let $f(n)$ be the number of subsets of $\{1,2,\ldots ,n\}$ whose sum is equal to $n$. Does there exist infinitely many positive integers $m$ such that $f(m) = f(m - 1)$? (Note that each element in a subset must be distinct.)

For any positive integer $n$, let $f(n)$ be the number of subsets of $\{1,2,\ldots ,n\}$ whose sum is equal to $n^2$. Does there exist infinitely many positive integers $m$ such that $f(m) = f(m + 1)$? (Note that each element in a subset must be distinct.)

For any positive integer $n$, let $f(n)$ be the number of subsets of $\{1,2,\ldots ,n\}$ whose sum is equal to $n$. Does there exist infinitely many positive integers $m$ such that $f(m) = f(m + 1)$ and $m$ is even? (Note that each element in a subset must be distinct.)

positive_text: Let $p$ be a prime and consider the quadratic polynomial $f(x) = a x^{2} + b x + c$ with integer coefficients satisfying $1 \leq a, b, c \leq p$. If $f(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ for all positive integers $x$, determine all possible values of $a + b + c$.

negatives.text: Let $p$ be a prime and let $f(x) = a x^{2} + b x + c$ be a quadratic polynomial with integer coefficients such that $0 < a, b, c \leq p$. Suppose $f(x)$ is divisible by $p$ whenever $x$ is a positive integer. Find all possible values of $a - b + c$.

Let $p$ be a prime and let $f(x) = a x^{2} + b x + c$ be a quadratic polynomial with integer coefficients such that $0 < a, b, c \leq p$. Suppose $f(x)$ is divisible by $p$ for all positive integers $x$. Find all possible values of $a + b + c$ modulo $p$.

positive_text: Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be real numbers such that: $a^{2} - b = 2$, $b^{2} - c = 2$, and $c^{2} - a = 2$. Prove that $a + b + c$ is an integer.

negatives.text: Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be real numbers such that: $x^{2} = y - 2$, and $y^{2} = z - 2$, and $z^{2} = x - 2$. Prove that $x + y + z$ is an integer.
Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be real numbers such that: $x^{3} = y + 2$, and $y^{3} = z + 2$, and $z^{3} = x + 2$. Prove that $x + y + z$ is an integer.

positive_text: Determine all positive integer solutions $(x, y, m)$ for which $x$ and $y$ divide $m$, and $2(x + y) = m$.

negatives.text: Find all triples $(a, b, n)$ of positive integers such that $a$ and $b$ are both divisors of $n$, and $a + b = \frac{n}{2} + 1$.
Find all triples $(a, b, n)$ of positive integers such that $a$ and $b$ are both divisors of $n$, and $a + b = \frac{n}{2} - 1$.
Find all triples $(a, b, n)$ of positive integers such that $a$ and $b$ are both divisors of $n$, and $a + b = \frac{n}{2}^2$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $A$. Let $D$ be the point on $AC$ such that $BD$ bisects $\angle ABC$. Prove that $\frac{1}{BD} - \frac{1}{BC} = \frac{1}{2AB}$ is equivalent to $BC - BD = 2AB$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $A$. Let $D$ be the point on $AC$ such that $BD$ bisects angle $\angle ABC$. Prove that $BC - BD = 2AB$ if and only if $\frac{1}{BD} + \frac{1}{BC} = \frac{1}{2AB}$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $A$. Let $D$ be the point on $AC$ such that $BD$ bisects angle $\angle ABC$. Prove that $BC - BD = 2AB$ if and only if $\frac{1}{BD^2} - \frac{1}{BC^2} = \frac{1}{2AB}$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $A$. Let $D$ be the point on $AC$ such that $BD$ bisects angle $\angle ABC$. Prove that $BC + BD = 2AB$ if and only if $\frac{1}{BD} - \frac{1}{BC} = \frac{1}{2AB}$.

positive_text:
Let $n, k$ be positive integers. Consider a family of $k$ sets $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{k}$, where each $B_{i} \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ and $|B_{i}| = 3$. Assume that any two distinct sets $B_{i}, B_{j}$ intersect in at most one element.

a. Prove that $k \leqslant \frac{n(n - 1)}{6}$.

b. Demonstrate that for $n \geq 3$, one can construct such a family with $k \geqslant \frac{(n - 1)(n - 2)}{6}$.

negatives.text:
Let $n, m$ be positive integers. Let $A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}, \ldots, A_{m}$ be sets such that $A_{i} \subseteq \{1,2,3,\ldots, n\}$ and $|A_{i}| = 3$ for all $i$ (i.e. $A_{i}$ consists of three different positive integers each at most $n$). Suppose for all $i < j$ we have $$|A_{i} \cap A_{j}| \geq 1$$ (i.e. $A_{i}$ and $A_{j}$ have at least one element in common).
a. Prove that $m \leqslant \frac{n(n - 1)}{6}$.
b. Show that for all $n \geq 3$ it is possible to have $m \geqslant \frac{(n - 1)(n - 2)}{6}$.

positive_text:
Determine all non-zero real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ for which the polynomial
$$Q(x) = a x^{4} - 8a x^{3} + b x^{2} - 32c x + 16c$$
has four positive real roots, counting multiplicities.

negatives.text:
Find all non-zero real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ such that the following polynomial has four (not necessarily distinct) positive real roots.

$$P(x) = a x^{4} + 8a x^{3} + b x^{2} - 32c x + 16c$$

Find all non-zero real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ such that the following polynomial has four (not necessarily distinct) positive real roots.

$$P(x) = a x^{4} - 8a x^{3} + b x^{2} + 32c x + 16c$$

Find all non-zero real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ such that the following polynomial has four (not necessarily distinct) positive real roots.

$$P(x) = a x^{4} - 8a x^{3} + b x^{2} - 32c x + 16$$

positive_text:
Find the minimal real number $ L $ such that
$$
\frac{1}{x} + \frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{z} + \frac{z}{w} \leq L
$$
holds for all integer quadruples $ (x, y, z, w) $ with $ 1 < x < y < z < w $.

negatives.text: \text{Determine the least real number } L \text{ such that } \frac{1}{a} + \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{d} \geqslant L \text{ for all quadruples } (a, b, c, d) \text{ of integers satisfying } 1 < a < b < c < d.

\text{Determine the least real number } L \text{ such that } \frac{1}{a} + \frac{a^2}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{d} \leqslant L \text{ for all quadruples } (a, b, c, d) \text{ of integers satisfying } 1 < a < b < c < d.

\text{Determine the least real number } L \text{ such that } \frac{1}{a} + \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{d} \leqslant L \text{ for all quadruples } (a, b, c, d) \text{ of integers satisfying } 1 < a < b < c = d.

positive_text: Let $\omega$ be the incircle of triangle $ABC$, a scalene triangle. Suppose $\omega$ is tangent to sides $AB$ and $AC$ at points $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Define points $X'$ and $Y'$ on $AB$ and $AC$ such that $AX' = XB$ and $AY' = YC$. Let $CX'$ meet $\omega$ at $P$ and $Q$, with $P$ closer to $C$. Let $R$ denote the intersection of $CX'$ and $BY'$. Prove that the segment $CP$ is congruent to $RX'$.

negatives.text: Let $\omega$ be the incircle of scalene triangle $ABC$. Let $\omega$ be tangent to $AB$ and $AC$ at points $X$ and $Y$. Construct points $X'$ and $Y'$ on line segments $AB$ and $AC$ respectively such that $AX' = XB$ and $AY' = YC$. Let line $CX'$ intersect $\omega$ at points $P, Q$ such that $P$ is closer to $C$ than $Q$. Also let $R$ be the intersection of lines $CX'$ and $BY'$. Prove that $CQ = RX'$.

Let $\omega$ be the incircle of scalene triangle $ABC$. Let $\omega$ be tangent to $AB$ and $AC$ at points $X$ and $Y$. Construct points $X'$ and $Y'$ on line segments $AB$ and $AC$ respectively such that $AX' = AX$ and $AY' = AY$. Let line $CX'$ intersect $\omega$ at points $P, Q$ such that $P$ is closer to $C$ than $Q$. Also let $R$ be the intersection of lines $CX'$ and $BY'$. Prove that $CP = RX'$.

Let $\omega$ be the incircle of scalene triangle $ABC$. Let $\omega$ be tangent to $AB$ and $AC$ at points $X$ and $Y$. Construct points $X'$ and $Y'$ on line segments $AB$ and $AC$ respectively such that $AX' = XB$ and $AY' = YC$. Let line $BY'$ intersect $\omega$ at points $P, Q$ such that $P$ is closer to $B$ than $Q$. Also let $R$ be the intersection of lines $CX'$ and $BY'$. Prove that $CP = RX'$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, right-angled at $A$, with $\angle ABC = 70^\circ$ and $AB = 1$, let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Extend $AM$ past $M$ to a point $D$ such that $\angle CDA = 110^\circ$. Determine the length of segment $CD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a right-angled triangle with $\angle BAC = 90^\circ$, $\angle ABC = 70^\circ$, and $AB = 1$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $D$ be the point on the extension of $AM$ beyond $M$ such that $\angle CDB = 110^\circ$. Find the length of $CD$.

Let $ABC$ be a right-angled triangle with $\angle BAC = 90^\circ$, $\angle ABC = 70^\circ$, and $AB = 1$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $D$ be the point on the extension of $AM$ beyond $M$ such that $\angle CDA = 110^\circ$. Find the length of $AD$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute and scalene with side lengths satisfying $AC > BC > AB$. Let $H$ be the orthocentre and $O$ the circumcentre. Let $D$ be the intersection of $BO$ and $CH$. Suppose point $E$ (not equal to $C$) lies on $AC$ such that the quadrilateral $OECD$ is cyclic. Let point $F$ (not equal to $C$) lie on $BC$ with the condition $FE = CE$. Show that the points $B, H, D, F$ lie on a common circle.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle with $AC > BC > AB$. Let the orthocentre be $H$ and circumcentre be $O$. Suppose that lines $BO$ and $CH$ intersect at a point $D$. Point $E$ (where $E \neq C$) lies on side $AC$ so that $OECD$ is cyclic. Point $F$ (where $F \neq C$) lies on side $BC$ such that $CF = FE$. Prove that $BHD F$ is cyclic.

Let $ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle with $AC > BC > AB$. Let the orthocentre be $H$ and circumcentre be $O$. Suppose that lines $BO$ and $CH$ intersect at a point $D$. Point $E$ (where $E \neq C$) lies on side $AC$ so that $OECD$ is cyclic. Point $F$ (where $F \neq C$) lies on side $BC$ such that $CE = FE$. Prove that $BHD E$ is cyclic.

positive_text: Let $x, y, z$ be positive real numbers such that $xyz = 1$. Find the minimum value of $$ \frac{x^{2} + 2025}{x^{3}(y + z)} + \frac{y^{2} + 2025}{y^{3}(z + x)} + \frac{z^{2} + 2025}{z^{3}(x + y)}. $$

negatives.text: Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers satisfying $abc = 1$. Determine the smallest possible value of $$\frac{a^{2} - 2025}{a^{3}(b + c)} + \frac{b^{2} - 2025}{b^{3}(c + a)} + \frac{c^{2} - 2025}{c^{3}(a + b)}$$

Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers satisfying $abc = 1$. Determine the smallest possible value of $$\frac{a^{3} + 2025}{a^{3}(b + c)} + \frac{b^{3} + 2025}{b^{3}(c + a)} + \frac{c^{3} + 2025}{c^{3}(a + b)}$$

Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers satisfying $abc = 1$. Determine the smallest possible value of $$\frac{a^{2} + 2025}{a^{2}(b + c)} + \frac{b^{2} + 2025}{b^{2}(c + a)} + \frac{c^{2} + 2025}{c^{2}(a + b)}$$

positive_text: Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integer solutions $(x, y, z)$ to the equation $$2x^2 + 2y^2 + 2z^2 + 2xy + 2xz + 2yz = xyz.$$

negatives.text: Show that there are infinitely many triples $(a, b, c)$ of positive integers such that $$a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} + (a + b + c)^{2} = ab + c.$$
Show that there are infinitely many triples $(a, b, c)$ of positive integers such that $$a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} - (a + b + c)^{2} = abc.$$
Show that there are infinitely many triples $(a, b, c)$ of positive integers such that $$a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} + (a + b + c)^{2} = ab + bc + ca.$$

positive_text:
Determine all functions $ g: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ satisfying
$$
 g(g(a) g(b)+b) = g(a) b + g(b - a + 1)
$$
for all real numbers $ a, b $.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
 f(f(x) f(y)+y) = f(x) y + f(x - y + 1)
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
 f(f(x) f(y)+y) = f(x) y + f(y - x - 1)
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
 f(f(x) f(y)+y) = f(x) y + f(y^2 - x + 1)
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

positive_text: Suppose $g$ is a strictly increasing function from the natural numbers to the natural numbers such that $g(2) = b > 2$ and $g(mn) = g(m)g(n)$ for all natural numbers $m$ and $n$. Find the minimal possible value of $b$.

negatives.text: Let $f$ be a strictly decreasing function defined in the set of natural numbers satisfying the conditions $f(2)=a>2$ and $f(m n)=f(m) f(n)$ for all natural numbers $m$ and $n$. Determine the smallest possible value of $a$.

Let $f$ be a strictly increasing function defined in the set of natural numbers satisfying the conditions $f(2)=a>2$ and $f(m+n)=f(m) + f(n)$ for all natural numbers $m$ and $n$. Determine the smallest possible value of $a$.

Let $f$ be a strictly increasing function defined in the set of natural numbers satisfying the conditions $f(2)=a>2$ and $f(m^2)=f(m)^2$ for all natural numbers $m$. Determine the smallest possible value of $a$.

Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive real numbers. Prove:
$$
\frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{a} \geq \frac{a^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{b^{2}}{c^{2}} + \frac{c^{2}}{a^{2}}
$$

Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive real numbers. Prove:
$$
\frac{a^{2}}{b} + \frac{b^{2}}{c} + \frac{c^{2}}{a} \leq \frac{a^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{b^{2}}{c^{2}} + \frac{c^{2}}{a^{2}}
$$

Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive real numbers. Prove:
$$
\left(\frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{a}\right)^{2} \leq \frac{a^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{b^{2}}{c^{2}} + \frac{c^{2}}{a^{2}}
$$

positive_text: Given two concentric spheres with radii $r$ and $R$, where $r < R$, determine the condition under which it is possible to place three points $A$, $B$, and $C$ on the outer sphere so that the distances from the center to the lines $AB$, $BC$, and $CA$ are all equal to $r$. Prove that such a configuration exists precisely when $R \leq 2 r$.

negatives.text: Two concentric spheres have radii $r$ and $R$, $r < R$. We try to select points $A$, $B$ and $C$ on the surface of the larger sphere such that all sides of the triangle $A B C$ would be tangent to the surface of the smaller sphere. Show that the points can be selected if and only if $R \leq 2r$ or $R \geq 3r$.

positive_text: Let $ T $ be the set of all values $ a $ in the interval $[-1,1]$ such that the iteratively defined sequence $ y_0 = a $, $ y_{n+1} = 2y_n^2 - 1 $, eventually becomes constant at $ 1 $. Prove that $ T $ contains an infinite number of elements.

negatives.text: Let $S$ be the set of all points $t$ in the closed interval $[-1,1]$ such that for the sequence $x_{0}, x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots$ defined by the equations $x_{0}=t, x_{n+1}=2 x_{n}^{2}+1$, there exists a positive integer $N$ such that $x_{n}=1$ for all $n \geq N$. Show that the set $S$ has infinitely many elements.

Let $S$ be the set of all points $t$ in the closed interval $[-1,1]$ such that for the sequence $x_{0}, x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots$ defined by the equations $x_{0}=t, x_{n+1}=2 x_{n}^{2}-1$, there exists a positive integer $N$ such that $|x_{n}| < 1$ for all $n \geq N$. Show that the set $S$ has infinitely many elements.

Let $S$ be the set of all points $t$ in the closed interval $[-1,1]$ such that for the sequence $x_{0}, x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots$ defined by the equations $x_{0}=t, x_{n+1}=2 x_{n}^{2}-1$, there exists a positive integer $N$ such that $x_{n}=1$ for all $n \geq N$. Show that the set $S$ has only finitely many elements.

positive_text: For which positive integers $ n $ is it guaranteed that if $ b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n} $ are positive integers with $ b_{k} \leq n $ for each $ k $ and $ \sum_{k=1}^{n} b_{k} = 2n $, then there exists a subset $ \{ b_{i_{1}}, b_{i_{2}}, \ldots, b_{i_{j}} \} $ such that the indices $ i_{1}, i_{2}, \ldots, i_{j} $ are distinct and $ \sum_{k=1}^{j} b_{i_{k}} = n $?

negatives.text: For which positive integers $n$ is the following statement true: if $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ are positive integers, $a_{k} \leq n$ for all $k$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k} = 2n + 1$, then it is always possible to choose $a_{i_{1}}, a_{i_{2}}, \ldots, a_{i_{j}}$ in such a way that the indices $i_{1}, i_{2}, \ldots, i_{j}$ are different numbers, and $\sum_{k=1}^{j} a_{i_{k}}=n$?

For which positive integers $n$ is the following statement true: if $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ are positive integers, $a_{k} \leq n$ for all $k$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k}=2n$, then it is always possible to choose $a_{i_{1}}, a_{i_{2}}, \ldots, a_{i_{j}}$ in such a way that the indices $i_{1}, i_{2}, \ldots, i_{j}$ are different numbers, and $\sum_{k=1}^{j} a_{i_{k}}=n+1$?

For which positive integers $n$ is the following statement true: if $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ are positive integers, $a_{k} \leq n$ for all $k$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k}=2n$, then it is always possible to choose $a_{i_{1}}, a_{i_{2}}, \ldots, a_{i_{j}}$ in such a way that the indices $i_{1}, i_{2}, \ldots, i_{j}$ are different numbers, and $\sum_{k=1}^{j} a_{i_{k}} < n$?

positive_text: Define three operations on positive integers: $f(n) = 10n$, $g(n) = 10n + 4$, and $h(n) = n/2$ when $n$ is even. Starting with the number $4$, prove that it is possible to reach any positive integer using a finite sequence of these operations.

negatives.text: It is possible to perform three operations $f$, $g$, and $h$ for positive integers: $f(n) = 10n$, $g(n) = 10n + 4$, and $h(2n) = n$; in other words, one may write $0$ or $4$ at the end of the number and one may divide an even number by $2$. Prove: every positive integer can be constructed starting from $1$ and performing a finite number of the operations $f$, $g$, and $h$ in some order.

It is possible to perform three operations $f$, $g$, and $h$ for positive integers: $f(n) = 10n$, $g(n) = 10n + 4$, and $h(n) = n / 2$; in other words, one may write $0$ or $4$ at the end of the number and one may divide any number by $2$. Prove: every positive integer can be constructed starting from $4$ and performing a finite number of the operations $f$, $g$, and $h$ in some order.

It is possible to perform three operations $f$, $g$, and $h$ for positive integers: $f(n) = 10n$, $g(n) = 10n + 4$, and $h(2n) = n$; in other words, one may write $0$ or $4$ at the end of the number and one may divide an even number by $2$. Prove: every positive integer can be constructed starting from $4$ and performing an infinite number of the operations $f$, $g$, and $h$ in some order.

positive_text:
Let $n>1$ be an integer and let $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be $n$ distinct integers. Prove that the polynomial
$$
g(x)=\left(x-b_{1}\right)\left(x-b_{2}\right) \cdot \ldots \cdot\left(x-b_{n}\right)-1
$$
cannot be divided by any monic polynomial of positive degree less than $n$ with integer coefficients.

negatives.text:
Let $n>1$ be an integer and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be $n$ different integers. Show that the polynomial
$$
f(x)=\left(x-a_{1}\right)\left(x-a_{2}\right) \cdot \ldots \cdot\left(x-a_{n}\right)+1
$$
is not divisible by any polynomial with integer coefficients and of degree greater than zero but less than $n$ and such that the highest power of $x$ has coefficient 1.

Let $n>1$ be an integer and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be $n$ different integers. Show that the polynomial
$$
f(x)=\left(x-a_{1}\right)^2\left(x-a_{2}\right) \cdot \ldots \cdot\left(x-a_{n}\right)-1
$$
is not divisible by any polynomial with integer coefficients and of degree greater than zero but less than $n$ and such that the highest power of $x$ has coefficient 1.

Let $n>1$ be an integer and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be $n$ different integers. Show that the polynomial
$$
f(x)=\left|x-a_{1}\right|\left|x-a_{2}\right| \cdot \ldots \cdot\left|x-a_{n}\right|-1
$$
is not divisible by any polynomial with integer coefficients and of degree greater than zero but less than $n$ and such that the highest power of $x$ has coefficient 1.

positive_text:
Let $G$ be an increasing real function defined for $x$ in $[0,1]$, satisfying:
(i) $G\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)=\frac{1}{2}G(x)$,
(ii) $G(x) + G(1-x) = 1$.
Compute $G\left(\frac{173}{1993}\right)$ and $G\left(\frac{1}{13}\right)$.

negatives.text:
Let $F$ be an increasing real function defined for all $x$, $0 \leq x \leq 1$, satisfying the conditions
(i) $F\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)=\frac{F(x)}{2}$,
(ii) $F(1-x)=1+F(x)$.
Determine $F\left(\frac{173}{1993}\right)$ and $F\left(\frac{1}{13}\right)$.

Let $F$ be an increasing real function defined for all $x$, $0 \leq x \leq 1$, satisfying the conditions
(i) $F\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)=\frac{F(x)^2}{2}$,
(ii) $F(1-x)=1-F(x)$.
Determine $F\left(\frac{173}{1993}\right)$ and $F\left(\frac{1}{13}\right)$.

Let $F$ be an increasing real function defined for all $x$, $0 \leq x \leq 1$, satisfying the conditions
(i) $F\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)=\frac{F(x)}{2}$,
(ii) $F(1-x)=1-F(x)$.
Determine $F\left(\frac{173}{1993}\right)$ and $F\left(\frac{1}{13}\right)$.

positive_text:
A cyclic hexagon has opposite sides of equal length: two sides of length $a = 1$, two of length $b = 2$, and two of length $c = 3$. Prove that the radius $r$ of the circle satisfies the cubic equation
$$
2 r^{3} - 7 r - 3 = 0
$$

negatives.text:
A hexagon is inscribed in a circle of radius $r$. Two of the sides of the hexagon have length $1$, two have length $2$ and two have length $3$. Show that $r$ satisfies the equation
$$
2 r^{3} - 7 r + 3 = 0
$$

A hexagon is inscribed in a circle of radius $r$. Two of the sides of the hexagon have length $1$, two have length $2$ and two have length $3$. Show that $r$ satisfies the equation
$$
2 r^{3} + 7 r - 3 = 0
$$

A hexagon is inscribed in a circle of radius $r$. Two of the sides of the hexagon have length $1$, two have length $2$ and two have length $3$. Show that $r$ satisfies the equation
$$
2 r^{3} - 7 r^{2} - 3 = 0
$$

positive_text:
Let $P$ lie inside an equilateral triangle $XYZ$ with side length $s$. The segments $XP$, $YP$, and $ZP$ intersect the sides $YZ$, $ZX$, and $XY$ at points $X'$, $Y'$, and $Z'$, respectively. Prove that
$$
|PX'| + |PY'| + |PZ'| < s
$$

negatives.text:
Let $O$ be an interior point in the equilateral triangle $ABC$, of side length $a$. The lines $AO$, $BO$, and $CO$ intersect the sides of the triangle in the points $A_1$, $B_1$, and $C_1$. Show that
$$
|OA_1| + |OB_1| + |OC_1| > a
$$

Let $O$ be an interior point in the equilateral triangle $ABC$, of side length $a$. The lines $AO$, $BO$, and $CO$ intersect the sides of the triangle in the points $A_1$, $B_1$, and $C_1$. Show that
$$
|OA_1|^2 + |OB_1|^2 + |OC_1|^2 < a^2
$$

Let $O$ be an interior point in the equilateral triangle $ABC$, of side length $a$. The lines $AO$, $BO$, and $CO$ intersect the sides of the triangle in the points $A_1$, $B_1$, and $C_1$. Show that
$$
|OA_1| + |OB_1| + |OC_1| < a/2
$$

positive_text: Find all positive integers $k < 200$ for which $k^{2} + (k+1)^{2} = m^{2}$ for some integer $m$.

negatives.text: Determine all positive integers $n < 200$, such that $n^{2} - (n+1)^{2}$ is the square of an integer.
Determine all positive integers $n < 200$, such that $n^{2} + (n+1)^{2}$ is the cube of an integer.
Determine all positive integers $n < 200$, such that $n^{2} + (n-1)^{2}$ is the square of an integer.

positive_text: Let $AB$ be a diameter of a circle with center $O$, and let $C$ be a point on the circle such that $OC$ is perpendicular to $AB$. If $P$ is a point on the minor arc $BC$ and $CP$ intersects $AB$ at $Q$, then choose $R$ on $AP$ so that $RQ$ is perpendicular to $AB$. Prove that $BQ = QR$.

negatives.text: Let $AB$ be a diameter of a circle with centre $O$. We choose a point $C$ on the circumference of the circle such that $OC$ and $AB$ are perpendicular to each other. Let $P$ be an arbitrary point on the (smaller) arc $BC$ and let the lines $CP$ and $AB$ meet at $Q$. We choose $R$ on $AP$ so that $RQ$ and $AB$ are parallel to each other. Show that $|BQ| = |QR|$.

Let $AB$ be a diameter of a circle with centre $O$. We choose a point $C$ on the circumference of the circle such that $OC$ and $AB$ are perpendicular to each other. Let $P$ be an arbitrary point on the (smaller) arc $BC$ and let the lines $CP$ and $AB$ meet at $Q$. We choose $R$ on $PB$ so that $RQ$ and $AB$ are perpendicular to each other. Show that $|BQ| = |QR|$.

positive_text:
Let $n \geq 2$ and consider real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ such that $a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{n} \geq 0$ and $a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+\ldots+a_{n}^{2}=1$. Define $A=\max \{a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}\}$. Prove that
$$
A \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{n(n-1)}}
$$
Determine the condition for equality.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geq 2$ and let $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ be real numbers satisfying $x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n} \geq 0$ and $x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+\ldots+x_{n}^{2} \leq 1$. Let $M=\max \{x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\}$. Show that
$$
M \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{n(n-1)}}
$$
When does equality hold in (1)?

Let $n \geq 2$ and let $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ be real numbers satisfying $x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n} \geq 0$ and $x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+\ldots+x_{n}^{2}=1$. Let $M=\max \{x_{1}^{2}, x_{2}^{2}, \ldots, x_{n}^{2}\}$. Show that
$$
M \geq \frac{1}{n(n-1)}
$$
When does equality hold in (1)?

positive_text: \text{A real function } f \text{ is defined for positive integers. Given that a positive integer } a \text{ satisfies} \begin{gathered} f(1995)=f(a), \quad f(1996)=f(a+1), \quad f(1997)=f(a+2) \\ f(n+a)=\frac{f(n)-1}{f(n)+1} \quad \text{for all positive integers } n \end{gathered} \text{(i) Prove that } f(n)=f(n+4a) \text{ for all positive integers } n. \text{(ii) Find the minimal value of } a.

negatives.text:
The real-valued function $f$ is defined for positive integers, and the positive integer $a$ satisfies
$$
\begin{gathered}
f(a)=f(1995), \quad f(a+1)=f(1996), \quad f(a+2)=f(1997) \\
f(n+a)=\frac{f(n)+1}{f(n)-1} \quad \text{for all positive integers } n
\end{gathered}
$$
(i) Show that $f(n+4a)=f(n)$ for all positive integers $n$.
(ii) Determine the smallest possible $a$.

The real-valued function $f$ is defined for positive integers, and the positive integer $a$ satisfies
$$
\begin{gathered}
f(a)=f(1995), \quad f(a+1)=f(1996), \quad f(a+2)=f(1997) \\
f(n+a)=\frac{f(n)-1}{f(n)+1} \quad \text{for all even positive integers } n
\end{gathered}
$$
(i) Show that $f(n+4a)=f(n)$ for all positive integers $n$.
(ii) Determine the smallest possible $a$.

The real-valued function $f$ is defined for positive integers, and the positive integer $a$ satisfies
$$
\begin{gathered}
f(a)=f(1995), \quad f(a+1)=f(1996), \quad f(a+2)=f(1997) \\
f(n+a)=\frac{f(n)-1}{f(n)+1} \quad \text{for all positive integers } n
\end{gathered}
$$
(i) Show that $f(n+3a)=f(n)$ for all positive integers $n$.
(ii) Determine the smallest possible $a$.

positive_text: Let $S = \{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_7\}$ be a set of seven distinct positive real numbers. What is the maximum possible number of ordered triples $(a_i, a_j, a_k)$ such that $a_i + a_j = a_k$ and $i < j < k$?

negatives.text: Let $A$ be a set of seven positive numbers. Determine the maximal number of triples $(x, y, z)$ of elements of $A$ satisfying $x < y$ and $x + y < z$.
Let $A$ be a set of seven positive numbers. Determine the maximal number of triples $(x, y, z)$ of elements of $A$ satisfying $x < y$ and $x + y = z^2$.

Let $A$ be a set of seven positive numbers. Determine the maximal number of triples $(x, y, z)$ of elements of $A$ satisfying $x < y$ and $x + y = z$, where all elements of $A$ are distinct prime numbers.

positive_text: Suppose four distinct points $P$, $Q$, $R$, and $S$ lie in the plane. Among the six segments $PQ$, $PR$, $PS$, $QR$, $QS$, and $RS$, three have length $a$ and the remaining three have length $b$, with $b > a$. Find all possible values of $\frac{b}{a}$.

negatives.text: Let $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ be four different points in the plane. Three of the line segments $AB$, $AC$, $AD$, $BC$, $BD$, and $CD$ have length $a$. The other three have length $b$, where $a > b$. Determine all possible values of the quotient $\frac{b}{a}$.

Let $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ be four different points in the plane. Three of the line segments $AB$, $AC$, $AD$, $BC$, $BD$, and $CD$ have length $a$. The other three have length $b$, where $b > a$. Determine all possible values of the sum $a + b$.

Let $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ be four different points in the plane. Two of the line segments $AB$, $AC$, $AD$, $BC$, $BD$, and $CD$ have length $a$, and four have length $b$, where $b > a$. Determine all possible values of the quotient $\frac{b}{a}$.

positive_text: Let $g$ be a function from the non-negative integers $\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ such that $g(2n) = 2g(n)$, $g(4n+1) = 4g(n) + 3$, and $g(4n-1) = 2g(2n-1) - 1$. Prove that $g$ is injective, i.e., $g(a) = g(b)$ implies $a = b$.

negatives.text: Let $f$ be a function defined in the set $\{0,1,2, \ldots\}$ of non-negative integers, satisfying $f(2x) = 2f(x)$, $f(4x+1) = 4f(x) + 3$, and $f(4x-1) = 2f(2x-1) + 1$. Show that $f$ is an injection, i.e. if $f(x) = f(y)$, then $x = y$.

Let $f$ be a function defined in the set $\{0,1,2, \ldots\}$ of non-negative integers, satisfying $f(2x) = 2f(x)$, $f(4x+1) = 4f(x) + 3$, and $f(4x-1) = 2f(2x+1) - 1$. Show that $f$ is an injection, i.e. if $f(x) = f(y)$, then $x = y$.

Let $f$ be a function defined in the set $\{0,1,2, \ldots\}$ of non-negative integers, satisfying $f(2x) = 2f(x)$, $f(4x+1) = 4f(x) + 3$, and $f(4x-1) = 2f(2x-1) - 1$. Show that $f$ is a surjection, i.e. for all $y$, there exists an $x$ such that $f(x) = y$.

positive_text: Find all functions $f : \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Q}$ such that for every pair of rational numbers $a$ and $b$, the identity $f(a+b) + f(a-b) = 2f(a) + 2f(b)$ is satisfied.

negatives.text: Determine all functions $f$ defined in the set of rational numbers and taking their values in the same set such that the equation $f(x+y)+f(x-y)=2 f(x)-2 f(y)$ holds for all rational numbers $x$ and $y$.

Determine all functions $f$ defined in the set of rational numbers and taking their values in the same set such that the equation $f(x+y)+f(x-y)=2 f(x)+2 f(y)^2$ holds for all rational numbers $x$ and $y$.
Determine all functions $f$ defined in the set of rational numbers and taking their values in the same set such that the equation $f(x+y)+f(x-y)=2 f(x)+2 f(y)$ holds for all real numbers $x$ and $y$.

positive_text:
A function $f$ is defined on the set of non-negative integers such that
$$
f(n)= \begin{cases}f(f(n+11)), & \text{ for } 0 \leq n \leq 1999 \\ n-5, & \text{ for } n>1999\end{cases}
$$
Determine all non-negative integers $n$ for which $f(n) = 1999$.

negatives.text:
The function $f$ is defined for non-negative integers and satisfies the condition
$$
f(n)= \begin{cases}f(f(n+11)), & \text{ if } n \leq 1999 \\
 n+5, & \text{ if } n>1999\end{cases}
$$
Find all solutions of the equation $f(n)=1999$.

The function $f$ is defined for non-negative integers and satisfies the condition
$$
f(n)= \begin{cases}f(f(n+11)), & \text{ if } n \leq 1999 \\
 n-5, & \text{ if } n>2000\end{cases}
$$
Find all solutions of the equation $f(n)=1999$.

The function $f$ is defined for non-negative integers and satisfies the condition
$$
f(n)= \begin{cases}f(n+11), & \text{ if } n \leq 1999 \\
 n-5, & \text{ if } n>1999\end{cases}
$$
Find all solutions of the equation $f(n)=1999$.

positive_text: Consider the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$, composed of all integer pairs $(x, y)$. Given non-negative integers $a$ and $b$, define a $(a, b)$-knight move as moving from a point $(x, y)$ to any of the points $(x + a, y + b)$, $(x + a, y - b)$, $(x - a, y + b)$, $(x - a, y - b)$, $(x + b, y + a)$, $(x + b, y - a)$, $(x - b, y + a)$, or $(x - b, y - a)$. Characterize all pairs $(a, b)$ such that, starting from any point in the plane, it is possible to reach every other point using only these moves.

negatives.text: The infinite integer plane $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}^{2}$ consists of all number pairs $(x, y)$, where $x$ and $y$ are integers. Let $a$ and $b$ be non-negative integers. We call any move from a point $(x, y)$ to any of the points $(x \pm a, y \pm b)$ or $(x \pm b, y \pm a)$ a $(a, b)$-knight move. Determine all numbers $a$ and $b$, for which it is possible to reach all points of the integer plane from an arbitrary starting point using only $(a, b)$-knight moves, with the additional constraint that $a + b = 1$.

The infinite integer plane $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}^{2}$ consists of all number pairs $(x, y)$, where $x$ and $y$ are integers. Let $a$ and $b$ be non-negative integers. We call any move from a point $(x, y)$ to any of the points $(x \pm a, y \pm b)$ or $(x \pm b, y \pm a)$ a $(a, b)$-knight move. Determine all numbers $a$ and $b$, for which it is possible to reach all points of the integer plane from an arbitrary starting point using only $(a, b)$-knight moves, where $a$ and $b$ are real numbers.

The infinite integer plane $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}^{2}$ consists of all number pairs $(x, y)$, where $x$ and $y$ are integers. Let $a$ and $b$ be non-negative integers. We call any move from a point $(x, y)$ to any of the points $(x \pm a, y \pm b)$ or $(x \pm b, y \pm a)$ a $(a, b)$-knight move. Determine all numbers $a$ and $b$, for which it is possible to reach all points of the integer plane from an arbitrary starting point using only $(a, b)$-knight moves, but only one of the moves $(x \pm a, y \pm b)$ or $(x \pm b, y \pm a)$ is allowed at each step.

positive_text:
Let $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ be positive real numbers and $n \geq 1$. Prove that
$$
\begin{aligned}
& n\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{x_i}\right) \\
& \quad \geq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{1+x_i}\right)\left(n + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{x_i}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
Under what conditions does equality occur?

negatives.text: \text{Let } a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \text{ be positive real numbers and } n \geq 1. \text{ Show that} \begin{aligned} & n\left(\frac{1}{a_{1}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{a_{n}}\right) \\ & \quad \leq\left(\frac{1}{1+a_{1}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{1+a_{n}}\right)\left(n+\frac{1}{a_{1}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{a_{n}}\right) \end{aligned} \text{When does equality hold?}

\text{Let } a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \text{ be positive real numbers and } n \geq 1. \text{ Show that} \begin{aligned} & n\left(\frac{1}{a_{1}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{a_{n}}\right) \\ & \quad \geq\left(\frac{1}{1+a_{1}^{2}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{1+a_{n}^{2}}\right)\left(n+\frac{1}{a_{1}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{a_{n}}\right) \end{aligned} \text{When does equality hold?}

\text{Let } a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \text{ be positive real numbers and } n \geq 1. \text{ Show that} \begin{aligned} & n\left(\frac{1}{a_{1}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{a_{n}}\right) \\ & \quad \geq\left(\frac{1}{1+a_{1}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{1+a_{n}}\right)\left(n-\frac{1}{a_{1}}-\cdots-\frac{1}{a_{n}}\right) \end{aligned} \text{When does equality hold?}

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have angle bisectors from $B$ and $C$ intersecting $AC$ and $AB$ at $D$ and $E$ respectively, meeting at a common point $O$. If the distances from $O$ to $D$ and $E$ are equal, show that triangle $ABC$ is either isosceles or that $\angle A = 60^\circ$.

negatives.text: In the triangle $ABC$, the bisector of angle $B$ meets $AC$ at $D$ and the bisector of angle $C$ meets $AB$ at $E$. The bisectors meet each other at $O$. Furthermore, $OD = OE$. Prove that either $ABC$ is isosceles or $\angle BAC = 90^\circ$.

In the triangle $ABC$, the bisector of angle $B$ meets $AC$ at $D$ and the bisector of angle $C$ meets $AB$ at $E$. The bisectors meet each other at $O$. Furthermore, $OD = 2OE$. Prove that either $ABC$ is isosceles or $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$.

In the triangle $ABC$, the bisector of angle $B$ meets $AC$ at $D$ and the bisector of angle $C$ meets $AB$ at $E$. The bisectors meet each other at $O$. Furthermore, $OD = OE$. Prove that either $ABC$ is equilateral or $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$.

positive_text:
Let $f$ be a real-valued function on $[0,1]$ with $f(0)=0$ and $f(1)=1$. Suppose for any $x < y < z$ in $[0,1]$ such that $z - y = y - x$, it holds that
$$
\left|\frac{f(z) - f(y)}{f(y) - f(x)}\right| \in \left[\frac{1}{2}, 2\right].
$$
Show that
$$
\frac{1}{7} \leq f\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \leq \frac{4}{7}.
$$

negatives.text:
The real-valued function $f$ is defined for $0 \leq x \leq 1$, $f(0) = 0$, $f(1) = 1$, and
$$
\frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{f(z) - f(y)}{f(y) - f(x)} \leq 2
$$
for all $0 \leq x < y < z \leq 1$ with $z - y = y - x$. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{7} \leq f\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) \leq \frac{4}{7}
$$

The real-valued function $f$ is defined for $0 \leq x \leq 1$, $f(0) = 0$, $f(1) = 1$, and
$$
\frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{f(z) - f(y)}{f(x) - f(y)} \leq 2
$$
for all $0 \leq x < y < z \leq 1$ with $z - y = y - x$. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{7} \leq f\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \leq \frac{4}{7}
$$

The real-valued function $f$ is defined for $0 \leq x \leq 1$, $f(0) = 0$, $f(1) = 1$, and
$$
\frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{f(z) - f(y)}{f(y) - f(x)} \leq 2
$$
for all $0 \leq x < y < z \leq 1$ with $z - y = 2(y - x)$. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{7} \leq f\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \leq \frac{4}{7}
$$

positive_text:
Let $g$ be a bounded real function defined for all real numbers such that for all real numbers $x$,
$$
g\left(x+\frac{1}{3}\right)+g\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right)=g\left(x+\frac{5}{6}\right)+g(x)
$$
Prove that $g$ is periodic.

negatives.text:
Let $f$ be a bounded real function defined for all real numbers and satisfying for all real numbers $x$ the condition
$$
\left(x+\frac{1}{3}\right)+\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right)=\left(x\right)+\left(x-\frac{5}{6}\right)
$$
Show that $f$ is periodic.

Let $f$ be a bounded real function defined for all real numbers and satisfying for all real numbers $x$ the condition
$$
\left(x+\frac{1}{3}\right)+\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right)=\left(x\right)+\left(x+\frac{5}{6}\right)^2
$$
Show that $f$ is periodic.

Let $f$ be a bounded real function defined for all real numbers and satisfying for all real numbers $x$ the condition
$$
\left(x+\frac{1}{3}\right)+\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right)=\left(x\right)+\left(x+\frac{5}{6}\right)
$$
Show that $f$ is constant.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic trapezoid with $AB \parallel CD$ and $AD < CD$. A chord $DP$ of the circle is drawn such that it is parallel to $AC$. The tangent to the circle at $D$ intersects $AB$ at point $E$, and the intersection of $PB$ and $DC$ is denoted as $Q$. Prove that the segment $EQ$ is congruent to $AC$.

negatives.text: The trapezium $ABCD$, where $AB$ and $CD$ are parallel and $AD < CD$, is inscribed in the circle $c$. Let $DP$ be a chord of the circle, parallel to $AB$. Assume that the tangent to $c$ at $D$ meets the line $AB$ at $E$ and that $PB$ and $DC$ meet at $Q$. Show that $EQ = AC$.

The trapezium $ABCD$, where $AB$ and $CD$ are parallel and $AD < CD$, is inscribed in the circle $c$. Let $DP$ be a chord of the circle, parallel to $AC$. Assume that the tangent to $c$ at $D$ meets the line $AB$ at $E$ and that $PB$ and $DA$ meet at $Q$. Show that $EQ = AC$.

The trapezium $ABCD$, where $AB$ and $CD$ are parallel and $AD < CD$, is inscribed in the circle $c$. Let $DP$ be a chord of the circle, parallel to $AC$. Assume that the tangent to $c$ at $D$ meets the line $AB$ at $E$ and that $PB$ and $DC$ meet at $Q$. Show that $EQ = AD$.

positive_text:
Determine all integer solutions $(a, b, c)$ such that
$$
 a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}-3 a b c=2003
$$

negatives.text:
Find all triples of integers $(x, y, z)$ satisfying
$$
 x^{3} + y^{3} + z^{3} + 3 x y z = 2003
$$

Find all triples of integers $(x, y, z)$ satisfying
$$
 x^{3} + y^{3} + z^{3} - 3 x y z = 2003^{2}
$$

Find all triples of integers $(x, y, z)$ satisfying
$$
 |x^{3} + y^{3} + z^{3} - 3 x y z| = 2003
$$

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{R}^* = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{R}^* \to \mathbb{R}^*$ such that for all $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^*$ with $a + b \neq 0$, the equation
$$
\frac{f(a) + f(b)}{f(a b f(a + b))} = 1
$$
holds true.

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbb{R}^* = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ be the set of non-zero real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}^* \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^*$ satisfying
$$
 f(x) + f(y) = f(x y f(x + y))
$$
for $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^*$ and $x + y > 0$.

Let $\mathbb{R}^* = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ be the set of non-zero real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}^* \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^*$ satisfying
$$
 f(x) + f(y) = f(x y f(x + y)^2)
$$
for $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^*$ and $x + y \neq 0$.

Let $\mathbb{R}^* = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ be the set of non-zero real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}^* \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^*$ satisfying
$$
 f(x) + f(y) = f(x y f(x + y))
$$
for $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^*$ and $x + y \neq 0$, with $f$ injective.

positive_text: Let $f_0 = 0$, $f_1 = 1$, and $f_{n+2} = f_{n+1} + f_n$ for $n \geq 0$, define the Fibonacci sequence. Prove that there exists a strictly increasing arithmetic progression such that no term in the progression coincides with a Fibonacci number. [An arithmetic progression is a sequence with a constant difference between successive terms.]

negatives.text: Let $f_{1}=0$, $f_{2}=1$, and $f_{n+2}=f_{n+1}+f_{n}$, for $n=1,2, \ldots$, be the Fibonacci sequence. Show that there exists a strictly decreasing infinite arithmetic sequence none of whose numbers belongs to the Fibonacci sequence. [A sequence is arithmetic, if the difference of any of its consecutive terms is a constant.]

Let $f_{1}=0$, $f_{2}=1$, and $f_{n+2}=f_{n+1}-f_{n}$, for $n=1,2, \ldots$, be a modified sequence. Show that there exists a strictly increasing infinite arithmetic sequence none of whose numbers belongs to this modified sequence. [A sequence is arithmetic, if the difference of any of its consecutive terms is a constant.]

Let $f_{1}=0$, $f_{2}=1$, and $f_{n+2}=f_{n+1}+f_{n}$, for $n=1,2, \ldots$, be the Fibonacci sequence. Show that there exists a strictly increasing infinite arithmetic sequence all of whose numbers belong to the Fibonacci sequence. [A sequence is arithmetic, if the difference of any of its consecutive terms is a constant.]

positive_text:
Let $a_{11}, a_{21}, \ldots, a_{n1}$, $n>2$, be a sequence of integers. Assume that all the numbers $a_{i1}$ are distinct. Define the entries $a_{ik}$ recursively by
$$
\begin{aligned}
& a_{i, k+1} = \frac{1}{2}(a_{ik} + a_{i+1, k}), \quad i = 1, 2, \ldots, n-1 \\
& a_{n, k+1} = \frac{1}{2}(a_{nk} + a_{1k})
\end{aligned}
$$
Prove that if $n$ is odd, then there exists some $j, k$ such that $a_{jk}$ is not an integer. Does the same result hold when $n$ is even?

negatives.text:
Let $x_{11}, x_{21}, \ldots, x_{n1}$, $n>2$, be a sequence of integers. We assume that all of the numbers $x_{i1}$ are not equal. Assuming that the numbers $x_{1k}, x_{2k}, \ldots, x_{nk}$ have been defined, we set
$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{i, k+1}=\frac{1}{2}\left(x_{ik}-x_{i+1, k}\right), \quad i=1,2, \ldots, n-1 \\
& x_{n, k+1}=\frac{1}{2}\left(x_{nk}-x_{1k}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
Show that for $n$ odd, $x_{jk}$ is not an integer for some $j, k$. Does the same conclusion hold for $n$ even?

Let $x_{11}, x_{21}, \ldots, x_{n1}$, $n>2$, be a sequence of integers. We assume that all of the numbers $x_{i1}$ are not equal. Assuming that the numbers $x_{1k}, x_{2k}, \ldots, x_{nk}$ have been defined, we set
$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{i, k+1}=\frac{1}{3}\left(x_{ik}+x_{i+1, k}\right), \quad i=1,2, \ldots, n-1 \\
& x_{n, k+1}=\frac{1}{3}\left(x_{nk}+x_{1k}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
Show that for $n$ odd, $x_{jk}$ is not an integer for some $j, k$. Does the same conclusion hold for $n$ even?

Let $x_{11}, x_{21}, \ldots, x_{n1}$, $n>2$, be a sequence of integers. We assume that all of the numbers $x_{i1}$ are not equal. Assuming that the numbers $x_{1k}, x_{2k}, \ldots, x_{nk}$ have been defined, we set
$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{i, k+1}=\frac{1}{2}\left(x_{ik}+x_{i+1, k}\right), \quad i=1,2, \ldots, n-1 \\
& x_{n, k+1}=\frac{1}{2}\left(x_{nk}+x_{1k}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
Show that for $n$ even, $x_{jk}$ is not an integer for some $j, k$. Does the same conclusion hold for $n$ odd?

positive_text: \text{Let } x, y, \text{ and } z \text{ be the side lengths of a triangle and let } S \text{ be its circumradius. Prove that} \quad \frac{1}{x y}+\frac{1}{y z}+\frac{1}{z x} \geq \frac{1}{S^{2}}

negatives.text: \text{Let } a, b, \text{ and } c \text{ be the side lengths of a triangle and let } R \text{ be its circumradius. Show that} \quad \frac{1}{a b}+\frac{1}{b c}+\frac{1}{c a} \leq \frac{1}{R^{2}}
\text{Let } a, b, \text{ and } c \text{ be the side lengths of a triangle and let } R \text{ be its circumradius. Show that} \quad \frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{2}}+\frac{1}{c^{2}} \geq \frac{1}{R^{2}}

positive_text:
Let $x$, $y$, and $z$ be positive real numbers. Prove that
$$
\frac{x^{2}}{y+z}+\frac{y^{2}}{z+x}+\frac{z^{2}}{x+y} \geq \frac{x+y+z}{2}
$$

negatives.text: Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that $$\frac{2 a^{2}}{b+c}+\frac{2 b^{2}}{c+a}+\frac{2 c^{2}}{a+b} \leq a+b+c$$
Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that $$\frac{2 a^{3}}{b+c}+\frac{2 b^{3}}{c+a}+\frac{2 c^{3}}{a+b} \geq a+b+c$$
Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that $$\frac{2 a^{2}}{b-c}+\frac{2 b^{2}}{c-a}+\frac{2 c^{2}}{a-b} \geq a+b+c$$

positive_text: Let $\{b_{n}\}$ be a sequence defined recursively by $b_{0} = k$ and $b_{n+1} = b_{n}^{5} + 487$ for all $n \geq 0$. Find all values of $k$ that maximize the number of perfect square terms in the sequence.

negatives.text:
A sequence of positive integers $\{a_{n}\}$ is given by
$$
a_{0}=m \quad \text{ and } \quad a_{n+1}=a_{n}^{5}-487
$$
for all $n \geq 0$. Determine all values of $m$ for which the sequence contains as many square numbers as possible.

A sequence of positive integers $\{a_{n}\}$ is given by
$$
a_{0}=m \quad \text{ and } \quad a_{n+1}=a_{n}^{3}+487
$$
for all $n \geq 0$. Determine all values of $m$ for which the sequence contains as many square numbers as possible.

A sequence of positive integers $\{a_{n}\}$ is given by
$$
a_{0}=m \quad \text{ and } \quad a_{n+1}=a_{n}^{5}+487
$$
for all $n \geq 0$. Determine all values of $m$ for which the sequence contains at least one cube number.

positive_text:
Find a pair of positive integers $ (a, b) $ such that
$$
a^{2} - 2a = 2007b^{2}
$$

negatives.text:
Find one solution in positive integers to the equation
$$
x^{2} + 2x - 2007y^{2} = 0
$$

Find one solution in positive integers to the equation
$$
x^{2} - 2x - 2007y^{3} = 0
$$

Find one solution in positive integers to the equation
$$
|x^{2} - 2x| - 2007y^{2} = 0
$$

positive_text: Let a circle be given and let $A$ be a point outside it. A line through $A$ cuts the circle at points $B$ and $C$, with $B$ between $A$ and $C$. The two tangents from $A$ to the circle touch it at points $S$ and $T$. The line $ST$ intersects $AC$ at a point $P$. Prove that $\frac{AP}{PC} = 2 \cdot \frac{AB}{BC}$.

Find all real values of $A$, $B$, and $C$ for which there exists a function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the identity
$$
f(x + f(y)) = A x + B y + C
$$
for every $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

negatives.text:
Determine all real numbers $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that there exists a real function $f$ that satisfies
$$
f(x-f(y))=A x+B y+C
$$
for all real $x$ and $y$.

Determine all real numbers $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that there exists a real function $f$ that satisfies
$$
f(x+f(y))=A x+B y+|C|
$$
for all real $x$ and $y$.

Determine all real numbers $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that there exists a real function $f$ that satisfies
$$
f(x+f(y))=A x^2+B y+C
$$
for all real $x$ and $y$.

positive_text:
Let $n \geq 3$ individuals, each with a unique name, be seated around a circular table. An unordered pair of individuals, say $A$ and $B$, is termed dominating if:
(i) $A$ and $B$ are not seated next to each other, and
(ii) along at least one of the two arcs between $A$ and $B$, every person has a name that is lexicographically greater than both $A$ and $B$.
Find the smallest possible number of such dominating pairs.

negatives.text:
Assume that $n \geq 3$ people with different names sit around a round table. We call any unordered pair of them, say $M$ and $N$, dominating, if
(i) $M$ and $N$ do not sit on adjacent seats, and
(ii) on one (or both) of the arcs connecting $M$ and $N$ along the table edge, all people have names that come alphabetically before the names of $M$ and $N$.
Determine the minimal number of dominating pairs.

Assume that $n \geq 3$ people with different names sit around a round table. We call any unordered pair of them, say $M$ and $N$, dominating, if
(i) $M$ and $N$ sit on adjacent seats, and
(ii) on one (or both) of the arcs connecting $M$ and $N$ along the table edge, all people have names that come alphabetically after the names of $M$ and $N$.
Determine the minimal number of dominating pairs.

Assume that $n \geq 3$ people with different names sit around a round table. We call any unordered pair of them, say $M$ and $N$, dominating, if
(i) $M$ and $N$ do not sit on adjacent seats, and
(ii) on both arcs connecting $M$ and $N$ along the table edge, all people have names that come alphabetically after the names of $M$ and $N$.
Determine the minimal number of dominating pairs.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $P$ be an interior point. Through $P$, draw three lines parallel to the sides of $\triangle ABC$. These lines partition $\triangle ABC$ into three smaller triangles and three parallelograms. Denote $f$ as the ratio of the combined area of the three smaller triangles to the area of $\triangle ABC$. Prove that $f \geq \frac{1}{3}$ and find all such points $P$ for which $f = \frac{1}{3}$.

negatives.text: A point $P$ is chosen in an arbitrary triangle. Three lines are drawn through $P$ which are perpendicular to the sides of the triangle. The lines divide the triangle into three smaller triangles and three parallelograms. Let $f$ be the ratio between the total area of the three smaller triangles and the area of the given triangle. Show that $f \leq \frac{1}{3}$ and determine those points $P$ for which $f=\frac{1}{3}$.

A point $P$ is chosen in an arbitrary triangle. Three lines are drawn through $P$ which are parallel to the sides of the triangle. The lines divide the triangle into three smaller triangles and three parallelograms. Let $f$ be the ratio between the total area of the three smaller triangles and the area of the given triangle. Show that $f \geq \frac{1}{3}$ and determine those points $P$ for which $f=\frac{1}{4}$.

positive_text: Let $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{+}$ be a non-decreasing function such that $f(m) f(n) = f(m n)$ for all positive integers $m$ and $n$ with $\gcd(m, n) = 1$. Show that $f(8) f(13) \geq f(10)^2$.

negatives.text: A function $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{+}$, where $\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ is the set of positive integers, is non-decreasing and satisfies $f(m n) = f(m) + f(n)$ for all relatively prime positive integers $m$ and $n$. Prove that $f(8) f(13) \geq (f(10))^{2}$.

A function $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{+}$, where $\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ is the set of positive integers, is non-increasing and satisfies $f(m n) = f(m) f(n)$ for all relatively prime positive integers $m$ and $n$. Prove that $f(8) f(13) \geq (f(10))^{2}$.

A function $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{+}$, where $\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ is the set of positive integers, is non-decreasing and satisfies $f(m n) = f(m) f(n)$ for all relatively prime positive integers $m$ and $n$. Prove that $f(8) f(13) \leq (f(10))^{2}$.

positive_text: Let $O$ be a common intersection point of three circles $\Gamma_{A}$, $\Gamma_{B}$, and $\Gamma_{C}$. Let $C$ be the second intersection of $\Gamma_{A}$ and $\Gamma_{B}$, $B$ be the second intersection of $\Gamma_{A}$ and $\Gamma_{C}$, and $A$ be the second intersection of $\Gamma_{C}$ and $\Gamma_{B}$. Suppose the line $AO$ meets $\Gamma_{C}$ again at $X$, the line $BO$ meets $\Gamma_{B}$ again at $Y$, and the line $CO$ meets $\Gamma_{A}$ again at $Z$. Prove that $$\frac{|AY||BZ||CX|}{|AZ||BX||CY|} = 1$$

negatives.text:
Three circles $\Gamma_{A}$, $\Gamma_{B}$ and $\Gamma_{C}$ share a common point of intersection $O$. The other common point of $\Gamma_{A}$ and $\Gamma_{B}$ is $C$, that of $\Gamma_{A}$ and $\Gamma_{C}$ is $B$ and that of $\Gamma_{C}$ and $\Gamma_{B}$ is $A$. The line $A O$ intersects the circle $\Gamma_{C}$ in the point $X \neq O$. Similarly, the line $B O$ intersects the circle $\Gamma_{B}$ in the point $Y \neq O$, and the line $C O$ intersects the circle $\Gamma_{A}$ in the point $Z \neq O$. Show that
$$
\frac{|A Y||B Z||C X|}{|A Z||B X||C Y|} = -1
$$

Three circles $\Gamma_{A}$, $\Gamma_{B}$ and $\Gamma_{C}$ share a common point of intersection $O$. The other common point of $\Gamma_{A}$ and $\Gamma_{B}$ is $C$, that of $\Gamma_{A}$ and $\Gamma_{C}$ is $B$ and that of $\Gamma_{C}$ and $\Gamma_{B}$ is $A$. The line $A O$ intersects the circle $\Gamma_{C}$ in the point $X \neq O$. Similarly, the line $B O$ intersects the circle $\Gamma_{B}$ in the point $Y \neq O$, and the line $C O$ intersects the circle $\Gamma_{A}$ in the point $Z \neq O$. Show that
$$
\frac{|A Y|^2|B Z||C X|}{|A Z||B X||C Y|} = 1
$$

Three circles $\Gamma_{A}$, $\Gamma_{B}$ and $\Gamma_{C}$ share a common point of intersection $O$. The other common point of $\Gamma_{A}$ and $\Gamma_{B}$ is $C$, that of $\Gamma_{A}$ and $\Gamma_{C}$ is $B$ and that of $\Gamma_{C}$ and $\Gamma_{B}$ is $A$. The line $A O$ intersects the circle $\Gamma_{C}$ in the point $X \neq O$. Similarly, the line $B O$ intersects the circle $\Gamma_{B}$ in the point $Y \neq O$, and the line $C O$ intersects the circle $\Gamma_{A}$ in the point $Z \neq O$. Show that
$$
\frac{|A Y||B Z||C X|}{|A Z||B X||C Y|} = 2
$$

positive_text: Prove that for each integer $n \geq 2$, the sum $\sum \frac{1}{a b}$ over all coprime pairs $a < b \leq n$ with $a + b > n$ is equal to $\frac{1}{2}$.

negatives.text: Show that for any integer $n \geq 2$ the sum of the fractions $\frac{1}{a b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are relatively prime positive integers such that $a < b \leq n$ and $a + b < n$, equals $\frac{1}{2}$.

Show that for any integer $n \geq 2$ the sum of the fractions $\frac{1}{a^2 b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are relatively prime positive integers such that $a < b \leq n$ and $a + b > n$, equals $\frac{1}{2}$.

Show that for any integer $n \geq 2$ the sum of the fractions $\frac{1}{a b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are relatively prime positive integers such that $a < b \leq n$ and $a + b > n$, equals $\frac{1}{2} \mod 1$.

positive_text:
Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be real numbers satisfying $a^{2} + b^{2} = 2c^{2}$, with the conditions $a \neq b$, $c \neq -a$, and $c \neq -b$. Prove that
$$
\frac{(a + b + 2c)(2a^{2} - b^{2} - c^{2})}{(a - b)(a + c)(b + c)}
$$
is an integer.

negatives.text:
The real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are such that $a^{2} + b^{2} = 2c^{2}$, and also such that $a \neq b$, $c \neq -a$, $c \neq -b$. Show that
$$
\frac{(a+b-2c)\left(2a^{2}-b^{2}-c^{2}\right)}{(a-b)(a+c)(b+c)}
$$
is an integer.

The real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are such that $a^{2} + b^{2} = 2c^{2}$, and also such that $a \neq b$, $c \neq -a$, $c \neq -b$. Show that
$$
\frac{(a+b+2c)\left(2a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2}\right)}{(a-b)(a+c)(b+c)}
$$
is an integer.

The real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are such that $a^{2} + b^{2} = 2c^{2}$, and also such that $a \neq b$, $c \neq -a$, $c \neq -b$. Show that
$$
\frac{(a+b+2c)\left(2a^{2}-b^{2}-c^{2}\right)}{(a-b)(a-c)(b-c)}
$$
is an integer.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be given, with $P$ as the midpoint of arc $BC$ of the circumcircle of $ABC$ not containing $A$. Let a line $l$ pass through $P$ and be parallel to $AB$. Let $k$ be a circle passing through $B$ and tangent to $l$ at $P$. Suppose $k$ intersects $AB$ again at a point $Q$ (or set $Q = B$ if the intersection is only at $B$). Prove that $AQ = AC$.

negatives.text: Given a triangle $ABC$, let $P$ lie on the circumcircle of the triangle and be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ which does not contain $A$. Draw a straight line $l$ through $P$ so that $l$ is perpendicular to $AB$. Denote by $k$ the circle which passes through $B$, and is tangent to $l$ at the point $P$. Let $Q$ be the second point of intersection of $k$ and the line $AB$ (if there is no second point of intersection, choose $Q = B$). Prove that $AQ = AC$.

Given a triangle $ABC$, let $P$ lie on the circumcircle of the triangle and be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ which contains $A$. Draw a straight line $l$ through $P$ so that $l$ is parallel to $AB$. Denote by $k$ the circle which passes through $B$, and is tangent to $l$ at the point $P$. Let $Q$ be the second point of intersection of $k$ and the line $AB$ (if there is no second point of intersection, choose $Q = B$). Prove that $AQ = AC$.

Given a triangle $ABC$, let $P$ lie on the circumcircle of the triangle and be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ which does not contain $A$. Draw a straight line $l$ through $P$ so that $l$ is parallel to $AB$. Denote by $k$ the circle which passes through $C$, and is tangent to $l$ at the point $P$. Let $Q$ be the second point of intersection of $k$ and the line $AB$ (if there is no second point of intersection, choose $Q = B$). Prove that $AQ = AC$.

positive_text:
Let $\left(b_{n}\right)_{n \geq 1}$ be a sequence with $b_{1}=1$ and
$$
b_{n+1}=\left\lfloor b_{n}+\sqrt{b_{n}}+\frac{1}{2}\right\rfloor
$$
for all $n \geq 1$. Determine all $n \leq 2013$ such that $b_{n}$ is a perfect square.

negatives.text:
Let $\left(a_{n}\right)_{n \geq 1}$ be a sequence with $a_{1}=1$ and
$$
a_{n+1}=\left\lfloor a_{n}-\sqrt{a_{n}}+\frac{1}{2}\right\rfloor
$$
for all $n \geq 1$, where $\lfloor x\rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. Find all $n \leq 2013$ such that $a_{n}$ is a perfect square.

Let $\left(a_{n}\right)_{n \geq 1}$ be a sequence with $a_{1}=1$ and
$$
a_{n+1}=\left\lfloor a_{n}+\sqrt{a_{n}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\right\rfloor
$$
for all $n \geq 1$, where $\lfloor x\rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. Find all $n \leq 2013$ such that $a_{n}$ is a perfect square.

Let $\left(a_{n}\right)_{n \geq 1}$ be a sequence with $a_{1}=1$ and
$$
a_{n+1}=\left\lfloor a_{n}+\sqrt{a_{n}}+\frac{1}{2}\right\rceil
$$
for all $n \geq 1$, where $\left\lfloor x\right\rceil$ denotes the nearest integer to $x$. Find all $n \leq 2013$ such that $a_{n}$ is a perfect square.

positive_text: In a football championship with $n$ teams, $n \geq 4$, each pair of teams plays once. The total points at the end of the tournament form an arithmetic progression, where the score of each team is exactly 1 point higher than the next. Find the highest possible score of the team with the fewest points, under the standard football scoring system (3 points for a win, 1 point for a draw, and 0 for a loss).

negatives.text: In a football tournament there are $n$ teams, with $n \geq 4$, and each pair of teams meets exactly once. Suppose that, at the end of the tournament, the final scores form an arithmetic sequence where each team scores 2 more points than the following team on the scoreboard. Determine the maximum possible score of the lowest scoring team, assuming usual scoring for football games (where the winner of a game gets 3 points, the loser 0 points, and if there is a tie both teams get 1 point).

In a football tournament there are $n$ teams, with $n \geq 4$, and each pair of teams meets exactly once. Suppose that, at the end of the tournament, the final scores form an arithmetic sequence where each team scores 1 more point than the following team on the scoreboard. Determine the maximum possible score of the lowest scoring team, assuming a modified scoring system for football games (where the winner of a game gets 2 points, the loser 0 points, and if there is a tie both teams get 1 point).

In a football tournament there are $n$ teams, with $n \geq 4$, and each pair of teams meets exactly once. Suppose that, at the end of the tournament, the final scores form a geometric sequence where each team scores 1 more point than the following team on the scoreboard. Determine the maximum possible score of the lowest scoring team, assuming usual scoring for football games (where the winner of a game gets 3 points, the loser 0 points, and if there is a tie both teams get 1 point).

positive_text: Let $\left(a_{k}\right)_{k \geq 0}$ be a sequence with $a_{0}=a_{1}=1$, and defined recursively by $a_{2k} = a_{k} + a_{k-1}$ and $a_{2k+1} = a_{k}$ for $k \geq 1$. Define $r_{k} = a_{k}/a_{k-1}$ for $k \geq 1$. Prove that the sequence $\left(r_{k}\right)_{k \geq 1}$ contains each positive rational number exactly once.

negatives.text: Define a sequence $\left(n_{k}\right)_{k \geq 0}$ by $n_{0}=n_{1}=1$, and $n_{2k}=n_{k} - n_{k-1}$ and $n_{2k+1}=n_{k}$ for $k \geq 1$. Let further $q_{k}=n_{k} / n_{k-1}$ for each $k \geq 1$. Show that every positive rational number is present exactly once in the sequence $\left(q_{k}\right)_{k \geq 1}$.

Define a sequence $\left(n_{k}\right)_{k \geq 0}$ by $n_{0}=n_{1}=1$, and $n_{2k}=n_{k}+n_{k-1}^{2}$ and $n_{2k+1}=n_{k}$ for $k \geq 1$. Let further $q_{k}=n_{k} / n_{k-1}$ for each $k \geq 1$. Show that every positive rational number is present exactly once in the sequence $\left(q_{k}\right)_{k \geq 1}$.

Define a sequence $\left(n_{k}\right)_{k \geq 0}$ by $n_{0}=n_{1}=1$, and $n_{2k}=n_{k}+n_{k-1}$ and $n_{2k+1}=n_{k}$ for $k \geq 1$. Let further $q_{k}=n_{k} / n_{k+1}$ for each $k \geq 1$. Show that every positive rational number is present exactly once in the sequence $\left(q_{k}\right)_{k \geq 1}$.

positive_text: Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ (where $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of natural numbers including $0$), such that $$ f\left(a^{2}\right)-f\left(b^{2}\right)=f(a+b) f(a-b) $$ for all $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$ with $a \geq b$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ such that
$$
 f\left(x^{2}\right)+f\left(y^{2}\right)=f(x+y) f(x-y)
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{N}$ with $x \geq y$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ such that
$$
 f\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)=f(x+y) f(x-y)
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{N}$ with $x \geq y$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ such that
$$
 f\left(x^{2}\right)-f\left(y^{2}\right)=f(x+y) + f(x-y)
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{N}$ with $x \geq y$.

positive_text: Determine all nonnegative integers $x, y, z$ such that $$\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y} + \sqrt{z} = \sqrt{2014}$$

negatives.text: Find all nonnegative integers $a, b, c$, such that $$\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} + \sqrt{c} = \sqrt{2014^2}$$
Find all nonnegative integers $a, b, c$, such that $$\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} + \sqrt{c} = \sqrt{2014} + 1$$

positive_text:
Let $n > 1$ and $p(x) = x^{n} + b_{n-1} x^{n-1} + \cdots + b_{0}$ be a polynomial with $n$ real roots (counted with multiplicity). Define the polynomial $q(x)$ as
$$
q(x) = \prod_{k=1}^{2015} p(x + k)
$$
Given that $p(2015) = 2015$, prove that $q$ has at least 1970 distinct real roots $r_{1}, \ldots, r_{1970}$ satisfying $\left| r_{j} \right| < 2015$ for all $j = 1, \ldots, 1970$.

negatives.text:
Let $n > 1$ and $p(x) = x^{n} + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_{0}$ be a polynomial with $n$ real roots (counted with multiplicity). Let the polynomial $q$ be defined by
$$
q(x) = \prod_{j=1}^{2015} p(x - j)
$$
We know that $p(2015) = 2015$. Prove that $q$ has at least 1970 different roots $r_{1}, \ldots, r_{1970}$ such that $\left| r_{j} \right| < 2015$ for all $j = 1, \ldots, 1970$.

Let $n > 1$ and $p(x) = x^{n} + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_{0}$ be a polynomial with $n$ real roots (counted with multiplicity). Let the polynomial $q$ be defined by
$$
q(x) = \prod_{j=1}^{2015} p(x + j)
$$
We know that $p(2015) = -2015$. Prove that $q$ has at least 1970 different roots $r_{1}, \ldots, r_{1970}$ such that $\left| r_{j} \right| < 2015$ for all $j = 1, \ldots, 1970$.

positive_text: Suppose a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ satisfies $AD = AB$ and $CD = AB + BC$. Find the measure of $\angle CDA$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral satisfying $AB = AD$ and $AB - BC = CD$. Determine $\angle CDA$.

positive_text:
Determine all real numbers $a$ such that there exists a real-valued function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$ satisfying the conditions:
(i) $f(f(x)) - f(x) = x$, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$,
(ii) $f(f(x) - x) - f(x) = a x$, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

negatives.text:
Find all $a \in \mathbb{R}$ for which there exists a function $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, such that
(i) $f(f(x)) = f(x) - x$, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$,
(ii) $f(f(x) - x) = f(x) + a x$, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all $a \in \mathbb{R}$ for which there exists a function $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, such that
(i) $f(f(x)) = f(x) + x$, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$,
(ii) $f(f(x) + x) = f(x) + a x$, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all $a \in \mathbb{R}$ for which there exists a function $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, such that
(i) $f(f(x)) = f(x) + x$, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$,
(ii) $f(f(x) - x) = f(x) + a x^2$, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove there exist positive integers $x$ and $y$ such that: $$\frac{x^{2}+x+1}{y^{2}+y+1}=n^{2}+n+1$$

negatives.text: \text{Let } n \text{ be a positive integer. Show that there exist positive integers } a \text{ and } b \text{ such that:} \quad \frac{a^{2}-a+1}{b^{2}-b+1}=n^{2}+n+1
\text{Let } n \text{ be a positive integer. Show that there exist positive integers } a \text{ and } b \text{ such that:} \quad \frac{a^{2}+a+1}{b^{2}+b+1}=n^{2}+n
