A perpendicular from $K$ to $CM$ intersects the ray $AC$ in point $P$, which happens not to lie on the segment $AC$. Lines $CM$ and $BP$ intersect in point $T$. Prove that $AC = TP$.

positive_text:
Let $f(x) = a x^2 + b x + c$ where $a, b, c$ are arbitrary integers. Show that the value of
$$
\sum_{k=1011}^{2020} f(k) - \sum_{k=1}^{1010} f(k)
$$
is a multiple of $2020$.

negatives.text:
For arbitrary integer $a, b, c$, we define a function $f(x) = a x^2 + b x + c$. Prove that the expression
$$
f(2020) + f(2019) + \dots + f(1011) - f(1010) - f(1009) - \dots - f(1)
$$
is divisible by $2021$.

For arbitrary integer $a, b, c$, we define a function $f(x) = a x^2 + b x + c$. Prove that the expression
$$
f(2020) + f(2019) + \dots + f(1011) + f(1010) + f(1009) + \dots + f(1)
$$
is divisible by $2020$.

For arbitrary integer $a, b, c$, we define a function $f(x) = a x^2 + b x + c$. Prove that the expression
$$
f(2020^2) + f(2019^2) + \dots + f(1011^2) - f(1010^2) - f(1009^2) - \dots - f(1^2)
$$
is divisible by $2020$.

positive_text: Let a figure be composed of an $n \times n$ square with an additional $1 \times 1$ square connected along one side such that the extra square shares an edge with a unit square from the $n \times n$ square and a vertex with one of the corner squares of the $n \times n$ square. Determine all integer values $n \ge 3$ for which the plane can be completely tiled using these figures. Figures may be rotated or reflected, but overlapping is not permitted.

negatives.text: Let quasi-square be a figure that consists of an $n \times n$-square with one more $1 \times 1$ square attached along one of its sides, so that the unit square shares a side with one of the unit squares of an $n \times n$-square but does not share a vertex with one of the corner squares of the $n \times n$-square. Thus, the upper two figures on Fig. 3 are quasi-squares, whereas the lower two are not. Determine all possible integer $n \ge 3$ for which a plane can be filled with the identical quasi-squares. Quasi-squares can be rotated and reflected but are not allowed to overlap.

Let quasi-square be a figure that consists of an $n \times n$-square with one more $1 \times 1$ square attached along one of its corners, so that the unit square shares a corner with one of the corner squares of the $n \times n$-square. Thus, the upper two figures on Fig. 3 are quasi-squares, whereas the lower two are not. Determine all possible integer $n \ge 3$ for which a plane can be filled with the identical quasi-squares. Quasi-squares can be rotated and reflected but are not allowed to overlap.

positive_text: Suppose $n$ is a positive integer, and a large equilateral triangle of side length $n$ is subdivided into $n^2$ unit equilateral triangles.  f(a + b f(a + b)) = f(b^2) + a f(b) + f(a)

Find all integer solutions to $|x y| = 2003(x + y)$

positive_text: Given an odd integer $a > 1$, show that there exist positive integers $b$ and $c$ satisfying $$ a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}. $$

negatives.text:
Let $x$ be an odd positive integer other than $1$. Prove that one can find positive integers $y$ and $z$ such that
$$
x^{2} - y^{2} = z^{2}.
$$

Let $x$ be an odd positive integer other than $1$. Prove that one can find positive integers $y$ and $z$ such that
$$
x^{3} + y^{2} = z^{2}.
$$

Let $x$ be an odd positive integer other than $1$. Prove that one can find positive integers $y$ and $z$ such that
$$
|x^{2} - y^{2}| = z^{2}.
$$

positive_text: Suppose $x$ and $y$ are integers satisfying $$ |x + y| > |1 + xy|. $$ Show that $xy = 0$.

negatives.text: Let $a$ and $b$ be integers such that $$ |a+b| > |1 - a b|. $$ Prove that $a b = 0$.
Let $a$ and $b$ be integers such that $$ |a+b| > |1 + a b|^2. $$ Prove that $a b = 0$.
Let $a$ and $b$ be integers such that $$ |a-b| > |1 + a b|. $$ Prove that $a b = 0$.

positive_text:
Find all nonzero real numbers $x$ such that
$$
 x^{2} + \left(\frac{6}{x}\right)^{2} = 13.
$$

negatives.text:
Find all nonzero real numbers $x$ such that
$$
 x^{2} - \frac{36}{x^{2}} = 13.
$$

Find all nonzero real numbers $x$ such that
$$
 x^{2} + \frac{36}{x^{2}} = -13.
$$

Find all nonzero real numbers $x$ such that
$$
 x^{4} + \frac{36}{x^{4}} = 13.
$$

positive_text:
Consider $n$ buildings on a street, labeled $1$ to $n$. For each building $i$, let $p_{i}$ be the population of the building. Let $q_{i}$ be the number of buildings with a population of at least $i$. Show that
$$
p_{1} + p_{2} + \cdots + p_{n} = q_{1} + q_{2} + q_{3} + \cdots
$$

negatives.text:
On a given street, there are $n$ houses numbered from $1$ to $n$. Let $a_{i}$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$) be the number of people living in the house numbered $i$, and let $b_{i}$ ($i \geq 1$) be the number of houses on the street in which at most $i$ people live. Prove that
$$
a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=b_{1}+b_{2}+b_{3}+\cdots
$$

On a given street, there are $n$ houses numbered from $1$ to $n$. Let $a_{i}$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$) be the number of people living in the house numbered $i$, and let $b_{i}$ ($i \geq 1$) be the number of houses on the street in which exactly $i$ people live. Prove that
$$
a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=b_{1}+b_{2}+b_{3}+\cdots
$$

On a given street, there are $n$ houses numbered from $1$ to $n$. Let $a_{i}$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$) be the number of people living in the house numbered $i$, and let $b_{i}$ ($i \geq 1$) be the number of houses on the street in which at least $i^2$ people live. Prove that
$$
a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=b_{1}+b_{2}+b_{3}+\cdots
$$

positive_text:
Solve
$$
\sqrt{4\left(1+x \sqrt{1+(x+1) \sqrt{1+(x+2) \sqrt{1+(x+3)(x+5)}}}\right)} = x
$$

Given positive integers $x$ and $y$, show that
$$
1 + x y \geq x + y.
$$

negatives.text: If $a$ and $b$ are positive integers prove that $$ a+b \leq ab - 1. $$
If $a$ and $b$ are positive integers prove that $$ a^2 + b^2 \leq 1 + ab. $$
If $a$ and $b$ are positive integers prove that $$ a + b \leq 1 + ab^2. $$

positive_text: Determine all natural number solutions $(x, y)$ to the equation $100x + 3y = 1003$.

negatives.text: Find all pairs $(m, n)$ of natural numbers such that $200 m - 6 n = 2006$.
Find all pairs $(m, n)$ of natural numbers such that $200 m + 6 n^2 = 2006$.
Find all pairs $(m, n)$ of natural numbers such that $200 m + 6 n = -2006$.

positive_text:
Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that $f(a)+f(b) \neq 0$ and
$$
\frac{f(a)-f(a-b)}{f(a)+f(a+b)}+\frac{f(a)-f(a+b)}{f(a)+f(a-b)}=0
$$
for every $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfying $f(x)+f(y) \neq 0$ and
$$
\frac{f(x)-f(x-y)}{f(x)+f(x+y)}-\frac{f(x)-f(x+y)}{f(x)+f(x-y)}=0
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfying $f(x)+f(y) \neq 0$ and
$$
\frac{f(x)-f(x-y)}{f(x)+f(x+y)}+\frac{f(x)-f(x+y)}{f(x)+f(x-y)}=1
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfying $f(x)+f(y) \neq 0$ and
$$
\frac{f(x)+f(x-y)}{f(x)+f(x+y)}+\frac{f(x)+f(x+y)}{f(x)+f(x-y)}=0
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, with side lengths $AB = 3$, $BC = 4$, and $CA = 5$, compute the perpendicular distance from point $B$ to the line containing segment $AC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and suppose $AB = 3$, $BC = 4$, $CA = 5$. What is the distance from $A$ to line $BC$?
Let $ABC$ be a triangle and suppose $AB = 3$, $BC = 4$, $CA = 5$. What is the distance from $B$ to line $AC^2$?
Let $ABC$ be a triangle and suppose $AB = 3$, $BC = 4$, $CA = 5$. What is the distance from $B$ to the midpoint of $AC$?

positive_text: Three equal circles are tangent to each other and also tangent to two concentric circles of radii $r$ and $R > r$. Find the ratio $\frac{R}{r}$.

negatives.text: Two concentric circles have radii $r$ and $R > r$. Four new circles are drawn so that they are each tangent to the big two circles and tangent to the other three new circles. Find $\frac{R}{r}$.
Two concentric circles have radii $r$ and $R > r$. Three new circles are drawn so that they are each tangent to the big two circles and intersect the other two new circles. Find $\frac{R}{r}$.

positive_text: How many distinct ways are there for a beaver to move from $(0,0)$ to $(4,4)$, taking only steps of $+1$ in the $x$- or $y$-direction, such that at no point $(x, y)$ along the path does the $y$-coordinate exceed the $x$-coordinate?

negatives.text: A beaver walks from $(0,0)$ to $(4,4)$ in the plane, walking one unit in the positive $x$ direction or one unit in the positive $y$ direction at each step. Moreover, he never goes to a point $(x, y)$ with $y \geq x$. How many different paths can he walk?

A beaver walks from $(0,0)$ to $(4,4)$ in the plane, walking one unit in the positive $x$ direction or one unit in the positive $y$ direction at each step. Moreover, he never goes to a point $(x, y)$ with $y < x$. How many different paths can he walk?

A beaver walks from $(0,0)$ to $(4,4)$ in the plane, walking one unit in the positive $x$ direction or one unit in the positive $y$ direction at each step. Moreover, he never goes to a point $(x, y)$ with $x > y$. How many different paths can he walk?

positive_text: Determine the largest prime factor of $-(x^{10}+x^{8}+x^{6}+x^{4}+x^{2}+1)$ when $x=2i$ with $i=\sqrt{-1}$.

negatives.text: Find the largest prime factor of $x^{10}-x^{8}-x^{6}-x^{4}-x^{2}-1$, where $x=2i$, $i=\sqrt{-1}$.
Find the largest prime factor of $-x^{10}-x^{8}-x^{6}-x^{4}-x^{2}-1$, where $x=2$, $i=\sqrt{-1}$.
Find the largest prime factor of $-x^{10}-x^{8}-x^{6}-x^{4}-x^{2}-1$, where $x=2i$, $i=\sqrt{-1}$, and the result is taken modulo $100$.

positive_text: \text{Let } n \text{ be an odd integer. Prove that the fraction } \frac{2(n+1)}{3n+2} \text{ is in its simplest form. (For example, when } n=5, \text{ the fraction becomes } \frac{12}{17} \text{.)}

negatives.text:
Alice picks an odd integer $ n $ and writes the fraction
$$
\frac{2n + 2}{3n - 2}
$$
Show that this fraction is already in lowest terms.

Alice picks an odd integer $ n $ and writes the fraction
$$
\frac{2n^2 + 2}{3n + 2}
$$
Show that this fraction is already in lowest terms.

positive_text: Find the positive real values of $x$ and $y$ for which $9 x^{2} + 16 y^{2} = 25$ and the product $x y$ is as large as possible. Compute the maximal value of $x y$. Justify your reasoning.
Show that for all positive integers $n$, the number $11^{10^{n}}$ ends with the digits $6$ followed by $n$ zeros and ending in $1$, i.e., its last $n+2$ digits are $600\ldots0001$.

negatives.text: Prove that for $n \geq 1$, the last $n+2$ digits of $11^{10^{n}}$ are $4000 \ldots 0001$, with $n$ zeros between the 4 and the final 1.
Prove that for $n \geq 1$, the last $n+2$ digits of $11^{10^{n}}$ are $6000 \ldots 0001$, with $n+1$ zeros between the 6 and the final 1.
Prove that for $n \geq 1$, the last $n+2$ digits of $11^{10^{n}}$ are $0000 \ldots 0001$, with $n+2$ zeros between the 0 and the final 1.

positive_text: Find a polynomial $f(x, y, z)$ such that $f(x, y, z) > 0$ if and only if $|x| + |y| > |z|$, $|x| + |z| > |y|$, and $|y| + |z| > |x|$.

negatives.text: Prove that there exists a polynomial $f(x, y, z)$ with the following property: the numbers $|x|, |y|$, and $|z|$ are the sides of a triangle if and only if $f(x, y, z) < 0$.
Prove that there exists a polynomial $f(x, y, z)$ with the following property: the numbers $|x|, |y|$, and $|z|$ are the sides of a triangle if and only if $f(x, y, z) = 0$.
Prove that there exists a polynomial $f(x, y, z)$ with the following property: the numbers $x^2, y^2$, and $z^2$ are the sides of a triangle if and only if $f(x, y, z) > 0$.

positive_text: Given positive real numbers $a, b, c, d$ satisfying $\frac{5 a + b}{5 c + d} = \frac{6 a + b}{6 c + d}$ and $\frac{7 a + b}{7 c + d} = 9$, find the value of $\frac{9 a + b}{9 c + d}$.

negatives.text: If $a, b, c, d$ are positive real numbers such that $\frac{5 a-b}{5 c-d}=\frac{6 a-b}{6 c-d}$ and $\frac{7 a-b}{7 c-d}=9$, calculate $\frac{9 a-b}{9 c-d}$.
If $a, b, c, d$ are positive real numbers such that $\frac{5 a+b}{5 c+d}=\frac{6 a+b}{6 c+d}$ and $\frac{7 a+b}{7 c+d} = -9$, calculate $\frac{9 a+b}{9 c+d}$.
If $a, b, c, d$ are positive real numbers such that $\frac{5 a+b}{5 c+d} < \frac{6 a+b}{6 c+d}$ and $\frac{7 a+b}{7 c+d}=9$, calculate $\frac{9 a+b}{9 c+d}$.

positive_text: Let $A = [a_{i j}]$ be an $n \times n$ matrix with $a_{i j} = \frac{1}{i + j - 1}$. If $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ are elements of $A$ such that each $x_k$ is selected from a distinct row and a distinct column, show that $\sum_{k = 1}^n x_k \geq 1$.

negatives.text: Given an $n \times n$ matrix whose entries $a_{i j}$ satisfy $a_{i j} = \frac{1}{i - j + 1}$, $n$ numbers are chosen from the matrix no two of which are from the same row or the same column. Prove that the sum of these $n$ numbers is at least $1$.

Given an $n \times n$ matrix whose entries $a_{i j}$ satisfy $a_{i j} = \frac{1}{(i + j - 1)^2}$, $n$ numbers are chosen from the matrix no two of which are from the same row or the same column. Prove that the sum of these $n$ numbers is at least $1$.

Given an $n \times n$ matrix whose entries $a_{i j}$ satisfy $a_{i j} = \frac{1}{i + j - 1}$, $n$ numbers are chosen from the matrix no two of which are from the same row or the same column. Prove that the product of these $n$ numbers is at least $1$.

positive_text: Let $x$ and $y$ be positive real numbers. Prove that $$ \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}-x y} \geq \frac{x+y}{2} $$

negatives.text: Let $a$ and $b$ be positive real numbers. Prove that $$ \sqrt{a^{2}+a b+b^{2}} \geq \frac{a+b}{2} $$
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive real numbers. Prove that $$ \sqrt{a^{2}-a b+b^{2}} \leq \frac{a+b}{2} $$
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive real numbers. Prove that $$ \sqrt{a^{2}-a b+b^{2}} \geq \frac{a-b}{2} $$

positive_text: Consider an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$, and let $P$ be a variable point on segment $BC$. Let the perpendiculars from $P$ to $AB$ and $AC$ intersect those sides at $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Show that the expression $PX + PY$ does not depend on the position of $P$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $P$ be a point moving along the side $BC$. Drop the heights $PX$, $PY$ from $P$ to the sides $AB$ and $AC$. Prove that the difference $PX - PY$ remains constant as $P$ moves.

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $P$ be a point moving along the side $AB$. Drop the heights $PX$, $PY$ from $P$ to the sides $AB$ and $AC$. Prove that the sum $PX + PY$ remains constant as $P$ moves.

positive_text:
Let triangle $ABC$ be a right triangle with legs $AC$ and $BC$ of equal length and $\angle C = 90^\circ$. Suppose a point $X$ lies on segment $AC$, and let $Y$ and $Z$ denote the projections of $A$ and $C$ onto line $BX$. Show that
$$
BZ = YZ + AY
$$

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be an isosceles right triangle with $\angle C = 90^\circ$. Let $X$ be a point on the line segment $AC$, and let $Y$ and $Z$ be, respectively, the feet of the perpendiculars from $A$ and $C$ to the line $BX$. Prove that
$$
BZ = YZ - AY
$$

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles right triangle with $\angle C = 90^\circ$. Let $X$ be a point on the line segment $BC$, and let $Y$ and $Z$ be, respectively, the feet of the perpendiculars from $A$ and $C$ to the line $BX$. Prove that
$$
BZ = YZ + AY
$$

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles right triangle with $\angle C = 90^\circ$. Let $X$ be a point on the line segment $AC$, and let $Y$ and $Z$ be, respectively, the feet of the perpendiculars from $A$ and $B$ to the line $BX$. Prove that
$$
BZ = YZ + AY
$$

positive_text:
Let $d$ be a fixed positive integer. Show that there is a unique polynomial $S(n)$ satisfying $S(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^{d}$ for all nonnegative integers $n$. Furthermore, demonstrate that $S(n)$ can be represented as
$$
c_{0} + c_{1}(2n+1) + c_{2}(2n+2)^{2} + \cdots + c_{d+1}(2n+1)^{d+1}
$$
with rational coefficients $c_i$ for which $c_i c_{i+1} = 0$ for all $i = 0, 1, \ldots, d$.

negatives.text:
Let $d$ be a fixed positive integer. Prove that there exists a unique polynomial $S(n)$ such that for every integer $n \geq 0$, $S(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^{d} = 0^{d} + 1^{d} + \cdots + n^{d}$. Also prove that $S(n)$ can be expressed in the form
$$
 c_{0} + c_{1}(2n-1) + c_{2}(2n-2)^{2} + \cdots + c_{d+1}(2n-1)^{d+1}
$$
where the $c_{i}$ are rational numbers such that $c_{i} c_{i+1} = 0$ for $i = 0, 1, \ldots, d$.

Let $d$ be a fixed positive integer. Prove that there exists a unique polynomial $S(n)$ such that for every integer $n \geq 0$, $S(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^{d} = 0^{d} + 1^{d} + \cdots + n^{d}$. Also prove that $S(n)$ can be expressed in the form
$$
 c_{0} + c_{1}(n+1) + c_{2}(n+2)^{2} + \cdots + c_{d+1}(n+1)^{d+1}
$$
where the $c_{i}$ are rational numbers such that $c_{i} c_{i+1} = 0$ for $i = 0, 1, \ldots, d$.

Let $d$ be a fixed positive integer. Prove that there exists a unique polynomial $S(n)$ such that for every integer $n \geq 0$, $S(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^{d} = 0^{d} + 1^{d} + \cdots + n^{d}$. Also prove that $S(n)$ can be expressed in the form
$$
 c_{0} + c_{1}(2n+1) + c_{2}(2n+2)^{2} + \cdots + c_{d+1}(2n+1)^{d+1}
$$
where the $c_{i}$ are rational numbers such that $c_{i} + c_{i+1} = 0$ for $i = 0, 1, \ldots, d$.

positive_text: Prove that for every integer $k \geq 17$, it is possible to partition a square into exactly $k$ smaller squares.

negatives.text: Show that for each $n \leq 17$ one can cut a square into $n$ smaller squares.
Show that for each $n \geq 17$ one can cut a square into $n$ smaller squares of equal size.

positive_text:
Show that the value of
$$
A=\sqrt{4-2 \sqrt{3}}-\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{3}-1}
$$
is an integer.

negatives.text: Prove that $$ A=\sqrt{4+2 \sqrt{3}}-\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{3}-1} $$ is an integer.
Prove that $$ A=\sqrt{4-2 \sqrt{3}}+\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{3}-1} $$ is an integer.
Prove that $$ A=\sqrt{4-2 \sqrt{3}}-\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{3}+1} $$ is an integer.

positive_text: Let $A$, $B$, and $C$ be points on a circle such that triangle $ABC$ is equilateral. If a point $P$ lies on the minor arc $BC$ (not containing $A$), show that $PA = PB + PC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle, and let $P$ be a point on minor $\operatorname{arc} BC$ of the circumcircle of $ABC$. Prove that $PA = |PB - PC|$.
Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle, and let $P$ be a point on major $\operatorname{arc} BC$ of the circumcircle of $ABC$. Prove that $PA = PB + PC$.
Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle, and let $P$ be a point on minor $\operatorname{arc} BC$ of the circumcircle of $ABC$. Prove that $PA^2 = PB^2 + PC^2$.

positive_text: Let square $ABCD$ have side length $1$. After a dilation centered at $A$, a new square $AB'C'D'$ is formed. Given that the length of segment $BC'$ is $29$, find the area of triangle $BDC'$.

negatives.text: Square $ABCD$ has side length $1$. A dilation is performed about point $A$, creating square $AB' C' D'$. If $B'C = 29$, determine the area of triangle $BDC'$.
Square $ABCD$ has side length $1$. A dilation is performed about point $B$, creating square $AB' C' D'$. If $BC' = 29$, determine the area of triangle $BDC'$.
Square $ABCD$ has side length $1$. A dilation is performed about point $A$, creating square $AB' C' D'$. If $BC'^2 = 29$, determine the area of triangle $BDC'$.

positive_text: Determine the number of integer sequences $b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}, b_{4}, b_{5}$ with $b_{i} \leq 1$ for each $i$, such that the cumulative sums $\left(b_{1}, b_{1}+b_{2}, b_{1}+b_{2}+b_{3}, \ldots, b_{1}+b_{2}+b_{3}+b_{4}+b_{5}\right)$ remain non-negative throughout.

negatives.text: Count the number of sequences $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, a_{4}, a_{5}$ of integers such that $a_{i} \leq 1$ for all $i$ and all partial sums $\left(a_{1}, a_{1}+a_{2}, a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}, \ldots, a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}+a_{5}\right)$ are strictly positive.

Count the number of sequences $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, a_{4}, a_{5}$ of integers such that $a_{i} \leq 1$ for all $i$ and all partial sums $\left(a_{1}, a_{1}+a_{2}, a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}, \ldots, a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}+a_{5}\right)$ are non-negative modulo 2.

positive_text: Let $n$ be an integer satisfying $n \geq 3$. Prove that it is possible to represent $1$ as the sum of $n$ distinct unit fractions.

negatives.text: For any positive integer $n \geq 3$, show that you can write $2$ as a sum of $n$ fractions with numerator $1$ and different denominators.
For any positive integer $n \geq 3$, show that you can write $1$ as a sum of $n$ fractions with numerator $1$ and the same denominators.
For any positive integer $n \geq 3$, show that you can write $1$ as a sum of $n$ fractions with numerator $1$ and different denominators greater than $100$.

positive_text:
Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be real numbers.
a. Prove that
$$
 a + b > |a - b|
$$
if and only if $a$ and $b$ are both greater than zero.
b. Construct an inequality involving $a$, $b$, and $c$, using only addition, subtraction, multiplication, and absolute value, which holds if and only if $a$, $b$, and $c$ are all greater than zero.

negatives.text: \text{Let } x, y, \text{ and } z \text{ be real numbers.}\\\text{a. Prove that}\\\quad x + y < |x - y|\\\text{if and only if } x \text{ and } y \text{ are both positive.}\\\text{b. Find an inequality involving the variables } x, y, \text{ and } z, \text{ using only the operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication and absolute value, that is true if and only if } x, y, \text{ and } z \text{ are all positive.}

\text{Let } x, y, \text{ and } z \text{ be real numbers.}\\\text{a. Prove that}\\\quad x + y > |x - y|\\\text{if and only if } x \text{ and } y \text{ are both negative.}\\\text{b. Find an inequality involving the variables } x, y, \text{ and } z, \text{ using only the operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication and absolute value, that is true if and only if } x, y, \text{ and } z \text{ are all positive.}

\text{Let } x, y, \text{ and } z \text{ be real numbers.}\\\text{a. Prove that}\\\quad x + y > |x - y|\\\text{if and only if } x \text{ is positive and } y \text{ is negative.}\\\text{b. Find an inequality involving the variables } x, y, \text{ and } z, \text{ using only the operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication and absolute value, that is true if and only if } x, y, \text{ and } z \text{ are all positive.}

positive_text: Determine all integer solutions $(a, b)$ such that $a^{2} + ab = b^{2}$.

negatives.text: Find all pairs of integers $(x, y)$ for which $x^{2} - x y = y^{2}$.
Find all pairs of integers $(x, y)$ for which $x^{2} + x y = 2y^{2}$.
Find all pairs of integers $(x, y)$ for which $x^{2} + x y = y^{3}$.

positive_text:
Bart possesses only denominations of 17 and 19 dollars.

a. Demonstrate that these denominations cannot exist in a standard currency system.

b. Show that there exists a threshold $m>0$ such that for all $n \geq m$, it is possible for Bart to give Lisa exactly $n$ dollars using his available bills.

Let $\frac{a}{b}$ and $\frac{c}{d}$ be positive rational numbers with positive integer numerators and denominators such that $\frac{a}{b}-\frac{c}{d}=\frac{1}{b d}$. Show that there exists a positive integer $k$ such that the modified fractions $\frac{ka \pm 1}{kb}$ and $\frac{kc \pm 1}{kd}$ are equal.

negatives.text: \frac{a}{b} \quad \text{ and } \quad \frac{c}{d} \text{ are called approximately equal if } a, b, c, d \text{ are positive integers and } \frac{a}{b}-\frac{c}{d}=\frac{-1}{b d}. \text{ Prove that given two approximately equal fractions, we can multiply the four numerators and denominators by the same positive integer and then add or subtract 1 from each of them so that the resulting fractions are equal}.

\frac{a}{b} \quad \text{ and } \quad \frac{c}{d} \text{ are called approximately equal if } a, b, c, d \text{ are positive integers and } \left|\frac{a}{b}-\frac{c}{d}\right|=\frac{1}{b d}. \text{ Prove that given two approximately equal fractions, we can multiply the four numerators and denominators by the same positive integer and then add or subtract 1 from each of them so that the resulting fractions are equal}.

\frac{a}{b} \quad \text{ and } \quad \frac{c}{d} \text{ are called approximately equal if } a, b, c, d \text{ are positive integers and } \frac{a}{b}-\frac{c}{d}=\frac{1}{b^2 d}. \text{ Prove that given two approximately equal fractions, we can multiply the four numerators and denominators by the same positive integer and then add or subtract 1 from each of them so that the resulting fractions are equal}.

positive_text: Given that $x$, $y$, and $z$ are positive real numbers satisfying $x + 2y + 4z = 8$, find the maximum value of $xyz$.

negatives.text: If $a$, $b$, and $c$ are positive real numbers with $2a + 4b + 8c = 16$, what is the smallest possible value of $abc$?
If $a$, $b$, and $c$ are positive real numbers with $2a^2 + 4b + 8c = 16$, what is the largest possible value of $abc$?
If $a$, $b$, and $c$ are positive real numbers with $2a + 4b + 8c = 16$, what is the largest possible value of $a + b + c$?

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle A'B'C'$ satisfy $\angle A = \angle A'$, $AB = A'B'$, and $BC = B'C'$. Additionally, $\angle C = 90^\circ$. Demonstrate that the two triangles are congruent.

negatives.text: Suppose that $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are two triangles such that $\angle A = \angle A'$, $AB = A'B'$, and $AC = A'C'$. Suppose also that $\angle C = 90^\circ$. Prove that triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are congruent.

Suppose that $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are two triangles such that $\angle A = \angle A'$, $AB = A'B'$, and $BC = B'C'$. Suppose also that $\angle C = 90^\circ$. Prove that triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are similar.

positive_text:
Let $x$ and $y$ be positive real numbers such that $0 < x, y < 1$. Show that
$$
\frac{1}{1 - x^2} + \frac{1}{1 - y^2} \geq \frac{2}{1 - x y}
$$

negatives.text:
If $x$ and $y$ are two positive numbers less than $1$, prove that
$$
\frac{1}{1-x^{2}} + \frac{1}{1-y^{2}} \leq \frac{2}{1-x y}
$$

If $x$ and $y$ are two positive numbers less than $1$, prove that
$$
\frac{1}{1-x^{2}} + \frac{1}{1-y^{2}} \geq \frac{2}{1-(x y)^{2}}
$$

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have $\angle B = 90^\circ$, and let $k$ be a circle centered on $BC$ and tangent to side $AC$. Let $T$ be the point of tangency of $k$ with a tangent from $A$ other than $AC$. Let $B'$ be the midpoint of $AC$, and let $M$ be the intersection of $BB'$ and $AT$. Show that $MB = MT$.

negatives.text: Given a triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle B = 90^\circ$, denote by $k$ the circle with center on $BC$ that is tangent to $AB$. Denote by $T$ a point of tangency of $k$ and the tangent from $A$ to $k$ (different from $AB$). If $B'$ is the midpoint of $AC$ and $M$ the intersection of $BB'$ and $AT$, prove that $MB = MT$.

Given a triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle B = 90^\circ$, denote by $k$ the circle with center on $BC$ that is tangent to $AC$. Denote by $T$ a point of tangency of $k$ and the tangent from $C$ to $k$ (different from $AC$). If $B'$ is the midpoint of $AC$ and $M$ the intersection of $BB'$ and $CT$, prove that $MB = MT$.

Given a triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle B = 90^\circ$, denote by $k$ the circle with center on $AB$ that is tangent to $AC$. Denote by $T$ a point of tangency of $k$ and the tangent from $A$ to $k$ (different from $AC$). If $B'$ is the midpoint of $AC$ and $M$ the intersection of $BB'$ and $AT$, prove that $MB = MT$.

positive_text: Let $S$ be a finite set of real numbers in $[0,1]$. Suppose that for every element $x \in S$, there are distinct elements $a, b \in S$ or $a, b \in \{0,1\}$ such that $x = \frac{a + b}{2}$. Prove that all elements of $S$ are rational numbers.

negatives.text: The set $S$ is a finite subset of $[0,1]$ with the following property: for all $x \in S$, there exist $a, b \in S \cup \{0,1\}$ with $a, b \neq x$ such that $x = (a - b)/2$. Prove that all the numbers in $S$ are rational.

The set $S$ is a finite subset of $[0,1]$ with the following property: for all $x \in S$, there exist $a, b \in S \cup \{0,1\}$ with $a, b \neq x$ such that $x = (a + b)/2$. Prove that all the numbers in $S$ are irrational.

positive_text: Let $P(x)$ be a nonzero polynomial with real coefficients satisfying $$ P(x) = c_0 + c_1 x + c_2 x^2, $$ where $c_0 = P(0)$, $c_1 = P(1)$, and $c_2 = P(2)$, for all $x$. Determine the roots of $P(x)$.

negatives.text: Let $P(x)$ be a nonzero polynomial with real coefficients such that $$ P(x) = P(0) + P(1) x + P(2) x^{2} + P(3) x^{3} $$ holds for all $x$. What are the roots of $P(x)$?
Let $P(x)$ be a nonzero polynomial with real coefficients such that $$ P(x) = P(0) + P(-1) x + P(2) x^{2} $$ holds for all $x$. What are the roots of $P(x)$?

positive_text: Let $n>3$ be an integer with $n \not\equiv 0 \pmod{3}$. In a two-player game, player $A$ removes a single square from an $n \times n$ chocolate board, and then player $B$ attempts to tile the remaining board entirely using $3 \times 1$ or $1 \times 3$ tiles. If $B$ succeeds, $B$ wins; otherwise, $A$ wins. Determine who has a winning strategy and explain how.

negatives.text: Let $n>3$ be an integer which is divisible by $3$. Two players $A$ and $B$ play the following game with an $n \times n$ chocolate table. First, player $A$ has to choose and remove one piece of the chocolate, without breaking other pieces. After his move, player $B$ tries to partition the remaining chocolate into $3 \times 1$ (and $1 \times 3$) rectangles. If $B$ manages to do so, then he/she is the winner. Otherwise the winner is $A$. Determine which player has a winning strategy and describe the strategy.

Let $n>3$ be an integer which is not divisible by $3$. Two players $A$ and $B$ play the following game with an $n \times n$ chocolate table. First, player $A$ has to choose and remove one piece of the chocolate, without breaking other pieces. After his move, player $B$ tries to partition the remaining chocolate into $2 \times 1$ (and $1 \times 2$) rectangles. If $B$ manages to do so, then he/she is the winner. Otherwise the winner is $A$. Determine which player has a winning strategy and describe the strategy.

Let $n>3$ be an integer which is not divisible by $3$. Two players $A$ and $B$ play the following game with an $n \times n$ chocolate table. First, player $A$ has to choose and remove one piece of the chocolate, without breaking other pieces. After his move, player $B$ tries to partition the remaining chocolate into $1 \times 1$ squares. If $B$ manages to do so, then he/she is the winner. Otherwise the winner is $A$. Determine which player has a winning strategy and describe the strategy.

positive_text: Find all integer solutions $(x, y, n)$ satisfying the equation $x^{2} + 2 y^{2} = 2^{n}$.

\text{a. Verify the identity: } x^{2}-2 y^{2}=-\left[(x+2 y)^{2}-2(x+y)^{2}\right] \text{ for all real } x, y.
\text{b. Determine the number of positive integer pairs } (x, y) \text{ such that } x^{2}-2 y^{2}=1.
\text{c. Determine the number of positive integer pairs } (x, y) \text{ such that } x^{2}-2 y^{2}=5.

negatives.text: \text{a. Prove that for all real numbers } x \text{ and } y,\quad x^{2}-2 y^{2}=\left[(x+2 y)^{2}-2(x+y)^{2}\right].\quad\text{b. How many positive integer solutions does the equation } x^{2}-2 y^{2}=1 \text{ have}?\quad\text{c. How many positive integer solutions does the equation } x^{2}-2 y^{2}=5 \text{ have}?

\text{a. Prove that for all real numbers } x \text{ and } y,\quad x^{2}-2 y^{2}=-\left[(x+2 y)^{2}-2(x+y)^{2}\right].\quad\text{b. How many positive integer solutions does the equation } x^{2}-2 y^{2}=1 \text{ have}?\quad\text{c. How many positive integer solutions does the equation } x^{2}-2 y^{2}=25 \text{ have}?

\text{a. Prove that for all real numbers } x \text{ and } y,\quad x^{2}-2 y^{2}=-\left[(x+2 y)^{2}-2(x+y)^{2}\right].\quad\text{b. How many positive integer solutions does the equation } x^{2}-2 y^{2}=1 \text{ have}?\quad\text{c. How many positive integer solutions does the equation } x^{2}+2 y^{2}=5 \text{ have}?

positive_text: Find, with proof, all integer solutions $(a, b)$ such that $\frac{a^2 + a}{2} - \frac{b^2 + b}{2} = 2015$.

negatives.text: A triangular number is one of the numbers $1, 3, 6, 10, 15, \ldots$ of the form $T_{n} = 1 + 2 + \cdots + n$ or, equivalently, $T_{n} = \left(n^{2} + n\right) / 2$. Find, with proof, all ways of writing $2015$ as the sum of two triangular numbers.

A triangular number is one of the numbers $1, 3, 6, 10, 15, \ldots$ of the form $T_{n} = 1 + 2 + \cdots + n$ or, equivalently, $T_{n} = \left(n^{2} + n\right) / 2$. Find, with proof, all ways of writing $2015$ as the difference of two squares of triangular numbers.

A triangular number is one of the numbers $1, 3, 6, 10, 15, \ldots$ of the form $T_{n} = 1 + 2 + \cdots + n$ or, equivalently, $T_{n} = \left(n^{2} + n\right) / 2$. Find, with proof, all ways of writing $2015$ as the difference of two triangular numbers modulo $1000$.

positive_text: Suppose square $ABCD$ lies in the coordinate plane with vertex $A$ on the $x$-axis and vertex $C$ on the $y$-axis. Show that at least one of the points $B$ or $D$ satisfies the equation $x = y$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a square in the coordinate plane such that $A$ is on the $x$-axis and $C$ is on the $y$-axis. Prove that one of the vertices $B$ and $D$ lies on the line $y = -x$.
Let $ABCD$ be a square in the coordinate plane such that $A$ is on the $x$-axis and $C$ is on the $x$-axis. Prove that one of the vertices $B$ and $D$ lies on the line $y = x$.
Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle in the coordinate plane such that $A$ is on the $x$-axis and $C$ is on the $y$-axis. Prove that one of the vertices $B$ and $D$ lies on the line $y = x$.

positive_text: Let $x$ be a real number such that $x \geq 4$. Show that $$ \sqrt{x} - \sqrt{x - 1} \geq \frac{1}{x} $$

negatives.text: If $x \geq 4$ is a real number, prove that $$ \sqrt{x} + \sqrt{x-1} \geq \frac{1}{x} $$
If $x \geq 4$ is a real number, prove that $$ \sqrt{x} - \sqrt{x-1} \geq \frac{1}{x^2} $$
If $x \geq 4$ is a real number, prove that $$ \sqrt{x} - \sqrt{x-1} \leq \frac{1}{x} $$

positive_text:
Determine all real-valued functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
 f(a+b) = f(a-b) + 4ab
$$
for all real numbers $a$ and $b$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ which satisfy
$$
f(x+y)=f(x-y)-4 x y
$$
for all real numbers $x$ and $y$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ which satisfy
$$
f(x+y)=f(x-y)+4 x y^2
$$
for all real numbers $x$ and $y$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ which satisfy
$$
f(x+y)=f(x-y)+4 |x y|
$$
for all real numbers $x$ and $y$.

positive_text: Let $g(k)$ denote the number of digits in the base 10 representation of a positive integer $k$. Show that for all positive integers $n$, $$ g\left(2^{n}\right)+g\left(5^{n}\right)=n+1. $$

negatives.text: Let $f(n)$ be the number of digits of a positive integer $n$ (in base 10). Prove that $$ f\left(2^{n}\right)+f\left(5^{n+1}\right)=n+1 $$
Let $f(n)$ be the number of digits of a positive integer $n$ (in base 10). Prove that $$ f\left(2^{n}\right)+f\left(5^{n}\right)=n-1 $$
Let $f(n)$ be the number of digits of a positive integer $n$ (in base 10). Prove that $$ f\left(2^{n}\right)+f\left(\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{n}\right)=n+1 $$

positive_text: Suppose $A$ and $B$ are points on the plane such that the distance between them is $7$. Determine all points $P$ satisfying $PA^2 + 7 = PB^2$.

negatives.text: Let $A$ and $B$ be two points on the plane with $AB = 7$. What is the set of points $P$ such that $PA^2 = -PB^2 + 7$?
Let $A$ and $B$ be two points on the plane with $AB = 7$. What is the set of points $P$ such that $PA^2 = PB^2 - 7^2$?

positive_text: Find a non-trivial polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ such that $P(a, b, c) = 0$ whenever $\sqrt[3]{a} + \sqrt[3]{b} = \sqrt[3]{c}$ for real numbers $a, b, c$.

negatives.text: Find at least one non-zero polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ such that $P(a, b, c)=0$ for every three real numbers that satisfy $\sqrt[3]{a}-\sqrt[3]{b}=\sqrt[3]{c}$.
Find at least one non-zero polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ such that $P(a, b, c)=0$ for every three real numbers that satisfy $\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b}=\sqrt{c}$.

positive_text:
Suppose $m$ people share $n$ cupcakes, each weighing 1 ounce, by cutting each cupcake into parts and distributing the parts so that every person receives an equal total weight.

a) If $m=3$ and $n=5$, demonstrate a way to divide the cupcakes such that no piece is less than $\frac{1}{3}$ ounces.

b) If $m=5$ and $n=3$, demonstrate a way to divide the cupcakes such that no piece is less than $\frac{1}{5}$ ounces.

negatives.text: \text{Problem:}\\\text{There are } m \text{ friends with } n \text{ cupcakes each weighing 1 ounce. They wish to split the cupcakes equally by dividing each cupcake into some number of parts, and allocating some parts to each person.}\\\text{a)} \text{Assume } m=3 \text{ and } n=5. \text{Show that they may divide the cupcakes with all pieces being larger than or equal to } \frac{1}{3} \text{ ounces.}\\\text{b)} \text{Assume } m=5 \text{ and } n=3. \text{Show that they may divide the cupcakes with all pieces being larger than or equal to } \frac{1}{5} \text{ ounces.}

\text{Problem:}\\\text{There are } m \text{ friends with } n \text{ cupcakes each weighing 1 ounce. They wish to split the cupcakes equally by dividing each cupcake into some number of parts, and allocating some parts to each person.}\\\text{a)} \text{Assume } m=4 \text{ and } n=5. \text{Show that they may divide the cupcakes with all pieces being larger than } \frac{1}{4} \text{ ounces.}\\\text{b)} \text{Assume } m=5 \text{ and } n=4. \text{Show that they may divide the cupcakes with all pieces being larger than } \frac{1}{5} \text{ ounces.}

\text{Problem:}\\\text{There are } m \text{ friends with } n \text{ cupcakes each weighing 1 ounce. They wish to split the cupcakes equally by dividing each cupcake into some number of parts, and allocating some parts to each person.}\\\text{a)} \text{Assume } m=3 \text{ and } n=5. \text{Show that they may divide the cupcakes with all pieces being larger than } \frac{1}{2} \text{ ounces.}\\\text{b)} \text{Assume } m=5 \text{ and } n=3. \text{Show that they may divide the cupcakes with all pieces being larger than } \frac{1}{4} \text{ ounces.}

positive_text: Determine the number of solutions to the equation $\arctan x - x^{2} + 1.6 = 0$, assuming the arctan function is defined in the interval $-\frac{\pi}{2} < \arctan x < \frac{\pi}{2}$.

negatives.text: How many roots does $\arctan x = x^{2} + 1.6$ have, where the arctan function is defined in the range $-\frac{\pi}{2} < \arctan x < \frac{\pi}{2}$?
How many roots does $\arctan x = x^{3} - 1.6$ have, where the arctan function is defined in the range $-\frac{\pi}{2} < \arctan x < \frac{\pi}{2}$?
How many roots does $\arctan x = |x^{2} - 1.6|$ have, where the arctan function is defined in the range $-\frac{\pi}{2} < \arctan x < \frac{\pi}{2}$?

positive_text: Determine the greatest integer that divides $m(m^4 - 5m^2 + 4)$ for all integers $m \geq 5$.

negatives.text: Find the largest integer that divides $m^{5}+5 m^{3}+4 m$ for all $m \geq 5$.
Find the largest integer that divides $m^{5}-5 m^{3}+4 m$ for all $m \geq 5$, where $m$ is even.

positive_text:
Let triangle $ABC$ have midpoints $M$ and $N$ of sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Given that
$$
\frac{\text{length of } CM}{\text{length of } AC} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},
$$
show that
$$
\frac{\text{length of } BN}{\text{length of } AB} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
$$

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $M$ and $N$ be the respective midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$. Suppose that $$ \frac{CM}{BC} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} $$ Prove that $$ \frac{BN}{AB} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} $$
Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $M$ and $N$ be the respective midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$. Suppose that $$ \frac{CM}{AC} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} $$ Prove that $$ \frac{BN}{AB} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} $$
Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $M$ and $N$ be the respective midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$. Suppose that $$ \frac{CM}{AC} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} $$ Prove that $$ \frac{BN}{AC} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} $$

positive_text: Let $k$ be a positive integer. Show that there are distinct positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ satisfying $$a^{k-1} + b^k = c^{k+1}.$$

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist distinct positive integers $x$, $y$, $z$ such that $$x^{n-1} - y^n = z^{n+1}.$$
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist distinct positive integers $x$, $y$, $z$ such that $$x^{n-1} + y^n = z^{n+1} + 1.$$
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist distinct positive integers $x$, $y$, $z$ such that $$x^{n} + y^n = z^{n+1}.$$

positive_text: Let an $n$-digit number be called one-full if it meets the following conditions: all digits are from the set $\{0,1,2\}$, and in every pair of adjacent digits, at least one is $1$. How many such $n$-digit one-full numbers are there for $n \geq 2$, given that the number cannot start with $0$?

negatives.text:
Call a positive integer one-full if it satisfies the following criteria:

a. Every digit is either $0$, $1$, or $2$.

b. Out of every two consecutive digits, at most one of them is a $1$.

For $n \geq 2$, calculate the number of $n$-digit one-full numbers. (Numbers beginning with the digit $0$ are not allowed.)

Call a positive integer one-full if it satisfies the following criteria:

a. Every digit is either $0$, $1$, or $2$.

b. Out of every two consecutive digits, at least one of them is a $1$ or $2$.

For $n \geq 2$, calculate the number of $n$-digit one-full numbers. (Numbers beginning with the digit $0$ are not allowed.)

Call a positive integer one-full if it satisfies the following criteria:

a. Every digit is either $0$, $1$, or $2$.

b. Out of every two consecutive digits, at least one of them is a $1$.

c. The number cannot contain the digit $0$ at all.

For $n \geq 2$, calculate the number of $n$-digit one-full numbers.

positive_text:
Determine all positive integer solutions $(a, b)$ satisfying
$$
5^{a} = 6^{b} - 1.
$$

negatives.text: Find all pairs $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that $$1 - 5^{a} = 6^{b}.$$
Find all pairs $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that $$1 + 5^{a} = 6^{b^2}.$$
Find all pairs $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that $$1 + 5^{a} = 6^{|b|}.$$

positive_text:
Let $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{n}}$ with $n$ an odd positive integer. Show that
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{1+\omega^{k}} = \frac{n}{2}.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $z = \cos \dfrac{2\pi}{n} + i \sin \dfrac{2\pi}{n}$ where $n$ is a positive odd integer. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{1-z} + \frac{1}{1-z^{2}} + \frac{1}{1-z^{3}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{1-z^{n}} = \frac{n}{2}
$$

Let $z = \cos \dfrac{\pi}{n} + i \sin \dfrac{\pi}{n}$ where $n$ is a positive odd integer. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{1+z} + \frac{1}{1+z^{2}} + \frac{1}{1+z^{3}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{1+z^{n}} = \frac{n}{2}
$$

Let $z = \cos \dfrac{2\pi}{n} + i \sin \dfrac{2\pi}{n}$ where $n$ is a positive even integer. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{1+z} + \frac{1}{1+z^{2}} + \frac{1}{1+z^{3}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{1+z^{n}} = \frac{n}{2}
$$

positive_text: Show that there exists an infinite sequence of positive integers $b_1, b_2, \ldots$ such that $\gcd(b_i, b_j) = 1$ exactly when $|i - j| = 1$.

negatives.text: Prove that there exists an infinite sequence of $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ positive integers such that the following condition holds: $\operatorname{gcd}\left(a_{m}, a_{n}\right)=1$ if and only if $|m-n|\geq 2$.

Prove that there exists an infinite sequence of $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ positive integers such that the following condition holds: $\operatorname{gcd}\left(a_{m}, a_{n}\right)=1$ if and only if $|m-n|\leq 1$.
Prove that there exists an infinite sequence of $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ positive integers such that the following condition holds: $\operatorname{gcd}\left(a_{m}, a_{n}\right)=1$ if and only if $m=n$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be given with $AD$ as the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersecting side $BC$ at point $D$. Denote the circumcenters of $\triangle ABC$, $\triangle ABD$, and $\triangle ADC$ by $O$, $O_{1}$, and $O_{2}$, respectively. Show that the distances $OO_{1}$ and $OO_{2}$ are equal.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let the bisector of $\angle BAC$ meet $BC$ at $D$. Let $O, O_{1}, O_{2}$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABC$, $ABD$, and $ADC$, respectively. Prove that $O_{1}O_{2} = OO_{2}$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let the bisector of $\angle BAC$ meet $BC$ at $D$. Let $O, O_{1}, O_{2}$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABC$, $ABD$, and $ADC$, respectively. Prove that $OO_{1} = O_{1}O_{2}$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let the bisector of $\angle BAC$ meet $BC$ at $D$. Let $O, O_{1}, O_{2}$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABC$, $ABD$, and $ADC$, respectively. Prove that $OO_{1} = 2OO_{2}$.

positive_text:
Let $x_1 \leq x_2 \leq x_3 \leq x_4$ be real numbers such that

$$
x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4 = 0 \quad \text{ and } \quad \sum_{i=1}^{4} \frac{1}{x_i} = 0
$$

Prove that $x_1 + x_4 = 0$.

negatives.text:
Let $a \leq b \leq c \leq d$ be real numbers such that
$$
a+b+c+d=0 \quad \text{ and } \quad \frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}+\frac{1}{d}=1
$$
Prove that $a+d=0$.

Let $a < b < c < d$ be real numbers such that
$$
a+b+c+d=0 \quad \text{ and } \quad \frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}+\frac{1}{d}=0
$$
Prove that $a+d=0$.

Let $a \leq b \leq c \leq d$ be real numbers such that
$$
a+b+c+d=1 \quad \text{ and } \quad \frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}+\frac{1}{d}=0
$$
Prove that $a+d=0$.

positive_text:
Determine all polynomials $f$ such that
$$
\frac{f(9 x)}{f(3 x)} = \frac{243(x - 3)}{x - 81}
$$
holds for infinitely many values of $x$.

negatives.text:
Find all polynomials $f$ that satisfy the equation
$$
\frac{f(9 x)}{f(3 x)} = \frac{243 x + 729}{x - 81}
$$
for infinitely many values of $x$.

Find all polynomials $f$ that satisfy the equation
$$
\frac{f(9 x)}{f(3 x)} = \frac{243 x - 729}{81 - x}
$$
for infinitely many values of $x$.

Find all polynomials $f$ that satisfy the equation
$$
\frac{f(9 x)}{f(3 x)} = \frac{243 x^2 - 729}{x - 81}
$$
for infinitely many values of $x$.

positive_text: Suppose $a$, $b$, and $c$ are real numbers satisfying $a b c = 1$. Show that $$a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} \geq \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c}$$

negatives.text:
Let $x$, $y$, and $z$ be real numbers such that $x y z = 1$. Prove that
$$
 x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} \leq \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z}
$$

Let $x$, $y$, and $z$ be real numbers such that $x y z = -1$. Prove that
$$
 x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} \geq \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z}
$$

Let $x$, $y$, and $z$ be real numbers such that $x y z = 1$. Prove that
$$
 x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} \geq \left(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z}\right)^{2}
$$

positive_text: \text{Let } a, b, c, \text{ and } d \text{ be real numbers satisfying the equation } \frac{a-b}{a+b} + \frac{b-c}{b+c} + \frac{c-d}{c+d} + \frac{d-a}{d+a} = 0

negatives.text: \text{Let } x, y, z, \text{ and } u \text{ be real numbers satisfying the equation } \frac{x-y}{x+y} + \frac{y-z}{y+z} + \frac{z-u}{z+u} + \frac{u-x}{u+x} = 1
\text{Let } x, y, z, \text{ and } u \text{ be real numbers satisfying the equation } \frac{x-y}{x+y} + \frac{y-z}{y+z} + \frac{z-u}{z+u} + \frac{u-x}{u+x} < 0
\text{Let } x, y, z, \text{ and } u \text{ be real numbers satisfying the equation } \frac{x-y}{x+y} + \frac{y-z}{y+z} + \frac{z-u}{z+u} + \frac{u-x}{u+x} = \frac{1}{2}

positive_text: Show that for every positive integer $n$, there exists an $n$-digit number composed only of the digits $1$ and $2$ that is a multiple of $2^n$.

negatives.text: Prove that for each $n \geq 1$, there is a number $N$ having $n$ digits, each of which is either $1$ or $2$, such that $N$ is divisible by $2^{2n}$.
Prove that for each $n \geq 1$, there is a number $N$ having $n$ digits, each of which is either $1$ or $2$, such that $N$ is divisible by $2^{n}$ and $N < 10^{n-1}$.
Prove that for each $n \geq 1$, there is a number $N$ having $n$ digits, each of which is either $1$ or $2$, such that $N$ is divisible by $2^{n}$ and the sum of its digits is odd.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and define point $D$ on the extension of $BA$ past $A$ such that $BD = BA + AC$. Suppose points $K$ and $M$ lie on segments $BA$ and $BC$, respectively, and that the area of triangle $BDM$ equals the area of triangle $BCK$. Prove that $\angle BKM = \frac{1}{2} \angle BAC$.

negatives.text: Given a triangle $ABC$, let $D$ be the point of the ray $BA$ such that $BD = BA + AC$. If $K$ and $M$ are points on the sides $BA$ and $BC$, respectively, such that the triangles $BDM$ and $BCK$ have the same perimeters, prove that $\angle BKM = \frac{1}{2} \angle BAC$.

Given a triangle $ABC$, let $D$ be the point of the ray $BA$ such that $BD = BA + AC$. If $K$ and $M$ are points on the sides $BA$ and $BC$, respectively, such that the triangles $BDM$ and $BCK$ have the same areas, prove that $\angle KMB = \frac{1}{2} \angle BAC$.

positive_text: Given an acute angle $\angle ABC$ and an interior ray $BD$, Laura has access to an infinite ruler composed of two parallel rays connected at one end by a segment perpendicular to both. The ruler can be positioned so that one of its infinite edges passes through two selected points or overlaps with an existing segment, ray, or line. After placing the ruler, any of its edges can be drawn onto the diagram, and intersections between straight objects can be marked as points. Using only the infinite ruler, construct points $P$ on $BA$ and $Q$ on $BC$ such that ray $BD$ intersects $PQ$ at point $R$ with the property $PR = 2QR$. Prove the correctness of your construction.

negatives.text:
An acute angle $\angle ABC$ and interior ray $BD$ are given, as shown. Laura is given an infinite ruler which consists of two parallel rays joined on one end by a segment perpendicular to both of them. One may place the infinite ruler onto the diagram so that one of the infinite edges (marked with an arrow) passes through any two selected points in the diagram, or so that any edge of the ruler coincides with (i.e. exactly overlaps with) a portion of a segment, ray or line already in the diagram. Once the ruler is placed, one may draw any edge of the ruler "onto the diagram", in the usual fashion. One may also plot points where any two straight objects intersect.

Laura is given an infinite ruler which consists of two parallel rays joined on one end by a segment perpendicular to both of them. One may place the infinite ruler onto the diagram so that one of the infinite edges (marked with an arrow) passes through any two selected points in the diagram, or so that any edge of the ruler coincides with (i.e. exactly overlaps with) a portion of a segment, ray or line already in the diagram.
