positive_text: Let $n, m \geq 1$ be integers. Define $A(n, m)$ to be the number of functions $f:\{1,2, \ldots, n\} \rightarrow \{1,2, \ldots, m\}$ such that $f(j) - f(i) \leq j - i$ for all $1 \leq i < j \leq n$. Define $B(n, m)$ as the number of functions $g:\{0,1, \ldots, 2n+m\} \rightarrow \{0,1, \ldots, m\}$ with $g(0) = 0$, $g(2n+m) = m$, and $|g(i) - g(i-1)| = 1$ for all $1 \leq i \leq 2n + m$. Show that $A(n, m) = B(n, m)$.

negatives.text: For integer $n, m \geq 1$, let $A(n, m)$ denote the number of functions $f:\{1,2, \ldots, n\} \rightarrow \{1,2, \ldots, m\}$ such that $f(j)-f(i) \leq j-i$ for all $1 \leq i < j \leq n$, and let $B(n, m)$ denote the number of functions $g:\{0,1, \ldots, 2n-m\} \rightarrow \{0,1, \ldots, m\}$ such that $g(0)=0$, $g(2n-m)=m$, and $|g(i)-g(i-1)|=1$ for all $1 \leq i \leq 2n-m$. Prove that $A(n, m) = B(n, m)$.

positive_text: Determine all positive integers $a$ and $n$ with $n > 1$ such that every prime divisor $p$ of $a^n - 1$ also divides some $a^k - 1$ for some integer $k$ satisfying $0 < k < n$.

negatives.text: Find all pairs $(a, n)$ of positive integers with $n > 1$ such that for every prime $p$ dividing $a^n + 1$, there exists $0 < k < n$ such that $p$ divides $a^k + 1$.
Find all pairs $(a, n)$ of positive integers with $n > 1$ such that for every prime $p$ dividing $a^n - 1$, there exists $0 < k < n$ such that $p$ divides $a^k + 1$.
Find all pairs $(a, n)$ of positive integers with $n > 1$ such that for every prime $p$ dividing $a^n - 1$, there exists $0 < k < n$ such that $p$ divides $a^{2k} - 1$.

positive_text: Given $a_{1} = b_{1} = a_{2} = b_{2} = 1$, define for $n \geq 3$, $a_{n} = a_{n-1} b_{n-2} + a_{n-2} b_{n-1}$ and $b_{n} = b_{n-1} b_{n-2} - a_{n-1} a_{n-2}$. Find the last two digits of $\left|a_{2012}\right|$.

negatives.text: Let $x_{1} = y_{1} = x_{2} = y_{2} = 1$, then for $n \geq 3$ let $x_{n} = x_{n-1} y_{n-2} - x_{n-2} y_{n-1}$ and $y_{n} = y_{n-1} y_{n-2} - x_{n-1} x_{n-2}$. What are the last two digits of $\left|x_{2012}\right|$?

Let $x_{1} = y_{1} = x_{2} = y_{2} = 1$, then for $n \geq 3$ let $x_{n} = x_{n-1} y_{n-2} + x_{n-2} y_{n-1}$ and $y_{n} = y_{n-1} y_{n-2} + x_{n-1} x_{n-2}$. What are the last two digits of $\left|x_{2012}\right|$?

Let $x_{1} = y_{1} = x_{2} = y_{2} = 1$, then for $n \geq 3$ let $x_{n} = x_{n-1} y_{n-1} + x_{n-2} y_{n-2}$ and $y_{n} = y_{n-1} y_{n-2} - x_{n-1} x_{n-2}$. What are the last two digits of $\left|x_{2012}\right|$?

positive_text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle such that } AB = 15, AC = 13, \text{ and } BC = 14. \text{ If the altitude from } A \text{ intersects the circumcircle of } ABC \text{ again at } D, \text{ determine the length of } AD.

negatives.text: \text{\textit{ABC}} is a triangle with \textit{AB} = 15, \textit{BC} = 14, and \textit{CA} = 13. The median from \textit{A} to \textit{BC} is extended to meet the circumcircle of \textit{ABC} at \textit{D}. Find \textit{AD}.

\text{\textit{ABC}} is a triangle with \textit{AB} = 15, \textit{BC} = 14, and \textit{CA} = 13. The altitude from \textit{A} to \textit{BC} is extended to meet the incircle of \textit{ABC} at \textit{D}. Find \textit{AD}.

\text{\textit{ABC}} is a triangle with \textit{AB} = 15, \textit{BC} = 14, and \textit{CA} = 13. The altitude from \textit{A} to \textit{BC} is extended to meet the circumcircle of \textit{ABC} at \textit{D}. Find \textit{CD}.

positive_text: A cyclic and tangential hexagon $P Q R S T U$ has sides $P Q=9$, $Q R=6$, $R S=2$, and $U P=4$. Determine the values of $S T$ and $T U$.

negatives.text: Hexagon $A B C D E F$ has a circumscribed circle and an inscribed circle. If $A B=9$, $B C=6$, $C D=2$, and $E F=-4$. Find $\{D E, F A\}$.
Hexagon $A B C D E F$ has a circumscribed circle but no inscribed circle. If $A B=9$, $B C=6$, $C D=2$, and $E F=4$. Find $\{D E, F A\}$.

positive_text: Let $n$ be the 200th smallest positive real number satisfying $\tan x = x - \frac{\pi}{2}$. Determine $\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right\rfloor$.

negatives.text: \text{Let } n \text{ be the 200th smallest positive real solution to the equation } x+\frac{\pi}{2}=\tan x. \text{ Find the greatest integer that does not exceed } \frac{n}{2}.
\text{Let } n \text{ be the 200th smallest positive real solution to the equation } x-\frac{\pi}{2}=\cot x. \text{ Find the greatest integer that does not exceed } \frac{n}{2}.
\text{Let } n \text{ be the 200th smallest positive real solution to the equation } x-\frac{\pi}{2}=\tan(\sqrt{x}). \text{ Find the greatest integer that does not exceed } \frac{n}{2}.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AB < AC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$. A line $l$ passes through $M$ and is perpendicular to $AM$, meeting $AB$ at $X$ and $AC$ at $Y$. Show that triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $A$ if and only if the points $X, B, Y, C$ lie on a circle.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Line $l$ is drawn through $M$ so that it is parallel to $AM$, and intersects line $AB$ at point $X$ and line $AC$ at point $Y$. Prove that $\angle BAC = 90^\circ$ if and only if quadrilateral $XBYC$ is cyclic.

positive_text: Find the number of real triples $(a, b, c)$ such that the polynomial $p(x)=x^{4}+a x^{3}+b x^{2}+a x+c$ has exactly three distinct real roots $\tan y, \tan 2 y, \tan 3 y$ for some real $y$, where one of the roots is repeated.

negatives.text: How many real triples $(a, b, c)$ are there such that the polynomial $p(x)=x^{4}+a x^{3}+b x^{2}+a x+c$ has exactly three distinct roots, which are equal to $\tan y, \cot 2 y$, and $\tan 3 y$ for some real $y$?

How many real triples $(a, b, c)$ are there such that the polynomial $p(x)=x^{4}+a x^{3}+b x^{2}+a x+c$ has exactly three distinct roots, which are equal to $\tan y, \tan 2 y$, and $\tan 4 y$ for some real $y$?

How many real triples $(a, b, c)$ are there such that the polynomial $p(x)=x^{4}+a x^{3}+b x^{2}+a x+c$ has exactly three distinct roots, which are equal to $\tan y, \tan 2 y$, and $-\tan 3 y$ for some real $y$?

positive_text:
Let $n$ be a positive integer and define $N=\sum_{k=1}^{n} \varphi(k)$. Prove that there exists a cyclic sequence
$$
\{b_1, b_2, \dots, b_N\}
$$
such that for each $k$ with $1 \leq k \leq n$, the number $k$ appears exactly $\varphi(k)$ times in the sequence, and
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{1}{b_i b_{i+1}} = 1,
$$
where $b_{N+1} = b_1$.

negatives.text:
For any positive integer $n$, let $N=\varphi(1)+\varphi(2)+\ldots+\varphi(n)$. Show that there exists a sequence
$$
a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{N}
$$
containing exactly $\varphi(k)$ instances of $k$ for all positive integers $k \leq n$ such that
$$
\frac{1}{a_{1} a_{2}}+\frac{1}{a_{2} a_{3}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{a_{N} a_{1}}=\frac{1}{2} .
$$

For any positive integer $n$, let $N=\varphi(1)+\varphi(2)+\ldots+\varphi(n)$. Show that there exists a sequence
$$
a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{N}
$$
containing exactly $\varphi(k)$ instances of $k$ for all positive integers $k \leq n$ such that
$$
\frac{1}{a_{1} a_{2}}+\frac{1}{a_{2} a_{3}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{a_{N} a_{1}}=1 .
$$
Additionally, all $a_i$ must be distinct.

For any positive integer $n$, let $N=\varphi(1)+\varphi(2)+\ldots+\varphi(n)$. Show that there exists a sequence
$$
a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{N}
$$
containing exactly $\varphi(k)$ instances of $k$ for all positive integers $k \leq n$ such that
$$
\frac{1}{a_{1} + a_{2}}+\frac{1}{a_{2} + a_{3}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{a_{N} + a_{1}}=1 .
$$

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle where $AB < AC$. The altitude from $A$ meets $\overline{BC}$ at $D$, the angle bisector from $A$ meets $\overline{BC}$ at $E$, and the median from $A$ meets $\overline{BC}$ at $F$. Suppose $\measuredangle BAD = 2 \measuredangle DAE = 2 \measuredangle EAF = \measuredangle FAC$. Determine all possible measures of $\angle ACB$.

negatives.text: Given $\triangle ABC$ with $AB < AC$, the altitude $AD$, angle bisector $AE$, and median $AF$ are drawn from $A$, with $D, E, F$ all lying on $\overline{BC}$. If $\measuredangle BAD = 2 \measuredangle DAE = 2 \measuredangle EAF = 2 \measuredangle FAC$, what are all possible values of $\measuredangle ACB$?

Given $\triangle ABC$ with $AB < AC$, the altitude $AD$, angle bisector $AE$, and median $AF$ are drawn from $A$, with $D, E, F$ all lying on $\overline{BC}$. If $\measuredangle BAD = 2 \measuredangle DAE = 2 \measuredangle EAF = \measuredangle FAB$, what are all possible values of $\measuredangle ACB$?

positive_text: Let $O, P, Q, R, S$ be points such that $P, O, R$ and $Q, O, S$ are collinear in that order, $OP=1$, $OQ=2$, $OR=\sqrt{2}$, $OS=2$, and $\angle POQ=45^\circ$. Let $\omega_P, \omega_Q, \omega_R, \omega_S$ be the circles with respective centers $P, Q, R, S$ that go through $O$. Let $A$ be the intersection of $\omega_P$ and $\omega_Q$, $B$ be the intersection of $\omega_Q$ and $\omega_R$, $C$ be the intersection of $\omega_R$ and $\omega_S$, and $D$ be the intersection of $\omega_S$ and $\omega_P$, with $A, B, C, D$ all distinct from $O$. What is the largest possible area of a convex quadrilateral $P'Q'R'S'$ such that $P'$ lies on $P$, $Q'$ lies on $Q$, $R'$ lies on $R$, $S'$ lies on $S$, and $A, B, C, D$ all lie on its perimeter?

negatives.text: Let $O, O_{1}, O_{2}, O_{3}, O_{4}$ be points such that $O_{1}, O, O_{3}$ and $O_{2}, O, O_{4}$ are collinear in that order, $OO_{1}=1$, $OO_{2}=2$, $OO_{3}=\sqrt{2}$, $OO_{4}=2$, and $\angle O_{1} O O_{2}=135^\circ$. Let $\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}, \omega_{3}, \omega_{4}$ be the circles with respective centers $O_{1}, O_{2}, O_{3}, O_{4}$ that go through $O$. Let $A$ be the intersection of $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$, $B$ be the intersection of $\omega_{2}$ and $\omega_{3}$, $C$ be the intersection of $\omega_{3}$ and $\omega_{4}$, and $D$ be the intersection of $\omega_{4}$ and $\omega_{1}$, with $A, B, C, D$ all distinct from $O$. What is the largest possible area of a convex quadrilateral $P_{1} P_{2} P_{3} P_{4}$ such that $P_{i}$ lies on $O_{i}$ and that $A, B, C, D$ all lie on its perimeter?

Let $O, O_{1}, O_{2}, O_{3}, O_{4}$ be points such that $O_{1}, O, O_{3}$ and $O_{2}, O, O_{4}$ are collinear in that order, $OO_{1}=1$, $OO_{2}=2$, $OO_{3}=\sqrt{2}$, $OO_{4}=2$, and $\angle O_{1} O O_{2}=45^\circ$. Let $\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}, \omega_{3}, \omega_{4}$ be the circles with respective centers $O_{1}, O_{2}, O_{3}, O_{4}$ that go through $O$. Let $A$ be the intersection of $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$, $B$ be the intersection of $\omega_{2}$ and $\omega_{3}$, $C$ be the intersection of $\omega_{3}$ and $\omega_{4}$, and $D$ be the intersection of $\omega_{4}$ and $\omega_{1}$, with $A, B, C, D$ all distinct from $O$. What is the largest possible area of a convex quadrilateral $P_{1} P_{2} P_{3} P_{4}$ such that $P_{i}$ lies on $\omega_{i}$ and that $A, B, C, D$ all lie on its perimeter?

Let $O, O_{1}, O_{2}, O_{3}, O_{4}$ be points such that $O_{1}, O, O_{3}$ and $O_{2}, O, O_{4}$ are collinear in that order, $OO_{1}=1$, $OO_{2}=2$, $OO_{3}=\sqrt{2}$, $OO_{4}=2$, and $\angle O_{1} O O_{2}=45^\circ$. Let $\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}, \omega_{3}, \omega_{4}$ be the circles with respective centers $O_{1}, O_{2}, O_{3}, O_{4}$ that go through $O$. Let $A$ be the intersection of $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$, $B$ be the intersection of $\omega_{2}$ and $\omega_{3}$, $C$ be the intersection of $\omega_{3}$ and $\omega_{4}$, and $D$ be the intersection of $\omega_{4}$ and $\omega_{1}$, with $A, B, C, D$ all distinct from $O$. What is the largest possible area of a convex quadrilateral $P_{1} P_{2} P_{3} P_{4}$ such that $P_{i}$ lies on the segment $OO_{i}$ and that $A, B, C, D$ all lie on its perimeter?

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths $BC = 7$, $CA = 8$, and $AB = 9$. Points $D$ and $E$ are the midpoints of $BC$ and $CA$, respectively. The lines $AD$ and $BE$ intersect at $G$. Let $G'$ be the point such that $D$ is the midpoint of segment $GG'$. If $G'E$ intersects $CG$ at point $P$, compute the length $PG$.

negatives.text: Consider triangle $ABC$ where $BC = 7$, $CA = 8$, and $AB = 9$. $D$ and $E$ are the midpoints of $BC$ and $CA$, respectively, and $AD$ and $BE$ meet at $G$. The reflection of $G$ across $E$ is $G'$, and $G'D$ meets $CG$ at $P$. Find the length $PG$.

Consider triangle $ABC$ where $BC = 7$, $CA = 8$, and $AB = 9$. $D$ and $E$ are the midpoints of $BC$ and $CA$, respectively, and $AD$ and $BE$ meet at $G$. The reflection of $G$ across $D$ is $G'$, and $G'E$ meets $BG$ at $P$. Find the length $PG$.

Consider triangle $ABC$ where $BC = 7$, $CA = 8$, and $AB = 9$. $D$ and $E$ are the midpoints of $BC$ and $CA$, respectively, and $AD$ and $BE$ meet at $G$. The reflection of $G$ across $D$ is $G'$, and $G'E$ meets $CG$ at $P$. Find the length $PG'$.

positive_text: Given a segment $AB$ with a point $M$ lying on it, define two circles $\omega_{l}$ and $\omega_{r}$ such that $\omega_{l}$ passes through $A$ and $M$ with center $O_{l}$, and $\omega_{r}$ passes through $M$ and $B$ with center $O_{r}$. Assume $O_{l}$ and $O_{r}$ lie on the same side of line $AB$ and satisfy $\angle A O_{l} M = \angle M O_{r} B = 2x$. Let $\omega_{l}$ and $\omega_{r}$ intersect at $M$ and another point $N$. Extend $AN$ to meet $\omega_{r}$ again at $D$. Prove that $\angle DBA = x$, and show that the lines $NM$ all pass through a fixed point $K$ in the plane. (For example, in the case of an equilateral triangle, $x = 60^\circ$; for a square, $x = 45^\circ$.)

negatives.text: Generalization: Given a segment $AB$ and a point $M$ inside of it, construct circle $\omega_{l}$ centered at $O_{l}$ passing through $A$ and $M$ and $\omega_{r}$ centered at $O_{r}$ passing through $M$ and $B$ so that $O_{l}$ and $O_{r}$ are on opposite sides of $AB$ and $\angle A O_{l} M = \angle M O_{r} B = 2x$. Then $\omega_{l}$ and $\omega_{r}$ intersect at $M$ and another point $N$. Extend $AN$ until it intersects $\omega_{r}$ again at a point $D$. Prove that $\angle DBA = x$, and moreover, all lines $NM$ pass through the same point $K$ in the plane. (Note that for triangles we have $x = 60^\circ$, and for squares we have $x = 45^\circ$.)

Generalization: Given a segment $AB$ and a point $M$ inside of it, construct circle $\omega_{l}$ centered at $O_{l}$ passing through $A$ and $M$ and $\omega_{r}$ centered at $O_{r}$ passing through $M$ and $B$ so that $O_{l}$ and $O_{r}$ are on the same side of $AB$ and $\angle A O_{l} M = \angle M O_{r} B = x$. Then $\omega_{l}$ and $\omega_{r}$ intersect at $M$ and another point $N$. Extend $AN$ until it intersects $\omega_{r}$ again at a point $D$. Prove that $\angle DBA = x$, and moreover, all lines $NM$ pass through the same point $K$ in the plane. (Note that for triangles we have $x = 60^\circ$, and for squares we have $x = 45^\circ$.)

Generalization: Given a segment $AB$ and a point $M$ inside of it, construct circle $\omega_{l}$ centered at $O_{l}$ passing through $A$ and $M$ and $\omega_{r}$ centered at $O_{r}$ passing through $M$ and $B$ so that $O_{l}$ and $O_{r}$ are on the same side of $AB$ and $\angle A O_{l} M = 2x$ and $\angle M O_{r} B = 3x$. Then $\omega_{l}$ and $\omega_{r}$ intersect at $M$ and another point $N$. Extend $AN$ until it intersects $\omega_{r}$ again at a point $D$. Prove that $\angle DBA = x$, and moreover, all lines $NM$ pass through the same point $K$ in the plane. (Note that for triangles we have $x = 60^\circ$, and for squares we have $x = 45^\circ$.)

positive_text: Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers with $a > b$ such that $a^{2} b^{2} + a^{2} + b^{2} + 2 a b = 40$ and $a b + a + b = 8$. Find the value of $a$.

negatives.text: Let $x$ and $y$ be real numbers with $x > y$ such that $x^{2} y^{2} - x^{2} + y^{2} + 2 x y = 40$ and $x y + x + y = 8$. Find the value of $x$.
Let $x$ and $y$ be real numbers with $x > y$ such that $x^{2} y^{2} + x^{2} + y^{2} + 2 x y = 40$ and $x y + x - y = 8$. Find the value of $x$.
Let $x$ and $y$ be real numbers with $x > y$ such that $x^{2} y^{2} + x^{2} + y^{2} + 2 x y = 40$ and $x y + x + y = -8$. Find the value of $x$.

positive_text: Suppose $x$ and $y$ are real numbers with $\frac{xy}{x^{2}+y^{2}}=\frac{1}{4}$. Determine all values of $\frac{|x^{2}-y^{2}|}{x^{2}+y^{2}}$.

negatives.text: Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers such that $\frac{a b}{a^{2}+b^{2}}=\frac{1}{4}$. Find all possible values of $\frac{\left|a+b\right|}{a^{2}+b^{2}}$.
Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers such that $\frac{a b}{a^{2}+b^{2}}=\frac{1}{4}$. Find all possible values of $\frac{\left|a^{2}-b^{2}\right|}{a^{2}-b^{2}}$.
Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers such that $\frac{a b}{a^{2}+b^{2}}=\frac{1}{4}$. Find all possible values of $\frac{\left|a^{2}+b^{2}\right|}{a^{2}+b^{2}}$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ have points $P, Q, R$ on sides $BC, CA, AB$, respectively. Denote the circumcircles of triangles $AQR, BRP, CPQ$ by $\omega_A, \omega_B, \omega_C$. Suppose segment $AP$ meets $\omega_A, \omega_B, \omega_C$ again at points $X, Y, Z$, respectively. Show that the ratio $\frac{YX}{XZ}$ is equal to $\frac{BP}{PC}$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, points $P, Q, R$ lie on sides $BC, CA, AB$, respectively. Let $\omega_A, \omega_B, \omega_C$ denote the circumcircles of triangles $AQR, BRP, CPQ$, respectively. Given the fact that segment $AP$ intersects $\omega_A, \omega_B, \omega_C$ again at $X, Y, Z$ respectively, prove that $\frac{YX}{XZ} = \frac{PC}{BP}$.

In triangle $ABC$, points $P, Q, R$ lie on sides $BC, CA, AB$, respectively. Let $\omega_A, \omega_B, \omega_C$ denote the circumcircles of triangles $AQR, BRP, CPQ$, respectively. Given the fact that segment $AP$ intersects $\omega_A, \omega_B, \omega_C$ again at $X, Y, Z$ respectively, prove that $\frac{YX}{XZ} = \left(\frac{BP}{PC}\right)^2$.

In triangle $ABC$, points $P, Q, R$ lie on sides $BC, CA, AB$, respectively. Let $\omega_A, \omega_B, \omega_C$ denote the circumcircles of triangles $AQR, BRP, CPQ$, respectively. Given the fact that segment $AP$ intersects $\omega_A, \omega_B, \omega_C$ again at $X, Y, Z$ respectively, prove that $\frac{YX}{XZ} = \frac{BP + PC}{BP}$.

positive_text: Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a set of $n$ elements, and let $k$ be a positive integer. Suppose there are $kn$ pairs $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_{kn}$ where each pair is a subset of $\mathcal{S}$ of size 2, and each element in $\mathcal{S}$ appears in exactly $2k$ of these pairs. Prove that it is possible to pick one element from each pair such that every element of $\mathcal{S}$ is selected exactly $k$ times.

negatives.text: Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a set of size $n$, and $k$ be a positive integer. For each $1 \leq i \leq k n$, there is a subset $S_{i} \subset \mathcal{S}$ such that $|S_{i}|=2$. Furthermore, for each $e \in \mathcal{S}$, there are exactly $k$ values of $i$ such that $e \in S_{i}$. Show that it is possible to choose one element from $S_{i}$ for each $1 \leq i \leq k n$ such that every element of $\mathcal{S}$ is chosen exactly $k$ times.

Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a set of size $n$, and $k$ be a positive integer. For each $1 \leq i \leq k n$, there is a subset $S_{i} \subset \mathcal{S}$ such that $|S_{i}|=2$. Furthermore, for each $e \in \mathcal{S}$, there are exactly $2k + 1$ values of $i$ such that $e \in S_{i}$. Show that it is possible to choose one element from $S_{i}$ for each $1 \leq i \leq k n$ such that every element of $\mathcal{S}$ is chosen exactly $k$ times.

Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a set of size $n$, and $k$ be a positive integer. For each $1 \leq i \leq k n$, there is a subset $S_{i} \subset \mathcal{S}$ such that $|S_{i}|=2$. Furthermore, for each $e \in \mathcal{S}$, there are at least $2k$ values of $i$ such that $e \in S_{i}$. Show that it is possible to choose one element from $S_{i}$ for each $1 \leq i \leq k n$ such that every element of $\mathcal{S}$ is chosen exactly $k$ times.

positive_text:
Let $M$ be a positive integer that includes the block $11235$ in its decimal digits, and suppose $m$ is a positive integer satisfying $10^{m} > M$. Determine the smallest possible value of
$$
\frac{10^{m}-1}{\gcd\left(M, 10^{m}-1\right)}
$$

negatives.text:
Let $N$ be a positive integer whose decimal representation contains $11235$ as a contiguous substring, and let $k$ be a positive integer such that $10^{k} > N$. Find the minimum possible value of
$$
\frac{10^{k}+1}{\operatorname{gcd}\left(N, 10^{k}+1\right)}
$$

Let $N$ be a positive integer whose decimal representation contains $11235$ as a contiguous substring, and let $k$ be a positive integer such that $10^{k} > N$. Find the minimum possible value of
$$
\frac{10^{2k}-1}{\operatorname{gcd}\left(N, 10^{2k}-1\right)}
$$

Let $N$ be a positive integer whose decimal representation contains $11235$ as a contiguous substring, and let $k$ be a positive integer such that $10^{k} > N$. Find the minimum possible value of
$$
\frac{10^{k}-1}{\operatorname{gcd}\left(N^2, 10^{k}-1\right)}
$$

positive_text:
Let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/727}$. Consider the imaginary part of the product
$$
\prod_{k=8}^{13} \left(1 + \omega^{3^{k-1}} + \omega^{2 \cdot 3^{k-1}}\right)
$$
and suppose it is equal to $\sin \alpha$ for some angle $\alpha$ in the interval $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$. Determine $\alpha$.

negatives.text:
Let $\omega = \cos \frac{2\pi}{727} + i \sin \frac{2\pi}{727}$. The imaginary part of the complex number
$$
\prod_{k=8}^{13}\left(1+\omega^{3^{k-1}}-\omega^{2 \cdot 3^{k-1}}\right)
$$
is equal to $\sin \alpha$ for some angle $\alpha$ between $-\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\frac{\pi}{2}$, inclusive. Find $\alpha$.

positive_text: Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, with $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$, $AB = 3$, and $AE = 4$, where $E$ is the intersection of the angle bisector of $\angle A$ with side $BC$. Let $D$ be the second intersection of the angle bisector with $\omega$. Define $D'$ as the reflection of $A$ over $D$, and $C'$ as the reflection of $A$ over $C$. The tangent at $A$ to $\omega$ intersects $BC$ at $P$, and the circumcircle of triangle $APD'$ intersects $BC$ again at $F$. Compute the length $FC'$.
How many functions $f:\{1,2, \ldots, n\} \rightarrow \{1,2, \ldots, n\}$ satisfy $f(j) - f(i) < j - i$ for all integers $i, j$ such that $1 \leq i < j \leq n$, where $n = 2013$?

negatives.text: How many functions $f:\{1,2, \ldots, 2013\} \rightarrow \{1,2, \ldots, 2013\}$ satisfy $f(j) > f(i) + j - i$ for all integers $i, j$ such that $1 \leq i < j \leq 2013$?
How many functions $f:\{1,2, \ldots, 2013\} \rightarrow \{1,2, \ldots, 2013\}$ satisfy $f(j) < f(i) + j^2 - i$ for all integers $i, j$ such that $1 \leq i < j \leq 2013$?
How many functions $f:\{1,2, \ldots, 2013\} \rightarrow \{1,2, \ldots, 2013\}$ satisfy $|f(j) - f(i)| < j - i$ for all integers $i, j$ such that $1 \leq i < j \leq 2013$?

positive_text: Consider a triangular grid with 10 vertices arranged so that each side contains 4 points, and adjacent points are 1 unit apart. Determine the number of Hamiltonian cycles where each vertex is visited exactly once, and consecutive vertices (including the last and first) are connected by an edge of unit length.

negatives.text: David has a unit triangular array of 10 points, 4 on each side. A looping path is a sequence $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{10}$ containing each of the 10 points exactly once, such that $A_{i}$ and $A_{i+1}$ are adjacent (exactly 1 unit apart) for $i=1,2, \ldots, 9$. (Here $A_{11}=A_{1}$.) Find the number of looping paths in this array.

David has a unit triangular array of 10 points, 4 on each side. A looping path is a sequence $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{10}$ containing each of the 10 points exactly once, such that $A_{i}$ and $A_{i+1}$ are adjacent (at most 1 unit apart) for $i=1,2, \ldots, 10$. (Here $A_{11}=A_{1}$.) Find the number of looping paths in this array.

David has a unit triangular array of 10 points, 4 on each side. A looping path is a sequence $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{10}$ containing each of the 10 points at least once, such that $A_{i}$ and $A_{10}$ are adjacent (exactly 1 unit apart) for $i=1,2, \ldots, 10$. (Here $A_{11}=A_{1}$.) Find the number of looping paths in this array.

positive_text: If $62^{2} + 122^{2} = 18728$, determine positive integers $(n, m)$ satisfying $n^{2} + m^{2} = 9364$.

negatives.text: Given that $62^{2} + 122^{2} = 18728$, find positive integers $(n, m)$ such that $n^{2} + m^{2} = 18728$.
Given that $62^{2} + 122^{2} = 18728$, find positive integers $(n, m)$ such that $n^{2} - m^{2} = 9364$.
Given that $62^{2} + 122^{2} = 18728$, find positive integers $(n, m)$ such that $n^{2} + m^{2} = -9364$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, it is given that $\angle A = 2 \angle B$. The internal angle bisector of $\angle A$ and the internal angle bisector of $\angle C$ meet at point $D$, and the angle bisector from $C$ meets side $\overline{AB}$ at point $E$. If $\frac{DE}{DC} = \frac{1}{3}$, find the value of $\frac{AB}{AC}$.

negatives.text: Consider triangle $ABC$ with $\angle A = 2 \angle C$. The angle bisectors from $A$ and $C$ intersect at $D$, and the angle bisector from $C$ intersects $\overline{AB}$ at $E$. If $\frac{DE}{DC} = \frac{1}{3}$, compute $\frac{AB}{AC}$.

Consider triangle $ABC$ with $\angle A = 2 \angle B$. The angle bisectors from $A$ and $C$ intersect at $D$, and the angle bisector from $C$ intersects $\overline{AB}$ at $E$. If $\frac{DE}{DC} = \frac{3}{1}$, compute $\frac{AB}{AC}$.

Consider triangle $ABC$ with $\angle A = 2 \angle B$. The angle bisectors from $A$ and $B$ intersect at $D$, and the angle bisector from $C$ intersects $\overline{AB}$ at $E$. If $\frac{DE}{DC} = \frac{1}{3}$, compute $\frac{AB}{AC}$.

positive_text: Determine all positive integer solutions $(a, b, c)$ to the system of equations $a^{2} + b - c = 100$ and $a + b^{2} - c = 124$.

negatives.text: Find all triples of positive integers $(x, y, z)$ such that $x^{2} + y + z = 100$ and $x + y^{2} - z = 124$.
Find all triples of positive integers $(x, y, z)$ such that $x^{2} + y - z = 100$ and $x + y^{2} + z = 124$.
Find all triples of positive integers $(x, y, z)$ such that $x^{2} + y - z = 100$ and $x + y^{3} - z = 124$.

positive_text: Determine all real values of $x$ in the interval $[0, 360]$ satisfying $$\sin x^\circ = \sqrt{3} \cos 10^\circ - \cos 40^\circ.$$

negatives.text: Find all real numbers $x$ between $0$ and $360$ such that $$\sqrt{3} \cos 10^\circ = \cos 40^\circ - \sin x^\circ.$$
Find all real numbers $x$ between $0$ and $360$ such that $$\sqrt{3} \cos 10^\circ = \cos 40^\circ + \cos x^\circ.$$
Find all real numbers $x$ between $0$ and $360$ such that $$\sqrt{3} \cos 10^\circ = \cos 40^\circ + \sin^2 x^\circ.$$

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be such that $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$, $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$, and $AB = 6$. If a ball is rolled from the midpoint of $BC$ toward $AB$, bounces off $AB$, then off $AC$, and returns to the starting point, determine the total distance traveled by the ball.

negatives.text: The walls of a room are in the shape of a triangle $ABC$ with $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$, $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$, and $AB = 6$. Chong stands at the midpoint of $BC$ and rolls a ball toward $AB$. Suppose that the ball bounces off $AB$, then $BC$, then returns exactly to Chong. Find the length of the path of the ball.

The walls of a room are in the shape of a triangle $ABC$ with $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$, $\angle BAC = 30^\circ$, and $AB = 6$. Chong stands at the midpoint of $BC$ and rolls a ball toward $AB$. Suppose that the ball bounces off $AB$, then $AC$, then returns exactly to Chong. Find the length of the path of the ball.

positive_text: Suppose the three medians of a triangle with perimeter $1$ are given by the lines $y = x$, $y = 2x$, and $y = 3x$. Determine the length of the triangle's longest side.

negatives.text: The lines $y = x$, $y = 2x$, and $y = -3x$ are the three medians of a triangle with perimeter $1$. Find the length of the longest side of the triangle.
The lines $y = x$, $y = 2x$, and $y = 3x^2$ are the three medians of a triangle with perimeter $1$. Find the length of the longest side of the triangle.
The lines $y = x$, $y = 2x$, and $y = 3x$ are the three medians of a triangle with area $1$. Find the length of the longest side of the triangle.

positive_text: Consider a sequence $\{b_n\}$ of positive integers defined by $b_1 = 1$, $b_2 = 3$, and for $n > 2$, $b_n$ is the base-$n$ interpretation of the base-$(n-1)$ representation of $b_{n-1}$, plus the value $2$ (interpreted in base $n$). For instance, since $b_2 = 3_{10} = 11_2$, then $b_3 = 11_3 + 2_3 = 6_{10}$. Determine the value of $b_{2013}$ in base ten.

negatives.text: Define the sequence of positive integers $\{a_n\}$ as follows. Let $a_1=1$, $a_2=3$, and for each $n>2$, let $a_n$ be the result of expressing $a_{n-1}$ in base $n-1$, then reading the resulting numeral in base $n$, then subtracting $2$ (in base $n$). For example, $a_2=3_{10}=11_2$, so $a_3=11_3-2_3=2_{10}$. Express $a_{2013}$ in base ten.

Define the sequence of positive integers $\{a_n\}$ as follows. Let $a_1=1$, $a_2=3$, and for each $n>2$, let $a_n$ be the result of expressing $a_{n-1}$ in base $n-1$, then squaring the resulting numeral (interpreted in base $n$), then adding $2$ (in base $n$). For example, $a_2=3_{10}=11_2$, so $a_3=(11_3)^2 + 2_3=121_3 + 2_3=123_3=42_{10}$. Express $a_{2013}$ in base ten.

Define the sequence of positive integers $\{a_n\}$ as follows. Let $a_1=1$, $a_2=3$, and for each $n>2$, let $a_n$ be the result of expressing $a_{n-1}$ in base $n-1$, then reading the resulting numeral in base $n$, then adding $2$ (in base $n$), but if $a_n > 100$, then $a_n = 1$. For example, $a_2=3_{10}=11_2$, so $a_3=11_3+2_3=6_{10}$. Express $a_{2013}$ in base ten.

positive_text: In an isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AB = 13$ and $CD = 17$, and height $3$, let $E$ be the point where the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect. Let $\Omega$ and $\omega$ be the circumcircles of triangles $ABE$ and $CDE$, respectively. Determine the total of the radii of $\Omega$ and $\omega$.

negatives.text: \text{An isosceles trapezoid } ABCD \text{ with bases } AB \text{ and } CD \text{ has } AB = 13, CD = 17, \text{ and height } -3. \text{ Let } E \text{ be the intersection of } AC \text{ and } BD. \text{ Circles } \Omega \text{ and } \omega \text{ are circumscribed about triangles } ABE \text{ and } CDE. \text{ Compute the sum of the radii of } \Omega \text{ and } \omega.

\text{An isosceles trapezoid } ABCD \text{ with bases } AB \text{ and } CD \text{ has } AB = 13, CD = 17, \text{ and height } 3. \text{ Let } E \text{ be the intersection of } AC \text{ and } BD. \text{ Circles } \Omega \text{ and } \omega \text{ are inscribed in triangles } ABE \text{ and } CDE. \text{ Compute the sum of the radii of } \Omega \text{ and } \omega.

\text{An isosceles trapezoid } ABCD \text{ with bases } AB \text{ and } CD \text{ has } AB = 13, CD = 17, \text{ and height } 3. \text{ Let } E \text{ be the intersection of } AC \text{ and } BD. \text{ Circles } \Omega \text{ and } \omega \text{ are circumscribed about triangles } ADE \text{ and } BCE. \text{ Compute the sum of the radii of } \Omega \text{ and } \omega.

positive_text: In quadrilateral $ABCD$ with equal diagonals $AC = BD$, the diagonals intersect at point $P$. Let $\omega_1$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABP$ with center $O_1$, and $\omega_2$ be the circumcircle of triangle $CDP$ with center $O_2$. Let segment $BC$ intersect $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ again at $S$ and $T$, respectively (distinct from $B$ and $C$). Define $M$ and $N$ as the centers of arcs $\widehat{SP}$ and $\widehat{TP}$ on $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ not containing $B$ and $C$, respectively. Prove that the line $MN$ is parallel to the segment $O_1O_2$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AC = BD$. Diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $P$. Let $\omega_1$ and $O_1$ denote the circumcircle and circumcenter of triangle $ABP$. Let $\omega_2$ and $O_2$ denote the circumcircle and circumcenter of triangle $CDP$. Segment $BC$ meets $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ again at $S$ and $T$ (other than $B$ and $C$), respectively. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of minor arcs $\widehat{BP}$ (not including $S$) and $\widehat{CP}$ (not including $T$). Prove that $MN \parallel O_1O_2$.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AC = 2BD$. Diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $P$. Let $\omega_1$ and $O_1$ denote the circumcircle and circumcenter of triangle $ABP$. Let $\omega_2$ and $O_2$ denote the circumcircle and circumcenter of triangle $CDP$. Segment $BC$ meets $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ again at $S$ and $T$ (other than $B$ and $C$), respectively. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of minor arcs $\widehat{SP}$ (not including $B$) and $\widehat{TP}$ (not including $C$). Prove that $MN \parallel O_1O_2$.

positive_text: Is there a pair of functions $ g, h : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that any function $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ commuting with both $ g $ and $ h $, i.e., satisfying $ f \circ g = g \circ f $ and $ f \circ h = h \circ f $, must be the identity function $ f(x) = x $?

negatives.text: Does there exist a pair $ (g, h) $ of functions $ g, h : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that the only function $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfying $ f(g(x)) = g(f(x)) $ and $ f(h(x)) = -h(f(x)) $ for all $ x \in \mathbb{R} $ is the identity function $ f(x) = x $?

Does there exist a pair $ (g, h) $ of functions $ g, h : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that the only function $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfying $ f(g(x)) = g(f(x)) $ and $ f(h(x)) = h(f(x)) $ for all $ x \in \mathbb{R} $ is the identity function $ f(x) = x $, and additionally $ f $ is continuous?

Does there exist a pair $ (g, h) $ of functions $ g, h : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that the only function $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfying $ f(g(x)) = g(f(x)) $ and $ f(h(x)) = h(f(x)) $ for all $ x \in \mathbb{R} $ is the identity function $ f(x) = x $, and additionally $ g $ is constant?

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be an isosceles trapezoid with $AB = 3$, $CD = 8$, and $AD = BC$. Suppose $E$ is a point satisfying $EC = BC$ and $\angle AEC = 90^\circ$. Find the length of $AE$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be an isosceles trapezoid such that $AD = BC$, $AB = 3$, and $CD = 8$. Let $E$ be a point in the plane such that $BC = EC$ and $AE \perp EB$. Compute $AE$.
Let $ABCD$ be an isosceles trapezoid such that $AD = BC$, $AB = 3$, and $CD = 8$. Let $E$ be a point in the plane such that $BC = 2EC$ and $AE \perp EC$. Compute $AE$.

positive_text: Let $E(n)$ denote the expected number of rolls Gary makes when starting with a fair $n$-sided die, labeled with the integers from $1$ to $n$. If $n = 1$, $E(1) = 0$; otherwise, he rolls the die, and the process restarts with a $k$-sided die, where $k$ is the outcome of the roll. What is $E(6)$?

negatives.text: Gary plays the following game with a fair $n$-sided die whose faces are labeled with the positive integers between $1$ and $n$, inclusive: if $n=1$, he stops; otherwise he rolls the die, and starts over with a $k$-sided die, where $k$ is the number his $n$-sided die lands on. (In particular, if he gets $k=1$, he will stop rolling the die.) If he starts out with a $6$-sided die, what is the expected number of times the die lands on 1?

Gary plays the following game with a fair $n$-sided die whose faces are labeled with the positive integers between $1$ and $n$, inclusive: if $n=1$, he stops; otherwise he rolls the die, and starts over with a $k$-sided die, where $k$ is the number his $n$-sided die lands on. (In particular, if he gets $k=1$, he will stop rolling the die.) If he starts out with a $6$-sided die, what is the expected number of rolls he makes until he rolls a number less than or equal to 3?

Gary plays the following game with a fair $n$-sided die whose faces are labeled with the positive integers between $1$ and $n$, inclusive: if $n=1$, he stops; otherwise he rolls the die, and starts over with a $k$-sided die, where $k$ is the number his $n$-sided die lands on. (In particular, if he gets $k=1$, he will stop rolling the die.) If he starts out with a $6$-sided die, what is the expected number of rolls he makes until he rolls the same number twice consecutively?

positive_text:
Determine all real-valued functions $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$ satisfying
$$
(f(x)-f(y))(x-y) = f(x - f(y)) f(f(x) - y)
$$
for every $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that, for all real numbers $x, y$,
$$
(x-y)(f(x)+f(y))=f(x-f(y)) f(f(x)-y)
$$

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that, for all real numbers $x, y$,
$$
(x-y)(f(x)-f(y))=f(x-f(y)) + f(f(x)-y)
$$

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that, for all real numbers $x, y$,
$$
(x-y)(f(x)-f(y))=f(x+f(y)) f(f(x)-y)
$$

positive_text: A snail crawls away from a fixed point at $1~\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{s}$. You begin a sequence of actions when the snail is $1$ meter from the fixed point. In the $n$-th action (where $n \geq 1$), you travel toward the snail at speed $(n+1)~\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{s}$ until you meet it, then travel back to the fixed point at the same speed. After each round, the next round begins. Determine the snail's distance from the fixed point at the start of the $100$-th action.

negatives.text: You are standing at a pole and a snail is moving directly away from the pole at $1~\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{s}$. When the snail is $1$ meter away, you start "Round 1". In Round $n$ ($n \geq 1$), you move directly toward the snail at $(n+1)~\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{s}$. When you reach the snail, you immediately turn around and move back to the starting pole at $(n+1)^2~\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{s}$. When you reach the pole, you immediately turn around and Round $n+1$ begins. At the start of Round $100$, how many meters away is the snail?

You are standing at a pole and a snail is moving directly away from the pole at $1~\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{s}$. When the snail is $1$ meter away, you start "Round 1". In Round $n$ ($n \geq 1$), you move directly toward the snail at $(n+1)~\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{s}$. When you reach the snail, you immediately turn around and move back to the starting pole at $(n+1)~\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{s}$. When you reach the pole, you immediately turn around and Round $n+1$ begins. However, the snail now moves at $2~\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{s}$ during each round. At the start of Round $100$, how many meters away is the snail?

You are standing at a pole and a snail is moving directly away from the pole at $1~\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{s}$. When the snail is $1$ meter away, you start "Round 1". In Round $n$ ($n \geq 1$), you move directly toward the snail at $(n+1)~\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{s}$. When you reach the snail, you immediately turn around and move back to the starting pole at $(n+1)~\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{s}$. When you reach the pole, you immediately turn around and Round $n+1$ begins. However, the snail now moves away from the pole at $1~\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{s}$ during the chase and $0~\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{s}$ during the return to the pole. At the start of Round $100$, how many meters away is the snail?

positive_text: Suppose $x = 1001a + 110b$ where $a, b$ are unique nonnegative integers from $0$ to $9$, and $x^2 = 57,108,249$. Compute $10a + b$.

negatives.text:
There exist unique nonnegative integers $A, B$ between $0$ and $9$, inclusive, such that
$$
(1001 \cdot A + 110 \cdot B)^3 = 57,108,249
$$
Find $10 \cdot A + B$.

There exist unique nonnegative integers $A, B$ between $0$ and $9$, inclusive, such that
$$
(1001 \cdot A - 110 \cdot B)^2 = 57,108,249
$$
Find $10 \cdot A + B$.

There exist unique nonnegative integers $A, B$ between $0$ and $9$, inclusive, such that
$$
(1001 \cdot A + 110 \cdot B)^2 = 57,108,250
$$
Find $10 \cdot A + B$.

positive_text:
Determine the count of positive integers $ j \leq 3^{2013} $ that can be expressed as
$$
j=\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}(-1)^{i-1} \cdot 3^{b_i}
$$
for some sequence $ b_1 < b_2 < \cdots < b_{n+1} $ of nonnegative integers. For example, $ 3 = 3^1 $, and $ 55 = 3^0 - 3^3 + 3^4 $, but 4 cannot be expressed in this way.

negatives.text:
Find the number of positive integers $ j \leq 3^{2013} $ such that
$$
j=\sum_{k=0}^{m}\left((-1)^{k} \cdot 2^{a_{k}}\right)
$$
for some strictly increasing sequence of nonnegative integers $ \{a_{k}\} $.

Find the number of positive integers $ j \leq 3^{2013} $ such that
$$
j=\sum_{k=0}^{m}\left(3^{a_{k}}\right)
$$
for some strictly increasing sequence of nonnegative integers $ \{a_{k}\} $.

Find the number of positive integers $ j \leq 3^{2013} $ such that
$$
j=\sum_{k=0}^{m}\left((-1)^{k} \cdot 3^{a_{k}}\right)
$$
for some non-decreasing sequence of nonnegative integers $ \{a_{k}\} $.

positive_text: Let $r > 0$ be a real number. Four circles of radius $r$ are placed with centers at $(0, r)$, $(r, 0)$, $(0, -r)$, and $(-r, 0)$. A larger circle $O$ is centered at the origin with radius $2r$. Determine the difference between the area of the union of the four smaller circles and the area of the region inside circle $O$ but outside the union of the smaller circles, expressed in terms of $r$.

negatives.text: Suppose $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ are four circles of radius $r>0$ centered about the points $(0, r)$, $(r, 0)$, $(0,-r)$, and $(-r, 0)$ in the plane. Let $O$ be a circle centered at $(0,0)$ with radius $r$. In terms of $r$, what is the area of the union of circles $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ subtracted by the area of circle $O$ that is not contained in the union of $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$?

Suppose $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ are four circles of radius $r>0$ centered about the points $(0, r)$, $(r, 0)$, $(0,-r)$, and $(-r, 0)$ in the plane. Let $O$ be a circle centered at $(0,0)$ with radius $2 r$. In terms of $r$, what is the area of the union of circles $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ subtracted by the area of circle $O$ that is contained in the union of $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$?

Suppose $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ are four circles of radius $r>0$ centered about the points $(0, r)$, $(r, 0)$, $(0,-r)$, and $(-r, 0)$ in the plane. Let $O$ be a circle centered at $(0,0)$ with radius $2 r$. In terms of $r$, what is the area of the intersection of circles $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ subtracted by the area of circle $O$ that is not contained in the intersection of $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$?

positive_text: Let $S$ be a subset of $\{1,2,3, \ldots, 12\}$ for which no partition of $S$ into two or more non-empty, disjoint subsets results in all subsets having equal total sum. Determine the largest possible sum of the elements in $S$.

negatives.text: Let $S$ be a subset of $\{1,2,3, \ldots, 12\}$ such that it is impossible to partition $S$ into $k$ disjoint subsets, each of whose elements sum to the same value, for any integer $k \geq 2$. Find the minimum possible sum of the elements of $S$.

Let $S$ be a subset of $\{1,2,3, \ldots, 12\}$ such that it is impossible to partition $S$ into $k$ disjoint subsets, each of whose elements sum to the same value, for any integer $k \geq 1$. Find the maximum possible sum of the elements of $S$.

Let $S$ be a subset of $\{1,2,3, \ldots, 12\}$ such that it is impossible to partition $S$ into $k$ disjoint subsets, each of whose elements product to the same value, for any integer $k \geq 2$. Find the maximum possible sum of the elements of $S$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram with side lengths $AB = 8$ and $AD = 11$, and angle $\angle BAD = 60^\circ$. A point $X$ lies on $CD$ such that $CX : XD = 1 : 3$, and a point $Y$ lies on $AD$ such that $AY : YD = 1 : 2$. Let $Z$ be on $AB$ such that the lines $AX$, $BY$, and $DZ$ intersect at a common point. Find the area of triangle $XYZ$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram with $AB = 8$, $AD = 11$, and $\angle BAD = 120^\circ$. Let $X$ be on segment $CD$ with $CX / XD = 1 / 3$ and $Y$ be on segment $AD$ with $AY / YD = 1 / 2$. Let $Z$ be on segment $AB$ such that $AX$, $BY$, and $DZ$ are concurrent. Determine the area of triangle $XYZ$.

Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram with $AB = 8$, $AD = 11$, and $\angle BAD = 60^\circ$. Let $X$ be on segment $CD$ with $CX / XD = 1 / 3$ and $Y$ be on segment $AD$ with $AY / YD = 2 / 1$. Let $Z$ be on segment $AB$ such that $AX$, $BY$, and $DZ$ are concurrent. Determine the area of triangle $XYZ$.

Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram with $AB = 8$, $AD = 11$, and $\angle BAD = 60^\circ$. Let $X$ be on segment $CD$ with $CX / XD = 3 / 1$ and $Y$ be on segment $AD$ with $AY / YD = 1 / 2$. Let $Z$ be on segment $AB$ such that $AX$, $BY$, and $DZ$ are concurrent. Determine the area of triangle $XYZ$.

positive_text: Let $A$, $B$, and $C$ be points in the plane such that $AB = 6$, $BC = 8$, $AC = 10$. Define a function $d(p, l)$ as the perpendicular distance from a point $p$ to a line segment $l$. Find the area of the set of all $(x, y)$ in the plane for which there exists a point $P$ inside triangle $ABC$ such that $d(P, AB) + x = d(P, BC) + y = d(P, AC)$.

negatives.text: Given a point $p$ and a line segment $l$, let $d(p, l)$ be the distance between them. Let $A$, $B$, and $C$ be points in the plane such that $AB = 6$, $BC = 8$, $AC = 10$. What is the area of the region in the $(x, y)$-plane formed by the ordered pairs $(x, y)$ such that there exists a point $P$ inside triangle $ABC$ with $d(P, AB) - x = d(P, BC) - y = d(P, AC)$?

Given a point $p$ and a line segment $l$, let $d(p, l)$ be the distance between them. Let $A$, $B$, and $C$ be points in the plane such that $AB = 6$, $BC = 8$, $AC = 10$. What is the area of the region in the $(x, y)$-plane formed by the ordered pairs $(x, y)$ such that there exists a point $P$ inside triangle $ABC$ with $d(P, AB)^2 + x = d(P, BC)^2 + y = d(P, AC)^2$?

Given a point $p$ and a line segment $l$, let $d(p, l)$ be the distance between them. Let $A$, $B$, and $C$ be points in the plane such that $AB = 6$, $BC = 8$, $AC = 10$. What is the area of the region in the $(x, y)$-plane formed by the ordered pairs $(x, y)$ such that there exists a point $P$ inside triangle $ABC$ with $d(P, AB) + x = d(P, BC) + y = 2d(P, AC)$?

positive_text:
Let $\left(w_{n}\right)$ be a sequence of complex numbers with the following properties:
- $w_{1}$ and $w_{2}$ are not real numbers.
- $w_{n+2}=w_{n+1}^{2} w_{n}$ for all integers $n \geq 1$.
- The quantity $\frac{w_{n+3}}{w_{n}^{2}}$ is real for all $n \geq 1$.
- It holds that $\left|\frac{w_{3}}{w_{4}}\right|=\left|\frac{w_{4}}{w_{5}}\right|=2$.
Determine the product of all possible values of $w_{1}$.

negatives.text:
The sequence $\left(z_{n}\right)$ of complex numbers satisfies the following properties:
- $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ are not real.
- $z_{n+2}=z_{n+1}^{2} + z_{n}$ for all integers $n \geq 1$.
- $\frac{z_{n+3}}{z_{n}^{2}}$ is real for all integers $n \geq 1$.
- $\left|\frac{z_{3}}{z_{4}}\right|=\left|\frac{z_{4}}{z_{5}}\right|=2$.
Find the product of all possible values of $z_{1}$.

The sequence $\left(z_{n}\right)$ of complex numbers satisfies the following properties:
- $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ are not real.
- $z_{n+2}=z_{n+1}^{2} z_{n}$ for all integers $n \geq 1$.
- $\frac{z_{n+3}}{z_{n}^{2}}$ is imaginary for all integers $n \geq 1$.
- $\left|\frac{z_{3}}{z_{4}}\right|=\left|\frac{z_{4}}{z_{5}}\right|=2$.
Find the product of all possible values of $z_{1}$.

The sequence $\left(z_{n}\right)$ of complex numbers satisfies the following properties:
- $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ are not real.
- $z_{n+2}=z_{n+1}^{2} z_{n}$ for all integers $n \geq 1$.
- $\frac{z_{n+3}}{z_{n}^{2}}$ is real for all integers $n \geq 1$.
- $\left|\frac{z_{3}}{z_{4}}\right|=\left|\frac{z_{4}}{z_{5}}\right|=\frac{1}{2}$.
Find the product of all possible values of $z_{1}$.

positive_text: A trapezoid $ABCD$ lies on the graph of $y = x^2$ with $A = (a, a^{2})$, $B = (b, b^{2})$, $C = (-b, b^{2})$, and $D = (-a, a^{2})$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive real numbers satisfying $a > b$. Given that $AB = \frac{3}{4}$ and the sum of the lengths $AD + BC$ equals $AB + CD$, find the value of $a$.

negatives.text: Trapezoid $ABCD$ is inscribed in the parabola $y = x^{2}$ such that $A = (a, a^{2})$, $B = (b, b^{2})$, $C = (-b, b^{2})$, and $D = (-a, a^{2})$ for some positive reals $a, b$ with $a > b$. If $AD + BC = AB - CD$, and $AB = \frac{3}{4}$, what is $a$?

Trapezoid $ABCD$ is inscribed in the parabola $y = x^{2}$ such that $A = (a, a^{2})$, $B = (b, b^{2})$, $C = (-b, b^{2})$, and $D = (-a, a^{2})$ for some positive reals $a, b$ with $a < b$. If $AD + BC = AB + CD$, and $AB = \frac{3}{4}$, what is $a$?

positive_text: Determine all real number triples $(x, y, z)$ satisfying the equations $x^{2} + 2 y^{2} - 2 y z = 16$ and $2 x y - z^{2} = 16$.

negatives.text: Find all triples of real numbers $(a, b, c)$ such that $a^{2}+2 b^{2}-2 b c=16$ and $2 a b+c^{2}=16$.
Find all triples of real numbers $(a, b, c)$ such that $a^{2}+2 b^{2}-2 b c=16$ and $2 a b-c^{2}=-16$.
Find all triples of real numbers $(a, b, c)$ such that $a^{2}+2 b^{2}-2 b c=16$ and $2 a b-c^{2}=16$ for all $b > 0$.

positive_text: Let $C$ be the 4-dimensional unit hypercube defined by $\{ (x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4}) \mid 0 \leq x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4} \leq 1 \}$. If a 3-dimensional section of $C$ is obtained by intersecting it with a hyperplane of the form $x_{1} + x_{2} + x_{3} + x_{4} = c$ for some $c \in \mathbb{R}$, what is the largest possible number of faces of this resulting polyhedron?

negatives.text: Let $W$ be the hypercube $\{ (x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4}) \mid 0 \leq x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4} \leq 1 \}$. The intersection of $W$ and a hyperplane parallel to $x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}-x_{4}=0$ is a non-degenerate 3-dimensional polyhedron. What is the maximum number of faces of this polyhedron?

Let $W$ be the hypercube $\{ (x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4}) \mid 0 \leq x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4} \leq 1 \}$. The intersection of $W$ and a hyperplane parallel to $x_{1}^2+x_{2}+x_{3}+x_{4}=0$ is a non-degenerate 3-dimensional polyhedron. What is the maximum number of faces of this polyhedron?

positive_text: Let $\triangle X Y Z$ be a right triangle with $\angle X Y Z=90^{\circ}$. An infinite sequence of equilateral triangles $X_{0} Y_{0} T_{0}, X_{1} Y_{1} T_{1}, \ldots$ is constructed such that $X_{0}=X$, $Y_{0}=Y$, each $X_{i}$ lies on segment $X Z$, each $Y_{i}$ lies on segment $Y Z$, each segment $X_{i} Y_{i}$ is perpendicular to $Y Z$, and $T_{i}$ lies on the side of $X Z$ opposite to $Y$. Furthermore, for each $i \geq 1$, $X_{i}$ lies on segment $Y_{i-1} T_{i-1}$. Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the union of all such equilateral triangles. If the area of $\mathcal{P}$ equals the area of $\triangle X Y Z$, determine $\frac{X Y}{Y Z}$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle X Y Z$ be a right triangle with $\angle X Y Z=90^{\circ}$. Suppose there exists an infinite sequence of equilateral triangles $X_{0} Y_{0} T_{0}, X_{1} Y_{1} T_{1}, \ldots$ such that $X_{0}=X$, $Y_{0}=Y$, $X_{i}$ lies on the segment $X Z$ for all $i \geq 0$, $Y_{i}$ lies on the segment $Y Z$ for all $i \geq 0$, $X_{i} Y_{i}$ is parallel to $Y Z$ for all $i \geq 0$, $T_{i}$ and $Y$ are separated by line $X Z$ for all $i \geq 0$, and $X_{i}$ lies on segment $Y_{i-1} T_{i-1}$ for $i \geq 1$. Let $\mathcal{P}$ denote the union of the equilateral triangles. If the area of $\mathcal{P}$ is equal to the area of $X Y Z$, find $\frac{X Y}{Y Z}$.

Let $\triangle X Y Z$ be a right triangle with $\angle X Y Z=90^{\circ}$. Suppose there exists an infinite sequence of isosceles triangles $X_{0} Y_{0} T_{0}, X_{1} Y_{1} T_{1}, \ldots$ such that $X_{0}=X$, $Y_{0}=Y$, $X_{i}$ lies on the segment $X Z$ for all $i \geq 0$, $Y_{i}$ lies on the segment $Y Z$ for all $i \geq 0$, $X_{i} Y_{i}$ is perpendicular to $Y Z$ for all $i \geq 0$, $T_{i}$ and $Y$ are separated by line $X Z$ for all $i \geq 0$, and $X_{i}$ lies on segment $Y_{i-1} T_{i-1}$ for $i \geq 1$. Let $\mathcal{P}$ denote the union of the isosceles triangles. If the area of $\mathcal{P}$ is equal to the area of $X Y Z$, find $\frac{X Y}{Y Z}$.

Let $\triangle X Y Z$ be a right triangle with $\angle X Y Z=90^{\circ}$. Suppose there exists an infinite sequence of equilateral triangles $X_{0} Y_{0} T_{0}, X_{1} Y_{1} T_{1}, \ldots$ such that $X_{0}=X$, $Y_{0}=Y$, $X_{i}$ lies on the segment $X Z$ for all $i \geq 0$, $Y_{i}$ lies on the segment $Y Z$ for all $i \geq 0$, $X_{i} Y_{i}$ is perpendicular to $Y Z$ for all $i \geq 0$, $T_{i}$ and $Y$ are separated by line $X Z$ for all $i \geq 0$, and $X_{i}$ lies on segment $Y_{i-1} T_{i-1}$ for $i \geq 1$. Let $\mathcal{P}$ denote the union of the equilateral triangles. If the area of $\mathcal{P}$ is equal to twice the area of $X Y Z$, find $\frac{X Y}{Y Z}$.

positive_text: Suppose there are $m$ sets $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{m}$, each of cardinality $2012$, and $m$ sets $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{m}$, each of size $2013$, such that $A_{i}$ and $B_{j}$ are disjoint if and only if $i = j$. Determine the largest possible value of $m$.

negatives.text: Let $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{m}$ be finite sets of size $2012$ and let $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{m}$ be finite sets of size $2013$ such that $A_{i} \cap B_{j} \neq \emptyset$ if and only if $i = j$. Find the maximum value of $m$.

Let $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{m}$ be finite sets of size $2012$ and let $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{m}$ be finite sets of size $2013$ such that $|A_{i} \cap B_{j}| = 1$ if and only if $i = j$. Find the maximum value of $m$.

positive_text: Let $P_{1} P_{2} P_{3} P_{4} P_{5} P_{6}$ be a convex hexagon such that $P_{i} P_{i+2} \parallel P_{i+3} P_{i+5}$ for $i=1,2,3$ (where $P_{i+6}=P_{i}$ for each $i$). The segments $P_{i} P_{i+2}$ and $P_{i+1} P_{i+3}$ intersect at point $Q_{i}$ for $1 \leq i \leq 6$. Suppose $\triangle P_{1} P_{3} P_{5} \cong \triangle P_{4} P_{6} P_{2}$. If $[P_{1} Q_{5} Q_{6}]=1$, $[P_{2} Q_{6} Q_{1}]=4$, and $[P_{3} Q_{1} Q_{2}]=9$, find the area of hexagon $Q_{1} Q_{2} Q_{3} Q_{4} Q_{5} Q_{6}$.

negatives.text: Let $A_{1} A_{2} A_{3} A_{4} A_{5} A_{6}$ be a convex hexagon such that $A_{i} A_{i+2} \parallel A_{i+3} A_{i+5}$ for $i=1,2,3$ (we take $A_{i+6}=A_{i}$ for each $i$). Segment $A_{i} A_{i+2}$ intersects segment $A_{i+1} A_{i+3}$ at $B_{i}$, for $1 \leq i \leq 6$, as shown. Furthermore, suppose that $\triangle A_{1} A_{3} A_{5} \sim \triangle A_{4} A_{6} A_{2}$. Given that $[A_{1} B_{5} B_{6}]=1$, $[A_{2} B_{6} B_{1}]=4$, and $[A_{3} B_{1} B_{2}]=9$ (by $[X Y Z]$ we mean the area of $\triangle X Y Z$), determine the area of hexagon $B_{1} B_{2} B_{3} B_{4} B_{5} B_{6}$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, where $\angle BCA = 90^\circ$, let $D$ denote the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$. Choose a point $X$ inside segment $CD$. Let $K$ be a point on segment $AX$ such that $BK = BC$, and let $L$ be a point on segment $BX$ such that $AL = AC$. Suppose the circumcircle of triangle $DKL$ intersects $AB$ again at a point $T$. Show that $\angle ACT = \angle BCT$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcenter $O$ and $AC = 7$. If the circle passing through $A$, $O$, and $C$ is tangent to side $BC$ at point $C$, and intersects $AB$ again at a point $F$, determine the length $BE$, where $E$ is the intersection of line $FO$ with $BC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcenter $O$ such that $AC = 7$. Suppose that the circumcircle of $AOC$ is tangent to $BC$ at $C$ and intersects the line $AB$ at $A$ and $F$. Let $FO$ intersect $AB$ at $E$. Compute $BE$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcenter $O$ such that $AC = 7$. Suppose that the circumcircle of $AOC$ is tangent to $BC$ at $C$ and intersects the line $AB$ at $A$ and $F$. Let $EO$ intersect $BC$ at $E$. Compute $BE$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcenter $O$ such that $AC = 7$. Suppose that the circumcircle of $AOC$ is tangent to $BC$ at $C$ and intersects the line $AB$ at $A$ and $F$. Let $FO$ intersect the extension of $BC$ beyond $C$ at $E$. Compute $BE$.

positive_text: Six distinct digits $1,2,3,4,5,6$ are randomly partitioned into two sets of three digits each, used to construct two three-digit numbers $M=\overline{A B C}$ and $N=\overline{D E F}$. Determine the expected value of the product $M \cdot N$.

negatives.text: The digits $1,2,3,4,5,6$ are randomly chosen (without replacement) to form the three-digit numbers $M=\overline{A B C}$ and $N=\overline{D E F}$. For example, we could have $M=413$ and $N=256$. Find the expected value of $M + N$.

The digits $1,2,3,4,5,6$ are randomly chosen (without replacement) to form the three-digit numbers $M=\overline{A B C}$ and $N=\overline{D E F}$. For example, we could have $M=413$ and $N=256$. Find the expected value of $M - N$.

positive_text: In a 24-hour clock format, how many distinct times $h: m: s$ exist such that the sum of the hour $h$ and the minute $m$ is equal to the second $s$, where $h \in \{0,1,\dots,23\}$, $m \in \{0,1,\dots,59\}$, and $s \in \{0,1,\dots,59\}$?

negatives.text: A 24-hour digital clock shows times $h: m: s$, where $h, m$, and $s$ are integers with $0 \leq h \leq 23$, $0 \leq m \leq 59$, and $0 \leq s \leq 59$. How many times $h: m: s$ satisfy $h + m = -s$?
A 24-hour digital clock shows times $h: m: s$, where $h, m$, and $s$ are integers with $0 \leq h \leq 23$, $0 \leq m \leq 59$, and $0 \leq s \leq 59$. How many times $h: m: s$ satisfy $h + m^2 = s$?
A 24-hour digital clock shows times $h: m: s$, where $h, m$, and $s$ are integers with $0 \leq h \leq 23$, $0 \leq m \leq 59$, and $0 \leq s \leq 59$. How many times $h: m: s$ satisfy $|h + m| = s$?

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths $AB = 5$, $BC = 4$, and $CA = 3$. At time $t = 0$, an ant is located at each vertex and begins moving along the perimeter in the order $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow A$, each with a constant speed of $1$ unit per second. Let $P(t)$, $Q(t)$, and $R(t)$ be the positions of the ants starting at $A$, $B$, and $C$ respectively after $t$ seconds. Define $A(t)$ as the area of triangle $PQR$ for $0 < t < 3$. Find the value of $t$ for which $A(t)$ is minimized.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = 5$, $BC = 4$, and $CA = 3$. Initially, there is an ant at each vertex. The ants start walking at a rate of $1$ unit per second, in the direction $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow A$ (so the ant starting at $A$ moves along ray $\overrightarrow{AB}$, etc.). For a positive real number $t$ less than $3$, let $A(t)$ be the area of the triangle whose vertices are the positions of the ants after $t$ seconds have elapsed. For what positive real number $t$ less than $3$ is $A(t)$ maximized?

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = 5$, $BC = 4$, and $CA = 3$. Initially, there is an ant at each vertex. The ants start walking at a rate of $1$ unit per second, in the direction $A \rightarrow C \rightarrow B \rightarrow A$ (so the ant starting at $A$ moves along ray $\overrightarrow{AC}$, etc.). For a positive real number $t$ less than $3$, let $A(t)$ be the area of the triangle whose vertices are the positions of the ants after $t$ seconds have elapsed. For what positive real number $t$ less than $3$ is $A(t)$ minimized?

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = 5$, $BC = 4$, and $CA = 3$. Initially, there is an ant at each vertex. The ants start walking at a rate of $1$ unit per second, in the direction $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow A$ (so the ant starting at $A$ moves along ray $\overrightarrow{AB}$, etc.). For a positive real number $t$ less than $4$, let $A(t)$ be the area of the triangle whose vertices are the positions of the ants after $t$ seconds have elapsed. For what positive real number $t$ less than $4$ is $A(t)$ minimized?

positive_text: Determine the count of ordered triples $(x, y, z)$ where $1 \leq x, y, z \leq 100$ and $x^{2} y + y^{2} z + z^{2} x = x y^{2} + y z^{2} + z x^{2}$.

negatives.text: Find the number of ordered triples of integers $(a, b, c)$ with $1 \leq a, b, c \leq 100$ and $a^{2} b + b^{2} c + c^{2} a = a b^{2} + b c^{2} + c a^{2} + 1$.
Find the number of ordered triples of integers $(a, b, c)$ with $1 \leq a, b, c \leq 100$ and $a^{2} b + b^{2} c + c^{2} a = a b^{2} + b c^{2} + c a^{2}$ and $a + b + c$ is even.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral on a unit circle centered at $O$, with $\angle AOB = \angle COD = 135^\circ$ and $BC = 1$. Reflect $A$ across $BO$ to get $B'$, and across $CO$ to get $C'$. Let $H_1$ be the orthocenter of triangle $AB'C'$, and $H_2$ be the orthocenter of triangle $BCD$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $OH_1$, and let $O'$ be the reflection of $O$ over the midpoint of $MH_2$. Find the length $OO'$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral inscribed in a unit circle with center $O$. Suppose that $\angle AOB = \angle COD = 135^\circ$, $BC = 1$. Let $B'$ and $C'$ be the reflections of $A$ across $BO$ and $CO$ respectively. Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the orthocenters of $AB'C'$ and $BCD$, respectively. If $M$ is the midpoint of $OH_1$, and $O'$ is the reflection of $O$ about the midpoint of $MH_2^2$, compute $OO'$.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral inscribed in a unit circle with center $O$. Suppose that $\angle AOB = \angle COD = 135^\circ$, $BC = 1$. Let $B'$ and $C'$ be the reflections of $A$ across $BO$ and $CO$ respectively. Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the orthocenters of $AB'C'$ and $BCD$, respectively. If $M$ is the midpoint of $OH_1$, and $O'$ is the reflection of $O$ about the midpoint of $MH_2$, compute $OO'$ modulo $3$.

positive_text: Two chords $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ of a circle $\omega$ intersect at point $E$, with $AE=8$, $BE=2$, and $CD=10$. Given $\angle AEC = 90^\circ$, determine the maximum area of a rectangle $R$ that can be inscribed in $\omega$ with its sides aligned parallel to $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$, and such that $R$'s interior does not intersect $\overline{AB}$, $\overline{CD}$, or the boundary of $\omega$.

negatives.text: Chords $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ of circle $\omega$ intersect at $E$ such that $AE=8$, $BE=2$, $CD=10$, and $\angle AEC=60^\circ$. Let $R$ be a rectangle inside $\omega$ with sides parallel to $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$, such that no point in the interior of $R$ lies on $\overline{AB}$, $\overline{CD}$, or the boundary of $\omega$. What is the maximum possible area of $R$?

Chords $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ of circle $\omega$ intersect at $E$ such that $AE=8$, $BE=2$, $CD=10$, and $\angle AEC=90^\circ$. Let $R$ be a square inside $\omega$ with sides parallel to $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$, such that no point in the interior of $R$ lies on $\overline{AB}$, $\overline{CD}$, or the boundary of $\omega$. What is the maximum possible area of $R$?

Chords $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ of circle $\omega$ intersect at $E$ such that $AE=8$, $BE=2$, $CD=10$, and $\angle AEC=90^\circ$. Let $R$ be a rectangle inside $\omega$ with sides parallel to $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$, such that no point in the interior of $R$ lies on $\overline{AB}$, $\overline{CD}$, or the boundary of $\omega$. What is the maximum possible perimeter of $R$?

positive_text:
Let $n$ be a positive integer greater than 2. Consider the sequence of $n-1$ fractions:
$$
\frac{2}{1}, \frac{3}{2}, \dots, \frac{n}{n-1}
$$
It is known that their product is $n$. Determine all values of $n$ such that flipping the numerator and denominator of some (but not necessarily all) of the fractions results in a total product of $1$.

negatives.text:
For a positive integer $n > 2$, consider the $n-1$ fractions
$$
\frac{2}{1}, \frac{3}{2}, \cdots, \frac{n}{n-1}
$$
The product of these fractions equals $n$, but if you reciprocate (i.e. turn upside down) some of the fractions, the product will change. Can you make the product equal $\frac{1}{2}$? Find all values of $n$ for which this is possible and prove that you have found them all.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths $AB = 4$, $BC = 7$, and $AC = 8$. If $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$ and $N$ lies on segment $AC$ such that points $M$, $B$, $C$, and $N$ are concyclic, determine the length of $BN$.

negatives.text: Consider triangle $ABC$ with side lengths $AB = 4$, $BC = 7$, and $AC = 8$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $AB$, and let $N$ be the point on the interior of segment $AC$ that also lies on the circumcircle of triangle $MBC$. Compute $AN$.

Consider triangle $ABC$ with side lengths $AB = 4$, $BC = 7$, and $AC = 8$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $AB$, and let $N$ be the point on the interior of segment $BC$ that also lies on the circumcircle of triangle $MBC$. Compute $BN$.

Consider triangle $ABC$ with side lengths $AB = 4$, $BC = 7$, and $AC = 8$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $AB$, and let $N$ be the point on the interior of segment $AC$ that also lies on the circumcircle of triangle $MBA$. Compute $BN$.

positive_text: Let two circles $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ have centers $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$, with radii $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$, respectively. Suppose $O_{2}$ lies on $\omega_{1}$. Let $A$ be a common point of intersection of $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$, and let $B$ be the point where line $O_{1} O_{2}$ intersects $\omega_{2}$, distinct from $O_{2}$. If the segment $AB$ is congruent to segment $O_{1} A$, determine all possible values of the ratio $\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}$.

negatives.text: Let $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ be circles with centers $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$, respectively, and radii $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$, respectively. Suppose that $O_{2}$ is on $\omega_{1}$. Let $A$ be one of the intersections of $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$, and $B$ be one of the two intersections of line $O_{1} O_{2}$ with $\omega_{2}$. If $AB = O_{1}B$, find all possible values of $\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}$.

Let $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ be circles with centers $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$, respectively, and radii $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$, respectively. Suppose that $O_{2}$ is on $\omega_{1}$. Let $A$ be one of the intersections of $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$, and $B$ be one of the two intersections of line $O_{1} O_{2}$ with $\omega_{2}$. If $AB = r_{2}$, find all possible values of $\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}$.

positive_text:
\textbf{a.} Let $X$ be a finite set of points in the plane. For each integer $n$, define $f_{X}(n)$ to be the maximum area of a polygon with at most $n$ vertices selected from $X$. Show that for all integers $m, n$ satisfying $m \geq n > 2$, the inequality $f_{X}(m) + f_{X}(n) \geq f_{X}(m+1) + f_{X}(n-1)$ holds.

\textbf{b.} Start with $P_{0}$ as a 1-by-2 rectangle (with interior). For each $i > 0$, construct $P_{i}$ by folding $P_{i-1}$ along a line that splits it into two connected subsets $A$ and $B$, and define $P_{i} = A \cup B_{l}$, where $B_{l}$ is the reflection of $B$ over the fold line $l$. The diameter of $P_{i}$ is the greatest distance between any two points in $P_{i}$. Find the minimal possible diameter of $P_{2013}$.

negatives.text:
\textbf{a.} Given a finite set $X$ of points in the plane, let $f_{X}(n)$ be the smallest possible area of a polygon with at most $n$ vertices, all of which are points of $X$. Prove that if $m, n$ are integers with $m \geq n > 2$, then $f_{X}(m) + f_{X}(n) \geq f_{X}(m+1) + f_{X}(n-1)$.

\textbf{b.} Let $P_{0}$ be a 1-by-2 rectangle (including its interior), and inductively define the polygon $P_{i}$ to be the result of folding $P_{i-1}$ over some line that cuts $P_{i-1}$ into two connected parts. The diameter of a polygon $P_{i}$ is the maximum distance between two points of $P_{i}$. Determine the smallest possible diameter of $P_{2013}$.

(In other words, given a polygon $P_{i-1}$, a fold of $P_{i-1}$ consists of a line $l$ dividing $P_{i-1}$ into two connected parts $A$ and $B$, and the folded polygon $P_{i} = A \cup B_{l}$, where $B_{l}$ is the reflection of $B$ over the line $l$.)

positive_text: Consider an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ and $E$ be the midpoints of sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. There is a point $F$ on the extension of segment $DE$ beyond $E$ such that triangle $BFA$ is similar to triangle $ABC$. Determine the value of $\frac{AB}{BC}$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ and $E$ be the midpoints of segments $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Suppose that there exists a point $F$ on ray $\overrightarrow{ED}$ outside of $ABC$ such that triangle $BFA$ is similar to triangle $ABC$. Compute $\frac{AB}{BC}$.

positive_text:
Suppose $Q(x)$ is a polynomial satisfying $Q(k) = \sum_{j=1}^{k} j^{2012}$ for all positive integers $k$. Determine the following:
(a) $Q(-2)$.
(b) $Q(\frac{1}{2})$.

negatives.text:
Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial such that for all integers $x \geq 1$,
$$
P(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{x} (-1)^n n^{2012}
$$
(a) Find $P(-2)$.
(b) Find $P(1 / 2)$.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial such that for all integers $x \geq 1$,
$$
P(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{x} n^{2011}
$$
(a) Find $P(-2)$.
(b) Find $P(1 / 2)$.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial such that for all integers $x \geq 1$,
$$
P(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{x} n^{2012} \mod 1000
$$
(a) Find $P(-2)$.
(b) Find $P(1 / 2)$.

positive_text: Let $c$ and $d$ be real numbers, and let $p$, $q$, and $r$ be the roots of the cubic polynomial $h(x) = x^{3} + c x^{2} + d x - 1$. Additionally, consider the cubic polynomial $k(x) = x^{3} + u x^{2} + v x + w$ whose roots are $p^{2}$, $q^{2}$, and $r^{2}$. If $k(-1) = -5$, determine the maximum possible value of $d$.

negatives.text: Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers, and let $r$, $s$, and $t$ be the roots of $f(x) = x^{3} + a x^{2} + b x - 1$. Also, $g(x) = x^{3} + m x^{2} + n x + p$ has roots $r^{2}$, $s^{2}$, and $t^{2}$. If $g(-1) = 5$, find the maximum possible value of $b$.

Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers, and let $r$, $s$, and $t$ be the roots of $f(x) = x^{3} + a x^{2} + b x - 1$. Also, $g(x) = x^{3} + m x^{2} + n x + p$ has roots $r$, $s$, and $t$. If $g(-1) = -5$, find the maximum possible value of $b$.

Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers, and let $r$, $s$, and $t$ be the roots of $f(x) = x^{3} + a x^{2} + b x + 1$. Also, $g(x) = x^{3} + m x^{2} + n x + p$ has roots $r^{2}$, $s^{2}$, and $t^{2}$. If $g(-1) = -5$, find the maximum possible value of $b$.

positive_text:
Let $k$ be an integer with $k \ge 2$. Define a sequence $(a_n)$ by $a_1 = 1$ and for $n \ge 2$, define $a_n$ as the minimal integer greater than $a_{n-1}$ satisfying
$$
a_n = 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \left\lfloor \sqrt[k]{\frac{a_n}{a_i}} \right\rfloor.
$$
Show that the sequence $a_1, a_2, \dots$ contains every prime number.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, point $D$ lies on $BC$ with $AB = \sqrt{2}$, $AC = \sqrt{3}$, and angles $\angle BAD = 30^\circ$ and $\angle CAD = 45^\circ$. Determine the length of segment $AD$.

positive_text:
Let $\omega$ be a complex number such that $\omega^{23}=1$ and $\omega \neq 1$. Evaluate
$$
\sum_{n=0}^{22} \frac{1}{1+\omega^{n}+\omega^{2n}}
$$

negatives.text:
Let $z$ be a non-real complex number with $z^{23}=1$. Compute

\sum_{k=0}^{22} \frac{1}{1-z^{k}+z^{2 k}}
$$

Let $z$ be a non-real complex number with $z^{23}=1$. Compute

positive_text:
Let $m$ be an odd positive integer with $m > 1$. Define the set $T_m$ to consist of all integers $a$ in $[0, m)$ such that there exist integers $x$ and $y$ with $x y \equiv 1 \pmod{m}$ and $a = x + y$. Let $g(m)$ count the number of elements in $T_m$.

a. Show that $g(m n) = g(m) g(n)$ when $m$ and $n$ are coprime odd integers both greater than $1$.

b. Derive an explicit formula for $g\left(p^k\right)$, where $p$ is an odd prime and $k$ is a positive integer.

negatives.text:
Let $m$ be an odd positive integer greater than $1$. Let $S_{m}$ be the set of all non-negative integers less than $m$ which are of the form $x+y$, where $x y+1$ is divisible by $m$. Let $f(m)$ be the number of elements of $S_{m}$.

a. Prove that $f(m n)=f(m) f(n)$ if $m, n$ are relatively prime odd integers greater than $1$.

b. Find a closed form for $f\left(p^{k}\right)$, where $k>0$ is an integer and $p$ is an odd prime.

Let $m$ be an odd positive integer greater than $1$. Let $S_{m}$ be the set of all non-negative integers less than $m$ which are of the form $x^2 + y^2$, where $x y - 1$ is divisible by $m$. Let $f(m)$ be the number of elements of $S_{m}$.

a. Prove that $f(m n)=f(m) f(n)$ if $m, n$ are relatively prime odd integers greater than $1$.

b. Find a closed form for $f\left(p^{k}\right)$, where $k>0$ is an integer and $p$ is an odd prime.

Let $m$ be an odd positive integer greater than $1$. Let $S_{m}$ be the set of all non-negative integers less than $m$ which are of the form $x + y$, where $x y - 1$ is divisible by $m$. Let $f(m)$ be the number of elements of $S_{m}$.

a. Prove that $f(m n)=f(m) + f(n)$ if $m, n$ are relatively prime odd integers greater than $1$.

b. Find a closed form for $f\left(p^{k}\right)$, where $k>0$ is an integer and $p$ is an odd prime.

positive_text:
Let $n = 2013$ and consider the set $S$ of all permutations of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. Define $f(\sigma)$ as the count of elements $k$ in $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ such that $\sigma(k) = k$. Compute the value of
$$
\sum_{\sigma \in S} [f(\sigma)]^4.
$$

negatives.text:
Given a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,2, \ldots, 2013\}$, let $f(\sigma)$ be the number of fixed points of $\sigma$—that is, the number of $k \in \{1,2, \ldots, 2013\}$ such that $\sigma(k) = k$. If $S$ is the set of all possible permutations $\sigma$, compute
$$
\sum_{\sigma \in S} f(\sigma)^3
$$

Given a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,2, \ldots, 2013\}$, let $f(\sigma)$ be the number of fixed points of $\sigma$—that is, the number of $k \in \{1,2, \ldots, 2013\}$ such that $\sigma(k) = -k$. If $S$ is the set of all possible permutations $\sigma$, compute
$$
\sum_{\sigma \in S} f(\sigma)^4
$$

Given a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,2, \ldots, 2012\}$, let $f(\sigma)$ be the number of fixed points of $\sigma$—that is, the number of $k \in \{1,2, \ldots, 2012\}$ such that $\sigma(k) = k$. If $S$ is the set of all possible permutations $\sigma$, compute
$$
\sum_{\sigma \in S} f(\sigma)^4
$$

positive_text: Let $ S $ be a set of $ n $ elements and define a binary operation $ \times $ on $ S $ to be *simple* if it is associative and for any $ x, y \in S $, $ x \times y $ is either $ x $ or $ y $. A *full* string is a sequence in $ S $ that contains every element of $ S $ at least once. Two such strings are *equivalent* if they evaluate to the same element for every simple operation $ \times $. For instance, $ x $, $ xx $, and $ xxx $ are equivalent, but they are full only when $ n = 1 $. Let $ T $ be a set of strings such that each full string is equivalent to exactly one string in $ T $. Find the size of $ T $.

negatives.text: Given a set $S$ of $n$ variables, a binary operation $\times$ on $S$ is called *simple* if it satisfies $(x \times y) \times z = x \times (y \times z)$ for all $x, y, z \in S$ and $x \times y \in \{x, y\}$ for all $x, y \in S$. Given a simple operation $\times$ on $S$, any string of elements in $S$ can be reduced to a single element, such as $xyz \rightarrow x \times (y \times z)$. A string of variables in $S$ is called *full* if it contains each variable in $S$ at least once, and two strings are *equivalent* if they evaluate to the same variable for a fixed simple $\times$. For example, $xxx$, $xx$, and $x$ are equivalent, but these are only full if $n = 1$. Suppose $T$ is a set of strings such that any full string is equivalent to exactly one element of $T$. Determine the number of elements of $T$.

Given a set $S$ of $n$ variables, a binary operation $\times$ on $S$ is called *simple* if it satisfies $(x \times y) \times z = x \times (y \times z)$ for all $x, y, z \in S$ and $x \times y \in \{x, y\}$ for all $x, y \in S$. Given a simple operation $\times$ on $S$, any string of elements in $S$ can be reduced to a single element, such as $xyz \rightarrow x \times (y \times z)$. A string of variables in $S$ is called *full* if it contains each variable in $S$ at least once, and two strings are *equivalent* if they evaluate to the same variable or set of variables regardless of which simple $\times$ is chosen. For example, $xxx$, $xx$, and $x$ are equivalent, but these are only full if $n = 1$. Suppose $T$ is a set of strings such that any full string is equivalent to exactly one element of $T$. Determine the number of elements of $T$.

positive_text:
In pentagon $A B C D E$, the following are known:
(i) $\angle B A D = 45^\circ$ and $\angle C B D + \angle D A E = 45^\circ$, $\angle B C D + \angle D E A = 300^\circ$
(ii) $\frac{B A}{D A} = \frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3},\ C D = \frac{7 \sqrt{5}}{3}$, and $D E = \frac{15 \sqrt{2}}{4}$
(iii) $A D^{2} \cdot B C = A B \cdot A E \cdot B D$

Determine the value of $B D$.

negatives.text:
Pentagon $A B C D E$ is given with the following conditions:
(a) $\angle C B D - \angle D A E = \angle B A D = 45^\circ$, $\angle B C D + \angle D E A = 300^\circ$
(b) $\frac{B A}{D A} = \frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3}$, $C D = \frac{7 \sqrt{5}}{3}$, and $D E = \frac{15 \sqrt{2}}{4}$
(c) $A D^{2} \cdot B C = A B \cdot A E \cdot B D$

Compute $B D$.

positive_text: Let $g(n)$ be the minimum value of $|a + b|$ where $a, b$ are integers satisfying $3a - 2b = n$ for $n \geq 0$. Compute the sum $g(0) + g(1) + g(2) + \cdots + g(2013)$.

negatives.text: For an integer $n \geq 0$, let $f(n)$ be the smallest possible value of $|x+y|$, where $x$ and $y$ are integers such that $3x + 2y = n$. Evaluate $f(0) + f(1) + f(2) + \cdots + f(2013)$.
For an integer $n \geq 0$, let $f(n)$ be the smallest possible value of $|x^2 + y^2|$, where $x$ and $y$ are integers such that $3x - 2y = n$. Evaluate $f(0) + f(1) + f(2) + \cdots + f(2013)$.

positive_text:
Given a regular $n$-gon with $n>3$, define a line as acceptable if it intersects the interior of the $n$-gon. Suppose $m$ such lines are drawn, partitioning the $n$-gon into multiple sub-polygons.

a. Show that there is an $m$, dependent only on $n$, such that every set of $m$ acceptable lines ensures that at least one of the sub-polygons is a triangle or quadrilateral.

b. Determine the minimal value of $m$ that guarantees at least one of the sub-polygons is a triangle or quadrilateral.

negatives.text:
Consider a regular $n$-gon with $n>3$, and call a line acceptable if it passes through the interior of this $n$-gon. Draw $m$ different acceptable lines, so that the $n$-gon is divided into several smaller polygons.

a. Prove that there exists an $m$, depending only on $n$, such that any collection of $m$ acceptable lines results in one of the smaller polygons having 5 or 6 sides.

b. Find the smallest possible $m$ which guarantees that at least one of the smaller polygons will have 5 or 6 sides.

Consider a regular $n$-gon with $n>3$, and call a line acceptable if it passes through the boundary of this $n$-gon. Draw $m$ different acceptable lines, so that the $n$-gon is divided into several smaller polygons.

a. Prove that there exists an $m$, depending only on $n$, such that any collection of $m$ acceptable lines results in one of the smaller polygons having 3 or 4 sides.

b. Find the smallest possible $m$ which guarantees that at least one of the smaller polygons will have 3 or 4 sides.

Consider a regular $n$-gon with $n>3$, and call a line acceptable if it passes through the interior of this $n$-gon. Draw $m$ different acceptable lines, so that the $n$-gon is divided into several smaller polygons.

a. Prove that there exists an $m$, depending only on $n$, such that any collection of $m$ acceptable lines results in one of the smaller polygons having 3 or 4 sides, or the original $n$-gon being entirely divided into triangles.

b. Find the smallest possible $m$ which guarantees that at least one of the smaller polygons will have 3 or 4 sides, or the entire $n$-gon is triangulated.

positive_text: Find $x$ such that $280 + x = 20 + 14x$.
